# Batch scheduler re-executes the whole graph write batch for every failing request

## Details
batch.TimeScheduler groups every graph write that arrives within BatchCommitInterval (500 ms default, lncfg/db.go:40; remote gossip is always LazyAdd, gossiper.go:2275-2278, so the batch waits the full window) into one DB transaction. batch.run executes each request's Do in arrival order inside that transaction; when any Do returns a non-serialization error it returns the error (sqldb rolls the whole transaction back and returns immediately, interfaces.go:300-317), swaps the last request into the failing slot, sends the failing request errSolo, and restarts the loop with every remaining request (batch/batch.go:56-102). There is no cap on re-runs and no way for a Do to report a per-request validation failure without aborting the others. Because the swap preserves the position of everything before the failing index, a request that precedes N failing requests is executed N+1 times; N failing requests therefore cost O(N x batch size) Do executions and N+1 transaction attempts.

Remote peers control what lands in the node scheduler's batch. The peer read loop hands every NodeAnnouncement1 to the gossiper without awaiting the result (peer/brontide.go:2478, 2243-2249); networkHandler spawns one goroutine per message after taking one of 1000 validation-barrier slots (gossiper.go:1585-1599); NodeAnnouncement1 jobs wait only on active ChannelAnnouncement1 parents, never on each other (validation_barrier.go:181-188). handleNodeAnnouncement accepts any node_announcement for a node already in the graph (one announced channel, both endpoints may be the attacker's) whose uint32 timestamp is newer than the stored one (builder.go:939-957); there is no rate limiter, reject cache (isRecentlyRejectedMsg keys only channel messages, gossiper.go:1800-1827) or ban score for node announcements, and an AddNode failure is only logged (gossiper.go:2605-2620). Failing announcements never commit, so the stored timestamp never advances and every one passes the freshness check.

A cheap always-failing request exists on the PostgreSQL native-SQL backend (db.use-native-sql=true with db.backend=postgres; supported and documented, non-default): SQLStore.AddNode.Do silences only sql.ErrNoRows (sql_store.go:261-270); NodeFromWireAnnouncement uses Alias.String(), which trims only leading/trailing NULs (models/node.go:246), and populateNodeParams passes the alias verbatim as a TEXT parameter (sql_store.go:4575-4578) to UpsertNode, the first statement of upsertNode (4695). lnwire accepts any 32-byte valid-UTF-8 alias including interior 0x00 (node_announcement.go:44-56). PostgreSQL rejects 0x00 in text with SQLSTATE 22021, which parsePostgresError maps to a plain error (sqlerrors.go:133-135), i.e. the failIdx path: a ~150-byte signed node_announcement whose Do fails before any work.

Attack: the attacker sends one expensive but valid node_announcement first (e.g. the all-ones 8 KB feature vector of the independently verified sql-store-node-features-row-per-bit-write-amplification: ~65k-145k single-row statements, seconds to minutes on PostgreSQL), then, within the same 500 ms window, N ~150-byte node_announcements carrying an interior-NUL alias and increasing timestamps. Since the heavy request precedes every failing one, each of the N+1 transaction attempts re-runs the heavy Do: the heavy write is multiplied by N+1 for N x 150 B of attacker bandwidth, and every honest node announcement that joined the window is also executed N+1 times (each tens of statements even without the heavy sibling) with its gossip goroutine and validation-barrier slot blocked for the whole series. Once the 1000 slots are held by blocked requests, networkHandler blocks in InitJobDependencies, ProcessRemoteAnnouncement blocks on the unbuffered networkMsgs channel, each peer's discStream fills (50) and that peer's readHandler blocks in discStream.AddMsg (brontide.go:2478), stalling all message processing from that peer. Later batches are separate SERIALIZABLE transactions on the same rows and are retried on conflict (DefaultNumTxRetries=20).

The same loop exists on the default bbolt backend (KVStore.AddNode.Do unsilenced, kv_store.go:1046-1057; putLightningNode returns ErrTooManyExtraOpaqueBytes for >10000 B of TLV-valid extra data before any bucket write, 4725-4727, while the wire layer allows ~65 KB), but there each failing request costs the attacker >10 KB and buys only one extra in-memory bbolt write-transaction attempt plus one cheap re-run of the batch's Do's, so the amplification is negligible; the impact rated here is the PostgreSQL native-SQL variant. SQLite stores NUL in TEXT without error, so the alias trigger does not apply there.

This is a defect of batch/ independent of any one store: the maintainers silence specific errors in each Do (ErrEdgeNotFound, ErrEdgeAlreadyExist, sql.ErrNoRows) precisely because an unsilenced error aborts the batch, but the scheduler offers no protection when an error path is missed, and remote-shaped field values reach the database unvalidated. It is distinct from the row-per-bit finding: that one sets the per-execution cost, this one lets ~150 B of input re-execute every other request in the window and blocks honest requests behind the repetitions.

Dependency assumptions (not verified in the checkout): PostgreSQL rejects 0x00 in text/varchar parameters with SQLSTATE 22021 (character_not_in_repertoire); pgx/v5 v5.11.0 and pgconn v1.14.3 (sqldb/go.mod) transmit Go string bytes to the server unmodified; per-statement cost on PostgreSQL is a network round trip.

## Impact
On native-SQL PostgreSQL the batch's write transaction re-runs every request that preceded the failing ones N+1 times: with the heavy node write of the verified row-per-bit sibling first, that is seconds-to-minutes of DB work multiplied by N for N x 150 B of attacker input; even without it, every honest node announcement in the window (tens of statements each) is re-executed N+1 times and its gossip goroutine blocked for the series. Blocked requests hold validation-barrier slots (1000); when exhausted, networkHandler and ProcessRemoteAnnouncement block and each peer's readHandler blocks in discStream.AddMsg, stalling all message processing from those peers. Graph ingestion for all peers stalls and the database absorbs N x (statements of the preceding requests) per round. On the default bbolt backend the same loop costs only cheap in-memory re-runs (degradation, not outage). No confidentiality or integrity impact.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker: any Lightning node that has one announced public channel in the victim's graph (both endpoints may be attacker nodes) and a brontide connection to the victim (restricted slot, no channel with the victim needed; or any relaying peer). It signs node_announcements for its own key: one heavy valid one first, then N tiny ones with an alias containing an interior 0x00, all with increasing timestamps, inside one 500 ms window. The peer layer forwards them fire-and-forget, the gossiper processes them concurrently, and no rate limit, reject cache or ban score applies to node announcements; the failing ones never commit so each passes the freshness check. Conditions outside the attacker's control: the node must be present in the victim's graph, and the rated variant needs db.use-native-sql on PostgreSQL (supported, documented, non-default) - attack_requirements PRESENT. Dependency assumption: PostgreSQL rejects 0x00 in text with SQLSTATE 22021 and pgx/v5 v5.11.0 passes the bytes through.

## Recommended fix
1. batch.run treats every non-serialization Do error as a reason to roll back and re-execute the entire remaining batch, with no bound on the number of re-runs, so the total work is proportional to (failing requests) x (batch size) and is controlled by whoever can inject failing requests. Fix criteria: A batch containing N failing requests must cost O(N + batch size) Do executions, not O(N x batch size): e.g. on the first failure fall back to executing each remaining request individually (or in a bounded number of sub-batches) instead of restarting the whole batch, or cap re-runs and hand the remainder to callers as errSolo. Verify by submitting one slow request followed by N always-failing requests in one window and confirming the slow Do runs a constant number of times.
2. Remote-shaped node announcement fields reach the database inside the batch transaction without validation: PostgreSQL rejects NUL bytes in the alias, and the bbolt serialiser rejects >10000 B of extra data, both only discovered inside Do where they abort the batch. Fix criteria: Node announcement content that any shipped store will refuse (alias containing 0x00, ExtraOpaqueData above MaxAllowedExtraOpaqueBytes, and equivalents for channel announcements/updates) must be rejected before a batch.Request is created (gossiper/builder validation) or converted to per-request local state inside Do as ErrEdgeNotFound already is, so that no remotely chosen value can abort a shared batch. Verify that such announcements produce a per-message error without causing a transaction rollback or re-run of co-batched requests.

# Single funding coordinator blocks on synchronous send to a non-reading peer, stalling all funding node-wide

## Details
The funding manager processes every funding-related wire message and every local open-channel request on one goroutine, reservationCoordinator (funding/manager.go:1040-1078). Inside that goroutine, fundeeProcessOpenChannel ends with `peer.SendMessage(true, &fundingAccept)` (manager.go:2001) — a synchronous send to whichever anonymous peer sent open_channel; fundeeProcessFundingCreated (2634) and continueFundingAccept (2447) do the same for funding_signed/funding_created.

Brontide's synchronous send has no caller-side timeout: sendMessage (peer/brontide.go:5190-5245) waits on errChan until the writeHandler reports a result or the peer exits, and the writeHandler (3052-3074) turns every 5 s write timeout into an unbounded `goto retry`. The outgoing-queue overflow teardown does not help: a Pong is charged only 128 B of the 16 MiB budget (queue_cost.go:70-74). So if the remote's TCP receive window is closed (the peer stops reading or ACKing, having first made us queue more than our socket send buffer — e.g. ~20 pings requesting 65531-byte pongs, admitted by the ping limiter's 200-token burst, ping_limits.go), the coordinator is parked until that peer is disconnected. Nothing else ends the stall; disconnection comes from the pong timeout 30-90 s later (ping_manager.go:148-200; pingInterval 1 min + pingTimeout 30 s; x3 for Tor peers), or after the 5 min idle timer if NoDisconnectOnPongFailure is set.

Attack: an anonymous inbound peer (restricted accessman slot; default config accepts inbound channels and open_channel is how a restricted peer upgrades, accessman.go:193) connects, fills our send buffer and stops reading, then sends one well-formed open_channel. The coordinator passes the generic checks and acceptor, builds the reservation and blocks in SendMessage for 30-90 s. With a second connection the attacker sends 50 junk funding messages (e.g. accept_channel for unknown ids) to fill the 50-slot fundingMsgs buffer (manager.go:104, 1422-1429). By staggering fresh connections roughly once a minute the stall is sustained indefinitely at negligible cost.

While stalled: (1) no open_channel/accept_channel/funding_created/funding_signed/channel_ready from any peer is processed — no channel can be opened in either direction and channels whose funding just confirmed do not become active (handleChannelReady is dispatched from this goroutine); (2) RPC OpenChannel/OpenChannelSync/BatchOpenChannel hang: server.go:5360 spawns the blocking InitFundingWorkflow send in a goroutine and the RPC handler waits for the coordinator's first update (rpcserver.go:2566-2576); (3) pruneZombieReservations does not run, so timed-out reservations and their locked UTXOs are not released; (4) once the buffer is full, the readHandler of any honest peer that sends a funding message blocks inside ProcessFundingMsg (brontide.go:2409, 2731), freezing all inbound processing on that connection (HTLC updates, its pings) until the coordinator drains, which causes that honest peer to disconnect us for pong failure and disrupts its channels.

The RPC channel acceptor round trip (manager.go:1564; up to acceptortimeout=15 s) runs on the same goroutine and adds to each stall when the operator's acceptor client is slow.

This is not volumetric: a single ~300-byte message from one connection removes the node's funding capability for up to 90 s; the defect is a synchronous, untimed remote I/O call inside a global single-threaded loop, plus a write path that retries timeouts without bound. The earlier dismissal of the writeHandler retry loop (per-peer bound of 5 min) did not consider that a global coordinator waits on it.

## Evidence
1. [funding/manager.go:2001–2005](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/funding/manager.go#L2001-L2005)
   fundeeProcessOpenChannel, which runs inline on the single reservationCoordinator goroutine, ends with peer.SendMessage(true, &fundingAccept): a synchronous send to the anonymous peer that sent open_channel. resMtx is released at 1898, before the send, so only the coordinator (not IsPendingChannel callers) is held. The coordinator cannot process any other funding message or local request until this returns.
2. [funding/manager.go:1040–1077](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/funding/manager.go#L1040-L1077)
   reservationCoordinator is the only consumer of fundingMsgs and fundingRequests and the only runner of pruneZombieReservations; every handler (fundeeProcessOpenChannel, funderProcessAcceptChannel, fundeeProcessFundingCreated, funderProcessFundingSigned, handleChannelReady, handleInitFundingMsg) is called inline, so one blocked handler stalls funding for every peer and every RPC caller.
3. [peer/brontide.go:3052–3073](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/peer/brontide.go#L3052-L3073)
   writeHandler: writeMessage sets a 5 s write deadline (writeMessageTimeout, :82, :2977); on a timeout it sets outMsg.msg = nil and `goto retry` with no retry count or total deadline. The sync caller's errChan (:3094-3096) is only signalled after the flush finally succeeds or fails non-transiently, so a peer whose TCP receive window is closed holds the message at the head of the write path, and the sync caller, until the peer is disconnected.
4. [peer/brontide.go:5190–5244](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/peer/brontide.go#L5190-L5244)
   sendMessage(sync=true) blocks on errChan with only p.cg.Done() / p.cfg.Quit as alternatives; there is no caller-side timeout, so the funding coordinator waits for whatever ends the peer.
5. [peer/brontide.go:849–872](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/peer/brontide.go#L849-L872)
   Ping manager wiring: SendPing only queues the ping (p.queueMsg), so a stalled write path never delivers it; OnPongFailure calls go p.Disconnect unless NoDisconnectOnPongFailure (default false, config.go:264). Disconnect (:1764-1816) stops the ping manager, closes the conn (ending the blocked flush with a non-timeout error) and calls p.cg.Quit(), which is what finally unblocks the coordinator's SendMessage.
6. [peer/ping\_manager.go:148–199](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/peer/ping_manager.go#L148-L199)
   The pong timer (TimeoutDuration = pingTimeout 30 s) is armed in setPingState before SendPing queues the ping, and pings are sent on a 1 min ticker first firing 1 min after connect. A non-reading peer is therefore disconnected between 30 s and 90 s after the stall begins (x3 for Tor peers, torTimeoutMultiplier=3, brontide.go:103); with NoDisconnectOnPongFailure set only the 5 min writeHandler idle timer (brontide.go:3036, idleTimeout :78) ends it.
7. [peer/queue\_cost.go:70–73](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/peer/queue_cost.go#L70-L73)
   The only other bound on the write path is the outgoing msgQueue overflow (maxQueuedMsgs 10000 / maxQueuedBytes 16 MiB, queue_limits.go:6-10) that tears the peer down; a Pong is charged only msgOverhead (128 B) because its payload aliases the shared PongBuf, so the ~20 x 65 KB pongs an attacker uses to fill the socket buffers cost ~2.5 KB of accounting and never trigger that teardown.
8. [peer/ping\_limits.go:9–47](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/peer/ping_limits.go#L9-L47)
   How the attacker fills the node's kernel send buffer before stalling: a 65531-byte pong (lnwire.MaxPongBytes, pong.go:11) costs 10 of a 200-token burst, so ~20 max-size pongs (~1.3 MB) are admitted at once plus one per second thereafter (brontide.go:2343-2347 enforces, :2395-2401 queues). Combined with the attacker closing its receive window or dropping ACKs, this makes the writeHandler's flush of the pong at the head of the queue time out indefinitely, with accept_channel queued behind it.
9. [funding/manager.go:1422–1428](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/funding/manager.go#L1422-L1428)
   ProcessFundingMsg is a blocking send into fundingMsgs (buffer msgBufferSize=50, :104, :703-705) with only f.quit as the alternative. Once the coordinator is stalled and 50 messages are buffered, every further caller blocks.
10. [peer/brontide.go:2403–2409](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/peer/brontide.go#L2403-L2409)
   readHandler calls FundingManager.ProcessFundingMsg inline for OpenChannel/AcceptChannel/FundingCreated/FundingSigned/ChannelReady (and at :2730-2731 for Error/Warning on pending channels). Pings are also handled inline on this goroutine (:2390-2401), so once the 50-slot buffer is full the readHandler of any honest peer that sends a funding message blocks, halting all inbound processing on that connection (HTLC updates, its pings) until the coordinator drains, which makes that honest peer disconnect us for pong failure.
11. [server.go:5360](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/server.go#L5360)
   server.OpenChannel spawns InitFundingWorkflow (a bare blocking send into the 50-slot fundingRequests, manager.go:4800-4802) in a goroutine and returns req.Updates/req.Err; rpcserver.OpenChannel/OpenChannelSync (rpcserver.go:2566-2576, 2626-2636) then wait for the first update, which only handleInitFundingMsg on the stalled coordinator produces, so RPC channel opens to any peer hang for the duration of the stall.
12. [funding/manager.go:2634–2638](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/funding/manager.go#L2634-L2638)
   fundeeProcessFundingCreated has the same synchronous send (funding_signed) on the coordinator; continueFundingAccept at :2447 (funding_created) likewise. open_channel is the cheapest trigger since it needs no funds and passes only generic checks (per-peer MaxPendingChannels, global pendingChansLimit, min/max size, channel_type, acceptor; :1480-1568).
13. [funding/manager.go:1564–1567](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/funding/manager.go#L1564-L1567)
   OpenChannelPredicate.Accept also runs synchronously on the coordinator; with an RPC channel acceptor registered this is a round trip to the operator's acceptor client bounded only by acceptortimeout (15 s default, config.go:106), compounding each stalled open_channel.

## Impact
Availability: the channel-funding subsystem is completely denied for the duration (no inbound/outbound opens, channel_ready not processed so confirmed channels stay inactive, RPC OpenChannel hangs, zombie reservations and locked UTXOs not released), and honest peers that send any funding message have their whole connection frozen, leading to disconnects. The daemon and existing HTLC forwarding on other connections keep running, so partial (LOW) rather than total loss. No confidentiality or integrity impact.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker is any anonymous peer able to complete the brontide handshake (no channel, restricted slot). It fills the node's send buffer (max-size pong requests or a gossip query), stops reading, and sends one valid open_channel. The coordinator deterministically blocks in SendMessage until the peer is disconnected (30-90 s). Repeating with a new connection per minute sustains the outage; a second connection fills the 50-slot funding buffer so honest peers' readHandlers also block. Works against default configuration with inbound channels enabled; no defenses to bypass.

## Recommended fix
1. The funding manager performs synchronous, untimed network sends (and the channel-acceptor round trip) to an untrusted peer from the single reservationCoordinator goroutine, so one peer's slow socket serializes and blocks all funding activity node-wide. Fix criteria: Funding message handling for one peer must not be able to delay funding messages of other peers or local open requests: sends to the remote (accept_channel, funding_created, funding_signed) are issued asynchronously or from per-peer/per-flow goroutines, and any synchronous wait is bounded by a timeout that fails only that flow. Verify by stalling one peer's socket after it sends open_channel and confirming that another peer's open_channel is answered and an RPC OpenChannel to a third peer completes within normal latency.
2. Brontide's synchronous SendMessage has no caller-visible deadline: the writeHandler retries write timeouts without bound and the sync caller waits until the peer is disconnected by the ping manager or idle timer. Fix criteria: A synchronous send must return an error to its caller within a bounded time when the peer is not draining its socket (e.g. a total deadline across retries, or disconnecting the peer after N consecutive write timeouts), so no subsystem that uses sync sends can be held longer than that bound. Verify by closing the remote receive window and confirming SendMessage(true, ...) returns an error within the bound.

# Graph SQL migration re-parses legacy opaque DNS/tcp6 addresses unvalidated, bricking startup

## Details
The KV-to-SQL graph migration (global migration 10, run on first start with db.use-native-sql) calls maybeOverrideNodeAddresses (graph/db/migration1/sql_migration.go:337-400) on every node read from channel.db. For each lnwire.OpaqueAddrs record it re-runs lnwire.ReadAddress over the stored payload and replaces the node's addresses with the parsed results. ReadAddress's DNS branch (lnwire/lnwire.go:923-944) returns DNSAddress{Hostname: string(rawBytes)} and its tcp6 branch returns a 16-byte net.IP; neither lnwire.ValidateDNSAddr (which the live gossip path applies in netann.ValidateNodeAnnFields, netann/node_announcement.go:98-120) nor the IPv4-mapped-to-tcp4 normalisation that the live KV encoder applies at storage time (graph/db/addr.go:72-76 encodeTCPAddr) is run. The re-parsed addresses then go to insertNodeSQLMig (:1486-1509) -> collectAddressRecords (migration1/sql_store.go:493-549) -> graph_node_addresses.address TEXT, and are read back by validateBatch (:185-231) via buildNodeWithBatchData -> buildNodeAddresses -> parseAddress (migration1/sql_store.go:1188-1280) and compared with sqldb.CompareRecords (strict reflect.DeepEqual, sqldb/migrations.go:544-547).

How the poisoned record gets into channel.db: lnd 0.19.x persisted node announcements whose address list contains a type unknown to it as one OpaqueAddrs blob holding the unknown type byte and ALL remaining address bytes (release-notes-0.19.0.md:74-77, PR 9474; lnwire ReadAddress default branch :946-958), and only 0.20 added type-5 DNS parsing and validation (release-notes-0.20.0.md:286-289). A remote node that owns one announced channel present in the victim's graph (graph/builder.go:939-948 assertNodeAnnFreshness is the only gate) therefore sends, while the victim runs 0.19.x, a validly signed node_announcement whose address block starts with a type-5 entry. The signature verifies because the opaque bytes are re-serialised verbatim. The record survives upgrades to 0.20/0.21 untouched: the live KV store writes OpaqueAddrs verbatim (graph/db/addr.go:160), no channeldb/graph KV migration re-parses them, the frozen migration reader returns them as OpaqueAddrs (migration1/addr.go:285-300), a re-received copy of the same announcement is rejected as not newer (builder.go:955-958) and a 0.20+ victim would in any case refuse the invalid hostname at ingest, leaving the KV record in place. The attacker only needs to not re-announce and keep its channel open.

Failure modes when the victim later enables native SQL:
(1) Both backends: a hostname containing '[' or ']' (e.g. "x]"). DNSAddress.String() yields "x]:9735" (net.JoinHostPort brackets only when the host contains ':'); validateBatch's parseAddress calls net.SplitHostPort, which returns "unexpected ']' in address"; buildNodeAddresses fails, 'could not build migrated node' aborts the migration.
(2) Both backends: a tcp6 (type 2) entry following the type-5 entry whose IP is IPv4-mapped (::ffff:a.b.c.d). The 16-byte TCPAddr is classified IPv4 by collectAddressRecords (IP.To4() != nil) and stored as "a.b.c.d:port"; parseAddress reads it back as a 4-byte IP (ResolveTCPAddr("tcp4") then To4()), so sqldb.CompareRecords(node, migNode) reports a mismatch and aborts. (Live gossip never produces this: encodeTCPAddr normalises v4-mapped IPs to tcp4 before KV storage, so KV-decoded addresses are always 4 or 16 bytes consistently.)
(3) PostgreSQL: a hostname containing 0x00 is rejected by the TEXT column at UpsertNodeAddress (SQLSTATE 22021) and insertNodeSQLMig's error is fatal (:274-280).
migrateNodes only skips nodes whose ReadAddress call itself errors (:262-270); all three paths above parse successfully and so are fatal rather than skipped.

Consequence: ApplyMigrations records a version only on success (sqldb/migrations.go:474-541), so migration 10 is rolled back and re-fails on every start, the ApplyAllMigrations error is fatal to startup (config_builder.go:1238-1248), while the already-committed version-7 invoice migration has set the KV invoice tombstone (config_builder.go:1138-1167) that makes starting without db.use-native-sql refused (config_builder.go:1351-1373). The node is offline (cannot resolve HTLCs or punish breaches) until the operator restores a pre-migration backup, hand-edits channel.db, or sets db.skip-native-sql-migration, which abandons the KV graph and payments data (lncfg/db.go:88). docs/db_migration_guide.md:144 lists the graph relational migration as 'Available with v0.20', so this is a supported shipped path. This complements graph-sql-migration-postgres-nul-alias-aborts-startup (same migration, different source and sink: alias vs legacy opaque addresses) and extends the impact to SQLite via paths (1) and (2); the dismissed ledger item at sql_migration.go:1486 only considered addresses as decoded by the KV reader, not the re-parsed opaque payloads.

Dependency assumptions: Go stdlib (go 1.26.8 per go.mod) net.SplitHostPort rejects an unbracketed host containing ']' with "unexpected ']' in address" and net.JoinHostPort brackets only hosts containing ':'; PostgreSQL rejects 0x00 in text and pgx v5 (github.com/jackc/pgx/v5 v5.11.0, sqldb/go.mod) forwards Go strings unmodified. The 0.19.x ReadAddress behaviour is inferred from the current default branch plus the 0.19.0/0.20.0 release notes, since this checkout carries no pre-0.21.4 history.

## Evidence
1. [graph/db/migration1/sql\_migration.go:337–400](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/migration1/sql_migration.go#L337-L400)
   maybeOverrideNodeAddresses re-parses every KV OpaqueAddrs payload with lnwire.ReadAddress in a loop and replaces node.Addresses with whatever comes out (DNSAddress with raw hostname bytes, 16-byte TCPAddr for tcp6). No ValidateDNSAddr / IPv4-mapped normalisation is applied; only a ReadAddress error is surfaced. This is where the fix belongs.
2. [graph/db/migration1/sql\_migration.go:262–280](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/migration1/sql_migration.go#L262-L280)
   migrateNodes skips a node only when maybeOverrideNodeAddresses returns an error; any error from insertNodeSQLMig ('could not persist node') is fatal and propagates to MigrateGraphToSQL.
3. [graph/db/migration1/sql\_migration.go:185–230](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/migration1/sql_migration.go#L185-L230)
   validateBatch rebuilds each migrated node with buildNodeWithBatchData and aborts on any build error ('could not build migrated node') or on sqldb.CompareRecords mismatch, so a re-parsed address that does not round-trip (unparseable hostname string or 16-byte v4-mapped IP read back as 4 bytes) fails the whole migration.
4. [graph/db/migration1/sql\_migration.go:1486–1509](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/migration1/sql_migration.go#L1486-L1509)
   insertNodeSQLMig writes the re-parsed addresses via collectAddressRecords/UpsertNodeAddress into graph_node_addresses.address (TEXT NOT NULL). On PostgreSQL a hostname containing 0x00 is rejected here (SQLSTATE 22021).
5. [graph/db/migration1/sql\_store.go:493–549](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/migration1/sql_store.go#L493-L549)
   collectAddressRecords stores addr.String() (net.JoinHostPort for DNSAddress) and classifies any *net.TCPAddr whose IP.To4() != nil as IPv4, so a v4-mapped IPv6 address recovered from an opaque payload is written as an IPv4 string.
6. [graph/db/migration1/sql\_store.go:1188–1280](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/migration1/sql_store.go#L1188-L1280)
   buildNodeAddresses -> parseAddress reads the DNS row back with net.SplitHostPort, which rejects any hostname containing '[' or ']' (and some ':' combinations), and reads the IPv4 row back as a 4-byte IP; both make validateBatch fail.
7. [sqldb/migrations.go:544–547](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/sqldb/migrations.go#L544-L547)
   CompareRecords is a strict reflect.DeepEqual, so a 16-byte v4-mapped net.IP in the KV node versus the 4-byte IP read back from SQL is a mismatch.
8. [lnwire/lnwire.go:923–958](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwire/lnwire.go#L923-L958)
   ReadAddress's dnsAddr branch builds DNSAddress{Hostname: string(hostname)} from raw bytes with no character validation; the default branch (the only branch a type-5 entry could reach in pre-0.20 lnd) swallows the type byte and all remaining address bytes into one OpaqueAddrs payload, which is what the migration re-parses.
9. [graph/db/addr.go:72–76](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/addr.go#L72-L76)
   The live KV encoder (encodeTCPAddr) normalises any TCPAddr whose IP.To4() != nil to a 4-byte tcp4 record at storage time, so KV-decoded addresses never carry a 16-byte v4-mapped IP; only the in-memory re-parse of an opaque payload in the migration does, which is what breaks the round-trip in failure mode (2).
10. [lnwire/dns\_addr.go:52–89](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwire/dns_addr.go#L52-L89)
   DNSAddress.String() is net.JoinHostPort(hostname, port). ValidateDNSAddr (charset [A-Za-z0-9.-], non-empty, <=255) exists but is only invoked from netann at live gossip ingest, never on the migration path.
11. [netann/node\_announcement.go:98–120](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/netann/node_announcement.go#L98-L120)
   The only DNS hostname validation in the codebase runs on freshly received node announcements; legacy KV records bypass it.
12. [graph/builder.go:939–959](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/builder.go#L939-L959)
   assertNodeAnnFreshness is the only gate on a node_announcement: the node must already be in the graph (own one known public channel) and the timestamp must be strictly newer. A re-received copy of the planted announcement is therefore rejected as outdated and cannot overwrite the legacy record.
13. [graph/db/migration1/addr.go:285–300](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/migration1/addr.go#L285-L300)
   The frozen KV reader returns opaqueAddrs rows verbatim as lnwire.OpaqueAddrs, so the attacker's bytes reach maybeOverrideNodeAddresses unchanged.
14. [docs/release-notes/release-notes-0.19.0.md:74–77](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/docs/release-notes/release-notes-0.19.0.md#L74-L77)
   lnd 0.19 began persisting (and relaying) node announcements with address types unknown to it (PR 9474) as OpaqueAddrs; this is the population of records the migration re-parses.
15. [docs/release-notes/release-notes-0.20.0.md:286–289](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/docs/release-notes/release-notes-0.20.0.md#L286-L289)
   DNS (type 5) parsing and BOLT 7 hostname validation were only added in 0.20, so a node that ran 0.19.x stored type-5 addresses opaquely and unvalidated.
16. [sqldb/sqlc/migrations/000008\_graph.up.sql:86–87](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/sqldb/sqlc/migrations/000008_graph.up.sql#L86-L87)
   graph_node_addresses.address is TEXT NOT NULL; PostgreSQL text cannot contain 0x00.
17. [sqldb/migrations.go:474–541](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/sqldb/migrations.go#L474-L541)
   Each migration runs in its own ExecTx and is recorded only on success; a failing version-10 graph migration is rolled back and re-attempted (and re-fails) on every start, while version 7 stays committed.
18. [config\_builder.go:1138–1167](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/config_builder.go#L1138-L1167)
   The version-7 invoice migration callback sets the KV invoice-bucket tombstone before the graph migration runs.
19. [config\_builder.go:1238–1248](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/config_builder.go#L1238-L1248)
   An ApplyAllMigrations error is fatal for startup.
20. [config\_builder.go:1351–1373](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/config_builder.go#L1351-L1373)
   With the tombstone set, starting without db.use-native-sql is refused, so the operator cannot fall back to KV mode once the graph migration keeps failing.
21. [graph/db/migration1/sql\_migration\_test.go:109–123](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/migration1/sql_migration_test.go#L109-L123)
   Context: the maintainers' only 'bad DNS' fixture is a length-corrupt payload that ReadAddress rejects (skipped); a well-formed but invalid hostname or a trailing v4-mapped tcp6 address is not modelled, and the fixtures confirm the maintainers expect legacy opaque payloads to begin with a type-5 entry.

## Impact
Availability: lnd cannot complete startup in native-SQL mode (migration 10 re-fails every start) and cannot revert to kvdb because of the version-7 tombstone; the node stays offline, unable to resolve HTLCs or respond to breaches, until manual DB surgery, a pre-migration backup restore, or db.skip-native-sql-migration. Integrity: the only in-product recovery discards the KV graph and payments history. No confidentiality impact.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker: any Lightning node with one announced public channel in the victim's graph. While the victim ran lnd 0.19.x it sent one signed node_announcement whose address list begins with a type-5 (DNS) entry carrying a hostname such as "x]" (or 0x00 for Postgres) or followed by an IPv4-mapped tcp6 entry; 0.19 stored it opaquely. The attacker then simply never re-announces. When the operator later enables db.use-native-sql (a documented, non-default migration path), migration 10 fails deterministically on every start and KV fallback is refused by the invoice tombstone. Requires the victim's version history and configuration choice (AT:PRESENT); no privileges, interaction or timing.

## Recommended fix
1. maybeOverrideNodeAddresses promotes bytes that were stored opaquely (never validated) into typed DNS/TCP addresses without applying the same validation and normalisation the live gossip path applies, so remote-chosen bytes reach the TEXT column and the string round-trip unchecked. Fix criteria: Re-parsed addresses must pass lnwire.ValidateDNSAddr (and IPv4-mapped IPv6 must be normalised to 4-byte IPv4, or kept opaque) before being stored; an address failing validation must cause the node to be skipped or the address kept opaque, never a migration abort. Verify by migrating KV nodes carrying opaque payloads with hostnames "x]", "a\x00b" and a trailing ::ffff:1.2.3.4 tcp6 entry on both SQLite and PostgreSQL: MigrateGraphToSQL completes and lnd starts.
2. migrateNodes treats every per-node insert or round-trip validation error as fatal, so a single malformed legacy record denies startup for the whole node. Fix criteria: Per-node data errors in insertNodeSQLMig/validateBatch should be logged and the node skipped (its channels get a shell node, as already done for TLV-invalid nodes) rather than aborting the migration. Verify that a deliberately unstorable node record does not prevent MigrateGraphToSQL from completing.

# bakemacaroon and constrainmacaroon write macaroon files world-readable (0644)

## Details
Two lncli macaroon commands persist bearer credentials with a world-readable mode.

`lncli bakemacaroon ... --save_to <file>` (cmd/commands/cmd_macaroon.go:244) bakes a macaroon either via the node's BakeMacaroon RPC or fully offline from `--root_key` (macaroons/bake.go:44), applies optional caveats, and writes the binary macaroon with `os.WriteFile(savePath, macBytes, 0644)`. The permission list is whatever the operator passed - broad entity:action sets or `uri:` entries - so the file can be as powerful as admin.macaroon, and in the offline case the server never sees it.

`lncli constrainmacaroon <in> <out>` (cmd_macaroon.go:523) reads an existing macaroon (the documented use is adding a timeout or IP lock to admin.macaroon), adds caveats, and writes the result with 0644. A macaroon lnd deliberately stored at 0640 (lnd.go:60, with the stated rationale that no other user may read the admin macaroon) inside a 0700 data directory (config.go:1049) is thereby re-persisted readable by every local account in whatever directory the operator names. Caveats narrow the window but do not close it: a timeout caveat is typically hours or days, and an ipaddr lock is satisfied by any process on the same host.

The mode is a hard-coded maximum; only a non-default umask (077) would tighten it. The project documents no chmod or protected-location requirement for these outputs - its own example (docs/macaroons.md:192) saves an offline-baked macaroon to /tmp - whereas it does document `chmod 0400` for the wallet password file (docs/wallet.md:90).

Attack path: another unprivileged account on the lncli host reads the file from a traversable directory (operator's cwd, 0755 home, /tmp, shared volume). tls.cert is 0644 by design, so the attacker can authenticate to the node's gRPC/REST port with whatever permissions the file carries. The threat model names the local host attacker via file permissions on secrets as in scope. Impact scales with the baked permissions; for the documented constrain-admin.macaroon case it is full node control including moving funds.

Root cause: credential files are created with 0644 rather than owner-only permissions, weaker than the daemon's own handling of admin.macaroon. The same defect exists at the stateless-init `--save_to` sink (cmd_walletunlocker.go:1018), filed separately.

## Evidence
1. [cmd/commands/cmd\_macaroon.go:244](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/cmd/commands/cmd_macaroon.go#L244)
   bakeMacaroon --save_to: the freshly baked and constrained macaroon (any permission set the operator names, including every admin op or uri:<method> entries) is persisted with os.WriteFile(savePath, macBytes, 0644). With the default umask 022 the file is world-readable; the mode is a hard-coded maximum, nothing in lncli tightens it.
2. [cmd/commands/cmd\_macaroon.go:523](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/cmd/commands/cmd_macaroon.go#L523)
   constrainMacaroon: the input macaroon (documented use is adding a timeout/IP lock to admin.macaroon) plus caveats is written to the destination with 0644, so a credential lnd stored at 0640 inside its 0700 data tree is re-persisted world-readable wherever the operator points it.
3. [cmd/commands/cmd\_macaroon.go:175–197](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/cmd/commands/cmd_macaroon.go#L175-L197)
   With --root_key the bake is fully offline (macaroons.BakeFromRootKey, macaroons/bake.go:44); the result is cryptographically identical to a node-issued macaroon for the given ops, so the server imposes no limit on how powerful the 0644 file is.
4. [lnd.go:60](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnd.go#L60)
   lnd writes admin.macaroon with 0640 and the comment above states the rationale: no other user may read the admin macaroon unless the administrator explicitly allowed it. lncli applies a laxer mode to macaroons that can carry identical privileges.
5. [config.go:1049](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/config.go#L1049)
   lnd creates its own data directories with 0700, so the 0644 readonly/invoice macaroons it writes are shielded by the directory. Files written by lncli --save_to / constrainmacaroon land in an operator-chosen directory with no such protection.
6. [docs/macaroons.md:192](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/docs/macaroons.md#L192)
   The project's own documented workflow saves an offline-baked macaroon to /tmp/info.macaroon, a world-traversable directory, with no chmod step; the only chmod guidance in docs (wallet.md:90) is for the wallet password file. No documented fencing requirement covers macaroon output permissions.

## Impact
The file is a bearer credential for the lnd node lncli administers. Its power depends on the baked permissions, but the documented workflows (constraining admin.macaroon, baking broad ops or offline from the root key) yield admin-equivalent access: full read of node data, fund movement and channel operations, daemon shutdown.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker is any other local account on the host where the operator runs lncli (AV:L, PR:L). Requires the operator to have used --save_to or constrainmacaroon and the output to sit in a directory the attacker can traverse - conditions outside the attacker's control (AT:P), but not a documented fencing requirement: the docs' own example writes to /tmp and no chmod step is documented. Reading the file needs no defence bypass; the mode is hard-coded and only a non-default umask would tighten it. tls.cert is world-readable by design, so the credential is immediately usable against the node's RPC port on loopback.

## Recommended fix
bakeMacaroon and constrainMacaroon create macaroon files with mode 0644, exposing bearer credentials to every local account, weaker than the daemon's own 0640 handling of admin.macaroon. Fix criteria: Macaroon files produced by bakemacaroon --save_to and constrainmacaroon are readable only by the invoking user (owner-only mode, no transient wider-permission window). Verify by producing a file with each command under a permissive umask and checking the resulting mode is at most 0600; also verify an existing more-permissive destination file does not retain its old mode.

# query_channel_range drives two policy point-queries per public channel in one uncancellable pinned SQL transaction

## Details
On the native SQL graph store (db.use-native-sql, a shipped non-default backend on sqlite or postgres) a single query_channel_range message from any gossip peer is answered by SQLStore.FilterChannelRange (graph/db/sql_store.go:2051-2208), which inside ONE serializable read transaction (sqldb/interfaces.go:355-392, 417-424) selects every public channel in the peer-chosen SCID range (GetPublicV1ChannelsBySCID, no LIMIT) and then, when the peer sets the timestamps query option (served by default; disabled only by --protocol.no-timestamp-query-option), issues two GetChannelPolicyByChannelAndNode single-row QueryRowContext statements per channel (sql_store.go:2128-2161). A ~50-byte QueryChannelRange{first_blocknum=0, number_of_blocks=0xffffffff, timestamps} therefore costs 1+2N statements for N = every public channel known (tens of thousands on mainnet), on postgres one network round trip each, while pinning one pooled connection for the whole transaction.

The only throttle in the path is the outbound byte rate limiter, applied per reply in sendMsgRateLimited (discovery/syncer.go:2132-2150) AFTER FilterChannelRange has returned (syncer.go:1410-1415). ChanSeries.FilterChannelRange (discovery/chan_series.go:247-254) calls the store with context.TODO(), so GossipSyncer.Stop (cg.Quit) on peer disconnect does not cancel the transaction; the replyHandler goroutine stays blocked in it until completion, and waitMsgDelay then returns ErrGossipSyncerExiting immediately, so a peer that disconnects is never throttled. QueryChannelRange is dispatched from the peer read loop into the syncer's 50-slot queryMsgs buffer (gossiper.go:898-924, syncer.go:1891-1903) with no per-peer or global budget on count or range. Every reconnecting peer gets a fresh syncer (brontide.go:2282 -> initGossipSync -> InitSyncState; createGossipSyncer always runs the replyHandler) and server.go:4828 prunes the old one without affecting the in-flight work; InboundPeerConnected has no per-IP or reconnect throttle and accessman releases the restricted slot on disconnect. The attack is: connect with a fresh key, send one maximal query, disconnect, repeat; each iteration costs the attacker a handshake and the node a full 1+2N-statement transaction that outlives the connection. Pending transactions queue on database/sql's pool without bound, so legitimate waiters see latency growing with the attacker's backlog.

Invoices, graph and payments stores all build their executors on the same baseDB (config_builder.go:1253-1340), so the connections pinned by peer-driven graph reads are the ones invoice settlement and payment-state writes need: a few dozen concurrent peer queries exhaust the default 50-connection postgres pool (lncfg/db.go:42); on sqlite the native store (lnd.sqlite, lncfg/db.go:34) has a 2-connection pool (sqldb/config.go:39), so two concurrent peer queries pin it entirely. The channel-state kvdb (channel.sqlite / kvdb postgres via sqlbase) uses a separate database and pool and is not directly stalled. Explicit assumption, not load-bearing: the DSN carries _txlock=immediate for every connection (sqldb/sqlite.go:113-116); whether modernc.org/sqlite v1.59.0 applies it to ReadOnly BeginTx could not be verified in the checkout -- if it does, each peer transaction also holds the sqlite writer lock on lnd.sqlite for its duration.

This is asymmetric amplification (one ~50 B message -> tens of thousands of statements and a pinned shared connection for seconds, uncancellable, unthrottled on the request side), not plain request volume: the bbolt sibling (kv_store.go:2910-3057) does the same per-channel policy lookups as in-process bucket gets under MVCC that pin no shared resource. The timestamp lookups can be a single joined range query (as GetChannelsBySCIDWithPolicies does elsewhere), the call should honour the syncer's context, and the request side needs a budget.

Holds only when the node runs the native SQL graph store (db.use-native-sql on sqlite or postgres). Open lead lead-syncer-1403-4c05 pointed at this call site.

## Evidence
1. [graph/db/sql\_store.go:2074–2188](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/sql_store.go#L2074-L2188)
   SQLStore.FilterChannelRange opens one ReadTxOpt transaction, fetches every public channel in the peer-chosen SCID range with GetPublicV1ChannelsBySCID, then for each row issues two separate GetChannelPolicyByChannelAndNode point queries (2128-2161) when withTimestamps is set. For a genesis-to-tip query on mainnet this is ~80k rows and ~160k additional statements inside the single transaction.
2. [discovery/syncer.go:1403–1415](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/syncer.go#L1403-L1415)
   replyChanRangeQuery takes withTimestamps from the peer's query option and passes the peer's whole FirstBlockHeight..LastBlockHeight range to FilterChannelRange before any reply is sent; the only early-out is a chain-hash mismatch.
3. [discovery/chan\_series.go:247–253](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/chan_series.go#L247-L253)
   ChanSeries.FilterChannelRange calls the graph with context.TODO(), so the SQL transaction cannot be cancelled when the peer disconnects or the syncer is stopped; the work always runs to completion.
4. [discovery/syncer.go:2132–2149](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/syncer.go#L2132-L2149)
   The per-peer and global rate limiters are applied in sendMsgRateLimited, i.e. only to the reply messages, after the DB work has already been done; waitMsgDelay (sync_manager.go:727-759) returns immediately with ErrGossipSyncerExiting once the syncer quits, so a disconnected attacker is never throttled at all.
5. [discovery/gossiper.go:898–923](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/gossiper.go#L898-L923)
   QueryChannelRange is dispatched from the peer read loop directly to the syncer's queryMsgs channel; there is no request-side rate limit, budget, or deduplication on the number or range of queries a peer may issue.
6. [peer/brontide.go:1090–1112](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/peer/brontide.go#L1090-L1112)
   Any peer advertising gossip_queries gets a fresh GossipSyncer with a replyHandler on every connection (InitSyncState); server.go:4828 prunes it on disconnect without affecting the in-flight transaction.
7. [sqldb/interfaces.go:355–391](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/sqldb/interfaces.go#L355-L391)
   ExecTx wraps the body in a *sql.Tx from BeginTx (417-424, LevelSerializable); a *sql.Tx holds one connection from the database/sql pool for the body's full duration.
8. [config\_builder.go:1253–1339](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/config_builder.go#L1253-L1339)
   With use-native-sql, the invoices, graph and payments stores all build their executors on the same baseDB, so the connections pinned by peer graph queries are the ones invoice settlement and payment state updates need.
9. [lncfg/db.go:42](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lncfg/db.go#L42)
   defaultPostgresMaxConnections = 50 bounds the shared pool; sqldb/config.go:39 sets DefaultSqliteMaxConns = 2 for sqlite.
10. [sqldb/sqlite.go:113–115](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/sqldb/sqlite.go#L113-L115)
   The sqlite DSN is built with _txlock=immediate for every connection. Explicit, unverified assumption about modernc.org/sqlite v1.59.0 (pinned in go.mod): if the driver applies this mode to ReadOnly BeginTx as well, each peer-driven FilterChannelRange transaction also holds the writer lock on lnd.sqlite; the pool-pinning impact (2 connections, sqldb/config.go:39) does not depend on this.
11. [sqldb/sqlc/queries/graph.sql:892–899](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/sqldb/sqlc/queries/graph.sql#L892-L899)
   GetPublicV1ChannelsBySCID returns every public channel whose scid lies in [start,end) with no LIMIT, and GetChannelPolicyByChannelAndNode (1128-1134) is a single-row lookup, confirming the 1 + 2N statement shape.

## Impact
Availability HIGH on the affected deployments: a sustained connect/query/disconnect loop keeps the native-SQL connection pool (50 on postgres, 2 on sqlite), shared by the invoice, payments and graph stores, occupied by uncancellable 1+2N-statement transactions, and pending ones queue without bound, so invoice settlement, payment-state and graph writes wait for as long as the attack runs. The process stays up and the channel-state kvdb is a separate DB/pool, so no direct loss of channel state; the impact is that database-backed HTLC/invoice processing is stalled at the attacker's discretion and negligible cost. No confidentiality or integrity impact.

## Reproduction steps
1. Unauthenticated remote peer: complete a brontide handshake to :9735 (restricted inbound slot, no channel needed; brontide.go:2282 starts gossip sync for every peer), advertise gossip_queries, send one maximal query_channel_range with the timestamps option, disconnect, repeat with fresh keys. No signatures, no state to guess, no defences to defeat; the only shipped control (the reply-side byte limiter) runs after the DB work and never engages once the peer is gone because the transaction is uncancellable (context.TODO()). Requires the node to run the native SQL graph store (db.use-native-sql, non-default) rather than bbolt, hence AT:PRESENT.

## Recommended fix
1. SQLStore.FilterChannelRange performs 2N dependent point queries inside one long-lived transaction for a peer-chosen N, pinning a shared pooled connection for the duration. Fix criteria: Serving a query_channel_range with timestamps must cost a bounded, small number of statements (e.g. one joined range query, paged) and must not hold a transaction open for the whole range. Verify: a genesis-to-tip query with timestamps executes O(pages) statements and no single transaction spans the full result.
2. ChanSeries uses context.TODO() so peer disconnect / syncer shutdown cannot cancel in-flight graph queries, and the only rate limit is applied to replies after the work is done. Fix criteria: Graph work done on behalf of a peer must be cancelled when that peer's syncer stops, and the node must bound the rate/size of query_channel_range work accepted per peer and globally before performing it. Verify: a peer that sends a maximal query and disconnects causes no further DB statements, and repeated reconnects cannot keep more than a small fixed number of range scans in flight.

# Stateless-init admin macaroon written world-readable by lncli --save_to

## Details
lncli's `create`, `createwatchonly` and `changepassword` commands accept `--stateless_init --save_to <file>`. The daemon then creates no macaroon files on its own disk and returns the serialized admin macaroon in the RPC response; `storeOrPrintAdminMac` (cmd/commands/cmd_walletunlocker.go:1011-1032) persists it with `os.WriteFile(macSavePath, adminMac, 0644)`.

Mode 0644 makes the file readable by every other account on the host (subject only to umask and the enclosing directory). The admin macaroon grants unrestricted access to every lnd RPC (send funds, close channels, bake further macaroons, stop the daemon). In stateless mode this file is deliberately the *only* copy of that credential, and the command's own help text says stateless init exists precisely so that no unencrypted macaroon file 'could leak information to the system'. The daemon side honours this: lnd writes admin.macaroon with 0640 (lnd.go:60). lncli, the component the documentation tells operators to use for stateless init, is laxer than the daemon for the same secret.

Attack path: an unprivileged local account on the host where the operator runs lncli (shared admin box, bastion, CI runner, container with a shared volume) reads `<save_to>` when it sits in a traversable directory (e.g. the operator's cwd or a 0755 home directory). tls.cert is 0644 by design (cert/selfsigned.go:297), so the attacker can dial the node's gRPC/REST endpoint with the stolen macaroon and operate it as admin, including draining the on-chain wallet via SendCoins. The threat model lists 'local host attacker via file permissions on secrets' as an in-scope adversary.

The root cause is choosing a world-readable mode for a credential file; nothing restricts the mode after the write, and the error path (`os.Remove` on failure) does not help. The same mistake appears in `bakemacaroon --save_to` and `constrainmacaroon` (filed separately).

## Evidence
1. [cmd/commands/cmd\_walletunlocker.go:1014–1023](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/cmd/commands/cmd_walletunlocker.go#L1014-L1023)
   storeOrPrintAdminMac persists the admin macaroon returned by InitWallet/ChangePassword to the operator-chosen --save_to path with os.WriteFile(macSavePath, adminMac, 0644) (line 1018). os.WriteFile applies that mode only at creation (masked by umask, 0644 under the common 022), so the file is readable by every account on the host; an existing file keeps whatever mode it had. In stateless mode this file is the only copy of the admin credential.
2. [cmd/commands/cmd\_walletunlocker.go:421–423](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/cmd/commands/cmd_walletunlocker.go#L421-L423)
   lncli create reaches the sink with response.AdminMacaroon when --stateless_init is set.
3. [cmd/commands/cmd\_walletunlocker.go:837–839](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/cmd/commands/cmd_walletunlocker.go#L837-L839)
   lncli changepassword reaches the same sink with the (possibly freshly rotated) admin macaroon.
4. [cmd/commands/cmd\_walletunlocker.go:1002–1004](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/cmd/commands/cmd_walletunlocker.go#L1002-L1004)
   lncli createwatchonly reaches the same sink.
5. [cmd/commands/cmd\_walletunlocker.go:480–484](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/cmd/commands/cmd_walletunlocker.go#L480-L484)
   The command's own help text states the purpose of stateless init: avoid 'unencrypted macaroon files which could leak information to the system that the daemon runs on'. The --save_to path defeats that purpose on the lncli host.
6. [lnd.go:47–60](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnd.go#L47-L60)
   The daemon's own constant and its comment state the project's stance: the admin macaroon must not be readable by any other user ('no other user can read admin macaroon unless the administrator explicitly allowed it'), which is why lnd writes admin.macaroon 0640 (lnd.go:826, 865) while invoice/readonly get 0644. lncli writes the identical credential 0644, contradicting this.
7. [cert/selfsigned.go:297](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/cert/selfsigned.go#L297)
   tls.cert is written 0644 by design, so a local reader who obtains the admin macaroon already has everything needed to authenticate to the gRPC/REST port.

## Impact
The disclosed file is the admin macaroon, which authenticates as full administrator to the lnd node lncli manages (treated here as part of the vulnerable system since lncli and lnd normally share a host). With it an attacker reads all node data, moves on-chain and channel funds, rotates macaroons and stops the daemon.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker is any other local account on the host where the operator runs lncli. The operator must have used --stateless_init --save_to and the file must sit in a directory the attacker can traverse (cwd, 0755 home, shared volume) — conditions outside the attacker's control, hence AT:PRESENT. No defence stands in the way of the read; tls.cert is 0644 by design, so the attacker can immediately authenticate to the node's RPC as admin. No victim interaction is needed beyond the normal command.

## Recommended fix
storeOrPrintAdminMac persists a full-privilege credential with a world-readable file mode (0644), weaker than the daemon's own 0640 for the same secret and contrary to the stated purpose of stateless init. Fix criteria: After the fix, a macaroon file written by lncli (create/createwatchonly/changepassword --save_to) is readable only by the invoking user (owner-only permissions, created without a window of broader access). Verify by running the command and checking the resulting file mode is at most 0600 regardless of umask, and that an existing more-permissive file at the target path is not left with its old mode.

# Bad reestablish secret on SCB-restored channel triggers force close with nil commitment, crashing lnd

## Details
A channel restored from a static channel backup (SCB) is persisted as a shell with ChanStatusRestored and no commitment state: channeldb.fetchChanCommitments returns empty LocalCommitment/RemoteCommitment for such channels, so LocalCommitment.CommitTx is nil. To run the data-loss-protection handshake, peer.loadActiveChannels still builds a LightningChannel and a link for Restored channels (brontide.go:1295). The link's syncChanStates hands the peer's channel_reestablish to lnwallet.ProcessChanSyncMsg.

ProcessChanSyncMsg checks the remote's your_last_per_commitment_secret first (channel.go:4452-4476), before the isRestoredChan branch that would classify the sync as local data loss. If the counterparty sends next_revocation_number != 0 together with a wrong secret, the function returns ErrInvalidLastCommitSecret. handleChanSyncErr (link.go:1235-1262) maps that error to LinkFailureForceClose; brontide.handleLinkFailure calls ChainArb.ForceCloseContract; the ChannelArbitrator moves to StateBroadcastCommit and calls arbChannel.ForceCloseChan, which marks the channel borked, reloads it and calls LightningChannel.ForceClose. ForceClose refuses only channels with ChanStatusLocalDataLoss (channel.go:8372) - a bit that is set only after a *successful* DLP classification, which this path skipped. It proceeds to getSignedCommitTx -> GetSignedCommitTx, which executes inputs.CommitTx.Copy() on the nil CommitTx (channel.go:6884) and panics in the arbitrator goroutine. No recover() exists in contractcourt, peer or htlcswitch, so the lnd process terminates.

The crash is repeatable: ForceCloseChan persisted ChanStatusBorked, but loadActiveChannels keys only on HasChanStatus(Restored), which stays true for Restored|Borked, so every reconnect re-creates the link and the same reestablish message crashes the node again. chanrestore.ConnectPeer connects the SCB peer with perm=true, so lnd reconnects to the attacker by itself after each restart, producing a crash loop until the operator abandons the channel or blocks the peer.

Attacker: the counterparty of any channel the victim restored from backup (SCB restore is exactly the situation in which the victim must trust this peer to come online and force close). The attacker needs only to answer the victim's channel_reestablish with one crafted message. Impact is loss of availability of the whole node, which during SCB recovery also prevents sweeping the remote force-closes of the victim's other restored channels and, for any channels opened after the restore, breach monitoring and HTLC resolution.

Assumption: (*wire.MsgTx).Copy in btcd v0.25.1-pre (go.mod) dereferences its receiver (it copies msg.Version etc.), so calling it on a nil *MsgTx panics; this is the standard btcd implementation.

The same ForceClose-on-shell path is reachable for ErrCommitSyncRemoteDataLoss/ErrInvalidLocalUnrevokedCommitPoint only on non-restored channels, which do have a commitment, so those are not affected.

## Evidence
1. [lnwallet/channel.go:8358–8379](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwallet/channel.go#L8358-L8379)
   ForceClose only refuses channels carrying ChanStatusLocalDataLoss. A channel restored from an SCB carries only ChanStatusRestored until the peer's channel_reestablish has been processed successfully, so the guard does not fire and getSignedCommitTx is called on a channel shell whose LocalCommitment is empty.
2. [lnwallet/channel.go:6881–6884](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwallet/channel.go#L6881-L6884)
   GetSignedCommitTx dereferences inputs.CommitTx via inputs.CommitTx.Copy(). For a restored shell LocalCommitment.CommitTx is nil, so this is a nil-pointer dereference (panic) in the channel arbitrator goroutine.
3. [lnwallet/channel.go:4452–4475](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwallet/channel.go#L4452-L4475)
   ProcessChanSyncMsg validates the remote's your_last_per_commitment_secret before the isRestoredChan branch (4541). A counterparty sending next_revocation_number != 0 with any wrong secret makes this return ErrInvalidLastCommitSecret even for a restored channel, so the designed DLP outcome (ErrCommitSyncLocalDataLoss -> MarkDataLoss) is never reached.
4. [htlcswitch/link.go:1235–1261](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/htlcswitch/link.go#L1235-L1261)
   handleChanSyncErr maps ErrInvalidLastCommitSecret (and ErrCommitSyncRemoteDataLoss / ErrInvalidLocalUnrevokedCommitPoint) to LinkFailureForceClose without checking whether the channel is a restored shell that has no commitment to broadcast.
5. [peer/brontide.go:4742–4774](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/peer/brontide.go#L4742-L4774)
   handleLinkFailure acts on LinkFailureForceClose by calling ChainArb.ForceCloseContract(chanPoint) for the restored channel.
6. [peer/brontide.go:1295–1299](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/peer/brontide.go#L1295-L1299)
   loadActiveChannels deliberately builds a LightningChannel and a link (addLink with syncStates=true, line 1486-1489) for ChanStatusRestored channels so the DLP handshake can run. hasChanStatus is a bitmask test (channeldb/channel.go:1287), so Restored|Borked still satisfies it: after the first crash the link is created again on every reconnect and the crash repeats.
7. [contractcourt/chain\_arbitrator.go:385–436](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/chain_arbitrator.go#L385-L436)
   arbChannel.ForceCloseChan first marks the channel borked, then re-reads it from the DB and calls LightningChannel.ForceClose(WithSkipContractResolutions) with no check for ChanStatusRestored. ChainArbitrator.Start (1351-1400) creates an arbitrator for every open channel including restored shells, so ForceCloseContract finds one.
8. [contractcourt/channel\_arbitrator.go:1116–1139](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/channel_arbitrator.go#L1116-L1139)
   StateBroadcastCommit, entered via userTrigger from the force-close request (channelAttendant 3058-3078, StateDefault userTrigger -> StateBroadcastCommit), calls c.cfg.Channel.ForceCloseChan(); it only special-cases ErrForceCloseLocalDataLoss, which is not returned for a Restored-only shell.
9. [channeldb/channel.go:5025–5032](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/channeldb/channel.go#L5025-L5032)
   fetchChanCommitments returns without reading any commitment for ChanStatusRestored channels, so LocalCommitment (and CommitTx) remain zero-valued on every load of the shell.
10. [channeldb/db.go:1724–1754](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/channeldb/db.go#L1724-L1754)
   RestoreChannelShells persists the shell with chanStatus |= ChanStatusRestored; no LocalDataLoss bit is set at restore time, which is the bit ForceClose checks.
11. [chanrestore.go:330–380](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/chanrestore.go#L330-L380)
   After an SCB restore the peer is connected with perm=true (persistent), and the restore writes a LinkNode that server.establishPersistentConnections reconnects to after every restart. lnd therefore reconnects to the attacker automatically, re-creating the link and re-triggering the crash.
12. [rpcserver.go:2785–2796](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/rpcserver.go#L2785-L2796)
   The project's own RPC close path refuses to force close a ChanStatusRestored channel ('cannot close channel with state'), and itest/lnd_channel_backup_test.go:323 asserts this; the comment says the arbitrator normally learns this only via ChanStatusLocalDataLoss after connecting. The link-failure force close is the path that reaches the arbitrator on a Restored-only shell before that bit is set.

## Impact
Unrecovered panic terminates the lnd process. Because the SCB peer is persistent and the restored channel is re-linked on every connection (Restored bit still set), the node re-crashes on each restart until the operator intervenes: full loss of availability of the node, including breach monitoring and HTLC handling for every other channel. No data is disclosed; the only state change is the Borked bit on the shell, which does not alter later behaviour.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker position: remote channel counterparty of a channel the victim restored from SCB (the victim connects to it on purpose, with a persistent connection). Delivery: after init and the victim's channel_reestablish, send channel_reestablish for that channel with next_revocation_number >= 1, any 32-byte your_last_per_commitment_secret that is not the victim's real secret, and a commitment point present. The victim's link returns ErrInvalidLastCommitSecret, requests a force close, and the arbitrator dereferences the nil commitment tx. No credentials, no user action, works on every reconnect; the only requirement is the restored-channel state, which is a runtime condition outside the attacker's control.

## Recommended fix
1. ProcessChanSyncMsg validates the remote's last commitment secret before recognising that the local channel is a restored shell, so a bad secret from the peer produces a force-close error on a channel that has nothing to broadcast. Fix criteria: For ChanStatusRestored channels, a channel_reestablish with an invalid your_last_per_commitment_secret must not lead to a force-close attempt; it should be treated like any other unrecoverable sync on a shell (fail/mark the channel without broadcasting). Verify by feeding a restored channel a reestablish with a wrong secret: the node must stay up and the channel must remain in restored/data-loss state.
2. LightningChannel.ForceClose/getSignedCommitTx and arbChannel.ForceCloseChan assume a commitment transaction exists; they gate only on ChanStatusLocalDataLoss and dereference a nil CommitTx for restored shells. Fix criteria: A force close requested for a channel with ChanStatusRestored (or any channel whose LocalCommitment.CommitTx is nil) must return an error instead of panicking, and the arbitrator must handle that error without crashing. Verify with a restored shell: ForceCloseContract returns an error and the process keeps running.
