# SetMissionControlConfig accepts NaN estimator parameters, driving pathfinding into an unbounded loop

## Details
routerrpc.SetMissionControlConfig (offchain:write) copies the proto double fields AprioriParameters.hop_probability/weight/capacity_fraction, BimodalParameters.node_weight and the deprecated float32 hop_probability/weight straight into routing.AprioriConfig/BimodalConfig (router_server.go:1218-1300) and installs the estimator via MissionControl.SetConfig. The only check on these values is validate(): `< 0 || > 1` (hop probability, apriori weight, bimodal node weight) and `< 0.75 || > 1` (capacity fraction). Every ordered comparison with IEEE-754 NaN is false, so NaN passes while +/-Inf is rejected. gRPC carries NaN as raw IEEE bits; the REST gateway (lnd.go:982, protojson UnmarshalOptions) accepts the string "NaN" for double fields.

NaN then reaches every probability: getNodeProbability returns NaN*capacityFactor (HopProbability NaN), NaN via aprioriFactor=1/(1-Weight)-1 for any from-node with history (Weight NaN), or NaN via capacityFactor for every edge with known capacity (CapacityFraction NaN); calculateProbability passes it through. LocalPairProbability is finite for the node's own channels, but processEdge multiplies it by the NaN cumulative probability of the rest of the route, so every heap entry carries probability NaN.

In findPath every guard is an ordered comparison: `edgeProbability == 0` (pathfind.go:841), `probability < MinProbability` (891), `dist > maxFloat` in getProbabilityBasedDist (which returns int64(NaN): MinInt64 on amd64, 0 on arm64), `tempDist > current.dist` (932) and `probability <= current.probability` (941). All are false, so every evaluation of every edge overwrites distance[fromVertex] and re-pushes the node (1005), including nodes already popped. distanceHeap.Less (heap.go:85-92) is always false for equal dist and NaN probability, so container/heap pops in insertion-dependent order. Dijkstra's invariants (a popped node is final; nextHop pointers strictly descend toward the target) no longer hold: when pivot P is popped it rewrites nextHop of all its neighbours to P, and the next adjacent pivot rewrites P's nextHop back, so the nextHop graph contains cycles.

Once the source is popped (1149-1156) the reconstruction loop (1159-1184) follows distance[current].nextHop until it reaches the target with no cycle detection and no hop bound, appending to pathEdges every iteration. With a cyclic chain it never terminates: the goroutine spins at 100% CPU and pathEdges grows until the process is OOM-killed. Minimal example, line graph target-A-B-source: step 0 writes A->target, step 1 writes B->A, step 2 (pivot B) rewrites A->B because the NaN guards accept it; the chain source->B->A->B->... never reaches the target. When the source is not reached quickly, the search phase itself also runs far beyond Dijkstra's bound because popped nodes are re-pushed indefinitely, limited only by per-walk CLTV/payload/fee checks.

findPath runs inside KVStore.GraphSession's bbolt read transaction (kv_store.go:4590-4600), which is therefore never released. The NaN estimator is shared by every payment and QueryRoutes until an admin re-sets it; UpdateRoutingConfig (server.go:1977) mirrors it into memory only, so a restart clears it, but an already-stuck goroutine ends only with the process. The verified record apriori-weight-zero-divide-by-zero-nan-probability-pathfinding reaches the same sink via 0/0 with a legal weight; this record covers the missing NaN rejection of RPC-supplied parameters.

## Evidence
1. [routing/probability\_apriori.go:98–115](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/probability_apriori.go#L98-L115)
   AprioriConfig.validate only checks `< 0 || > 1` (and `< minCapacityFraction || > 1`). Every ordered comparison with NaN is false, so AprioriHopProbability, AprioriWeight and CapacityFraction equal to NaN all pass validation; +/-Inf is rejected, NaN is not. This is the fix location.
2. [routing/probability\_bimodal.go:82–98](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/probability_bimodal.go#L82-L98)
   BimodalConfig.validate applies the same `< 0 || > 1` check to the float64 BimodalNodeWeight, so NaN passes (ScaleMsat/DecayTime are integers and unaffected); a NaN NodeWeight makes calculateProbability NaN for every from-node without fresh direct results.
3. [lnrpc/routerrpc/router\_server.go:1218–1299](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnrpc/routerrpc/router_server.go#L1218-L1299)
   SetMissionControlConfig copies proto double fields (AprioriParameters.HopProbability/Weight/CapacityFraction, BimodalParameters.NodeWeight, and the deprecated float32 fields) straight into routing.AprioriConfig / BimodalConfig and installs the estimator via MissionControl.SetConfig; no NaN check exists on this path.
4. [lnrpc/routerrpc/router\_server.go:123–126](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnrpc/routerrpc/router_server.go#L123-L126)
   The RPC requires only the offchain:write macaroon permission, held by the stock router.macaroon and any payment-capable non-admin macaroon.
5. [routing/probability\_apriori.go:180–248](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/probability_apriori.go#L180-L248)
   getNodeProbability multiplies AprioriHopProbability by capacityFactor and mixes in aprioriFactor = 1/(1-AprioriWeight)-1; a NaN in any of the three parameters makes the node probability NaN for every affected edge.
6. [routing/probability\_apriori.go:337–376](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/probability_apriori.go#L337-L376)
   calculateProbability returns nodeProbability (NaN) for untried pairs and nodeProbability*(1-weight) (NaN) for penalised pairs, so NaN reaches ProbabilitySource in pathfinding.
7. [routing/pathfind.go:841–1005](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/pathfind.go#L841-L1005)
   processEdge never prunes a NaN edge: `edgeProbability == 0` (841), `probability < cfg.MinProbability` (891), `tempDist > current.dist` (932) and `probability <= current.probability` (941) are all false for NaN / int64(NaN), so every evaluation of every edge overwrites distance[fromVertex].nextHop and re-pushes the node via PushOrFix (1005), including nodes already popped. This is what lets consecutive adjacent pivots point their nextHop entries at each other.
8. [routing/pathfind.go:1143–1184](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/pathfind.go#L1143-L1184)
   The search ends when the source is popped (1149-1156); the reconstruction loop (1159-1184) then follows distance[currentNode].nextHop until it equals the target with no cycle detection and no hop bound, appending to pathEdges every iteration. With the cyclic nextHop chain produced above it never terminates: 100% CPU and unbounded memory growth until OOM.
9. [routing/pathfind.go:1557–1576](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/pathfind.go#L1557-L1576)
   getProbabilityBasedDist computes dist = weight + penalty/NaN = NaN; `dist > maxFloat` is false, so int64(NaN) is returned (implementation-defined: MinInt64 on amd64, 0 on arm64), giving every entry the same dist.
10. [routing/heap.go:85–91](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/heap.go#L85-L91)
   Less ties on equal dist and compares NaN probabilities (always false): all entries are incomparable, so container/heap pops in insertion-dependent order and the min-heap provides no Dijkstra ordering.
11. [routing/missioncontrol.go:494–518](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/missioncontrol.go#L494-L518)
   SetConfig re-validates only MaxMcHistory/MinFailureRelaxInterval and installs the estimator used by GetProbability for all subsequent pathfinding (payments and QueryRoutes).
12. [graph/db/kv\_store.go:4590–4599](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/kv_store.go#L4590-L4599)
   GraphSession runs the whole findPath callback inside a bbolt read transaction (db.View), so the stuck pathfinding goroutine also holds the graph read transaction open indefinitely.

## Impact
Availability: a pathfinding goroutine never returns, pins a CPU core, holds the graph read transaction and grows pathEdges without bound until lnd is OOM-killed; until then every payment and QueryRoutes on the node uses the NaN estimator and hangs or returns an arbitrary route. The threat model treats node downtime as a funds-safety issue (missed HTLC/breach deadlines). Integrity: routes that do complete are not fee/probability-optimal and QueryRoutes success probability is NaN. No confidentiality impact.

## Reproduction steps
1. An RPC client holding a macaroon with offchain:write (e.g. the stock router.macaroon, or any payment-capable non-admin macaroon) calls SetMissionControlConfig over gRPC (NaN as IEEE bits) or REST (protojson "NaN") with hop_probability, weight, capacity_fraction or node_weight = NaN. validate() accepts it and the estimator is installed. The next pathfinding run - any SendPaymentV2 or QueryRoutes, which the same caller can also trigger - enters the degenerate search and the cyclic reconstruction loop deterministically. No shipped control checks for NaN; the attack works against default deployments.

## Recommended fix
1. AprioriConfig.validate and BimodalConfig.validate use ordered range comparisons that NaN passes, so SetMissionControlConfig installs a non-numeric probability/weight/fraction as a valid estimator parameter. Fix criteria: Both validate() methods must reject NaN (and keep rejecting Inf) for every float64 parameter, so SetMissionControlConfig with any NaN field returns an error and leaves the active estimator unchanged. Verify by sending NaN in each double/float field over gRPC and REST and confirming rejection, with GetMissionControlConfig still reporting the previous config.
2. findPath assumes ProbabilitySource returns a finite value in [0,1]; a NaN disables edge pruning, the Dijkstra improvement guards and heap ordering, and the route-reconstruction loop has no cycle or hop bound, so a corrupt distance map loops forever. Fix criteria: Pathfinding must treat a non-finite or out-of-range edge probability as zero (skip the edge), and route reconstruction must terminate with an error on a cyclic or over-long nextHop chain instead of looping. Verify with a ProbabilitySource stub returning NaN: findPath must return errNoPathFound promptly with bounded memory.

# Script-based spend request spent in two blocks crashes lnd at reorg-safety pruning

## Details
TxNotifier keeps two indexes for spend requests: spendNotifications (SpendRequest -> *spendNtfnSet holding the clients and the spend details) and spendsByHeight (height -> set of SpendRequests spent at that height), the latter driving Reorg dispatch on DisconnectTip and the Done/prune pass 144 blocks (reorgSafetyLimit) later in ConnectTip. For outpoint-based requests a single chain can spend the outpoint only once, so a request appears under at most one height. For script-based requests (OutPoint == ZeroOutPoint, created when chainrpc.ChainNotifier/RegisterSpendNtfn is called without an Outpoint and the backend forwards the nil outpoint to TxNotifier.RegisterSpend) filterTx (txnotifier.go:1589-1596) re-derives the spent pkScript from every input and performs a zero-outpoint lookup, so every later spend of any output carrying that script matches the same request. handleSpendDetailsAtTip (1704-1737) then overwrites spendSet.details and adds the request to spendsByHeight[newHeight] with no already-spent guard, unlike handleConfDetailsAtTip (1658-1664) which explicitly refuses address reuse. A script spent in block H1 and again (a different output, same script) in block H2 with H1 < H2 <= H1+144 is therefore indexed under both heights.

At ConnectTip(H1+144) the prune loop (1506-1521) sends Done, deletes spendNotifications[request] and spendsByHeight[H1]; spendsByHeight[H2] still references the request. At ConnectTip(H2+144) the loop executes `spendSet := n.spendNotifications[spendRequest]` -> nil *spendNtfnSet, then `for _, ntfn := range spendSet.ntfns` -> nil pointer dereference. ConnectTip is called from each backend's single notification-dispatcher goroutine (bitcoindnotify/bitcoind.go:658, btcdnotify/btcd.go:724, neutrinonotify/neutrino.go:679) with no recover in chainntnfs, so the unrecovered panic terminates the lnd process. DisconnectTip (1910-1926) dereferences the same lookup without a nil check, so a reorg of block H2 after the H1 prune also crashes; and before pruning, disconnecting H2 alone nils the details of the still-confirmed H1 spend and emits a spurious Reorg to the clients.

CancelSpend (1215) only deletes the client's entry from spendSet.ntfns and leaves the set in spendNotifications, so the attacker may close the RPC stream immediately after registering; the request and its index entries persist until pruned. Attack: any holder of a macaroon carrying onchain:read (the shipped readonly.macaroon, chainnotifier.macaroon, or any custom macaroon granting it) calls RegisterSpendNtfn with Outpoint unset and Script set to a non-taproot output script (P2PKH/P2SH/P2WPKH/P2WSH, the classes btcd txscript.ComputePkScript can re-derive) that is spent from in two different blocks within 144 blocks of each other -- a busy third-party address, or the attacker's own address spent from twice. The crash is deterministic 144 blocks after the second spend, requires no race or victim action, and recurs after every restart as long as the attacker re-registers (or a legitimate script-based registration on a reused address exists), taking the node offline so it misses HTLC timeout and breach-remedy windows (threat model: availability is funds). The maintainers' tests cover address reuse only on the confirmation side (TestTxNotifierFutureConfDispatchReuseSafe) and a single script spend plus reorg on the spend side; no test spends a registered script in two blocks.

## Evidence
1. [chainntnfs/txnotifier.go:1704–1736](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/chainntnfs/txnotifier.go#L1704-L1736)
   handleSpendDetailsAtTip unconditionally overwrites spendSet.details and inserts the SpendRequest into spendsByHeight[spendHeight] every time filterTx matches, with no 'already spent' guard. For a script-based request (ZeroOutPoint) a second output carrying the same script spent in a later block therefore indexes the same request under two heights. Contrast handleConfDetailsAtTip (lines 1658-1664) which refuses address reuse.
2. [chainntnfs/txnotifier.go:1506–1520](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/chainntnfs/txnotifier.go#L1506-L1520)
   ConnectTip's pruning loop iterates spendsByHeight[matureBlockHeight], looks up n.spendNotifications[spendRequest] and immediately ranges over spendSet.ntfns with no nil check, then deletes the set. 144 blocks after the first spend height the set is deleted; 144 blocks after the second spend height the stale index entry yields a nil *spendNtfnSet and `spendSet.ntfns` panics, crashing the process (no recover in any notifier goroutine).
3. [chainntnfs/txnotifier.go:1589–1595](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/chainntnfs/txnotifier.go#L1589-L1595)
   filterTx re-derives the spent pkScript from every input and performs a zero-outpoint lookup, so any spend of any output carrying the registered script in any later block is treated as a spend of the request.
4. [chainntnfs/txnotifier.go:1910–1925](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/chainntnfs/txnotifier.go#L1910-L1925)
   DisconnectTip also dereferences n.spendNotifications[op] without a nil check for every op in spendsByHeight[blockHeight]; with a double entry, disconnecting only the second block nils the details of the first (still-valid) spend and emits a false Reorg to the client.
5. [lnrpc/chainrpc/chain\_server.go:498–508](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnrpc/chainrpc/chain_server.go#L498-L508)
   The ChainNotifier RPC passes a nil outpoint when the request omits Outpoint, producing a script-based SpendRequest. This is the only production path that creates zero-outpoint spend registrations; all in-tree callers pass concrete outpoints.
6. [lnrpc/chainrpc/chain\_server.go:66–69](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnrpc/chainrpc/chain_server.go#L66-L69)
   RegisterSpendNtfn requires only onchain:read.
7. [rpcserver.go:105–109](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/rpcserver.go#L105-L109)
   readPermissions (readonly.macaroon) include onchain:read, so a read-only macaroon holder reaches the vulnerable registration.
8. [chainntnfs/bitcoindnotify/bitcoind.go:442–444](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/chainntnfs/bitcoindnotify/bitcoind.go#L442-L444)
   ConnectTip runs inside the notifier's dispatcher goroutine (same for btcd.go:724 and neutrino.go:679); an unrecovered panic there terminates lnd.

## Impact
An unrecovered nil pointer dereference in the chain notifier dispatcher goroutine terminates the whole lnd process. No data is read or altered, but the node is down until restarted and can be re-crashed at will by re-registering, so a limited read-only principal can keep the node from reacting to on-chain events (HTLC timeouts, breaches) -- an availability loss the project reserves to info:write (StopDaemon).

## Reproduction steps
1. The attacker holds any macaroon with onchain:read -- the shipped readonly.macaroon (lnd.go:859 bakes it from readPermissions, which include onchain:read at rpcserver.go:105-110) suffices -- and can reach the gRPC or REST listener; chainrpc is compiled into release builds (make/release_flags.mk RELEASE_TAGS includes chainrpc). One RegisterSpendNtfn call with Outpoint unset and a frequently spent non-taproot script (or two self-spends from one address in separate blocks within 144 blocks) is enough; the stream may be closed immediately since CancelSpend leaves the set registered. No race, no control to bypass, no victim action. The crash occurs deterministically 144 blocks after the second spend and is repeatable after restart. Assumption: btcd v0.25.1-pre txscript.ComputePkScript re-derives P2PKH/P2SH/P2WPKH/P2WSH scripts from an input's sigScript/witness, as filterTx and NewSpendRequest's taproot exclusion already rely on.

## Recommended fix
1. handleSpendDetailsAtTip (and dispatchSpendDetails) may index one SpendRequest under multiple heights in spendsByHeight because script-based requests can match more than one spend; the conf side guards against address reuse, the spend side does not. Fix criteria: A SpendRequest is present in spendsByHeight under at most one height at any time: either ignore further matches once details are set (as handleConfDetailsAtTip does) or remove the previous height entry when details are replaced. Verify by registering a script-based spend, spending two outputs with that script in blocks H1 and H2 < H1+144, connecting through H2+144 and confirming no panic, exactly one Done per client, and no Reorg when only H2 is disconnected.
2. ConnectTip, DisconnectTip and NotifyHeight dereference the result of n.spendNotifications[...] (and n.confNotifications[...]) without checking for a missing set, so any index inconsistency becomes a process crash. Fix criteria: Index lookups in ConnectTip/DisconnectTip/NotifyHeight tolerate a missing set (skip and clean the stale index entry, logging an error) so that an inconsistent index can never terminate the notifier goroutine. Verify with a unit test that seeds a stale spendsByHeight entry and connects/disconnects the corresponding heights without panic.

# Apriori estimator returns 0/0 = NaN with AprioriWeight=0, breaking Dijkstra termination and route reconstruction in pathfinding

## Details
routing/probability_apriori.go getNodeProbability converts AprioriWeight w into aprioriFactor = 1/(1-w) - 1 and uses it as the weight of the a-priori term in a weighted average (lines 209-248). The w == 1 extreme is guarded (line 192) but w == 0 is not, although validate() accepts it (line 107) and the field documentation (probability_apriori.go:81-88, lnrpc/routerrpc/routing_config.go:57-64, sample-lnd.conf:1349-1351 'Valid values are in [0, 1]') advertises 0 as a legitimate setting that 'only base[s] the probability on historical results, unless there are none available'. With w == 0 both probabilitiesTotal and totalWeight start at 0; the loop adds weight only for results with amt <= SuccessAmt or (FailTime set and amt >= FailAmt). Whenever the from-node has mission-control history but no result matches the queried amount, the function returns 0/0 = NaN (Go float division does not panic). calculateProbability (337-377) returns that NaN for every untried pair of the node and nodeProbability*(1-weight) = NaN for penalized pairs, so NaN reaches findPath's ProbabilitySource via MissionControl.GetProbability.

The results that create the unmatched condition are authored by remote routing nodes: a node returning temporary_channel_failure makes result_interpretation.failPairBalance record FailAmt = attempted amount for its outgoing pair (481-482, 853-858); any forwarded success records SuccessAmt via successPairRange (862-868); missioncontrol_state.setLastPairResult (56-139) stores exactly these ranges. A later query for a smaller amount (failure case) or larger amount (success case) through any channel of that node then matches neither clause. With a single result per node this is the common case, so on a node running routerrpc.apriori.weight=0 one failure message or one successful forward by a routing node is sufficient and deterministic.

In routing/pathfind.go processEdge a NaN probability is never pruned: `edgeProbability == 0` (841) and `probability < cfg.MinProbability` (891) are false; getProbabilityBasedDist (1557-1577) computes weight + penalty/NaN = NaN, `dist > maxFloat` is false and int64(NaN) is returned (implementation-dependent per the Go spec: MinInt64 on amd64, 0 on arm64; either sorts at or before every real distance). The 'worse route' guards `tempDist > current.dist` (932) and `probability <= current.probability` (941) are both false, so every relaxation of a NaN edge is accepted, distance[fromVertex] is overwritten and the node is re-pushed (PushOrFix, 1005) even after it was popped; since probability = toNodeDist.probability * edgeProbability (886), NaN propagates to every predecessor. heap.go Less (85-92) puts int64(NaN) entries ahead of all real distances and cannot order them among themselves (NaN > NaN is false), so the loop at 1055-1157 degenerates into an exhaustive re-exploration of all walks back from the target, bounded only by the per-path CLTV (870), onion payload size (981) and fee-limit (823) accumulations (tens of hops) - exponential work with no context cancellation, pinning a CPU core for the payment lifecycle goroutine or the QueryRoutes handler. Because relaxations are accepted unconditionally, nextHop pointers no longer form a tree: two adjacent NaN nodes A and B each popped once end up with A.nextHop -> B and B.nextHop -> A, and the reconstruction loop at 1163-1184 has no hop bound and no cycle check, so when the source is popped it appends to pathEdges forever (unbounded memory growth) instead of returning. Any route that is returned has NaN probability and is chosen arbitrarily.

Mission control state is in memory and persisted, so the condition survives restarts until ResetMissionControl or a weight change. The finding holds only when the operator has configured routerrpc.apriori.weight=0 (lnd.conf, server.go:1029-1042) or set weight 0 via SetMissionControlConfig (router_server.go:1240-1268); this is a documented valid value, not a disabled security control, and the bimodal estimator's explicit NaN checks (probability_bimodal.go:550-562) show the project's own standard that an estimator must not emit NaN. This is distinct from the pending candidate about NaN-valued config fields passing validate() (needs an offchain:write RPC caller): here the configuration is valid and the trigger is an ordinary remote routing outcome.

## Evidence
1. [routing/probability\_apriori.go:202–248](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/probability_apriori.go#L202-L248)
   With AprioriWeight == 0, aprioriFactor = 1/(1-0)-1 = 0, so probabilitiesTotal and totalWeight both start at 0 (227-228). The loop adds weight only for results with amt <= SuccessAmt or (FailTime set and amt >= FailAmt). When the from-node has history but no result matches the queried amount, line 248 returns 0/0 = NaN. The weight == 1 extreme is guarded at 192; weight == 0 is not. This is the code the fix must change.
2. [routing/probability\_apriori.go:98–115](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/probability_apriori.go#L98-L115)
   validate() accepts AprioriWeight == 0 (107); the field documentation at 81-88 (mirrored in lnrpc/routerrpc/routing_config.go:57-64 and sample-lnd.conf:1349-1351) advertises 0 as a valid setting that only uses historical results, so the operator is following the documentation when the bug is reachable.
3. [routing/probability\_apriori.go:337–376](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/probability_apriori.go#L337-L376)
   calculateProbability returns the NaN nodeProbability unchanged for every untried pair of that node (348, 364) and nodeProbability*(1-weight) = NaN for penalized pairs (374); PairProbability (308-317) is what MissionControl.GetProbability (missioncontrol.go:554) hands to findPath's ProbabilitySource for every non-local edge.
4. [routing/pathfind.go:827–944](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/pathfind.go#L827-L944)
   processEdge cannot prune a NaN probability: `edgeProbability == 0` (841) and `probability < cfg.MinProbability` (891) are false; probability = toNodeDist.probability * edgeProbability (886) propagates NaN to every predecessor; the 'worse route' guards `tempDist > current.dist` (932) and `probability <= current.probability` (941) are both false, so every relaxation is accepted, distance[] overwritten and the node re-pushed via PushOrFix (1005) even after it has been popped.
5. [routing/pathfind.go:1557–1576](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/pathfind.go#L1557-L1576)
   getProbabilityBasedDist: probability == 0 is false for NaN, dist = weight + penalty/NaN = NaN, `dist > maxFloat` is false, and int64(NaN) is returned (implementation-dependent per the Go spec; MinInt64 on amd64, 0 on arm64), a value that sorts at or before every real distance.
6. [routing/heap.go:85–91](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/heap.go#L85-L91)
   Less orders by dist then by probability; int64(NaN) entries sort ahead of all real distances and are mutually unordered (NaN > NaN is false), so the search services only NaN entries, in an order that is DFS-like, until the walk bounds exhaust or the source happens to be popped.
7. [routing/pathfind.go:1163–1183](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/pathfind.go#L1163-L1183)
   Route reconstruction follows nextHop pointers with no hop bound or cycle check. Once relaxations are accepted unconditionally, two adjacent popped NaN nodes end up pointing at each other, so this loop never reaches target and appends to pathEdges without bound.
8. [routing/result\_interpretation.go:478–482](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/result_interpretation.go#L478-L482)
   A remote routing node returning temporary_channel_failure causes failPairBalance (853-858) to record FailAmt = attempted amount for its outgoing pair; ordinary successes recorded via successPairRange (862-868) create the condition the same way for larger queried amounts. Any later query for a non-matching amount through another channel of that node yields the 0/0 case.
9. [routing/missioncontrol\_state.go:56–138](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/missioncontrol_state.go#L56-L138)
   setLastPairResult stores the SuccessAmt/FailAmt ranges whose gaps trigger the unmatched case; the values are driven by remote failure messages and payment outcomes, not by the operator, and persist across restarts.

## Impact
Availability: pathfinding for payments and QueryRoutes becomes an exhaustive walk enumeration with no cancellation (CPU core pinned per payment/QueryRoutes goroutine), and the unbounded route reconstruction loop can grow pathEdges without limit (memory exhaustion); since NaN spreads to every predecessor of any node with history, most searches are affected once the node has made a few payments, and the MC state persists across restarts, so the node's payment-sending function is lost until the operator resets mission control or changes the weight. HTLC resolution and breach handling do not depend on pathfinding, so this is loss of a primary function rather than of the whole node unless memory exhaustion kills the process. Integrity: any route that is returned has NaN probability and is chosen arbitrarily. No confidentiality impact.

## Reproduction steps
1. Precondition: the victim runs the apriori estimator with routerrpc.apriori.weight=0 (non-default but documented valid, validate() accepts it) - a deployment condition, hence AT:P. From there a remote routing node on one of the victim's attempted routes needs only to return temporary_channel_failure (or simply forward the HTLC) once; mission control records an amount-specific result and every later pathfinding whose candidate edges touch that node for a non-matching amount receives NaN and degenerates. No authentication, no special position beyond being a routing node the victim tries, no user interaction, and the effect is deterministic for a given MC state and amount. Assumption: Go (toolchain 1.26.8 per go.mod) float64 0/0 yields NaN without panic and int64(NaN) is implementation-dependent (MinInt64 on amd64, 0 on arm64); both values sort at or before every real distance, so the analysis holds on either architecture.

## Recommended fix
1. getNodeProbability divides probabilitiesTotal by totalWeight with totalWeight == 0 when AprioriWeight == 0 and no historical result matches the queried amount, yielding NaN instead of a defined probability. Fix criteria: getNodeProbability must return a finite value in [0,1] for every input: when totalWeight is zero it must fall back to the a-priori probability (as the len(results)==0 branch does), or the weight-0 extreme must be handled like the weight-1 extreme. Verify with a unit test using AprioriWeight 0 and a results map whose SuccessAmt < amt < FailAmt (and one with only a FailAmt above amt), asserting a finite result.
2. findPath trusts ProbabilitySource to return a finite probability; NaN defeats edge pruning, the probability-based distance and the Dijkstra improvement guards, so nodes are re-relaxed without bound. Fix criteria: Pathfinding must treat non-finite (NaN/Inf) edge probabilities as zero and skip the edge, and getProbabilityBasedDist must never convert a non-finite float to int64. Verify that findPath terminates immediately with a ProbabilitySource stub returning NaN.
3. Route reconstruction follows nextHop pointers with no hop limit or cycle detection, so a corrupted distance map (pointers forming a cycle) loops forever while growing pathEdges. Fix criteria: The reconstruction loop must bound its iterations (e.g. by the maximum hop count / routing payload size) or detect revisited vertices and return an error instead of looping. Verify with a unit test whose distance map contains a two-node cycle.

# Unmapped RBF publish rejection strands force close in StateBroadcastCommit, skipping anchor CPFP

## Details
When the ChannelArbitrator decides to go on chain it enters StateBroadcastCommit: it marks the channel borked, persists the commitment via MarkCommitmentBroadcasted and calls PublishTx (contractcourt/channel_arbitrator.go:1162-1180). Only lnwallet.ErrDoubleSpend and lnwallet.ErrMempoolFee are treated as 'a conflicting or low-fee commitment is already out there, continue'; any other error returns StateError. advanceState (1689-1696) commits no new state, so the arbitrator remains in StateBroadcastCommit on disk and in memory, and nothing re-drives it: handleBlockbeat advances the state machine only from StateDefault (3139-3147), ForceCloseContract answers errAlreadyForceClosed for any other state (3062-3075), and on restart the channel is still in the open bucket (IsPendingClose=false, chain_arbitrator.go:511) so the same publish is re-executed and fails identically while the conflict persists. sweepAnchors, which offers the anchors of all commitment versions (local, remote, remote-pending) to the sweeper so that whichever commitment is in the mempool gets CPFP'd, runs only in StateCommitmentBroadcasted (1185-1212) and is never reached.

The unmapped error is reachable from a channel counterparty. Commitment transactions carry the obfuscated state hint in nSequence (lnwallet/transactions.go:191; 0x80xxxxxx < 0xFFFFFFFE) and therefore signal BIP125 replaceability (bitcoind >= 28 defaults to full-RBF anyway). If the counterparty's commitment already sits unconfirmed in our backend's mempool, our commitment, which pays the same absolute fee because both sides derive it from the same feerate and weight, is evaluated as a replacement and rejected with 'insufficient fee, rejecting replacement'. BtcWallet.PublishTransaction takes that reject reason from TestMempoolAccept and converts it via chain.MapRPCErr (btcwallet.go:1371-1397); mapRpcclientError (1285-1308) maps mempool-conflict/missing-inputs/already-known to ErrDoubleSpend and min-fee rejections to ErrMempoolFee but passes chain.ErrInsufficientFee through unchanged. lnd's own wallet interface test asserts that exactly this scenario surfaces chain.ErrInsufficientFee from PublishTransaction (lnwallet/test/test_interface.go:1915-1922), and the arbitrator test comment 'We map a rejected rbf transaction to ErrDoubleSpend in lnd' (channel_arbitrator_test.go:3606-3611) shows the StateBroadcastCommit safeguard was meant to cover this case but does not.

Consequence: while the counterparty's low-fee commitment lingers in the mempool our node has no commitment of its own pending and CPFPs no anchor, so the counterparty alone decides when the channel closes. The chain watcher dispatches the close only after CloseConfsForCapacity (>=3) confirmations (chain_watcher.go:821-850, confscale_prod.go:12-25), so our HTLC resolvers start several blocks after the commitment confirms; a counterparty that confirms its commitment at or after an incoming HTLC's expiry can spend the pre-signed timeout path before our success resolver runs, stealing an HTLC we already paid downstream.

Dependency assumption (btcwallet v0.16.20-pre per go.mod): chain.MapRPCErr maps the replacement-fee rejection reason to chain.ErrInsufficientFee, as sweep/fee_bumper.go:582 and the wallet test rely on. Distinct from fundee-no-commit-feerate-floor-unrelayable-commitment (funding-time feerate acceptance).

## Evidence
1. [contractcourt/channel\_arbitrator.go:1162–1180](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/channel_arbitrator.go#L1162-L1180)
   After MarkCommitmentBroadcasted, PublishTx errors other than ErrDoubleSpend/ErrMempoolFee return StateError; only those two let the arbitrator proceed to StateCommitmentBroadcasted. A conflicting-commitment replacement rejection (chain.ErrInsufficientFee) falls into the StateError branch and the arbitrator stays in StateBroadcastCommit with the channel already borked.
2. [contractcourt/channel\_arbitrator.go:1185–1212](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/channel_arbitrator.go#L1185-L1212)
   Anchor resolutions for all commitment versions (local, remote, remote-pending) are offered to the sweeper only in StateCommitmentBroadcasted. The stranded arbitrator never reaches this state, so the remote's conflicting commitment is never CPFP'd by us.
3. [lnwallet/btcwallet/btcwallet.go:1285–1308](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwallet/btcwallet/btcwallet.go#L1285-L1308)
   mapRpcclientError translates mempool-conflict/missing-inputs/already-known into ErrDoubleSpend and min-fee errors into ErrMempoolFee, but passes chain.ErrInsufficientFee (BIP125 'insufficient fee, rejecting replacement') through unmapped.
4. [lnwallet/btcwallet/btcwallet.go:1371–1397](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwallet/btcwallet/btcwallet.go#L1371-L1397)
   Production publish path for btcd/bitcoind: the TestMempoolAccept reject reason is converted with chain.MapRPCErr and then mapRpcclientError, so the replacement-fee rejection reaches the arbitrator as the raw chain.ErrInsufficientFee.
5. [contractcourt/channel\_arbitrator.go:1689–1696](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/channel_arbitrator.go#L1689-L1696)
   advanceState returns on a stateStep error without committing a new state, leaving c.state at the last committed value (StateBroadcastCommit).
6. [contractcourt/channel\_arbitrator.go:3137–3147](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/channel_arbitrator.go#L3137-L3147)
   handleBlockbeat only calls advanceState when c.state == StateDefault, so once stuck in StateBroadcastCommit the force close is never retried on subsequent blocks.
7. [contractcourt/channel\_arbitrator.go:3058–3074](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/channel_arbitrator.go#L3058-L3074)
   A user force-close request is refused with errAlreadyForceClosed whenever state != StateDefault, so the operator cannot kick the stuck arbitrator either.
8. [contractcourt/chain\_arbitrator.go:511](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/chain_arbitrator.go#L511)
   Arbitrators for channels still in the open bucket start with IsPendingClose=false, so progressStateMachineAfterRestart re-runs StateBroadcastCommit with a chainTrigger and the same publish fails identically while the conflicting commitment persists.
9. [lnwallet/transactions.go:191](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwallet/transactions.go#L191)
   Commitment input nSequence is the obfuscated state hint OR'd with SequenceLockTimeDisabled (0x80xxxxxx < 0xFFFFFFFE), so commitments signal BIP125 replaceability and a conflicting commitment is evaluated as a replacement rather than rejected as txn-mempool-conflict.
10. [lnwallet/test/test\_interface.go:1915–1922](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwallet/test/test_interface.go#L1915-L1922)
   lnd's own wallet interface test asserts that publishing a transaction conflicting with a mempool transaction without paying enough additional fee returns chain.ErrInsufficientFee from PublishTransaction, establishing that this raw error reaches callers.
11. [contractcourt/channel\_arbitrator\_test.go:3603–3619](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/channel_arbitrator_test.go#L3603-L3619)
   The arbitrator test documents the maintainers' belief that 'a rejected rbf transaction' maps to ErrDoubleSpend and expects StateCommitmentBroadcasted; an 'unmatched error' is expected to stay in StateBroadcastCommit. The belief contradicts mapRpcclientError and the wallet test.
12. [contractcourt/chain\_watcher.go:821–850](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/chain_watcher.go#L821-L850)
   In production the chain watcher waits CloseConfsForCapacity (>=3, confscale_prod.go:12-25) confirmations of the spending commitment before dispatching the close event, so our HTLC resolvers start several blocks after the remote's commitment confirms and the remote can already have spent the HTLC timeout path.

## Impact
Loss of the full value of in-flight incoming HTLCs whose preimage we know (funds already paid downstream), i.e. direct theft from the node, plus the channel being left borked with no on-chain progress or anchor fee bumping until the attacker chooses to confirm their commitment. No confidentiality impact.

## Reproduction steps
1. The attacker is a channel counterparty (a P2P peer). It routes an HTLC to us whose preimage we learn and withholds the off-chain settlement; before our IncomingBroadcastDelta (16 blocks) cutoff it broadcasts its own commitment at a feerate that enters our backend's mempool but does not confirm (as funder it sets that feerate via update_fee, accepted down to FeePerKwFloor). Our force close is rejected as an insufficient-fee replacement, the arbitrator strands and never offers anchors, so nothing is CPFP'd. The attacker confirms its commitment via its own anchor at or after HTLC expiry and spends the timeout path first.

## Recommended fix
1. The arbitrator treats only ErrDoubleSpend and ErrMempoolFee as 'a conflicting or low-fee commitment is pending, proceed to StateCommitmentBroadcasted and sweep anchors', while the wallet surfaces BIP125 replacement rejections (chain.ErrInsufficientFee) as an unmapped error, so a conflicting remote commitment in the mempool aborts the transition. Fix criteria: A publish rejection caused by a conflicting transaction already in the mempool (including insufficient-fee replacement rejections) must lead to StateCommitmentBroadcasted and to anchors of all commitment versions being offered to the sweeper. Verify by publishing the local commitment while the remote commitment is in the mempool and asserting the state transition and anchor sweep requests.
2. After a failed force-close step the arbitrator remains in StateBroadcastCommit and nothing re-drives the state machine: handleBlockbeat advances only from StateDefault and ForceCloseContract refuses non-default states, so a transient publish failure strands the channel until the remote's commitment confirms. Fix criteria: A force-close attempt that fails after MarkCommitmentBroadcasted must be retried on subsequent blocks (or the state must be re-evaluated so anchors are offered and the published tx is rebroadcast). Verify by injecting a transient PublishTx error, delivering further blockbeats, and asserting the arbitrator reaches StateCommitmentBroadcasted without a restart.

# Unsynchronized concurrent access to ChannelArbitrator.activeHTLCs map across arbitrator goroutines

## Details
ChannelArbitrator.activeHTLCs (channel_arbitrator.go:343) is a plain Go map created once in NewChannelArbitrator and never reassigned. updateActiveHTLCs (2891-2904) writes three keys of it while holding only unmergedMtx.RLock, a shared lock that guards unmergedSet and does not serialize two concurrent writers of activeHTLCs. The owning attendant goroutine writes and iterates the map lock-free on every blockbeat while in StateDefault (971-975 → checkLocalChainActions/checkRemoteDanglingActions range over it and index it) and in sweepAnchors/prepareAnchorSweeps (1432-1437, 3353-3410).

ChainArbitrator.FindOutgoingHTLCDeadline (chain_arbitrator.go:1298-1332) breaks this goroutine confinement: for an outgoing HTLC on channel B it locates the arbitrator of the incoming channel A in activeChannels, calls A.updateActiveHTLCs() and ranges over A.activeHTLCs, from B's goroutine, holding only the ChainArbitrator mutex that A's attendant never takes. B reaches it on its attendant goroutine from (a) sweepAnchors → prepareAnchorSweeps → createSweepRequest → findCommitmentDeadlineAndValue (1495), executed on every block while B sits in StateCommitmentBroadcasted waiting for confirmation (1191-1202), once per non-dust outgoing HTLC per commitment set (up to three sets); (b) prepContractResolutions (2613, 2686) when the commitment confirms; and (c) relaunchResolvers (792) at startup. ChainArbitrator.handleBlockbeat (837-857) delivers each beat first to the chain watchers and then to every ChannelArbitrator concurrently via chainio.DispatchConcurrent (one goroutine per consumer); the arbitrator's handleBlockbeat (3112-3155) drains the buffered close-event channels and advances state within that same beat, so B's cross-arbitrator accesses to A's map and A's own StateDefault write/iterate of it run in the same dispatch window on different goroutines, on every block.

The result is an unsynchronized write/write, read/write and iterate/write data race on one map. Go (go.mod: go 1.26.8) detects an overlapping access via the map's writing flag and calls runtime fatal ('concurrent map writes', 'concurrent map read and map write', 'concurrent map iteration and map write'), which terminates the process and cannot be recovered. lnd dies while it is resolving an on-chain contract; until restarted it cannot sweep HTLCs, CPFP its commitment or react to a breach, and the same accesses recur on restart through relaunchResolvers.

Trigger from the network: a routing counterparty forwards HTLCs through the node (incoming on channel A, outgoing on channel B) and withholds settlement on B; shouldGoOnChain (1830) forces B on chain at expiry-OutgoingBroadcastDelta without any further action by the peer. From then on B's goroutine performs three writes plus an iteration of A's map per outgoing HTLC per commitment set on every block until B's commitment confirms, and again for every HTLC when it does, while A's goroutine performs its own writes, reads and iterations of that map on each of those blocks. Whether a given pair of accesses overlaps is decided by the scheduler, so the attacker must win a race, but the number of attempts scales with the number of forwarded HTLCs (up to the channel's max_accepted_htlcs) times the blocks the close stays unconfirmed (which an upstream peer that chose a long incoming CLTV lengthens, since the deadline-aware anchor budget then bids low), and the race also fires during ordinary multi-channel operation with no attacker. (The description's earlier citation of a 0.14.0 'concurrent map writes' fix refers to a crash in the btcwallet dependency — docs/release-notes/release-notes-0.14.0.md:603 — and is background on the crash class, not a prior fix of this code.)

## Evidence
1. [contractcourt/chain\_arbitrator.go:1298–1332](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/chain_arbitrator.go#L1298-L1332)
   FindOutgoingHTLCDeadline runs on the calling arbitrator's (channel B's) goroutine. For an outgoing HTLC whose incoming circuit is on channel A it takes only the ChainArbitrator mutex, then calls A.updateActiveHTLCs() (three map writes to A.activeHTLCs) and ranges over A.activeHTLCs. Channel A's own attendant goroutine never acquires the ChainArbitrator mutex, so nothing orders these accesses against A's.
2. [contractcourt/channel\_arbitrator.go:2891–2904](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/channel_arbitrator.go#L2891-L2904)
   updateActiveHTLCs writes three keys of c.activeHTLCs while holding only unmergedMtx.RLock, a shared lock that does not serialize two concurrent writers of activeHTLCs; it protects unmergedSet only.
3. [contractcourt/channel\_arbitrator.go:965–976](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/channel_arbitrator.go#L965-L976)
   On every block in StateDefault, channel A's channelAttendant goroutine calls updateActiveHTLCs (write) and then hands c.activeHTLCs to checkLocalChainActions, which ranges over the map (iteration) without any lock.
4. [contractcourt/channel\_arbitrator.go:1430–1441](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/channel_arbitrator.go#L1430-L1441)
   sweepAnchors also writes activeHTLCs via updateActiveHTLCs and prepareAnchorSweeps then reads it; this path calls FindOutgoingHTLCDeadline for each outgoing HTLC, i.e. it is the writer into *other* channels' maps.
5. [contractcourt/chain\_arbitrator.go:837–857](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/chain_arbitrator.go#L837-L857)
   ChainArbitrator.handleBlockbeat copies the arbitrators and fans the blockbeat out with chainio.DispatchConcurrent, which spawns one goroutine per consumer; each ChannelArbitrator processes the beat on its own channelAttendant goroutine. Channel A's per-block write/iterate of its map and channel B's FindOutgoingHTLCDeadline write/iterate of the same map therefore execute concurrently on every beat.

## Impact
A detected concurrent map access is a fatal runtime error that terminates lnd; the node is offline until restarted, during which it cannot resolve HTLCs, punish breaches or fee-bump closes. No data is disclosed or persistently corrupted (state is persisted before the crash).

## Reproduction steps
1. A routing peer with no privileges establishes forwarded HTLCs spanning two of the victim's channels and withholds settlement on the outgoing channel; the arbitrator goes on chain by itself at the deadline and, from then on, B's goroutine writes and iterates A's activeHTLCs on every block, concurrently with A's own lock-free per-block accesses. The attacker cannot control goroutine scheduling, so a detectable overlap must be won (AC:H) and specific runtime state is required (two channels, forwarded HTLCs at their deadline, an unconfirmed force close) (AT:P). Attempts repeat per HTLC per commitment set per block, so cumulative probability grows with the number of forwarded HTLCs and the blocks the close stays unconfirmed.

## Recommended fix
activeHTLCs is mutated and iterated from the owning arbitrator's goroutine and from other arbitrators' goroutines (via ChainArbitrator.FindOutgoingHTLCDeadline) without a mutex that covers the map itself; updateActiveHTLCs only holds a shared read lock on a different structure. Fix criteria: Every read, write and iteration of a ChannelArbitrator's activeHTLCs must be serialized by a lock owned by that arbitrator (or FindOutgoingHTLCDeadline must query the arbitrator through a message to its goroutine instead of touching its map). Verify with the Go race detector on a test in which one arbitrator processes blocks while another concurrently calls FindOutgoingHTLCDeadline for an HTLC whose incoming circuit is on the first.

# Hostile tower replying AlreadyExists drives unbounded negotiation loop and burns global session key-index space

## Details
The watchtower client negotiates sessions round-robin across the operator's registered towers (candidate_iterator.go). In sessionNegotiator.negotiate() (session_negotiator.go:300-336) a CreateSessionReply with code CreateSessionCodeAlreadyExists is interpreted as 'our session key was already used, derive another one': tryAddress returns ErrSessionKeyAlreadyUsed, createSession propagates it, and negotiate() sets forceNextKey=true and `continue`s immediately. Each iteration (1) runs DB.NextSessionKeyIndex(tower, blobType, true), a bbolt write transaction that advances the single bucket-wide sequence of cSessionKeyIndexBkt by 1000 and persists a new reservation; (2) derives a new session key (an RPC when a remote signer is used); (3) dials the tower (TCP + brontide handshake) and performs Init/CreateSession; (4) never closes the connection. There is no backoff, no attempt limit and no fallthrough to the next candidate tower, and the loop never re-consults the candidate iterator, so `lncli wtclient remove` (RemoveCandidate only deletes a map entry) cannot stop it; only an lnd restart does.

A tower that the operator has added (an explicit adversary in the threat model: 'a tower this node backs up to may lie') simply answers every CreateSession with code 60. Consequences, all remote and deterministic:

1. Negotiation is monopolised: negotiate() never returns, so the honest towers in the candidate list are never tried again. backupDispatcher sits in awaitSession (client.go:709-754) and every new revoked state for that blob type piles up in the pipeline; nothing is backed up anywhere until the loop ends. Without this bug a hostile tower only captures its own round-robin share of sessions.

2. Persistent resource burn: a continuous stream of fsync'd DB transactions, key derivations and outbound brontide handshakes, plus leaked sockets, for as long as the hostile tower keeps replying. The Manager runs one negotiator per blob policy (four in server.go), so a tower lying on every blob type drives four such loops in parallel over the same DB.

3. Permanent, restart-surviving DoS of the whole tower client: the key-index sequence is global (one bucket for every tower and blob type, client_db.go:709-741). After ~2.1M forced iterations (+1000 each) the sequence passes MaxInt32-1000 and every forced call fails forever (the failing transaction rolls back, leaving the sequence at the cap); non-forced calls can hand out fewer than 1000 further indexes to all honest towers combined before they too fail with 'exhausted session key indexes'. lnd exposes no way to reset the sequence, so the node can never create another tower session without discarding wtclient.db.

The honest lnd wtserver only sends AlreadyExists when LastApplied>0 for an existing session (wtserver/create_session.go:32-37), and the project's own test ('continue after client database deletion', client_test.go:2098-2105) shows the +1000 jump was designed for client state loss, not for an adversarial peer; the client trusts the code unconditionally.

## Evidence
1. [watchtower/wtclient/session\_negotiator.go:300–335](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtclient/session_negotiator.go#L300-L335)
   Inner for-loop in negotiate(): on ErrSessionKeyAlreadyUsed it sets forceNextKey=true and immediately `continue`s, calling DB.NextSessionKeyIndex (a write transaction) and createSession (new TCP+brontide dial, Init, CreateSession) again against the same `tower` pointer. There is no backoff, no attempt counter, no re-consultation of the candidate iterator (so RemoveTower cannot stop it) and no move to the next candidate tower; the loop only ends when NextSessionKeyIndex errors.
2. [watchtower/wtclient/session\_negotiator.go:502–510](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtclient/session_negotiator.go#L502-L510)
   tryAddress maps the tower-supplied CreateSessionReply code CreateSessionCodeAlreadyExists (60) directly to ErrSessionKeyAlreadyUsed with no validation; the tower can return this for every fresh session key.
3. [watchtower/wtclient/session\_negotiator.go:363–367](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtclient/session_negotiator.go#L363-L367)
   createSession returns ErrSessionKeyAlreadyUsed to negotiate() immediately (no other addresses tried, no ErrFailedNegotiation/backoff path).
4. [watchtower/wtdb/client\_db.go:704–770](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtdb/client_db.go#L704-L770)
   NextSessionKeyIndex uses the bucket-wide Sequence() of cSessionKeyIndexBkt, shared by all towers and all blob types. With forceNext it advances by 1000 per call and commits. The MaxInt32 check runs after SetSequence inside the kvdb.Update closure, so on failure the transaction rolls back and the sequence stays at the last committed value: once it exceeds MaxInt32-1000 every forced call fails, and non-forced calls (+1) can hand out at most the remaining <1000 indexes to all honest towers combined before every call fails. Nothing in the codebase resets the sequence.
5. [watchtower/wtclient/candidate\_iterator.go:161–183](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtclient/candidate_iterator.go#L161-L183)
   RemoveCandidate (reached from lncli wtclient remove via handleStaleTower, client.go:1302-1347) only deletes the tower from the candidates map; the running negotiate() loop already holds the *Tower and never calls Next()/IsActive again, so the operator cannot stop the loop short of restarting lnd.
6. [watchtower/wtclient/manager.go:213–218](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtclient/manager.go#L213-L218)
   NewManager creates one client (and one sessionNegotiator) per blob policy; server.go:1866-1897 passes four policies (legacy, anchor, taproot, taproot-final) sharing one DB, so a tower answering code 60 on every blob type drives four parallel loops against the same global sequence.
7. [watchtower/wtclient/session\_negotiator.go:403–406](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtclient/session_negotiator.go#L403-L406)
   The brontide connection opened per attempt is never closed by tryAddress on any path (c.dial at client.go:977-981 is a bare brontide.Dial), so each loop iteration leaves a socket open until the Go GC finalizer runs.
8. [watchtower/wtclient/client.go:700–754](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtclient/client.go#L700-L754)
   backupDispatcher blocks in awaitSession until the negotiator delivers a session; while the negotiator is captured by the hostile tower no session for any other tower is produced, so all new backups for this blob type stall.

## Impact
No data is disclosed or altered. Availability of the watchtower client is lost: while the loop runs no new session is negotiated with any tower so all new backups stall, and the node continuously performs fsync'd DB writes, key derivations and outbound handshakes; after the shared sequence reaches MaxInt32 the client can never negotiate a session again across restarts. lnd itself keeps running, but the security component is permanently disabled, which is the component's entire function.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker runs a watchtower the victim has registered via AddTower (the threat model's hostile-tower adversary; the attacker needs no credentials on the victim). It implements the wtwire protocol normally but answers every CreateSession with CreateSessionCodeAlreadyExists. The next time the victim's negotiator reaches this tower in its round-robin (within one exhausted session, 1024 updates by default) the client enters the unbounded loop: it never tries other towers, stops producing sessions, and burns the persisted key-index sequence until it is exhausted. Works over the network against default configuration; the only precondition is that the victim added the attacker's tower.

## Recommended fix
1. negotiate() retries on ErrSessionKeyAlreadyUsed without any bound or backoff and without advancing to the next candidate tower, treating a remote-controlled reply code as a trusted instruction to keep looping. Fix criteria: A tower returning AlreadyExists repeatedly must not be able to keep the negotiator busy: after a small bounded number of AlreadyExists replies for one tower the negotiator applies the normal exponential backoff and moves to the next candidate (or marks the tower failed). Verify that with a tower that always replies code 60 and one honest tower, sessions with the honest tower continue to be created.
2. NextSessionKeyIndex with forceNext advances a single global bucket sequence by 1000 on every call and the exhaustion at MaxInt32 is irreversible, so a remote party can exhaust key-index space for every tower. Fix criteria: Key-index consumption must not be driven unboundedly by remote replies: either the forced jump is rate-limited/bounded per tower, or the index space is per tower so one tower cannot exhaust others, or exhaustion is recoverable. Verify that after many AlreadyExists replies from one tower, NextSessionKeyIndex still succeeds for other towers.
3. tryAddress never closes the brontide connection it opens. Fix criteria: Every connection opened in tryAddress is closed before return on all paths; verify no open sockets remain after a failed or successful negotiation.

# AMP set ID re-use after settlement accepted; payer can persistently fail exit-hop link

## Details
updateMpp (invoices/update.go:257-318) decides whether an incoming AMP HTLC may join an HTLC set purely from inv.State (always ContractOpen for AMP invoices, since addHTLCs never moves the top-level AMP invoice out of Open) and from the set's currently *accepted* HTLCs (inv.HTLCSet(setID, HtlcStateAccepted)). It never consults inv.AMPState[setID].State. A sender who completed and settled a set earlier can therefore send a brand-new HTLC (new circuit key, so resolveReplayedHtlc does not fire; new onion, so sphinx replay protection does not fire) carrying the same payment_addr and the same AMP set_id. Because the set's HTLCs are all Settled, the accepted set is empty, every check passes and the HTLC is admitted into the already-settled set.

The registry then runs idb.UpdateInvoice with that setID as hint. Both stores load *all* HTLCs of the set regardless of state (channeldb fetchInvoice → fetchAmpSubInvoices → fetchFilteredAmpInvoices; sql_store fetchInvoice with HtlcSetOnlyModifier → fetchAmpState → FetchAMPSubInvoiceHTLCs), so addHTLCs iterates the old Settled HTLCs.

Variant A (zero cost, availability): the new HTLC is a partial payment (amtPaid < total_msat, e.g. the channel's min HTLC with total_msat >= invoice value). update.State is nil, so settleEligibleAMP is false and getUpdatedHtlcState(oldSettledHtlc, ContractOpen, nil) returns ErrHTLCAlreadySettled (update_invoice.go:818-819). The DB transaction rolls back and the error is returned from UpdateInvoice; notifyExitHopHtlcLocked only converts ErrDuplicateSetID/ErrInvoiceNotFound/ErrInvRefEquivocation into fail resolutions, so its default branch (invoiceregistry.go:1196-1198) returns the error as a Go error, NotifyExitHopHtlc returns it, processExitHop returns it, and processRemoteAdds calls l.failf(LinkFailureError{code: ErrInternalError}) (link.go:3193-3202). handleLinkFailure (peer/brontide.go) wipes the channel from the switch and, because ShouldSendToPeer is true for ErrInternalError, sends an lnwire.Error to the upstream peer — the code's own comment notes that 'sending an error can lead some nodes to force close the channel'. The HTLC is neither settled nor failed, so its forwarding package is never acked; the channel stays inactive until the peer reconnects, and on every reconnect resolveFwdPkg replays the add (link.go:1148-1149), the same error recurs and the link fails again. The only way the HTLC clears without going on-chain is a replay once its expiry is within the invoice's final CLTV delta of the current height (updateMpp's ResultExpiryTooSoon check then fails it back), which requires a reconnect in that window; otherwise the upstream peer must force close to time the HTLC out, and peers that treat a received error as fatal (BOLT 1) force close immediately. The attacker's only cost is a minimal HTLC amount locked until expiry. The upstream peer can be an innocent routing node chosen by the attacker's route, so the attacker selects which of the victim's channels is disabled.

Variant B (integrity): if the new HTLC alone satisfies total_msat, the set 'completes' again. reconstructAMPPreimages runs over an empty prior set, so the attacker computes the child hash from their own single share; getUpdatedInvoiceState passes because the new HTLC is in the accepted set, settleEligibleAMP makes trySettle tolerate the old Settled HTLCs and the update succeeds. In the kv store, UpdateAmpState sees the pre-existing state Settled, initialises updatedAmpHtlcs[setID] empty and marks settledSetIDs[setID] (channeldb/invoices.go:846-856); storeAddHtlcsUpdate then writes a second settle-index entry for the same set (setSettleMetaFields) and updateAMPInvoices overwrites key invoiceNum||setID with only the new HTLC, erasing the stored records of the original settled HTLCs. A second SETTLED notification for the same set_id is emitted and InvoicesSettledSince replays the set twice.

Preconditions: the victim has an AMP invoice the attacker previously paid (a static AMP invoice issued with --amp, or spontaneous AMP via --accept-amp where the attacker first pays an arbitrary tiny amount to create the invoice). Both kv (bbolt/etcd) and SQL backends are affected by variant A. Pre-recurring AMP invoices that store HTLCs inline (shouldFetchAMPHTLCs returns false) hit variant A for any new set, not only a re-used one.

## Evidence
1. [invoices/update.go:257–318](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/update.go#L257-L318)
   updateMpp gates acceptance on inv.State (always Open for AMP) and on the set's Accepted HTLCs only; an HTLC naming a set whose HTLCs are all Settled sees an empty accepted set, passes every check and is recorded as a partial (update.State nil) or settled (complete). inv.AMPState[*setID].State is never checked. This is the code the fix must change.
2. [invoices/update\_invoice.go:302–352](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/update_invoice.go#L302-L352)
   addHTLCs iterates every HTLC loaded for the set, including the old Settled ones; for a partial accept update.State is nil so htlcContextState is ContractOpen and getUpdatedHtlcState is asked to align a Settled HTLC with an Open invoice.
3. [invoices/update\_invoice.go:816–820](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/update_invoice.go#L816-L820)
   Returns ErrHTLCAlreadySettled for a Settled HTLC when the invoice state is not Settled; this aborts the whole update and the transaction.
4. [invoices/invoiceregistry.go:1178–1199](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/invoiceregistry.go#L1178-L1199)
   Only ErrDuplicateSetID, ErrInvoiceNotFound and ErrInvRefEquivocation are converted into fail resolutions; any other UpdateInvoice error (here ErrHTLCAlreadySettled) is returned as a Go error to the link.
5. [htlcswitch/link.go:3193–3203](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/htlcswitch/link.go#L3193-L3203)
   processRemoteAdds treats an error from processExitHop (which returns the registry error unchanged at 3522-3528) as a link failure: failf(ErrInternalError), which wipes the channel and sends an lnwire.Error to the peer (ShouldSendToPeer is true for ErrInternalError).
6. [htlcswitch/link.go:1148–1149](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/htlcswitch/link.go#L1148-L1149)
   On every link restart resolveFwdPkg replays all un-acked adds through processRemoteAdds; the stuck HTLC is never acked, so the failure recurs on each reconnect until the HTLC is near enough to expiry for the ResultExpiryTooSoon check to fail it back.
7. [channeldb/invoices.go:1466–1491](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/channeldb/invoices.go#L1466-L1491)
   fetchFilteredAmpInvoices loads every HTLC stored under invoiceNum||setID regardless of state, so the settled HTLCs of the re-used set are present in the update.
8. [invoices/sql\_store.go:604–615](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/sql_store.go#L604-L615)
   The SQL store likewise loads all AMP HTLCs for the set ID with no state filter, so the same error path is reached on SQL backends.
9. [channeldb/invoices.go:818–861](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/channeldb/invoices.go#L818-L861)
   Variant B: when the pre-existing AMP set state is Settled, UpdateAmpState starts updatedAmpHtlcs[setID] as an empty map and adds the set to settledSetIDs, so the later write replaces the set's stored HTLCs with only the new one and a second settle-index entry is created (storeAddHtlcsUpdate 907-961, updateAMPInvoices 1031-1052).

## Impact
Availability: the channel link to the upstream peer is persistently disabled (link failure loop) and the HTLC can only be resolved by on-chain timeout/force close, with any other HTLCs on that channel stuck. Integrity (variant B, kv store): records of previously settled HTLCs are overwritten, a duplicate settle-index entry and duplicate SETTLED notification with cumulative amt_paid are produced for the same set_id, which can mislead downstream accounting. No confidentiality impact.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker is any Lightning node that once paid an AMP set to the victim (static AMP invoice, or --accept-amp spontaneous payment of a trivial amount) and so knows payment_addr and its own set_id. It routes one more HTLC to the victim with that payment_addr/set_id, total_msat >= invoice value, and a small amount. The victim's exit-hop link fails deterministically, re-fails on every reconnect, and the HTLC stays locked until expiry; stricter upstream peers force close on the error message. Needs no credentials or user action; requires the victim to have AMP enabled/issued.

## Recommended fix
1. updateMpp admits an AMP HTLC into a set based only on the invoice's top-level Open state and the set's currently accepted HTLCs; it does not check that the set identified by the sender-chosen set_id is still pending, so terminal (settled) sets can be re-entered. Fix criteria: An HTLC whose set_id refers to an AMP set whose AMPState is Settled (or otherwise terminal) must be rejected with a fail resolution before any DB update. Verify by replaying a new HTLC with a previously settled set_id: the HTLC is failed back to the sender, the invoice/AMP state and stored HTLC records are unchanged, and no settle event is emitted.
2. Errors from idb.UpdateInvoice other than a few whitelisted ones propagate from NotifyExitHopHtlc as Go errors, and the link converts any such error into a link failure, turning a per-HTLC data-dependent condition into loss of the whole channel link that recurs on replay. Fix criteria: A remote-triggerable invoice-update failure for a single HTLC must resolve that HTLC (fail it back) rather than fail the link; verify that a malformed/inconsistent exit-hop HTLC leaves the link running and the HTLC failed, including after a restart replay.

# Web fee API response body decoded with no size limit; gzip-amplified body exhausts memory during lnd startup and on every refresh

## Details
SparseConfFeeSource.GetFeeInfo fetches the operator-configured fee URL (lncfg/fee.go: 'Must be set for neutrino on mainnet'; the documented example, sample-lnd.conf:614 and docs/neutrino_headers_import.md, is the third-party endpoint https://nodes.lightning.computer/fees/v1/btc-fee-estimates.json) and parses the body with json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(). No size limit is applied anywhere on the path: there is no io.LimitReader or http.MaxBytesReader, no Content-Length check, and the custom http.Transport leaves DisableCompression at its default, so Go's net/http requests gzip and transparently inflates the body. encoding/json's Decoder buffers the entire JSON value in a doubling in-memory buffer before unmarshalling, so the heap grows with whatever the server sends.

The only guard is http.Client.Timeout = 10 s (WebAPIResponseTimeout), which bounds the time spent reading, not the bytes buffered. With a gzip-encoded body of a few megabytes that inflates ~1000:1 (e.g. a JSON object padded with whitespace or millions of key/value pairs), the amount buffered within the window is set by single-core inflate + JSON-scan throughput rather than by the attacker's bandwidth: on the order of a gigabyte or more per fetch, with transient peaks of roughly two to three times that from the doubling copies. That is enough to have the process OOM-killed on the 1-4 GB hosts lnd is commonly run on, and is in any case a multi-GB allocation forced by a remote party on every fetch.

Because WebAPIEstimator.Start() performs the first fetch synchronously inside chainreg.NewPartialChainControl (called from config_builder.go during startup), the crash happens before the node is operational and recurs on every restart for as long as the server serves the payload; after startup it recurs on the 5-20 minute refresh ticker. The threat model lists the web fee estimator as a 'mostly trusted' supplier whose trust extends to fee values, and marks remote crash/OOM as a security issue because the node must stay online to resolve HTLCs and punish breaches. The code itself (comment at estimator.go:685-689, error tolerance in updateFeeEstimates) shows the design intends a down or misbehaving fee service to degrade gracefully, not to terminate lnd. A malicious or compromised fee server (including compromise of the shared default endpoint, its DNS or CDN) therefore gains the ability to take every dependent node offline deterministically, which the project does not concede to it.

This is distinct from a server lying about fee values (filed separately at estimator.go:902): here the content of the response is irrelevant, only its size.

Assumed standard-library behaviour (Go 1.26.8 per go.mod): http.Transport with DisableCompression=false adds Accept-Encoding: gzip when the request sets none and wraps the body in a gzip reader; http.Client.Timeout interrupts Body reads after the deadline; json.Decoder.Decode reads the whole value into dec.buf, growing it by doubling, before unmarshalling.

## Evidence
1. [lnwallet/chainfee/estimator.go:661–679](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwallet/chainfee/estimator.go#L661-L679)
   parseResponse hands the raw HTTP body to json.NewDecoder(r).Decode(&resp) with no io.LimitReader, http.MaxBytesReader or Content-Length check (no such limiter exists anywhere on this path). encoding/json's Decoder reads the complete JSON value into one in-memory buffer that doubles on each refill before unmarshalling, so heap use is proportional to the (decompressed) body the server chooses to send; a successfully parsed body with millions of fee_by_block_target keys additionally materialises a map[uint32]uint32 of that size.
2. [lnwallet/chainfee/estimator.go:685–721](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwallet/chainfee/estimator.go#L685-L721)
   GetFeeInfo builds a custom http.Transport that leaves DisableCompression at its default (false) and issues a plain Get with no Accept-Encoding header, so Go's transport (go 1.26.8 per go.mod) requests gzip and transparently inflates the body before parseResponse reads it (deflate allows ~1000:1). The only guard is http.Client.Timeout = WebAPIResponseTimeout (10 s), whose stated purpose (comment at 685-689) is to survive a service that is 'down or overloaded'; it bounds how long the body is read, not how many bytes are buffered.
3. [lnwallet/chainfee/estimator.go:842–869](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwallet/chainfee/estimator.go#L842-L869)
   WebAPIEstimator.Start calls updateFeeEstimates() synchronously before returning, and feeUpdateManager repeats it every fee.min-update-timeout..fee.max-update-timeout (default 5-20 min). updateFeeEstimates (1004-1021) treats a fetch error as non-fatal and keeps the cache, i.e. the design intends a misbehaving fee service to degrade fee quality, not to end the process.
4. [chainreg/chainregistry.go:706–744](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/chainreg/chainregistry.go#L706-L744)
   A fee.url is mandatory for neutrino on mainnet (708-712) and, whenever set, replaces the backend estimator with a WebAPIEstimator over SparseConfFeeSource{URL: cfg.Fee.URL} (715-733); cc.FeeEstimator.Start() is then called inline (742-744), so the first unbounded fetch happens inside NewPartialChainControl.
5. [config\_builder.go:657–665](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/config_builder.go#L657-L665)
   NewPartialChainControl runs during lnd's startup sequence (after wallet unlock, before the wallet, server and listeners are built), so the fee fetch and its allocation occur before the node is operational; a process killed here never comes online, and the same happens again on every restart while the server keeps serving the payload.

## Impact
The lnd process is terminated by the OS (or, on larger hosts, forced into multi-GB allocations on every fetch). Because the first fetch is synchronous inside NewPartialChainControl, a node pointed at a hostile server cannot complete startup and stays offline across restarts, unable to sweep HTLCs or punish breaches. No confidentiality or integrity effect on data.

## Reproduction steps
1. The triggering input is the HTTP response body authored by whoever controls the server behind fee.url: the fee API operator or anyone who compromises that service, its DNS or its CDN (the documented default is a single shared third-party endpoint that every neutrino mainnet node must point at). lnd connects on startup and every 5-20 min; the server answers with Content-Encoding: gzip and a few MB of highly compressible JSON. Go's transport inflates it transparently and json.Decoder buffers the whole value, so the process allocates gigabytes within the 10 s window and is OOM-killed on constrained hosts. No lnd privileges or user interaction are needed; the precondition (attack requirement) is that the node's configured fee endpoint is under the attacker's control.

## Recommended fix
parseResponse/GetFeeInfo read and decode an HTTP body whose size is chosen by the remote fee server with no byte cap; the 10 s client timeout bounds wire time but not decompressed or buffered size, and transparent gzip decoding decouples the two. Fix criteria: The decoder must never buffer more than a small fixed number of decompressed bytes of body (e.g. wrap resp.Body in io.LimitReader/http.MaxBytesReader with a limit of a few KB-MB and treat reaching it as an error), and the transport should disable transparent compression or bound the inflated size. Verify: a response inflating beyond the limit is rejected with a logged error, the estimator keeps its previous cache, process memory stays flat, and startup proceeds instead of crashing.
