# Unexpected RBF close message tears down and recreates FSM, leaking spend registrations and goroutines per message

## Details
Reachable only when the victim runs with RBF cooperative close enabled: `--protocol.rbf-coop-close`, which `--protocol.simple-taproot-chans` (without taproot-overlay) auto-enables (server.go:732-736), and the remote peer also signals feature bit 61/161 (brontide.go:1133-1142, rbfCoopCloseAllowed). Under that condition `initRbfChanCloser` builds a protofsm state machine for every active non-aux channel at connect time (brontide.go:1509) and on new channels (brontide.go:5846), and registers it with the per-peer message router.

`RbfMsgMapper.MapMsg` (lnwallet/chancloser/rbf_coop_msg_mapper.go) maps every `shutdown`, `closing_complete` and `closing_sig` carrying the channel ID from that peer into an event irrespective of FSM state; the state transition functions return `ErrInvalidStateTransition` for any event not expected in the current state (`ChannelActive`, rbf_coop_transitions.go:376-381; likewise ShutdownPending :550-553, ChannelFlushing :676-679, ClosingNegotiation :1051-1052). protofsm treats any `ProcessEvent` error as fatal: `driveMachine` calls `ErrorReporter.ReportError` then `go s.Stop()` (protofsm/state_machine.go:693-707). `chanErrorReporter.ReportError` (brontide.go:4151-4197) sends an `lnwire.Error` to the peer and synchronously calls `initRbfChanCloser(lnChan)` to build a replacement machine.

Nothing releases what the dead machine acquired. (1) Its `RegisterSpend` InitEvent (brontide.go:4358-4364) created a chain-notifier spend registration for the funding outpoint; the protofsm goroutine that consumes it exits on `ctx.Done()` without calling `spendEvent.Cancel()` (state_machine.go:497-520), so the `SpendNtfn` and its three buffered channels stay in `TxNotifier.spendNotifications[request].ntfns` (chainntnfs/txnotifier.go:1098-1106) until the funding outpoint is spent or lnd restarts — `CancelSpend` (:1188-1216) is the only other removal. (2) `chanFlushEventSentinel` (brontide.go:4202-4268), spawned per init while a link exists (:4430), subscribed to the dead machine's state events via `RegisterStateEvents`; no further state is ever published and the EventReceiver's channels are never closed, so the sentinel blocks until `p.cg.Done()` (peer disconnect, brontide.go:1814), pinning its goroutine, the two `ConcurrentQueue` goroutines of its `EventReceiver` (fn/events.go:47-60, fn/conc_queue.go:52-56), and the whole dead machine object graph it references. Each re-init additionally performs `GetBestBlock`, `EstimateFeePerKW`, a `RegisterSpendNtfn` against the chain notifier, actor unregister/spawn, and two error log lines.

The attacker's message rate is bounded only by how fast `ReportError` completes (the FSM's one-slot event buffer back-pressures the peer's readHandler during the re-init), i.e. by the victim's own backend latency; the total leaked set is unbounded in the number of messages sent. Nothing in the peer layer rate-limits or disconnects for repeated protocol errors. Honest peers never hit this path, so an out-of-order close message has no legitimate reason to recreate the machine with fresh, never-released registrations.

Dependency assumption: for the bitcoind backend, `BitcoindNotifier.RegisterSpendNtfn` (chainntnfs/bitcoindnotify/bitcoind.go:719-751) calls `chainConn.NotifySpent` per registration; whether that is an RPC or a local filter update is behaviour of btcwallet v0.16.20-pre (go.mod) and is not asserted here.

## Evidence
1. [peer/brontide.go:4151–4196](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/peer/brontide.go#L4151-L4196)
   chanErrorReporter.ReportError: on every FSM error it sends an lnwire.Error and immediately calls initRbfChanCloser(lnChan) to build a brand-new state machine, turning each remote-triggered error into a full allocate-and-register cycle.
2. [protofsm/state\_machine.go:693–706](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/protofsm/state_machine.go#L693-L706)
   driveMachine treats any ProcessEvent error as fatal: ReportError then go s.Stop(). Stop cancels goroutine contexts but releases nothing registered on the machine's behalf.
3. [protofsm/state\_machine.go:485–526](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/protofsm/state_machine.go#L485-L526)
   RegisterSpend: the SpendEvent returned by RegisterSpendNtfn is only read until ctx.Done(); spendEvent.Cancel() is never called, so the chain notifier keeps the registration after the machine dies.
4. [lnwallet/chancloser/rbf\_coop\_transitions.go:376–381](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwallet/chancloser/rbf_coop_transitions.go#L376-L381)
   ChannelActive.ProcessEvent returns ErrInvalidStateTransition for any event other than SendShutdown/ShutdownReceived/SpendEvent, so a remote closing_complete or closing_sig sent before shutdown is a fatal error. ShutdownPending (:550-553), ChannelFlushing (:676-679) and ClosingNegotiation (:1051-1052) behave the same for out-of-order messages.
5. [peer/brontide.go:4358–4385](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/peer/brontide.go#L4358-L4385)
   initRbfChanCloser registers a RegisterSpend InitEvent on every construction, so every re-init adds another never-cancelled spend registration for the same funding outpoint; it also calls GetBestBlock, EstimateFeePerKW and the actor system each time.
6. [peer/brontide.go:4202–4267](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/peer/brontide.go#L4202-L4267)
   chanFlushEventSentinel (spawned per init at :4430 when a link exists) subscribes to the machine's state events and blocks until ChannelFlushing or peer exit; when the machine is torn down after an error, no event or close ever arrives, so the goroutine and its subscriber leak until disconnect.
7. [fn/events.go:47–59](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/fn/events.go#L47-L59)
   Each state subscriber creates two ConcurrentQueues, each starting its own goroutine (fn/conc_queue.go:52-56), so every leaked sentinel holds two more goroutines.
8. [chainntnfs/txnotifier.go:1098–1106](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/chainntnfs/txnotifier.go#L1098-L1106)
   RegisterSpend retains every registration in spendNotifications[request].ntfns until CancelSpend or the spend; BitcoindNotifier.RegisterSpendNtfn additionally issues NotifySpent/GetTxOut RPCs to the backend per call.
9. [peer/brontide.go:2361–2371](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/peer/brontide.go#L2361-L2371)
   Incoming messages are offered to the msgRouter first; RbfMsgMapper maps any Shutdown/ClosingComplete/ClosingSig for the channel to an FSM event regardless of state, so the remote can reach the fatal branch directly.

## Impact
No confidentiality or integrity impact. Availability HIGH: per message the node permanently retains a chain-notifier spend registration (until the channel is spent or restart) and three blocked goroutines plus the dead FSM's object graph (until the peer disconnects), performs several synchronous chain-backend/notifier operations and emits error logs. Growth is unbounded in attacker messages, bounded in rate only by the victim's own backend latency; sustained from one peer it drives heap and goroutine count toward OOM on a node whose liveness protects funds (HTLC timeouts, breach response).

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker is a channel counterparty whose connection negotiated option_simple_close; this requires the victim's non-default --protocol.rbf-coop-close (or --protocol.simple-taproot-chans) flag and an open channel with the attacker (AT:P). It repeatedly sends closing_complete (or closing_sig) for the channel without any shutdown. Each message is routed by the per-peer msgRouter to the FSM, hits ErrInvalidStateTransition in ChannelActive, and triggers ReportError's synchronous re-init. No rate limit, back-off or disconnect exists on this path; cycle time is bounded only by the victim's GetBestBlock/EstimateFeePerKW/RegisterSpendNtfn latency.

## Recommended fix
1. protofsm tears down the whole machine on any ProcessEvent error but never releases the resources it acquired on the daemon's behalf: the RegisterSpend/RegisterConf goroutines exit on context cancellation without calling the notifier's Cancel, and state subscribers are never closed or detached, so the peer's chanFlushEventSentinel blocks forever. Fix criteria: A stopped state machine must cancel every outstanding spend/confirmation registration it created and must close or detach its state-event subscribers so dependent goroutines exit. Verify: after N forced error/re-init cycles on one channel, TxNotifier holds no SpendNtfn attributable to dead machines and the goroutine count returns to its pre-attack baseline without a peer disconnect.
2. Unexpected remote close messages (closing_complete/closing_sig outside the state that expects them) are treated as fatal errors that destroy and immediately rebuild the FSM, giving the remote peer a cheap, unbounded allocate loop. Fix criteria: Out-of-order remote close messages must be rejected without destroying and rebuilding the machine (ignore, or send a single error/disconnect), and any ReportError re-initialisation path must be bounded or back off so a peer cannot force unbounded re-initialisations. Verify: a flood of closing_complete to an active channel produces at most a bounded number of FSM constructions and no growth in registrations or goroutines.

# Every AMP exit-hop HTLC loads full set history under registry lock; zero-cost partial sets inflate it

## Details
For every exit-hop HTLC, notifyExitHopHtlcLocked (holding the global InvoiceRegistry lock) first calls idb.LookupInvoice(invoiceRef) with the default modifier. For an AMP invoice the ref is InvoiceRefByAddr(payment_addr), and both stores interpret the default modifier as 'load all HTLCs of all sets ever paid to this invoice':
- channeldb: fetchInvoice -> fetchAmpSubInvoices(nil) -> forEachAMPInvoice walks a cursor over every invoiceNum||setID key and deserializes every HTLC set; the main invoice body also carries the whole AMPState map (one entry per set) which is deserialized here and re-serialized on every UpdateInvoice.
- sql_store: fetchInvoice -> fetchInvoiceData -> fetchAmpState(setID=nil, fetchHtlcs=true) runs FetchAMPSubInvoices and FetchAMPSubInvoiceHTLCs with set_id IS NULL (all rows) plus GetInvoiceHTLCCustomRecords for all HTLCs, then executes a nested loop over every set x every HTLC (sql_store.go:709-733) to recompute per-set totals: O(sets * htlcs).

The history is attacker-inflatable at zero cost. updateMpp accepts a partial AMP HTLC (amount < total_msat) into any fresh sender-chosen set_id (resultPartialAccepted); acceptHtlcsAmp creates a new AMPState entry and an AMP HTLC record for it. After HtlcHoldDuration (120 s) the registry auto-releases it via cancelSingleHtlc, which fails the HTLC back to the sender with FailMPPTimeout (funds returned) but only flips the entry/record to Canceled; nothing ever removes canceled sets or their HTLC records from the invoice. The sender needs only the invoice's payment_addr, which is public in a static (reusable) AMP invoice, or, with --accept-amp, the attacker creates its own spontaneous AMP invoice and inflates that.

After n such HTLCs, every further HTLC to that invoice (from the attacker or anyone else) costs O(n) deserialization in the kv store or O(n^2) in the SQL store, executed while i.Lock() is held, so all exit-hop HTLC processing for every invoice on the node, as well as SettleHodlInvoice/CancelInvoice RPCs, waits behind it. With n in the tens of thousands (hours of HTLC traffic) the SQL path spends seconds to minutes per HTLC; sustained, this stalls invoice settlement node-wide, causing payments to the node to fail or time out and pushing held HTLCs toward the incoming broadcast window. The maintainers already avoided this for the UpdateInvoice call by passing a setID hint (only that set is loaded), but the preceding LookupInvoice ignores the hint and reads everything; the loaded result is used only for replay detection and for the (optional) interceptor's view.

## Evidence
1. [invoices/invoiceregistry.go:1028–1034](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/invoiceregistry.go#L1028-L1034)
   Per-HTLC LookupInvoice with ctx.invoiceRef() (DefaultModifier, no set-ID scope) for every exit-hop HTLC; runs inside notifyExitHopHtlcLocked while the registry RWMutex taken at lines 972-976 is held, so AddInvoice, SettleHodlInvoice, cancelInvoiceImpl and every other link's exit-hop processing wait behind it. The fix belongs here: scope the lookup to the HTLC's own set.
2. [invoices/update.go:42–57](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/update.go#L42-L57)
   For an AMP HTLC (amp != nil && mpp != nil) invoiceRef() returns InvoiceRefByAddr(payAddr) with the default modifier; the set ID the HTLC carries is not placed on the ref, so both stores load every set.
3. [channeldb/invoices.go:355–382](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/channeldb/invoices.go#L355-L382)
   kv LookupInvoice: for a pay-addr ref with DefaultModifier neither modifier case matches, setID stays nil and fetchInvoice is called with []*SetID{nil}, which selects the full-history path.
4. [channeldb/invoices.go:1498–1566](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/channeldb/invoices.go#L1498-L1566)
   fetchAmpSubInvoices with a nil set ID falls through to forEachAMPInvoice, which cursors over every invoiceNum||setID key of the invoice and deserializes every HTLC set: O(total HTLCs ever recorded). deserializeInvoice additionally decodes the AMPState map (tlv type 15) with one entry per set, which serializeAndStoreInvoice (line 1054) rewrites on every update.
5. [invoices/sql\_store.go:536–734](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/sql_store.go#L536-L734)
   SQL fetchAmpState with setID=nil: FetchAMPSubInvoices, GetInvoiceHTLCCustomRecords and FetchAMPSubInvoiceHTLCs all run unfiltered (sqlc.narg set_id IS NULL), then lines 709-733 loop every set x every HTLC to recompute per-set totals: O(sets * htlcs) per lookup.
6. [invoices/update.go:305–318](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/update.go#L305-L318)
   A partial AMP HTLC (newSetTotal < totalAmt) under any fresh sender-chosen set_id is recorded via AddHTLCsUpdate and returned as resultPartialAccepted; the only authorisation is the payment_addr comparison at line 262, and no cap on the number of sets or HTLCs per invoice exists anywhere in the package.
7. [invoices/invoiceregistry.go:1317–1320](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/invoiceregistry.go#L1317-L1320)
   An accepted HTLC on a still-open invoice gets autoRelease=true, so NotifyExitHopHtlc (lines 990-1003) starts a HtlcHoldDuration (120 s, server.go:765) timer that refunds the attacker's HTLC.
8. [invoices/invoiceregistry.go:663–760](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/invoiceregistry.go#L663-L760)
   cancelSingleHtlc marks the timed-out HTLC Canceled (CancelHTLCsUpdate) and fails it back to the sender; the set's AMPState entry and HTLC record remain on the invoice.
9. [invoices/update\_invoice.go:16–68](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/update_invoice.go#L16-L68)
   acceptHtlcsAmp creates an AMPState entry per new set; cancelHtlcsAmp only flips it to Canceled. No code path deletes a set's state or HTLC records, so each attacker set is permanent for the invoice's lifetime (AMP default expiry 30 days, lnrpc/invoicesrpc/addinvoice.go:39).

## Impact
Availability: every exit-hop HTLC, AddInvoice, SettleHodlInvoice and CancelInvoice serialises behind the registry RWMutex, so attacker-inflated lookups stall settlement of all invoices node-wide and block the affected links' message processing; sustained traffic to the inflated invoice keeps the lock saturated, failing or timing out payments to the node and pushing held HTLCs toward their CLTV deadlines. Persistent storage also grows without bound. No confidentiality or integrity impact.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker is any Lightning sender able to route an HTLC to the victim who holds one of its static AMP invoices (payment_addr is in the BOLT11 string), or, if the victim runs --accept-amp, any sender at all (processAMP creates the invoice from the sender's own payment_addr). It sends partial AMP HTLCs, each with a distinct set_id and mpp total_msat >= invoice value; updateMpp records each one, the 120 s hold timer refunds it, and the set record persists. The link calls NotifyExitHopHtlc synchronously (htlcswitch/link.go:3522) and the registry lock is global, so after n sets every HTLC to that invoice costs O(n) (bbolt) or O(n^2) (native SQL) work with all invoice processing blocked. Cost to the attacker is HTLC slots and a 120 s liquidity lock per set; no credentials, no user interaction. Requires the victim to have an open AMP invoice or accept-amp enabled (AT:P).

## Recommended fix
1. The pre-update LookupInvoice in notifyExitHopHtlcLocked loads the complete multi-set history of an AMP invoice on every HTLC, and the SQL fetch additionally performs a sets x HTLCs nested loop, while holding the registry-wide lock. Fix criteria: Per-HTLC work for an AMP invoice must be bounded by the size of the HTLC's own set (e.g. look up with the set-ID hint / HtlcSetOnly modifier, and compute per-set totals in O(htlcs)). Verify that the time to process an HTLC to an AMP invoice does not grow with the number of other sets on that invoice.
2. Partial AMP sets that time out leave permanent AMPState entries and HTLC records on the invoice, so an unauthenticated sender can grow the invoice's history without bound at no cost. Fix criteria: Canceled/timed-out AMP sets must not accumulate indefinitely on a live invoice (prune them on cancellation or cap/evict canceled set state). Verify that after N partial sets are auto-released the invoice's stored set count and lookup cost do not grow by N.

# EstimateRouteFee lets offchain:read macaroons originate real HTLC probe payments

## Details
The Router service classifies `EstimateRouteFee` as a read operation (`offchain:read`, lnrpc/routerrpc/router_server.go:107-110), but when the request carries a `payment_request` the handler (`probePaymentRequestWithSender` -> `sendProbePayment` -> `SendPaymentV2`) originates one or more genuine Lightning payments: it opens a payment in the payments DB (`PreparePayment`/`InitPayment`), runs pathfinding, and dispatches HTLCs across the node's channels (`SendPaymentAsync` with a background context). Every economically relevant parameter of that payment is taken from the caller-supplied invoice: destination node, amount (`AmtMsat = invoice amount`; `lnrpc.UnmarshallAmt` only rejects negatives, there is no upper bound), route hints (which steer the probe through channels the attacker names), final CLTV delta (up to `MaxTotalTimelock`, default 2016 blocks), and up to three extra LSP probes whose amounts are inflated by attacker-chosen hop fees. The fee limit is hard-coded to 1 BTC. The only safeguard is a random payment hash, which prevents the probe from settling but does nothing to prevent the HTLC from being *held*: the probe `Timeout` only governs `checkContext` in routing/payment_lifecycle.go:364-405, which marks the payment failed and stops new attempts while an already-dispatched HTLC remains in flight until the destination fails it or it expires.

A holder of readonly.macaroon (or any macaroon with offchain:read; such credentials are routinely handed to dashboards, monitoring agents and third-party services) can therefore:
- make the node send outgoing HTLCs of arbitrary size to a node the attacker controls (reachable via attacker-supplied route hints or a direct channel), which holds them until just before expiry (up to ~2 weeks), repeating the call to exhaust outbound liquidity and the HTLC slots of every channel - free jamming of the victim's own channels from the inside, with no cost to the attacker;
- force on-chain resolution/force-close of the victim's channel if the attacker is the direct peer and simply never fails the HTLC;
- persist an unbounded number of payment records (and mission-control results) in the victim's databases that the read-only caller cannot delete;
- do all of this while `SendPaymentV2`/`SendToRouteV2` remain correctly protected by offchain:write, i.e. the permission model is bypassed through a sibling method.

This contradicts both the threat model's RPC boundary ("the macaroon permission tables ... are all that separates a limited macaroon from full control") and the project's own documentation, which describes readonly.macaroon as permitting "only methods that don't change the state of lnd" (docs/macaroons.md:55-57): the table itself places an HTLC-originating, state-persisting operation at read level. The `dest`+`amt_sat` variant (`probeDestination`) is a pure local graph query and is not affected.

## Evidence
1. [lnrpc/routerrpc/router\_server.go:107–109](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnrpc/routerrpc/router_server.go#L107-L109)
   macPermissions gates /routerrpc.Router/EstimateRouteFee behind offchain:read only, the same level as TrackPaymentV2/QueryMissionControl, while SendPaymentV2 and SendToRouteV2 (lines 95-102) require offchain:write. This is the entry the fix must change.
2. [lnrpc/routerrpc/router\_server.go:530–587](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnrpc/routerrpc/router_server.go#L530-L587)
   probePaymentRequestWithSender decodes the caller-supplied invoice and builds a SendPaymentRequest whose Dest, AmtMsat (invoice amount, no upper bound: lnrpc.UnmarshallAmt only rejects negatives), FinalCltvDelta, DestFeatures, PaymentAddr and RouteHints all come from the caller's invoice, with FeeLimitSat fixed at routeFeeLimitSat (1 BTC) and a random payment hash; it then dispatches it as a real payment.
3. [lnrpc/routerrpc/router\_server.go:975–995](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnrpc/routerrpc/router_server.go#L975-L995)
   sendProbePayment calls s.SendPaymentV2 directly from inside the EstimateRouteFee handler, so the offchain:write check that protects SendPaymentV2 on the RPC surface is bypassed; the probe is indistinguishable from an operator-initiated payment for the router and switch.
4. [lnrpc/routerrpc/router\_server.go:349–409](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnrpc/routerrpc/router_server.go#L349-L409)
   SendPaymentV2 calls Router.PreparePayment (persists a new payment record) and Router.SendPaymentAsync with context.Background() (the probe request never sets Cancelable); the resulting HTLC is dispatched to the network and lives until the destination resolves it, independent of the RPC call.
5. [routing/payment\_lifecycle.go:364–404](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/payment_lifecycle.go#L364-L404)
   checkContext handles the probe timeout: it calls Control.FailPayment but, as the comment states, the payment stays StatusInflight while HTLCs are outstanding and only prevents new attempts. An HTLC already in flight cannot be withdrawn by the sender; it is held until the destination fails or it expires on-chain.
6. [lnrpc/routerrpc/router\_server.go:615–676](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnrpc/routerrpc/router_server.go#L615-L676)
   In the LSP branch up to MaxLspsToProbe (3) further probe payments are sent per call, each with its own payment hash and with the amount increased by caller-chosen hop fees, so one read-only request can lock several outgoing HTLCs.
7. [rpcserver.go:105–113](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/rpcserver.go#L105-L113)
   readPermissions, baked into readonly.macaroon, includes offchain:read, so the stock read-only credential suffices.
8. [routing/router.go:1035–1037](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/router.go#L1035-L1037)
   PreparePayment calls Control.InitPayment, persisting each probe as a payment in the payments DB; the read-only caller thereby writes durable state it cannot remove.

## Impact
Funds are not stolen (random hash cannot settle), but the node's core function is denied: outbound liquidity and HTLC slots on all channels can be locked for up to the maximum CLTV at zero cost, and a direct-peer attacker can force the victim on-chain. Integrity is affected at low level: durable payment DB records and mission-control state are written by a credential meant to be read-only. No confidentiality impact beyond what offchain:read already grants.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker: RPC client holding readonly.macaroon or any offchain:read macaroon, reaching gRPC 10009 or REST 8080 (/v2/router/route/estimatefee). They craft a BOLT11 invoice to a node they control (optionally with route hints and a large final CLTV), submit it in EstimateRouteFee, and have their node hold the resulting HTLC; repeat concurrently with minimal invoice amounts to fill HTLC slots or with large amounts to drain liquidity. No race, no user interaction, works against default configuration.

## Recommended fix
1. An operation that originates payments (persists payment state and dispatches HTLCs) is placed under the offchain:read permission, so the macaroon permission table does not enforce the read/write boundary for this method. Fix criteria: Any EstimateRouteFee path that sends a probe payment must require the same authority as SendPaymentV2 (offchain:write), or probing must be split into a separately-gated method so that an offchain:read-only macaroon can never cause an HTLC to be dispatched or a payment record to be created. Verify that a readonly.macaroon call with a payment_request is rejected before any payment is initialised.
2. Probe parameters (amount, CLTV, hints, up to four probes per call) are taken verbatim from the caller's invoice with no node-side bounds, so even an authorised probe can lock arbitrary liquidity for the maximum timelock. Fix criteria: Probe payments should be bounded by node policy (maximum probe amount / CLTV / concurrent probes) independent of the invoice contents, so that a single request cannot lock a channel's full capacity or HTLC slots for the maximum timelock. Verify that invoices exceeding those bounds are refused or clamped.

# query_short_channel_ids reply materialises every announcement before sending; per-peer memory unbounded

## Details
Any peer that completes the brontide handshake and advertises gossip_queries in its init message, including one with no channel occupying one of the 100 default restricted inbound slots, gets a GossipSyncer (peer/brontide.go:1093-1112) and can send BOLT 7 `query_short_channel_ids`. The gossiper dispatches it straight to that syncer (gossiper.go:898-924) and `replyShortChanIDs` (syncer.go:1553) answers it.

The handler accepts the full decoded SCID list with no upper bound of its own. The only limit is lnwire's decode cap of 100,000 SCIDs, and with the spec-permitted zlib encoding a single 65 KiB wire message names on the order of 10^4 real public channels (the public SCID set is learnable by the same attacker via `query_channel_range`). `ChanSeries.FetchChanAnns` then calls `FetchChanInfos`, which deserialises for every existing channel the edge info with its 4-signature proof, both channel policies and both complete node records (addresses, feature maps, alias, extra TLV; shared hub nodes are re-materialised once per channel), and builds for each a `ChannelAnnouncement1`, up to two `ChannelUpdate1` and node announcements into a single `[]lnwire.Message` before anything is sent. Only after the whole slice exists does the syncer write it one message at a time through `sendToPeerSync`, which blocks on the 50 KiB/s per-peer limiter, the 1000 KiB/s global limiter and the synchronous wire write. Serialised, a 15k-channel reply is roughly 10-12 MB (~430 B per announcement, ~140 B per update, plus node announcements), so the slice, several tens of MB of Go heap objects, stays resident for ~4 minutes per query at the per-peer rate and proportionally longer when many peers share the global budget. `replyHandler` is strictly serial with a 50-entry `queryMsgs` buffer plus 50 more in the peer's discStream, so one peer can pipeline ~100 such queries (each retaining its decoded SCID slice at 12 B/SCID) and keep its syncer busy for hours from a single burst; there is no per-peer or node-wide cap on in-flight materialised replies. `ApplyGossipFilter` in the same file shows the maintainers' intended pattern for this class of work: a pull-based iterator (`UpdatesInHorizon`, 1000-row batches) gated by the shared 5-slot `syncerSema`; `replyShortChanIDs` has neither. lnd's own syncer, by contrast, never asks a peer for more than 500 SCIDs per query (`requestBatchSize`, syncer.go:190), so the shape this handler accepts is 30-100x beyond the sanctioned request.

Result: a ~64 KiB request yields tens of MB of resident memory for minutes, repeatable and parallel across all connected peers. With the default 100 restricted inbound slots an unauthenticated attacker using 100 identities can hold multiple GB resident on the target (plus ~15k full edge deserialisations per query of CPU), enough to OOM-kill nodes on small hosts; the slot limit bounds the multiplier, not the per-connection cost. Loss of the daemon means unattended HTLC deadlines and breach windows.

Assumptions: zlib ratios are from a stdlib calculation on synthetic sorted SCID sets (0.3-0.6 of raw size); object sizes are estimates from the model structs; limiter semantics are those of golang.org/x/time v0.3.0 (ReserveN then sleep for Delay). This record answers ledger lead lead-syncer-1553-19d9.

## Evidence
1. [discovery/syncer.go:1571–1607](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/syncer.go#L1571-L1607)
   replyShortChanIDs only rejects an empty list; it passes the peer's entire decoded SCID list to FetchChanAnns, receives one []lnwire.Message holding every announcement, and only then streams it one message at a time through sendToPeerSync (blocking on the per-peer and global byte-rate limiters and on the synchronous wire write). The whole slice stays live until the last message is written. No cap on len(query.ShortChanIDs) exists here or anywhere upstream of lnwire's 100,000 decode cap.
2. [discovery/chan\_series.go:264–354](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/chan_series.go#L264-L354)
   FetchChanAnns fetches every requested channel via FetchChanInfos, then builds a ChannelAnnouncement1, up to two ChannelUpdate1 and the node announcements for all of them into one slice (preallocated len(channels)*3) before returning; nothing is yielded incrementally.
3. [graph/db/kv\_store.go:3082–3173](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/kv_store.go#L3082-L3173)
   fetchChanInfos deserialises, for every requested SCID that exists, the ChannelEdgeInfo (incl. the 4-signature auth proof), both policies and both full models.Node records (addresses, features, extra data) and appends all of them to one slice; hub nodes shared by many channels are re-deserialised once per channel. Unknown SCIDs cost one bucket Get and are skipped.
4. [graph/db/sql\_store.go:3031–3097](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/sql_store.go#L3031-L3097)
   The SQL backend has the same shape: all channel rows are collected, batchBuildChannelEdges materialises every edge, and the whole result is returned at once.
5. [lnwire/query\_short\_chan\_ids.go:206–289](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwire/query_short_chan_ids.go#L206-L289)
   With EncodingSortedZlib (a spec-permitted encoding the decoder accepts from any peer) a single <=65,535-byte message decompresses to up to maxDecodedShortChanIDs=100,000 sorted SCIDs; a sorted real-channel SCID set fits on the order of 10^4 real public channels in one message. The cap bounds decoded SCIDs, not the reply they select.
6. [discovery/syncer.go:832–858](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/syncer.go#L832-L858)
   replyHandler is one goroutine per peer draining a 50-deep queryMsgs buffer, with no node-wide concurrency limit; contrast ApplyGossipFilter (syncer.go:1641-1653), which gates its backlog send behind the shared 5-slot syncerSema and streams via a pull iterator. Every connected peer can hold a fully materialised reply simultaneously.
7. [discovery/sync\_manager.go:763–771](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/sync_manager.go#L763-L771)
   maybeRateLimitMsg reserves the serialized size of each reply message against the limiter and sleeps for the resulting delay before the message is handed to the peer; with sendToPeerSync's sync=true the syncer additionally blocks until the peer's writeHandler has written the message (peer/brontide.go:5190-5244). The materialised slice is therefore retained for the whole drain.
8. [discovery/sync\_manager.go:39–49](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/sync_manager.go#L39-L49)
   Outgoing gossip is limited to 50 KiB/s per peer (burst 100 KiB, syncer.go:481-486) and 1000 KiB/s globally (burst 2000 KiB). These limits slow the drain of the materialised slice, so each reply's allocation is retained for minutes, and proportionally longer when many peers share the global budget.
9. [peer/brontide.go:1090–1112](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/peer/brontide.go#L1090-L1112)
   initGossipSync registers a GossipSyncer (via InitSyncState) for any connected peer whose init message advertises gossip_queries, whether or not it has a channel; sync_manager.go:1091-1095 returns inactive (passive) syncers from GossipSyncer(), so every such peer has a live replyHandler.
10. [discovery/gossiper.go:898–923](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/gossiper.go#L898-L923)
   ProcessRemoteAnnouncement dispatches QueryShortChanIDs straight to the peer's syncer via ProcessQueryMsg before the main processing loop; the gossiper's ban logic (isBanned/ShouldDisconnect, gossiper.go:3904-3934) only scores invalid announcements and is not consulted for queries.

## Impact
Per connection tens of MB resident for minutes plus a full deserialisation of every requested channel; across the 100 default restricted inbound slots this reaches multiple GB and sustained DB/CPU load, sufficient to OOM-kill or render unresponsive a Lightning node on typical small hosts. No confidentiality or integrity effect; availability of the node, and hence its ability to meet HTLC and breach deadlines, is lost while the attack runs or after the process is killed.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker connects as an ordinary inbound peer (no channel, no credentials) advertising gossip_queries, using any number of node identities up to the restricted-slot limit, learns the public SCID set via query_channel_range, then sends zlib query_short_channel_ids messages naming on the order of 10^4 real channels, optionally pipelining ~100 per connection. Each query deterministically materialises the full reply in memory and holds it for minutes while the rate limiters drain it. Works against the default configuration; no ban, auth or cap stands in the way.

## Recommended fix
1. replyShortChanIDs/FetchChanAnns build the entire reply for an attacker-sized SCID list in memory before sending, so retained memory per query is proportional to the number of real channels the peer names rather than to anything the responder controls. Fix criteria: Replies to query_short_channel_ids must be produced incrementally (a bounded batch of SCIDs fetched and sent at a time, as UpdatesInHorizon already does) and/or the number of SCIDs accepted per query must be capped to a value whose full reply is small; a 100k-SCID zlib query must not raise resident memory by more than a small constant regardless of graph size. Verify by sending a query naming every public SCID and observing heap growth bounded to one batch.
2. replyHandler work is unbounded across peers: every connected syncer may hold a materialised query_short_channel_ids reply concurrently, unlike ApplyGossipFilter which is gated by syncerSema. Fix criteria: Concurrent expensive query replies must be limited node-wide, e.g. via the same shared semaphore, so total in-flight reply memory and DB fetch concurrency is bounded independent of peer count; verify that N malicious peers cannot drive more than the configured number of concurrent FetchChanAnns calls.

# Watchtower lookout permanently skips a block after transient fetch/processing failure, missing breaches in it

## Details
The tower's lookout (watchtower/lookout/lookout.go) is the only component that detects a client's revoked commitment on chain and publishes the justice transaction; a tower client is offline by assumption and relies on the tower never missing a block. watchBlocks() fetches every block epoch via fetchBlockWithRetries(), which returns an error after cfg.MaxNumRetries failed BlockFetcher.GetBlock calls (standalone.go:69-71 sets MinBackoff 1s, MaxBackoff 1m, MaxNumRetries 5, i.e. six attempts over ~31 s of lookout back-off). On that error watchBlocks only logs and `continue`s (lookout.go:186-192); a processEpoch error such as a QueryMatches DB failure is likewise only logged (196-200). No record of the unprocessed height is kept. When the next epoch is processed successfully, processEpoch ends with DB.SetLookoutTip(epoch) (309), persisting a single (hash,height) tip (watchtower/wtdb/tower_db.go:484-493) that lies beyond the skipped block. Lookout.Start() resumes from that tip (83-99) and the notifier's historical dispatch delivers only heights startingHeight+1.. (chainntnfs/interface.go:557-561), so the skipped block is never scanned in this run or any later one.

If the skipped block confirms a revoked commitment for which a client uploaded a blob, the hint is never queried, no justice transaction is built, and the breaching counterparty's to_local output matures after its CSV delay: the client loses its channel balance and nobody is alerted beyond an error line in the tower log.

In production (lnd.go:558-572, when watchtower.active is set) BlockFetcher is activeChainControl.ChainIO, i.e. btcwallet's GetBlock (lnwallet/btcwallet/blockchain.go:136-149) over the configured backend. Triggering condition: GetBlock fails for the duration of the retry budget. With bitcoind/btcd this is a backend restart, reindex, RPC overload (e.g. 'Work queue depth exceeded') or connectivity blip; with neutrino the block is served by untrusted P2P peers, and GetBlock errors when none of the connected peers serves it within neutrino's bounded retries (eclipse-level control). The breaching counterparty does not control the outage in a bitcoind deployment, so the attack is opportunistic — but the window is per block, a long outage spanning the breach block suffices, and the loss is silent and permanent. Dependency assumptions: btcd rpcclient (v0.25.1-pre) in HTTP POST mode retries a failed connection itself (lengthening but not removing the bounded window) and returns RPC errors immediately; neutrino v0.17.1 GetBlock returns an error rather than blocking when no peer serves the block.

The design elsewhere intends full coverage: the tip is persisted and EpochRegistrar must support historical dispatch from it (lookout/interface.go:48-58) precisely so that no block is skipped across restarts. The `continue` paths fail open and break that invariant.

## Evidence
1. [watchtower/lookout/lookout.go:186–191](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/lookout/lookout.go#L186-L191)
   watchBlocks: when fetchBlockWithRetries returns an error the epoch is only logged and the loop `continue`s to the next epoch. The block's transactions are never hashed to hints or queried, and nothing records that this height was skipped. This is the code the fix must change.
2. [watchtower/lookout/lookout.go:304–309](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/lookout/lookout.go#L304-L309)
   processEpoch for the next successfully fetched block ends with SetLookoutTip(epoch), persisting a tip past the skipped height; the tip carries no notion of a gap.
3. [watchtower/lookout/lookout.go:128–165](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/lookout/lookout.go#L128-L165)
   fetchBlockWithRetries gives up after MaxNumRetries attempts (attempt > MaxNumRetries) and returns an error instead of blocking until the block is available.
4. [watchtower/standalone.go:64–71](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/standalone.go#L64-L71)
   The shipped tower configures MinBackoff=1s, MaxBackoff=1m, MaxNumRetries=5: six failed GetBlock calls spanning ~1+2+4+8+16 = 31 s of lookout back-off are enough to abandon a block.
5. [watchtower/lookout/lookout.go:196–199](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/lookout/lookout.go#L196-L199)
   A processEpoch error (e.g. QueryMatches DB error, returned at 235-238 before SetLookoutTip) is likewise only logged; the block is not retried and the next block advances the tip past it.
6. [watchtower/lookout/lookout.go:83–98](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/lookout/lookout.go#L83-L98)
   Start resumes block-epoch delivery from the stored tip, so after a restart the skipped block (below the tip) is never examined.
7. [chainntnfs/interface.go:557–561](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/chainntnfs/interface.go#L557-L561)
   GetClientMissedBlocks, used by every production notifier for historical dispatch, delivers only heights startingHeight+1 .. tip, so a height at or below the persisted lookout tip is never re-delivered.
8. [watchtower/wtdb/tower\_db.go:484–493](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtdb/tower_db.go#L484-L493)
   SetLookoutTip overwrites a single (hash,height) record; there is no store of unprocessed heights that a recovery path could consult.
9. [lnd.go:558–572](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnd.go#L558-L572)
   Production wiring when watchtower.active is set: BlockFetcher is activeChainControl.ChainIO (btcwallet GetBlock over bitcoind/btcd/neutrino) and EpochRegistrar is the ChainNotifier, so backend fetch failures reach the skip path in the release binary.

## Impact
The tower node (lnd with watchtower.active) loses no funds or confidentiality of its own; its persisted lookout tip comes to misrepresent its coverage (it records a height beyond a block it never scanned), a limited integrity loss on the tower's own state, and its monitoring stays available. Subsequent-system impact: The tower's client is a separate node that delegated breach detection to this tower. A breach in the skipped block is never punished, so the counterparty's revoked state settles and the client loses its channel balance — an unauthorized, irreversible transfer of the client's funds. No confidentiality or availability impact on the client.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker is a channel counterparty of any tower client — remote and unauthenticated with respect to the tower. They broadcast a revoked commitment; if the tower's BlockFetcher.GetBlock fails for the whole retry budget on the confirming block (bitcoind/btcd restart, reindex or RPC overload; under neutrino, no connected peer serving the block), the lookout logs, continues, and the next block advances the persisted tip past the gap. No privileges or user interaction. The attack requires the backend-failure condition to coincide with the breach block, which the attacker does not control in a bitcoind deployment and can only force under neutrino with eclipse-level control of the tower's peers (AT:PRESENT).

## Recommended fix
1. watchBlocks treats a failed block fetch or a failed processEpoch as a per-block warning and advances to later epochs, after which the persisted lookout tip moves past the unprocessed height. The invariant that every block between the persisted tip and the chain tip has been scanned is violated, and the failure is silent. Fix criteria: The lookout must never persist a tip beyond a block that has not been successfully scanned: either keep retrying the fetch/processing (with capped back-off, cancellable only on shutdown) until the block is processed, or persist the unprocessed height(s) and re-scan them before advancing the tip. Verify: make GetBlock fail for one block containing a stored hint for longer than the retry budget, let later blocks arrive, then restore the backend (and/or restart) and confirm the justice transaction for that block is still published.
2. A skipped block produces only an error log line; neither the tower operator nor the client has any signal that coverage was lost. Fix criteria: Surface persistent fetch/processing failure as an operator-visible condition (e.g. health check failure or tower status) rather than a debug/error log, so that an outage spanning a block cannot pass unnoticed.

# Funding timeout while peer offline leaves stale pending count granting permanent unrestricted access

## Details
The access manager tracks, per remote pubkey, how many pending-open channels exist (`peerChanInfo[pub].PendingOpenCount`); a non-zero count grants `peerStatusTemporary`, which bypasses both the restricted-slot limit (`num-restricted-slots`, default 100) and the gossip ban check in `assignPeerPerms` (accessman.go:140-164, early return at 143-145), and also makes `checkAcceptIncomingConn` (accessman.go:506-514) accept unconditionally. docs/gossip_rate_limiting.md:90-99 documents temporary status as belonging to peers *currently* opening a channel.

The count is incremented in `newPendingOpenChan` while the peer is connected (restricted -> temporary, accessman.go:245-268) and is supposed to be decremented in `newPendingCloseChan` when the funding manager gives up on the channel. But `newPendingCloseChan` (accessman.go:298-304) first requires a `peerScores` entry, which only exists while the peer is connected, and returns `ErrNoPeerScore` without modifying `peerChanInfo` otherwise. `removePeerAccess` (accessman.go:655-659), run on disconnect, intentionally keeps the `peerChanInfo` record while `PendingOpenCount != 0`. The funding timeout is purely block-height driven (`waitForTimeout`, funding/manager.go:3300-3322: 2016 blocks after BroadcastHeight, no peer-online condition) and `fundingTimeout` (funding/manager.go:2917-2946) closes the channel in the DB and calls `NotifyFundingTimeout` -> `notifyFundingTimeoutPeerEvent` (server.go:4457-4478), which only logs the error. The result is a record `{HasOpenOrClosedChan:false, PendingOpenCount:1}` for a channel that no longer exists.

An anonymous peer can create this state at no on-chain cost: connect (taking a restricted slot), run open_channel/accept_channel/funding_created with a fabricated funding outpoint — as fundee lnd persists the pending channel on a valid commitment signature alone (`CompleteReservationSingle`, funding/manager.go:2527-2533, then `NotifyPendingOpenChannelEvent` at 2664) and never sees the funding tx — then disconnect and wait ~2 weeks. From then until the daemon restarts (the maps are rebuilt from the DB only in `newAccessMan`, and `FetchPermAndTempPeers` excludes funding-cancelled channels), that key is admitted by the listener filter and by `assignPeerPerms` as Temporary: it never consumes a restricted slot, is admitted when all slots are full, and is admitted even after the gossiper has banned it (ban enforcement at connect time only applies to restricted keys; `handleBadPeer` disconnects it, but it simply reconnects). The accumulation rate is bounded by the funding manager's limits — `MaxPendingChannels` (default 1 per key) and the global `pendingChansLimit` of 50 pending channels (funding/manager.go:109, 1496-1505) — so roughly 50 fresh keys per 2016-block window can be converted to permanently privileged identities, growing without bound over the process lifetime and eroding the inbound connection ceiling and the gossip ban for those keys.

The same early return affects `newOpenChan` when a channel confirms while the peer is offline (peer stays Temporary instead of Protected), which is benign, and the outbound-upgrade path (`addPeerAccess` writes a `{false,0}` record) is cleaned by `removePeerAccess`, so the pending-count path is the one that leaks.

## Evidence
1. [accessman.go:286–304](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/accessman.go#L286-L304)
   newPendingCloseChan looks the peer up in peerScores first and returns ErrNoPeerScore without touching peerChanInfo when the peer is not currently connected (298-304). The pending-open count for the peer is therefore never decremented when the funding timeout fires while the peer is offline. This is the code the fix must change.
2. [accessman.go:614–663](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/accessman.go#L614-L663)
   removePeerAccess (run on disconnect via server.go:5138) deletes the peerScores entry but deliberately keeps the peerChanInfo entry while PendingOpenCount != 0 (655-659). Combined with the early return above, the {HasOpenOrClosedChan:false, PendingOpenCount:1} record outlives the channel it describes.
3. [accessman.go:84–189](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/accessman.go#L84-L189)
   hasPeer consults peerChanInfo first: a stale PendingOpenCount != 0 yields peerStatusTemporary (103-109), which assignPeerPerms returns at 143-145 before the ban check (shouldDisconnect, 150-164) and before the restricted-slot check (172-187).
4. [accessman.go:492–544](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/accessman.go#L492-L544)
   checkAcceptIncomingConn (the brontide listener filter, server.go:1944) also accepts any key found in peerChanInfo (506-514), so the listener admits the key regardless of slot availability.
5. [server.go:4457–4478](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/server.go#L4457-L4478)
   notifyFundingTimeoutPeerEvent is the only caller of newPendingCloseChan; it logs ErrNoPeerScore and continues, so the inconsistency is silently kept for the process lifetime (the maps are rebuilt from the DB only in newAccessMan at startup).
6. [funding/manager.go:3273–3322](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/funding/manager.go#L3273-L3322)
   waitForTimeout is driven solely by block epochs: it fires when height >= BroadcastHeight + 2016 (DefaultMaxWaitNumBlocksFundingConf), with no condition on the peer being connected; the goroutine is spawned from handleFundingCreated (2686) and re-spawned from start() for every pending channel after a restart.
7. [funding/manager.go:2917–2946](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/funding/manager.go#L2917-L2946)
   fundingTimeout closes the channel in the DB (CloseChannel, FundingCanceled) and calls NotifyFundingTimeout(c.FundingOutpoint, c.IdentityPub), which is wired to server.notifyFundingTimeoutPeerEvent (server.go:1734).
8. [funding/manager.go:2527–2533](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/funding/manager.go#L2527-L2533)
   As fundee, lnd persists the pending channel (IsPending) on funding_created once the remote commitment signature verifies; the funding outpoint is never checked on-chain at this point, so the attacker needs no real funds. NotifyPendingOpenChannelEvent (2664) then upgrades the connected peer to Temporary. MaxPendingChannels (default 1) and pendingChansLimit (50, line 109 / 1496-1505) bound the rate at which keys can be converted.

## Impact
The restricted-slot and ban controls are DoS mitigations for the P2P boundary; the defect lets an attacker-chosen set of keys bypass them indefinitely, so the integrity of the access-control state is affected (Low). It does not by itself exhaust resources or touch funds; availability impact arises only indirectly through the extra always-admitted connections, rated None here to avoid double counting.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker: any Internet host that can complete a brontide handshake. It opens one unfunded inbound channel per throw-away key (default config accepts), disconnects, and waits for the 2016-block funding timeout. No race, no privileges, no user interaction, default configuration. After the timeout each such key has permanent (until restart) unrestricted inbound admission.

## Recommended fix
newPendingCloseChan gates the peerChanInfo update on a live connection (peerScores entry), so a channel-lifecycle event delivered while the peer is offline leaves the pending-open count, and the Temporary status derived from it, permanently stale. Fix criteria: The pending-open count in peerChanInfo must be decremented (and the record removed when it reaches zero with no open/closed channel) on funding timeout regardless of whether the peer is connected; equivalently, access status must be derivable from the DB state at connection time. Verify by creating an inbound pending channel, disconnecting, triggering the funding timeout, and confirming the key is treated as restricted (slot check and ban check applied) on reconnect.

# Tor-mode DNS seed bootstrap panics on non-SRV answer record, crashing lnd

## Details
lnd bootstraps peers from BOLT-10 DNS seeds. When the node runs with `tor.active=1` (the common configuration for privacy-preserving nodes), `cfg.net` is a `*tor.ProxyNet` and `DNSSeedBootstrapper.SampleNodeAddrs` (discovery/bootstrapper.go:473) resolves the `_nodes._tcp.<seed>` SRV record via `tor.LookupSRV` (tor/tor.go:151). That function opens a plaintext TCP DNS connection through the Tor SOCKS proxy to the configured `tor.dns` server (default `soa.nodes.lightning.directory:53`), reads one `dns.Msg`, and then does `for _, rr := range resp.Answer { srv := rr.(*dns.SRV); ... }` (tor/tor.go:189-190). The type assertion is unchecked. A DNS answer section is not guaranteed to contain only records of the queried type: a CNAME at the queried name is legitimately returned in the answer section ahead of the target's records, and a hostile responder can put any RR type there. The first non-SRV RR panics the goroutine.

The panic is not recovered. `peerBootstrapper`/`initialPeerBootstrap` (server.go:3200-3210, 3337-3398) are launched with `go s.peerBootstrapper(...)` (server.go:2736) and contain only `defer s.wg.Done()`; the only `recover()` in the discovery/peer/server code is the gossiper's `finalizeGossipProcessing`, which covers a different goroutine. Per Go semantics an unrecovered panic in any goroutine terminates the process, so lnd exits with all channels unattended until the operator restarts it.

Who can trigger it: (1) the operator of the configured DNS server (a third party by default), (2) any Tor exit node that happens to carry the stream, since the DNS query is unauthenticated plaintext TCP (Tor exits can and do tamper with plaintext), or (3) anyone who can answer for that name on the path. The bootstrapper runs at every start while the node has fewer than `defaultMinPeers` (3) connected peers (server.go:3362-3368, 3237-3244), and keeps retrying with backoff until it has them; the bootstrappers are shuffled, so the DNS seed is consulted with high probability for a fresh or poorly connected node. A node that cannot reach its channel peers (e.g. after they went offline) will keep hitting this path every 15 s to 5 min.

The maintainers already fixed the identical pattern in the clearnet fallback in the same package (discovery/bootstrapper.go:429-435 uses `srv, ok := rr.(*dns.SRV)` and skips non-SRV records), and Go's `net.DefaultResolver.LookupSRV` used on clearnet filters record types safely, so only the Tor path is exposed.

Impact: full process crash of a Lightning node from a single forged DNS response; the node is offline until manually restarted, during which HTLC timeouts and breach-remedy windows can be missed. Note also that `netann`/`tor` use of `dnsCodes[resp.Rcode]` is a map lookup and safe; `LookupHost` indexes `ip[0]` but btcd's `connmgr.TorLookupIP` (v0.25.1-pre) is assumed to return a non-empty slice or an error.

## Evidence
1. [tor/tor.go:187–197](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/tor/tor.go#L187-L197)
   LookupSRV iterates resp.Answer and performs an unchecked type assertion `srv := rr.(*dns.SRV)` on every RR. Any non-SRV record in the answer section (a CNAME, A, TXT or anything the responder chooses) panics the calling goroutine. There is no recover anywhere on this call path.
2. [discovery/bootstrapper.go:468–475](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/bootstrapper.go#L468-L475)
   DNSSeedBootstrapper.SampleNodeAddrs calls d.net.LookupSRV for every configured seed. When lnd runs with tor.active=1, d.net is a *tor.ProxyNet so this resolves to tor.LookupSRV above with attacker-influenceable DNS data.
3. [discovery/bootstrapper.go:424–442](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/bootstrapper.go#L424-L442)
   The clearnet fallback path in the same file handles exactly this case with a comma-ok assertion and a `continue`, showing the maintainers know the answer section can contain non-SRV records; the Tor sibling lacks the check.
4. [tor/net.go:120–128](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/tor/net.go#L120-L128)
   ProxyNet.LookupSRV forwards to tor.LookupSRV with the configured p.DNS server; the query is plaintext DNS over TCP through the Tor SOCKS proxy, so the Tor exit node or the DNS server itself controls the response.
5. [config.go:1322–1328](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/config.go#L1322-L1328)
   cfg.net becomes a tor.ProxyNet whenever tor.active is set, which is the condition under which the vulnerable LookupSRV is used. The default DNS server is soa.nodes.lightning.directory:53 (config.go:82-83,347).
6. [server.go:2728–2738](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/server.go#L2728-L2738)
   Unless nobootstrap is set, server start launches peerBootstrapper as a bare goroutine; it and initialPeerBootstrap (server.go:3200-3210, 3337-3398) call discovery.MultiSourceBootstrap with no deferred recover, so the panic terminates the whole lnd process.

## Impact
An unrecovered panic terminates the lnd process. No data is read or modified, but the node is fully offline until an operator restarts it, which for a Lightning node means missed HTLC deadlines and breach-response windows.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker is the configured tor.dns server operator (a third party by default), a Tor exit node carrying the plaintext TCP DNS stream (tor/tor.go:126-133 dials the clearnet DNS server through SOCKS with no authentication or integrity protection), or any on-path party; they answer lnd's `_nodes._tcp.<seed>` SRV query with an answer section containing any non-SRV RR (a CNAME at the queried name is a legitimate, non-malicious example). tor/tor.go:190 does `srv := rr.(*dns.SRV)` without the comma-ok form, so the first such RR panics; the calling goroutine (server.go:2736 `go s.peerBootstrapper` → initialPeerBootstrap/peerBootstrapper → discovery.MultiSourceBootstrap → SampleNodeAddrs, bootstrapper.go:473) carries no recover (the only recovers in the tree are gossiper.go:1724 and the gRPC interceptor at rpcperms/interceptor.go:686/726, both on other goroutines), so the process exits. Preconditions: lnd runs with tor.active=1 (so cfg.net is a *tor.ProxyNet, config.go:1322-1329) on a network with DNS seeds (mainnet/testnet/testnet4/signet, chainreg/chainregistry.go:878) without --nobootstrap, and is in a bootstrap round (fewer than defaultMinPeers=3 connected peers: every startup, and every 15 s to 5 min thereafter while under-connected). No credentials, no user interaction; the panic is deterministic. Dependency assumption: github.com/miekg/dns v1.1.43 (go.mod:48) `Conn.ReadMsg` unpacks each answer RR into its concrete Go type (*dns.CNAME, *dns.A, *dns.RFC3597 for unknown types), so a non-SRV wire record yields a value whose dynamic type is not *dns.SRV; the project's own fallBackSRVLookup (bootstrapper.go:424-443) is written on exactly that premise.

## Recommended fix
1. tor.LookupSRV trusts that every RR in a remote DNS answer section is a *dns.SRV and uses an unchecked type assertion, so attacker-controlled DNS data can panic the process. Fix criteria: Non-SRV records in the answer section must be skipped or cause an error return, never a panic; a response consisting of CNAME/A/TXT records must leave lnd running and simply fail that bootstrap attempt. Verify with a stub DNS server returning a CNAME-only answer while lnd runs with tor.active.
2. The peer bootstrapper goroutines process untrusted network data with no panic isolation, so any defect in the DNS/bootstrap parsing path is a whole-process crash. Fix criteria: A failure while sampling bootstrap addresses must be contained to that bootstrap round (logged and retried), and must not terminate the daemon; confirm by injecting a panic in a bootstrapper and observing the node keeps serving channels.

# Persistent peer's inbound ephemeral address appended per disconnect, each becoming a permanent dial

## Details
The server keeps, per persistent peer, an in-memory list of addresses to redial (`persistentPeerAddrs`). `peerTerminationWatcher` (server.go:4890-4956) extends that list on every disconnect with the address the peer last used. For an inbound connection `p.NetAddress().Address` is `conn.RemoteAddr()` (server.go:4488/4517): the remote IP plus the ephemeral source port of the TCP connection that just closed. When the peer has no node announcement in the graph, `fetchNodeAdvertisedAddrs` returns a FetchNode error that lands in the `default:` branch; when it is in the graph without addresses, a non-Tor victim `break`s out of the `errNoAdvertisedAddr` case. Both keep the inbound address. Entries are de-duplicated only against the existing list by `IP:port`, never capped or replaced, and `cancelConnReqs` (server.go:4361-4398, run when the peer reconnects) clears the ConnReqs and retry canceller but not the address list.

An anonymous remote peer becomes persistent for free: as fundee, lnd stores a pending channel on `funding_created` without on-chain evidence and `handleFundingCreated` (funding/manager.go:2652) calls `WatchNewChannel`, which sets `persistentPeers[pub]=false` (server.go:1669-1688). Because a pending channel counts as an open channel, `prunePersistentPeerConnection` (server.go:3863-3880) does not clear the state for the 2016-block (~2 weeks) funding-timeout window. (The verified finding inbound-pending-channel-global-cap-sybil-exhaustion covers the pending-channel sybil itself; this record is the distinct server-side reconnect sink.) The attacker can also keep its own node announcement off the network, so the gossip path at server.go:532 that would replace the list never runs.

The attacker then repeatedly connects inbound from a fresh source port (any NAT'd client does this by default), completes the brontide handshake and drops the connection. Each cycle appends one address and reschedules the reconnect; the next inbound connection cancels that reconnect without trimming the list. After the last disconnect, the scheduled reconnect fires (after at most MaxBackoff = 1 h) and `connectToPersistentPeer` (server.go:5000-5087) turns every entry into a `connmgr.ConnReq{Permanent: true}` and calls `connMgr.Connect` for it, one every 10 s. If the attacker's host silently drops SYNs, each dial blocks for `ConnectionTimeout` (120 s default) holding a goroutine and a socket. Assumption (btcd connmgr, pinned github.com/btcsuite/btcd v0.25.1-0.20260310163610-1c55c7c18179): a failed Permanent ConnReq is re-dialled via time.AfterFunc after min(retryCount*RetryDuration, 1 min), indefinitely, until Remove is called. The number of concurrent in-flight dials therefore grows linearly with the number of connect/disconnect cycles the attacker performed — bounded only by the distinct IP:port pairs the attacker can source from, not by the code — for the lifetime of the pending channel, and is multiplied by the number of attacker identities holding a pending channel. The state is in-memory: a restart rebuilds the list from the single persisted link-node address, after which the attacker simply re-runs the cycles.

Impact is resource consumption on the victim (goroutines, sockets, timers, outbound SYNs toward the attacker's own IP) that persists after the attacker leaves and is not self-healing until the pending channel times out. No funds or confidentiality are affected.

## Evidence
1. [server.go:4890–4955](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/server.go#L4890-L4955)
   peerTerminationWatcher seeds addrs with p.NetAddress().Address (for an inbound peer this is conn.RemoteAddr(): the remote IP plus the ephemeral source port of the connection that just ended, set at server.go:4488/4517). A node absent from the graph makes fetchNodeAdvertisedAddrs return a FetchNode error that lands in the default branch; a node present without addresses hits errNoAdvertisedAddr and, for a non-Tor victim, breaks out — both keep the inbound address. Entries are de-duplicated only by addr.String() (IP:port) and appended to s.persistentPeerAddrs[pubStr]; nothing caps the slice, so every fresh source port is a new permanent entry.
2. [server.go:5000–5086](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/server.go#L5000-L5086)
   connectToPersistentPeer turns every entry of persistentPeerAddrs into a connmgr.ConnReq{Permanent: true} and hands it to connMgr.Connect, one every multiAddrConnectionStagger (10 s). Each accumulated address becomes an independent, indefinitely retried outbound dial.
3. [server.go:4361–4397](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/server.go#L4361-L4397)
   cancelConnReqs (run on the attacker's next inbound connection from InboundPeerConnected) closes the retry canceller and removes the ConnReqs but never touches persistentPeerAddrs, so the address list only ever grows across connect/disconnect cycles.
4. [funding/manager.go:2652](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/funding/manager.go#L2652)
   The fundee's handleFundingCreated calls WatchNewChannel after storing the pending channel, before any on-chain evidence exists, so an anonymous peer that sends open_channel/funding_created with a fabricated outpoint is marked persistent.
5. [server.go:1669–1687](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/server.go#L1669-L1687)
   WatchNewChannel sets persistentPeers[pub]=false for any peer whose pending channel is accepted, which is the gate peerTerminationWatcher checks before extending the address list.
6. [server.go:3863–3879](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/server.go#L3863-L3879)
   prunePersistentPeerConnection is the only path that deletes persistentPeerAddrs for an auto-added peer and it runs only when the peer has no open channels; a pending channel counts as open, so the list survives for the 2016-block funding-timeout window.
7. [server.go:1957–1960](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/server.go#L1957-L1960)
   connmgr is configured with noiseDial and cfg.ConnectionTimeout (default tor.DefaultConnTimeout = 120 s, config.go:725), so a dial to a host that silently drops SYNs holds a goroutine and a socket for two minutes before connmgr retries the permanent request.

## Impact
Availability only: growth of goroutines, sockets, timers and outbound dial attempts proportional to attacker effort, sustained for ~2 weeks per pending channel and renewable after restart. The 10 s stagger per identity makes the ramp slow (10k dials needs ~28 h per identity, parallel across identities) and Go raises the fd soft limit, so this degrades the node rather than deterministically crashing it; rated Low availability impact.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker is any Internet host able to reach port 9735 knowing the node pubkey (the threat model's primary adversary). Step 1: open one unfunded inbound channel (open_channel/accept_channel/funding_created with a fabricated outpoint) to be marked persistent; default config accepts. Step 2: loop N times: connect inbound from a new source port, complete the brontide handshake, close. Step 3: go offline and drop SYNs. After at most 1 h the victim creates N permanent dial requests, one per 10 s, each retried forever. Deterministic, no race, no privileges, no user interaction, no non-default configuration.

## Recommended fix
1. peerTerminationWatcher treats the transient inbound remote address (IP plus ephemeral source port) as a durable reconnect address and appends it to an unbounded per-peer list; connectToPersistentPeer dials every entry with a permanent request. Fix criteria: The set of reconnect addresses for a peer must be bounded independently of how many times the peer connected: the inbound-fallback address replaces the previous fallback rather than accumulating (or inbound ephemeral addresses are not used as reconnect targets at all), and the per-peer address list and the number of concurrent permanent ConnReqs are capped. Verify by performing many inbound connect/disconnect cycles from distinct source ports with a pending channel and confirming persistentPeerAddrs[pub] and the outstanding ConnReqs stay at a small constant.
2. Peers with only an unfunded pending channel are marked persistent and keep that status, and the associated reconnect state, for the full 2016-block funding-timeout window. Fix criteria: Persistent-peer reconnect state for a peer whose only channels are unconfirmed inbound pending channels is bounded or dropped (for example, not treating fundee-side pending channels as grounds for persistence until the funding transaction is seen, or pruning reconnect state when the peer has no confirmed channels). Verify that an unfunded inbound channel alone does not cause the node to retain reconnect addresses or schedule permanent dials for that peer.
