# Custom messages from any peer buffered without bound per RPC subscriber

## Details
`readHandler` (peer/brontide.go:2531) routes every `lnwire.Custom` message (types >= 32768, body up to 65533 arbitrary bytes, copied into a fresh buffer by `Custom.Decode`) to `handleCustomMessage` -> `server.handleCustomMessage` -> `subscribe.Server.SendUpdate`. In `subscriptionHandler` the update is pushed into each subscriber's `queue.ConcurrentQueue`, whose output channel holds 20 items and whose overflow is an unbounded `container/list`; the push never blocks, so the peer is never back-pressured. The only consumer is `rpcServer.SubscribeCustomMessages`, which performs one gRPC `Send` per item.

Every other unsolicited message class a no-channel peer can send on this switch is bounded by a shipped control: pings by `pingLimiter` (disconnect on flood), onion messages by a channel-presence gate plus per-peer and global byte-bucket limiters (docs/onion_message_rate_limiting.md), peer errors by `storeError`'s active-channel requirement (whose comment names the 'dos vector where a peer costlessly connects to us'), gossip by the gossiper's rate limits. Custom messages have none of these: no channel gate, no per-peer rate or byte limit, and no cap on the retained queue.

Therefore, whenever any RPC client holds an open `SubscribeCustomMessages` stream (the documented way to consume custom messages; `lncli subscribecustom` and custom-channel daemons use it), an anonymous remote peer that has merely completed the brontide handshake — admitted by accessman into one of the default 100 restricted slots, no channel needed — can stream maximum-size custom messages, and every byte the gRPC consumer does not drain at ingress rate is retained in the subscriber's overflow list indefinitely. With a remote or slow subscriber (e.g. a wallet over Tor), or once the subscriber's HTTP/2 receive window is exhausted so `Send` blocks, resident memory grows as attacker-bandwidth x time with no ceiling until the daemon is OOM-killed; the retention is per subscriber, so N streams multiply it. The node must stay online to resolve HTLCs and punish breaches.

The finding is conditional on at least one active `SubscribeCustomMessages` stream; without subscribers `SendUpdate` discards the update. The sink lives in `subscribe/`/`queue/`, but the missing admission control is at the peer entry point, which forwards unlimited untrusted bytes from a no-channel identity into retained server state.

## Evidence
1. [peer/brontide.go:2531–2536](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/peer/brontide.go#L2531-L2536)
   readHandler's dispatch switch forwards every *lnwire.Custom (type >= 32768, body up to 65533 bytes freshly allocated by Custom.Decode) to handleCustomMessage with no channel gate, per-peer rate limiter or byte budget. The sibling classes on the same switch are all bounded: pings hit pingLimiter (2343), onion messages hit the channel gate + per-peer/global byte limiters (2487-2493), errors are only retained via storeError when the peer has an active channel (2671-2675).
2. [peer/brontide.go:2564–2570](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/peer/brontide.go#L2564-L2570)
   handleCustomMessage passes the message straight to cfg.HandleCustomMessage, wired to server.handleCustomMessage at server.go:4630.
3. [server.go:4402–4410](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/server.go#L4402-L4410)
   server.handleCustomMessage wraps the message (retaining msg.Data) in a CustomMessage and calls customMessageServer.SendUpdate; the send into s.updates is consumed immediately by subscriptionHandler, so the peer's readHandler is never back-pressured.
4. [subscribe/subscribe.go:202–208](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/subscribe/subscribe.go#L202-L208)
   subscriptionHandler pushes each update into every client's ConcurrentQueue ChanIn; the queue goroutine always accepts from ChanIn, so this never blocks on a slow consumer.
5. [queue/queue.go:76–90](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/queue/queue.go#L76-L90)
   ConcurrentQueue is documented as 'unbounded capacity': once the 20-slot chanOut is full every further item is appended to a container/list overflow with no size cap, drop policy or consumer eviction.
6. [rpcserver.go:8709–8741](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/rpcserver.go#L8709-L8741)
   SubscribeCustomMessages (offchain:read macaroon, used by `lncli subscribecustom` and custom-channel daemons) is the only drain: one gRPC Send per item. A consumer slower than the peer's ingress rate, or one whose HTTP/2 receive window is exhausted so Send blocks, leaves everything else accumulating in the overflow list for as long as the peer keeps sending.

## Impact
Memory grows without bound in the subscriber's container/list overflow (one ~65 KB buffer per message, roughly 1:1 with bytes sent, never freed until drained) until the daemon is OOM-killed, taking all channels offline and risking missed HTLC/breach timeouts; no confidentiality or integrity impact on its own.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker: any host that can reach port 9735 (or the onion service) and knows the victim's pubkey completes the Noise_XK handshake and init exchange, is admitted by accessman as a restricted-slot peer (default 100 slots, config.go:249), then sends a continuous stream of 65 KB Custom messages; no channel, funds or other relationship is needed, and the readHandler applies no per-peer rate or byte limit to this class. Condition outside the attacker's control: an RPC client with an offchain:read macaroon must hold an open SubscribeCustomMessages stream, and the consumer must drain slower than the peer's ingress rate. The attacker ensures the latter by sending at line rate, possibly from several restricted slots; a remote or Tor-connected subscriber makes it trivially true. Dependency assumption: in grpc-go v1.83.1 (go.mod) the server-side stream Send is gated by a per-stream write quota that is only replenished as the client's HTTP/2 flow-control window allows, so a stalled client blocks Send entirely and the entire ingress is retained; even without that assumption, growth equals the ingress/drain rate difference times duration, which the attacker sets.

## Recommended fix
1. The peer forwards custom messages from any authenticated-but-unrelated peer into retained server state without any admission control (no channel gate, no per-peer rate or byte limit), unlike pings, onion messages, errors and gossip on the same dispatch path. Fix criteria: A remote peer must not be able to grow lnd's memory without bound via custom messages: bound the custom-message ingress per peer (byte-bucket rate limit, and/or gate on an active channel as storeError and the onion path do, with an explicit opt-out for operators who need unsolicited custom messages). Verification: a no-channel peer streaming max-size custom messages at line rate must be throttled or disconnected regardless of subscriber state.
2. subscribe.Server delivers to each client through queue.ConcurrentQueue, whose overflow list has no size cap, drop policy or slow-consumer eviction, so any producer faster than the gRPC consumer accumulates unbounded state. Fix criteria: The per-subscriber queue must have a bounded footprint: cap the overflow by item count or bytes and, when exceeded, drop the oldest/newest updates or cancel the subscriber with an error. Verification: with a stalled SubscribeCustomMessages consumer and a peer streaming custom messages, resident memory attributable to the subscription stays below the configured cap.

# Pre-auth commitment_signed decode pre-allocates up to ~4.7 MB from an unchecked 2-byte HTLC signature count

## Details
The wire codec's ReadElement handles `*[]Sig` by reading a 2-byte big-endian count and pre-allocating `make([]Sig, numSigs)` before it has read a single signature byte (lnwire/lnwire.go:567-583). The count is bounded only by its uint16 type; nothing compares it to the bytes remaining in the message. Each signature occupies 64 bytes on the wire and a message body is at most 65533 bytes, so no legitimate message can carry more than ~1022 signatures, yet a peer may declare 65535. Each Sig is 72 bytes in memory (a [64]byte plus a `uint` sigType), so the declared count forces a zeroed ~4.7 MB heap allocation from a message whose entire body is 32 (ChanID) + 64 (CommitSig) + 2 (count) = 98 bytes. The subsequent io.ReadFull on the first element fails with EOF, but only after the allocation has been made.

Reachability: `CommitSig.Decode` (lnwire/commit_sig.go:75-89) reads HtlcSigs through this arm. `peer.(*Brontide).readNextMessage` (peer/brontide.go:1912-1945) calls `lnwire.ReadMessage` for every message received from any peer that completed the brontide handshake, inside a read-pool worker, before the message is matched to a channel or otherwise authorized. The accessman admits unknown peers into restricted slots (default 100; brontide listener runs 50 handshakes in parallel), so no channel or prior relationship is needed. The decode error is fatal in readHandler (peer/brontide.go:2334-2335), so the peer is disconnected after each such message; no ban score accrues and the slot is released on termination, so the attacker reconnects under a fresh random identity key and repeats, from many connections in parallel.

Impact: an unauthenticated remote peer obtains roughly 47,000x memory-allocation amplification per ~100 wire bytes (plus one handshake). The allocation becomes garbage immediately, so it does not accumulate as live heap: Go's GC pacer bounds heap growth to roughly GOGC (lnd does not tune GOGC or a memory limit), and the realistic effect is sustained allocation, zeroing and GC-cycle pressure rather than OOM. Because every GC cycle marks the node's entire live heap, driving several GB/s of garbage from ~100 KB/s of attacker upload imposes a CPU load far above the per-connection cost the project already concedes (three ECDH operations and a 65 KB-per-message read), degrading message processing for all peers on a node whose availability is required to resolve HTLCs and punish breaches. This is a length-prefix trust defect: the declared count is honoured without comparing it to the bytes that can actually follow. Other count/length-prefixed arms in the same function (OpaqueReason, ErrorData, PingPayload, []net.Addr) allocate at most 65535 bytes, proportional to the input, and are not affected to the same degree.

## Evidence
1. [lnwire/lnwire.go:567–583](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwire/lnwire.go#L567-L583)
   ReadElement(*[]Sig) reads a 2-byte big-endian numSigs from the peer-controlled stream and executes make([]Sig, numSigs) before reading a single signature byte. The only bound is the uint16 type (65535); nothing compares the count to the bytes remaining in the message, even though no message body (<= 65533 bytes) can carry more than ~1022 64-byte signatures.
2. [lnwire/signature.go:40–44](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwire/signature.go#L40-L44)
   Sig is a [64]byte plus a sigType (declared `type sigType uint` at line 25, 8 bytes on 64-bit targets), so each element is 72 bytes and a count of 65535 forces a zeroed allocation of 4,718,520 bytes.
3. [lnwire/commit\_sig.go:75–88](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwire/commit_sig.go#L75-L88)
   CommitSig.Decode passes &c.HtlcSigs to ReadElements immediately after ChanID and CommitSig, so the vulnerable arm runs for every commitment_signed (type 132) regardless of whether the ChanID names a channel this node has with the peer.
4. [lnwire/message.go:442–462](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwire/message.go#L442-L462)
   ReadMessage dispatches on the 2-byte type via makeEmptyMessage and calls Decode with a reader over the raw body; the 65535-byte brontide body limit bounds the bytes supplied, not the element count a message declares.
5. [peer/brontide.go:1912–1947](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/peer/brontide.go#L1912-L1947)
   readNextMessage decrypts the body inside a read-pool worker (Workers.Read, default 100) and calls lnwire.ReadMessage for every message from every connected peer, before the message is routed to a channel link, the funding manager or any other authorizing component.
6. [peer/brontide.go:2334–2335](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/peer/brontide.go#L2334-L2335)
   A decode error that is not UnknownMessage/ErrUnknownAddrType/ErrInvalidNodeAlias breaks out of readHandler and disconnects the peer. This bounds the attack to one allocation per connection; it does not ban or penalise the peer, and accessman releases the restricted slot on termination, so the attacker reconnects with a fresh random key.

## Impact
No confidentiality or integrity effect. Availability: each ~100-byte message forces a zeroed ~4.7 MB allocation that is immediately garbage, so sustained reconnect churn converts a small attacker upload into gigabytes per second of allocation and continuous GC cycles that each mark the node's whole live heap, slowing all mutator goroutines (channel state machines, HTLC handling) and consuming CPU on small VPS-class hosts. The allocation does not persist, GC pacing bounds heap growth, a single message does not crash the node and each attempt costs a reconnect, so this is degradation rather than outage: LOW, not HIGH.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker is any Internet host knowing the victim's node pubkey (public, in gossip). It completes the brontide handshake into a restricted slot (accessman checkAcceptIncomingConn admits unknown keys while numRestricted < 100), sends Init, then a ~100-byte commitment_signed whose HTLC-signature count is 0xFFFF. The victim's read worker allocates ~4.7 MB before the decode fails and the peer is disconnected; no ban is recorded, so the attacker reconnects under a fresh random key and repeats, or runs up to the 50 parallel handshakes / 100 restricted slots concurrently. No credentials, user interaction, channel or special configuration are required and the behaviour is deterministic.

## Recommended fix
ReadElement(*[]Sig) trusts a peer-declared uint16 element count and sizes a heap allocation from it before confirming that the stream can supply that many 64-byte signatures, so allocation is decoupled from the bytes actually received. Fix criteria: A declared signature count that cannot be satisfied by the remaining message bytes (greater than MaxMsgBody/64, i.e. about 1023) is rejected before any allocation, or signatures are read incrementally (append per element, or cap the initial capacity) so memory grows only with bytes consumed. Verify by decoding a commitment_signed with count 0xFFFF and a 98-byte body: it must fail without allocating more than a small multiple of the message's own size, with a unit test asserting allocation stays proportional to input length.

# Breach arbiter finalises justice at one confirmation; reorg to counterparty HTLC spend abandons the channel

## Details
When a counterparty broadcasts a revoked commitment, the chain watcher dispatches the breach only after the commitment reaches lnwallet.CloseConfsForCapacity confirmations (minimum 3, chain_watcher.go:1405-1413) — reorg protection for the breach tx. The breach arbiter then gives the justice transaction no such protection. BreachArbitrator.exactRetribution publishes a justice tx spending every output of the revoked commitment (our to_remote, their revocable to_local and every HTLC output, breach_arbitrator.go:1250-1411) and waits for spends via RegisterSpendNtfn. The TxNotifier dispatches Spend as soon as the spending tx is in a connected block (txnotifier.go:1400-1425) and tracks it in spendsByHeight precisely so it can signal a reorg on Event.Reorg (2085-2108). waitForSpendEvent (478-511) selects only on Spend/exit/quit; Reorg is never read and the subscriptions are dropped from the map. On the first block containing the justice tx, updateBreachInfo (596-692) drops every output as terminal and, with none left, cleanupBreach (950-974) marks the channel fully closed, deletes the retribution record and closes the breach resolver's reply channel; the resolver marks itself resolved and checkpoints (breach_resolver.go:70-77), the channel arbitrator reaches StateFullyResolved and ChainArbitrator.ResolveContract (584-621) stops the chain watcher and arbitrator and wipes the arbitrator log. On restart start() (227-317) resumes only store entries and prunes records for fully-closed channels, so the decision is irreversible.

The counterparty controls a conflicting spend of one of the justice inputs: for any HTLC on the revoked state whose preimage it knows (an HTLC we offered it) it holds our pre-signed HTLC-success signature, and for any HTLC it offered us whose CLTV has passed it holds the HTLC-timeout signature. It can therefore shape the revoked state (a high balance plus an HTLC it can claim, followed by payments to us) and, after our justice tx is mined in block N, needs the competing block N' that replaces N to carry its HTLC transaction (own hash power, a cooperating miner, or a natural stale-block fork where the other miner's mempool held the HTLC tx). The justice tx is then permanently invalid (it conflicts on that input) and lnd has already forgotten the breach: nothing re-registers for the remaining outputs or rebuilds the justice tx. Assumption about btcwallet v0.16.20-pre: its rebroadcaster re-announces the reorged-out justice tx only until a conflicting tx confirms, then drops it as a double spend. The counterparty's revocable to_local (its full revoked balance) becomes spendable by it after the CSV delay, the second-level HTLC output (ours via the revocation key) is theirs after its CSV, and our own to_remote output is no longer swept by any lnd component (recoverable only with external tooling). The breach attempt succeeds and the channel shows as fully closed.

This is contrary to BOLT 5, which requires monitoring until outputs are 'irrevocably resolved' (100 blocks deep), and to the project's own reorg standard: release notes 0.21.0 (PR #10331) state that treating a spend as final 'immediately on spend detection with no confirmation waiting' was unsafe and raised close finality to 3-6 confirmations; the irreversible breach cleanup was not given that gate. The same one-confirmation defect is recorded for the HTLC timeout resolver (htlc-timeout-resolver-fails-upstream-at-one-conf-reorg-loses-htlc); here the stake is the whole channel and no preimage-withholding is needed — only the conflicting tx in the replacement block.

## Evidence
1. [contractcourt/breach\_arbitrator.go:808–840](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/breach_arbitrator.go#L808-L840)
   exactRetribution treats the first spend notifications for the breached outputs as final: updateBreachInfo removes the spent outputs and, when none remain, cleanupBreach is called immediately. No confirmation depth is awaited and no reorg signal is consulted before the breach is declared served. Primary fix location.
2. [contractcourt/breach\_arbitrator.go:478–510](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/breach_arbitrator.go#L478-L510)
   waitForSpendEvent's per-output goroutines select only on spendEv.Spend (and exit/quit). SpendEvent.Reorg is never read, so a spend later disconnected from the chain cannot be observed, and the spend subscriptions are dropped from the map once consumed.
3. [contractcourt/breach\_arbitrator.go:950–973](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/breach_arbitrator.go#L950-L973)
   cleanupBreach irreversibly marks the channel fully closed, deletes the retribution record and closes the breach resolver's reply channel. Nothing in the breach arbiter refers to the channel afterwards.
4. [contractcourt/breach\_resolver.go:70–76](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/breach_resolver.go#L70-L76)
   The breach resolver marks itself resolved and checkpoints as soon as replyChan is closed, driving the channel arbitrator to StateFullyResolved.
5. [contractcourt/chain\_arbitrator.go:584–620](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/chain_arbitrator.go#L584-L620)
   ResolveContract, reached when the breach resolver resolves, marks the channel fully closed, stops the ChannelArbitrator and chainWatcher and wipes the arbitrator log, so no component remains that watches the commitment outputs or the justice transaction.
6. [contractcourt/breach\_arbitrator.go:227–316](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/breach_arbitrator.go#L227-L316)
   On restart, start() resumes only retributions still in the store and prunes any record whose channel is marked fully closed; after cleanupBreach a restart cannot recover the abandoned justice.
7. [chainntnfs/txnotifier.go:1400–1424](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/chainntnfs/txnotifier.go#L1400-L1424)
   A spend notification is dispatched on Event.Spend as soon as the spending tx is included in a connected block (one confirmation); the request is then tracked in spendsByHeight because the spend may still be reorged out.
8. [chainntnfs/txnotifier.go:2085–2108](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/chainntnfs/txnotifier.go#L2085-L2108)
   dispatchSpendReorg drains Spend and sends on Event.Reorg when the block containing a dispatched spend is disconnected; the breach arbiter never consumes this signal.
9. [contractcourt/breach\_arbitrator.go:1356–1402](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/breach_arbitrator.go#L1356-L1402)
   Every HTLC output of the revoked commitment is an input of the justice transaction. The counterparty holds our pre-signed HTLC-success/HTLC-timeout signatures for that state, so for an HTLC whose preimage it knows (or whose CLTV has passed) it can author a conflicting spend of the same input.
10. [contractcourt/breach\_arbitrator.go:596–691](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/breach_arbitrator.go#L596-L691)
   updateBreachInfo permanently drops every spent output from breachedOutputs; no path re-adds an output whose spend was reorged out.
11. [contractcourt/chain\_watcher.go:1405–1413](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/chain_watcher.go#L1405-L1413)
   requiredConfsForSpend gates the breach (commitment) spend at CloseConfsForCapacity confirmations before dispatching to the breach arbiter, showing reorg-aware handling exists for the breach tx but not for the justice spend that triggers irreversible cleanup.
12. [lnwallet/confscale\_prod.go:8–24](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwallet/confscale_prod.go#L8-L24)
   The project's own standard for acting on a channel-close spend is a minimum of 3 confirmations 'to provide better reorg protection'; the irreversible breach cleanup has no equivalent depth gate.

## Impact
On success the breach is never punished: the counterparty keeps its entire revoked balance and the contested HTLC after the CSV delays, and the node's own to_remote output is left unclaimed (recoverable only manually). The channel is recorded as fully closed with justice served, so the loss is silent. Funds integrity impact is high; no confidentiality or availability impact.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker is a channel counterparty (any peer may open a channel; PR:LOW). It broadcasts a revoked commitment that contains an HTLC it can spend with a pre-signed HTLC-success (preimage known) or HTLC-timeout (CLTV passed). After lnd's justice tx is mined, the attacker needs its conflicting HTLC transaction included in a competing block that replaces that block (one-block reorg via own hash power or a cooperating miner, or a natural stale-block fork where the other miner received the attacker's tx out of band). Winning that reorg is the requirement (AT:PRESENT); all other steps are deterministic from the code, no user interaction, reachable over the Lightning P2P network.

## Recommended fix
1. exactRetribution/cleanupBreach treat a one-confirmation spend of the breached outputs as final and irreversibly tear down all breach state, contrary to the project's own multi-confirmation standard for close finality. Fix criteria: The retribution record must only be removed, and the channel only marked fully closed, after the justice spends have reached a reorg-safe depth (at least the depth used for close detection). Verify that a justice tx reorged out after one confirmation and replaced by a counterparty HTLC spend results in a rebuilt justice transaction for the remaining outputs rather than a fully-closed channel.
2. waitForSpendEvent ignores the notifier's SpendEvent.Reorg channel, so a disconnected justice spend cannot be detected and the spent outputs cannot be restored to the pending set. Fix criteria: The breach arbiter must consume reorg notifications for the spends it has acted on and, when a spend is disconnected before the required depth, restore the affected outputs (converting to second-level where the replacement spend requires it) and re-enter the justice broadcast loop. Verify with a simulated one-block reorg replacing the justice tx.

# Accepted tower backups held only in memory are lost on crash and never re-presented

## Details
Manager.BackupState is the single hand-off by which the link gives a freshly revoked remote commitment to the watchtower client (wtclient.active). Its documented contract is that a nil return guarantees the backup, and the link honours it: on each RevokeAndAck it first durably advances the revocation log in channel.db (link.go:4486, lnwallet.ReceiveRevocation -> channeldb.AdvanceCommitChainTail) and then presents CommitHeight-1 exactly once (link.go:4524). It is the only caller of BackupState in the tree and nothing replays earlier heights on link, peer or daemon restart.

In the implementation a nil return only means the BackupID was appended to DiskOverflowQueue.inputList in process memory (queue.go:281) and the channel's MaxHeight was bumped in the in-memory chanInfos map (manager.go:693). Durable state is written later and only on two paths: (a) wtdb.CommitUpdate, which sessionQueue.nextStateUpdate calls immediately before a send attempt; (b) the on-disk wtdb.Queue, written when memQueue is full (toDisk mode) or when DiskOverflowQueue.stop drains memory on a clean shutdown. Between hand-off and one of those events the only copies of a revoked state's backup intent are inputList, memQueue (capacity MaxTasksInMemQueue-2, default 1998), the three leftOver slots, the dispatcher's prevTask and each sessionQueue.pendingQueue (up to MaxUpdates-seqNum, default 1024).

If lnd exits without running the Stop path (OOM kill, panic, SIGKILL, power loss) all of these are discarded. channel.db already records the state as revoked, so the counterparty does not re-send the revocation on reestablish and the link never re-presents it. On restart FetchChanInfos reloads MaxHeight from cChanMaxCommitmentHeight, which only CommitUpdate and the disk queue's onItemWrite ever wrote, and nothing compares it with the channel's actual revocation height. Those revoked states permanently have no tower copy. A counterparty holding one can broadcast it while the node is offline and claim the channel balance, which is precisely the scenario docs/watchtower.md says the tower client covers ('in the event that the client's node is offline or unable to respond at the time of a breach').

The window is widest when protection matters most. drainBackups returns on dial failure before nextStateUpdate runs, so while a tower is unreachable nothing is committed: pendingQueue fills to session capacity, the dispatcher requests a new session (which cannot be negotiated) and blocks in awaitSession, and memQueue fills to ~2000 before any task reaches disk. The counterparty controls how many states enter this window through its revocation rate. No configuration closes it: max-tasks-in-mem-queue must be >= 2 and pendingQueue/inputList are always memory. RemoveTower and TerminateSession make it worse: sessionQueue.Stop(final=true) re-queues every durably committed update into the in-memory pipeline and then calls DeleteCommittedUpdates, converting crash-safe backups into volatile ones.

The queue's own comment calls it 're-start safe' and the only durability test ('in-mem updates not lost on restart', client_test.go:2154) exercises a clean Stop; no documentation or release note (0.17.0, PR 7380) concedes that an unclean exit loses accepted backups. The exploit holds only when the node later exits uncleanly and then stays offline past the channel's CSV delay; those are runtime conditions outside the counterparty's control, reflected in AT:PRESENT.

## Evidence
1. [watchtower/wtclient/queue.go:269–288](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtclient/queue.go#L269-L288)
   QueueBackupID appends the BackupID to the in-memory inputList and returns nil; the only error path is a stopped queue. Nothing durable is written at hand-off, so a nil return does not mean the backup survives an unclean exit.
2. [watchtower/wtclient/manager.go:654–714](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtclient/manager.go#L654-L714)
   BackupState's contract: a nil return means the backup is guaranteed. It bumps chanInfos[].MaxHeight only in memory (line 693) and returns QueueBackupID's in-memory result; no durable record that the height was handed over is written.
3. [htlcswitch/link.go:4486–4534](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/htlcswitch/link.go#L4486-L4534)
   ReceiveRevocation (4486) durably advances the revocation log in channel.db (lnwallet AdvanceCommitChainTail -> channeldb putRevocationLog) before BackupState is called (4524) exactly once with CommitHeight-1. After a crash the counterparty's revocation is already persisted so it is never re-sent on reestablish, and this is the only caller of BackupState in the tree, so the height is never re-presented.
4. [watchtower/wtclient/queue.go:34–97](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtclient/queue.go#L34-L97)
   inputList, memQueue (capacity MaxTasksInMemQueue-2, default 1998) and the three leftOver slots are process memory. The type comment calls the queue 're-start safe', but items reach disk only on overflow (pushToActiveQueue in toDisk mode) or via the clean stop() path at 186-267.
5. [watchtower/wtclient/session\_queue.go:264–334](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtclient/session_queue.go#L264-L334)
   AcceptTask appends accepted tasks to the in-memory pendingQueue (line 323); a session holds up to MaxUpdates-seqNum (default 1024) uncommitted tasks.
6. [watchtower/wtclient/session\_queue.go:371–466](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtclient/session_queue.go#L371-L466)
   drainBackups returns on dial failure (389-411) before nextStateUpdate runs, so while the tower is unreachable nothing in pendingQueue is committed; wtdb.CommitUpdate (line 560) is the first durable write and happens only immediately before a send.
7. [watchtower/wtclient/client.go:699–756](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtclient/client.go#L699-L756)
   When the active session is exhausted and no candidate exists, the dispatcher blocks in awaitSession and stops reading the pipeline; memQueue then fills to capacity before the queue switches to toDisk mode, so up to ~3000 BackupIDs (memQueue + pendingQueue) sit in memory for as long as a tower is unreachable.
8. [watchtower/wtdb/client\_db.go:1351–1406](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtdb/client_db.go#L1351-L1406)
   On restart FetchChanInfos reloads MaxHeight from cChanMaxCommitmentHeight, written only by CommitUpdate (line 2034) and the disk queue's onItemWrite (GetDBQueue 2252-2260 -> maybeUpdateMaxCommitHeight 2890-2937). Heights that were only in memory are absent and nothing compares this value against the channel's revocation log to find the gap.
9. [watchtower/wtclient/session\_queue.go:198–222](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtclient/session_queue.go#L198-L222)
   Stop(final=true), reached from RemoveTower/TerminateSession, re-queues each durably committed update into the in-memory pipeline (206-213) and then DeleteCommittedUpdates removes the durable copy (216-222), downgrading crash-safe backups to volatile ones.
10. [watchtower/wtdb/client\_db.go:2311–2374](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtdb/client_db.go#L2311-L2374)
   DeleteCommittedUpdates drops the session's cSessionCommits bucket in one transaction; afterwards the only copy of those BackupIDs is process memory until the pipeline overflows to disk or stops cleanly.

## Impact
The lost states silently lose the breach protection the operator configured and believes they have (BackupState's 'guaranteed' contract, 're-start safe' queue comment, num_pending_backups stats). When the gap is exploited the counterparty takes the node's balance in that channel: a direct funds (integrity) loss for the node. No confidentiality or availability effect on lnd itself.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker is a channel counterparty (remote peer holding a channel with the node; channels are accepted without further authorisation, so the position costs only a funded channel). It drives revocations normally; each revoked state enters the in-memory window, which is milliseconds while a tower is reachable and unbounded (up to ~3000 states at defaults) while the tower is unreachable or a new session cannot be negotiated. The attack succeeds only if the node then exits uncleanly before those states are committed or overflowed to disk and later stays offline longer than the CSV delay, at which point the counterparty broadcasts one of the unbacked revoked commitments and no tower holds justice material. The crash and the offline period are runtime conditions the attacker does not control, hence AT:PRESENT; no shipped security mechanism needs to be defeated and no interaction from the operator is needed.

## Recommended fix
1. BackupState returns success after an in-memory append; the hand-off of a revoked height from the link to the client is not durable, yet the link treats it as final and never re-presents. Fix criteria: A revoked height for which BackupState returned nil must survive an unclean process exit: either persist the BackupID (or the per-channel 'handed-over' height) before returning, or on startup compare the persisted per-channel max height with the channel's actual revocation log height and re-enqueue the gap. Verify by killing the process with tasks in memQueue/pendingQueue and checking that every revoked state is eventually acked by a tower after restart.
2. sessionQueue.Stop(final=true) deletes durable committed updates after re-queuing them only into volatile memory, downgrading durability during RemoveTower/TerminateSession. Fix criteria: Committed updates must not be deleted until their replacement BackupIDs are durably recorded (e.g. pushed to the disk queue within the same transaction, or deletion deferred until re-commit). Verify by killing the process immediately after RemoveTower on a tower with committed-unacked updates and confirming the updates are still delivered to another tower after restart.

# Read-only QueryScores races active autopilot agent on shared centrality map, crashing lnd

## Details
The autopilot TopCentrality heuristic wraps a single BetweennessCentrality object that is shared between two independent executors: (1) the autopilot Agent's controller goroutine, which calls a.cfg.Heuristic.NodeScores on every wake-up while it is below its channel budget (agent.go:652-654), and (2) the autopilotrpc QueryScores handler, which calls Manager.QueryHeuristics -> queryHeuristics -> every heuristic in availableHeuristics plus the agent's weightedcomb heuristic (manager.go:327-358), i.e. TopCentrality.NodeScores twice per call. Both ultimately execute BetweennessCentrality.Refresh and GetMetric on the same instance, because availableHeuristics/AvailableHeuristics (interface.go:190-206) hold one NewTopCentrality() pointer and pilot.go:43-57 hands that same pointer to the agent.

BetweennessCentrality has no mutex. Refresh (betweenness_centrality.go:225-245) writes bc.min and bc.max, then does `bc.centrality = make(map[NodeID]float64)` followed by a loop `bc.centrality[cache.Nodes[u]] = value / 2.0` that re-reads the struct field on every iteration. GetMetric (lines 252-267) ranges over bc.centrality. The Manager mutex taken by QueryHeuristics is never taken by the agent, so nothing orders these two goroutines. If the RPC goroutine executes the `make` assignment while the agent goroutine is inside its fill loop (or vice versa), the agent's subsequent iterations write into the RPC goroutine's new map while that goroutine is also filling it: an unsynchronized concurrent map write. The Go runtime (go.mod pins go 1.26.8; assumption: the runtime's swiss-table maps retain the concurrent-write detector) aborts the process with `fatal error: concurrent map writes` (or `concurrent map iteration and map write` when one side is in GetMetric). This is runtime.fatal, not a panic, so the gRPC panic-recovery interceptor cannot catch it; lnd dies. Short of the crash, a caller can observe a partially filled map or torn min/max, producing wrong normalized scores for the agent's channel-open choice.

Attack: the holder of a readonly.macaroon (info:read) calls QueryScores (gRPC or REST GET /v2/autopilot/scores) in a loop against a node whose autopilot agent is active and under budget. Each call takes tens of seconds to minutes on a mainnet-sized graph (4 full graph-DB walks + 2 Brandes passes, ctx ignored after the walk), and the agent is re-running the same computation on every gossip NodeUpdates batch, so their Refresh/GetMetric phases repeatedly overlap. The racy windows are the millisecond-scale fill/iteration loops at the end of each computation, so a single attempt rarely hits, but the attacker can repeat indefinitely with no rate limit or cap, and an attacker who is also a Lightning peer can time node_announcements to wake the agent in lock-step with their RPC calls. The outcome is a hard process crash of a funds-holding node, which the threat model lists as a security impact (missed HTLC/breach windows).

This is distinct from the recorded sigma-overflow finding at betweenness_centrality.go:104 (different root cause, no process crash) and from the dismissed cost item dismissed-top-centrality-54-df2a (cost, not shared-state corruption). Preconditions: autopilot.active=true (or admin ModifyStatus enable) with a top_centrality-weighted heuristic (the default), agent below budget, and an info:read macaroon holder.

## Evidence
1. [autopilot/betweenness\_centrality.go:225–245](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/autopilot/betweenness_centrality.go#L225-L245)
   Refresh mutates shared state with no synchronization: it writes bc.min/bc.max, assigns bc.centrality = make(map...) and then fills it in a loop that re-loads the bc.centrality field on every iteration. Two goroutines in this loop at once (or one here while another ranges over the map in GetMetric) is an unsynchronized concurrent map write, which the Go runtime treats as an unrecoverable fatal error.
2. [autopilot/betweenness\_centrality.go:252–267](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/autopilot/betweenness_centrality.go#L252-L267)
   GetMetric ranges over bc.centrality and reads bc.min/bc.max without a lock; concurrent with a Refresh fill loop this is 'concurrent map iteration and map write' (fatal), and at best yields a partially filled map / torn min,max normalization.
3. [autopilot/top\_centrality.go:21–40](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/autopilot/top_centrality.go#L21-L40)
   TopCentrality owns a single *BetweennessCentrality created once with runtime.NumCPU() workers; NodeScores (lines 54-64) calls Refresh then GetMetric on it with no mutex. The struct has no lock of its own.
4. [autopilot/interface.go:187–207](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/autopilot/interface.go#L187-L207)
   availableHeuristics is a package-level singleton list containing one NewTopCentrality() instance, and AvailableHeuristics maps the name to that same pointer. Both the Manager's query path and the agent's configured heuristic therefore share one BetweennessCentrality.
5. [pilot.go:42–60](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/pilot.go#L42-L60)
   validateAtplCfg builds the agent's WeightedCombAttachment from autopilot.AvailableHeuristics[name] (the shared instance); default config is top_centrality:1.0 (config.go:744-746), so the agent's scoring always runs the shared TopCentrality.
6. [autopilot/manager.go:270–360](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/autopilot/manager.go#L270-L360)
   QueryHeuristics takes only the Manager mutex and then runs every heuristic in availableHeuristics plus PilotCfg.Heuristic (the weightedcomb wrapper, not deduped by name, so TopCentrality.NodeScores runs twice per call). The Manager lock serialises RPC callers against each other but is never taken by the agent, so it does not serialise this path against the agent's own scoring.
7. [autopilot/agent.go:650–659](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/autopilot/agent.go#L650-L659)
   The agent controller goroutine calls a.cfg.Heuristic.NodeScores -> WeightedCombAttachment -> TopCentrality.NodeScores -> Refresh/GetMetric on the same shared instance, without the Manager lock. The controller is woken by every NodeUpdates topology batch (manager.go:229-231), so on mainnet an under-budget agent is almost continuously inside this computation.
8. [lnrpc/autopilotrpc/autopilot\_server.go:41–43](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnrpc/autopilotrpc/autopilot_server.go#L41-L43)
   QueryScores requires only info:read, which rpcserver.go readPermissions (lines 105-141) includes and which is baked into readonly.macaroon (lnd.go:859). QueryScores (lines 220-243) calls Manager.QueryHeuristics directly with the caller's pubkey list.
9. [lnd.go:642–660](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnd.go#L642-L660)
   The Manager is created and wired into the RPC server on every node regardless of autopilot.active; the race additionally needs the agent running (lnd.go:783-787 with autopilot.active=true, or an admin ModifyStatus enable).

## Impact
A concurrent map write is an unrecoverable runtime fatal: the whole lnd process exits, taking channel monitoring, HTLC resolution and breach remediation offline until an operator or supervisor restarts it, and it can be re-triggered. No data is disclosed. Integrity of the agent's scoring can be perturbed by a torn/partially filled map but has no direct funds effect, so rated NONE.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker holds a readonly.macaroon (info:read, baked in via readPermissions at rpcserver.go:105-141 / lnd.go:859) and network access to gRPC or REST. QueryScores (autopilot_server.go:41-44) -> Manager.QueryHeuristics takes only the Manager mutex (manager.go:270-283) and runs the singleton TopCentrality (interface.go:190-206) twice per call; the agent controller (agent.go:500, 652-654) runs the same *BetweennessCentrality via the WeightedCombAttachment built from AvailableHeuristics (pilot.go:43-57, 162-174) with no lock at all, having released chanStateMtx/pendingMtx before NodeScores. BetweennessCentrality has no mutex: Refresh reassigns and fills bc.centrality (betweenness_centrality.go:241-245) re-loading the field each iteration, and GetMetric ranges over it (line 260). Overlap of one side's fill loop with the other's fill or range is an unsynchronized concurrent map write / iteration, which the Go runtime (go.mod go 1.26.8; assumption: the map implementation retains the concurrent-write and iteration+write detectors, which call runtime fatal and are not recoverable by the gRPC panic interceptor) aborts the process on. Deployment conditions: autopilot.active=true (non-default; the threat model lists autopilot as a supported deployment mode) with a top_centrality-weighted heuristic (the default) and the agent below its channel budget so the controller actually scores -- hence AT:PRESENT, as is the need to win the race, which the attacker retries indefinitely with no rate limit (Refresh ignores ctx after the graph walk, so cancelled calls still run). No security control is bypassed; AC:LOW. No victim interaction.

## Recommended fix
1. BetweennessCentrality mutates its centrality map and min/max fields in Refresh and reads them in GetMetric with no synchronization, while a single instance is shared between the agent goroutine and RPC handler goroutines. Fix criteria: Concurrent Refresh/GetMetric calls on one BetweennessCentrality (or TopCentrality) must be memory-safe: either guard the instance with a mutex so Refresh+GetMetric execute atomically per caller, or build results into a local map and publish them atomically and have callers consume a snapshot. Running TestBetweennessCentrality-style workloads from two goroutines under -race must report no races and never fatal.
2. The Manager's QueryHeuristics path and the Agent's scoring path both use the package-level singleton heuristics, so the Manager mutex gives a false sense of serialization that does not extend to the agent. Fix criteria: Either give the RPC query path its own heuristic/metric instances (as GetNodeMetrics in rpcserver.go already does) or make the shared heuristics internally thread-safe; QueryScores issued while the agent is mid-scoring must not be able to corrupt or crash the agent's computation.

# Unauthenticated reply_channel_range timestamps resurrect zombies, one fsync'd write tx each under cacheMu

## Details
When lnd runs a historical gossip sync it sends QueryChannelRange (with the timestamp query option, on by default: syncer.go:1338, lncfg/protocol.go:69) to one peer and feeds that peer's ReplyChannelRange stream into VersionedGraph.FilterKnownChanIDs (graph/db/graph.go:754-810). For every SCID that the store reports as a known zombie, the code consults isZombieChan(info) using ONLY the timestamps the remote peer put in the reply (syncer.go:1162-1169) and, if they look fresh, calls c.db.MarkEdgeLive. The reply timestamps carry no signature, the zombie entry's stored node keys are ignored (unlike processZombieUpdate at gossiper.go:2318-2347, which demands a ChannelUpdate signed by a stored key, and contrary to builder.go:964-968 which records zero keys precisely so a failed-validation zombie 'can't be resurrected'), and the resurrected SCID is not added to the `unknown` list, so the net effect is an unauthenticated bulk delete of zombie-index entries.

Attacker: any node that completes a brontide handshake (a restricted inbound slot suffices, no channel needed) and advertises gossip_queries (peer/brontide.go:1093 creates a syncer for every such peer). Replies are only accepted while a query is outstanding (syncer.go:1920-1924), so it must be the peer our SyncManager picks for a historical sync: the first peer after startup / while the graph is unsynced (sync_manager.go:402-477), or the random hourly pick among all chansSynced syncers (sync_manager.go:577-657, 979-997, 1005-1026). With 100 restricted inbound slots an attacker holding k of N connections is picked with probability k/N every hour.

Payload: a reply stream of up to 100,000 SCIDs (syncer.go:1137-1147) each with two current timestamps. Candidate SCIDs are (a) channels the victim pruned as stale -- the same 14-day rule every node applies, so the attacker's own graph predicts the victim's zombie set; (b) zombies the attacker minted itself via fake ChannelAnnouncements (gossiper.go:3975/4013/4030 -> Builder.MarkZombieEdge with zero keys), which the code assumes unresurrectable -- this path resurrects them regardless of keys.

Cost imposed: per matching SCID, MarkEdgeLive takes the store's exclusive cacheMu and commits one write transaction (kv_store.go:4383-4439 via kvdb.Update on a bbolt DB opened without NoSync; sql_store.go:2252-2299 via WriteTxOpt with sqlite synchronous=full). N zombies => N serialized fsync-bound commits on the syncer goroutine, each holding cacheMu. At a few ms per commit, tens of thousands of zombies is minutes of serialized writes; gossip ingestion batches (batch/batch.go:46-52 take the same cacheMu) and reject-cache misses (HasV1ChannelEdge takes cacheMu.Lock) interleave behind each one, and on the default bbolt backend channel-state writes share the same channel.db file and writer lock (lncfg/db.go:735-738). On the SQL backend the read half also issues one IsZombieChannel point query per unknown SCID (sql_store.go:3174-3200). The attack repeats every time the attacker is selected.

Integrity: the zombie index -- lnd's defence against replaying announcements/updates for stale channels (IsKnownEdge builder.go:1394-1400 fast-rejects announcements for zombies; IsStaleEdgePolicy builder.go:1430-1446 rejects >14-day-old updates only for zombies) -- is wiped for the chosen SCIDs on the word of an unauthenticated peer, after which replayed, validly signed historical gossip for those channels is re-validated and re-admitted.

## Evidence
1. [graph/db/graph.go:754–810](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/graph.go#L754-L810)
   VersionedGraph.FilterKnownChanIDs iterates every SCID the store reports as a known zombie and, whenever isZombieChan(info) is false for the peer-supplied freshness values, calls c.db.MarkEdgeLive for it. Nothing checks the zombie's stored node keys or any signature; the TODO/NOTE at 774-785 acknowledges the data is unverified. Resurrected SCIDs are not appended to `unknown` (despite the comment at 790-792), so the loop's only effect is one zombie-index delete per matching SCID.
2. [discovery/syncer.go:1157–1199](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/syncer.go#L1157-L1199)
   bufferChanRangeReply copies msg.Timestamps[i].Timestamp1/2 from the peer's ReplyChannelRange straight into ChannelUpdateInfo.Node1Freshness/Node2Freshness; only both-stale/both-skewed combinations (14-day DefaultChannelPruneExpiry either side of now) are dropped, so two 'now' values pass.
3. [discovery/syncer.go:1137–1147](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/syncer.go#L1137-L1147)
   A single query's reply stream may carry up to maxChanRangeReplySCIDs (100,000, const at 175-177) SCIDs before FilterKnownChanIDs runs at 1237, so one reply stream drives up to 100k candidate resurrections.
4. [graph/builder.go:544–552](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/builder.go#L544-L552)
   IsZombieChannel (wired as isStillZombieChannel at server.go:1210) decides purely from the supplied freshness values via isTimestampStale (473-487, time.Since(t) >= ChannelPruneExpiry); with default non-strict pruning both-fresh means 'not a zombie', triggering MarkEdgeLive.
5. [graph/builder.go:962–978](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/builder.go#L962-L978)
   MarkZombieEdge records zero keys for channels that failed validation expressly 'so this edge can't be resurrected'. The FilterKnownChanIDs loop never reads the stored keys, so this invariant is violated: zero-key zombies are resurrected by peer timestamps alone.
6. [graph/db/kv\_store.go:4383–4438](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/kv_store.go#L4383-L4438)
   KVStore.MarkEdgeLive takes cacheMu.Lock (exclusive) and runs markEdgeLiveUnsafe with tx==nil, i.e. kvdb.Update: one committed bbolt write transaction per zombie, not a Batch. kvdb/backend.go:95-112 opens bbolt without NoSync, so each commit is fsync'd (assumption: go.etcd.io/bbolt v1.4.3 default sync-on-commit).
7. [graph/db/sql\_store.go:2252–2298](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/sql_store.go#L2252-L2298)
   SQLStore.MarkEdgeLive likewise takes cacheMu.Lock and opens one WriteTxOpt transaction per call (DELETE + commit); sqldb/sqlite.go:76-82 sets synchronous=full, so on sqlite every commit is an fsync.
8. [graph/db/sql\_store.go:3174–3199](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/sql_store.go#L3174-L3199)
   On the SQL backend the read half of the same path additionally issues one IsZombieChannel point query per SCID not found in graph_channels, inside one read transaction, for up to 100k peer-supplied SCIDs.
9. [batch/batch.go:46–51](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/batch/batch.go#L46-L51)
   Every gossip write batch (chanScheduler constructed with &cacheMu at kv_store.go:228-231 / sql_store.go:237-239) takes the same cacheMu for its commit, so channel/policy ingestion must interleave with each of the N exclusive-locked write transactions.
10. [lncfg/db.go:735–737](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lncfg/db.go#L735-L737)
   With the default bbolt backend GraphDB and ChanStateDB are the same channel.db backend, so each of the N serialized graph write commits also competes with channel-state commits for bbolt's single writer.
11. [discovery/gossiper.go:2318–2346](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/gossiper.go#L2318-L2346)
   The maintainers' own resurrection path, processZombieUpdate, requires a ChannelUpdate signed by one of the keys stored in the zombie entry and refuses zero-key zombies. The syncer path bypasses that invariant entirely.
12. [discovery/sync\_manager.go:979–996](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/sync_manager.go#L979-L996)
   forceHistoricalSync picks a random chansSynced syncer from all active+inactive syncers (hourly via HistoricalSyncTicker at 577-657, and on initial sync at 402-477), which is how an attacker peer becomes the recipient of our QueryChannelRange (sent with the timestamp QueryOption by default, syncer.go:1338) and the source of the trusted reply.
13. [discovery/syncer.go:1907–1924](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/syncer.go#L1907-L1924)
   ProcessQueryMsg accepts a ReplyChannelRange only while the syncer is in waitingQueryRangeReply/waitingQueryChanReply, so the attacker cannot push unsolicited replies; it must be the peer we queried. Once queried, the reply is dispatched from the peer's read loop (gossiper.go:898-924) with no further budget than the 100k SCID cap.

## Impact
Integrity LOW: arbitrary zombie-index entries, including zero-key ones the code declares unresurrectable, are deleted on unauthenticated input, removing replay protection for stale channels so old signed gossip can re-pollute the graph. Availability LOW: up to 100k serialized, fsync-bound write transactions each under the exclusive graph cache lock stall gossip ingestion and compete with channel.db writes for minutes per selection; it is a sustained degradation, not a crash or hang, and pathfinding (in-memory graph cache) continues. Assumes go.etcd.io/bbolt v1.4.3 fsyncs on commit when NoSync is unset (kvdb/backend.go never sets it) and modernc.org/sqlite v1.59.0 honours synchronous=full (sqldb/sqlite.go:80-82). No confidentiality impact.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker connects as an ordinary gossip-query peer (restricted inbound slot, no channel, no auth beyond brontide) and waits to be selected as historical-sync target: guaranteed if it is the first peer after a restart or while the graph is unsynced, otherwise k/N per hour via the random pick (sync_manager.go:979-997). It then answers our QueryChannelRange with up to 100k SCIDs and two fresh timestamps each; lnwire only requires len(Timestamps)==len(ShortChanIDs). No defence mechanism stands in the way; the dependency is on runtime selection state, hence AT:PRESENT.

## Recommended fix
1. VersionedGraph.FilterKnownChanIDs performs a privileged state change (deleting a zombie entry) based solely on unauthenticated timestamps from a ReplyChannelRange, ignoring the keys recorded with the zombie. Fix criteria: A zombie must not leave the zombie index on the basis of reply_channel_range data alone. Either the SCID is only added to the query set and resurrection happens through the signature-checked processZombieUpdate path, or the entry's stored keys/strict-pruning side are honoured before any write. Verify: a peer replying with fresh timestamps for zombie SCIDs (including zero-key ones) leaves the zombie index unchanged.
2. Each resurrection is its own exclusive-locked, fsync'd write transaction, so a single reply stream of up to 100k SCIDs becomes up to 100k serialized commits. Fix criteria: Any legitimate bulk zombie-index maintenance driven by a peer reply must be bounded and batched (single transaction or kvdb.Batch, bounded per query) so that one peer cannot force more than a small constant number of write commits under cacheMu per query. Verify: a 100k-SCID reply causes O(1) write transactions.

# lncli payment confirmation prompt prints payee-controlled invoice description with raw terminal escape sequences

## Details
lncli's `payinvoice` and `sendpayment --pay_req` flows (cmd/commands/cmd_payments.go, SendPaymentRequest, lines 597-628) decode the invoice with DecodePayReq and, unless `--force` is passed (default false), call confirmPayReq (lines 298-311). That function is the only safeguard that lets the operator verify what they are about to pay: it prints the payment hash, the invoice description, the amount, the fee limit and the destination, then waits for `yes`/`no`.

The description is attacker-controlled: the payee writes the BOLT11 `d` field. zpay32.parseDescription (zpay32/decode.go:476-489) only requires valid UTF-8, so LF, CR, BEL, ESC (0x1b) and the whole ANSI/VT escape repertoire pass through; the field can hold up to 639 bytes. rpcserver.DecodePayReq (rpcserver.go:7221-7223, 7266) copies it unchanged into PayReq.Description, and confirmPayReq prints it with `fmt.Printf("Description: %v\n", ...)` with no escaping, before the Amount/Fee limit/Destination lines and the prompt.

Because the description is rendered first, a malicious invoice can rewrite what the operator sees. Example description for a 5,000,000 sat invoice:

  "Coffee\nAmount (in satoshis): 5000\nFee limit (in satoshis): 50\nDestination: 03aa...\nConfirm payment (yes/no): \x1b[?25l\x1b[30;40m"

The fake lines appear as normal lncli output; the trailing sequences hide the cursor and set foreground=background (SGR 8 'conceal' is an alternative on terminals that honour it), so the real `Amount (in satoshis): 5000000`, `Fee limit`, `Destination` lines, the genuine prompt and the echoed answer are invisible on terminals that honour these sequences (xterm, VTE/gnome-terminal, iTerm2, Windows Terminal, etc.). The operator, who received the invoice believing it is for a small purchase, reads the forged amount and types `yes`; SendPaymentV2 then pays the invoice's real amount (server-side the amount is taken from the invoice, router_backend.go:1058-1068). Other sequences (OSC title/clipboard writes, bell flooding) extend the deception. Plain embedded newlines alone already let the payee inject lines that look like lncli output.

The same weakness exists in the live payment table (formatPayment, lines 864-900): node aliases fetched from the graph (aliasCache.get -> GetNodeInfo -> rpcserver.go:6612) are placed unescaped into the table that PrintLivePayment prints and repeatedly redraws with clearLines (lines 752-767). Aliases are set by arbitrary gossip participants and are only checked for length and UTF-8 validity (lnwire/node_announcement.go:43-57), so any hop on the route or the destination can inject sequences that hide or forge the `Payment status`/`preimage` footer (e.g. make a settled keysend look FAILED to provoke a repeat payment; a repeat of an invoice payment is refused by lnd, so this secondary path is weaker than the primary one).

All other lncli output paths in this unit (`printRespJSON`/`printJSON`) go through protojson/encoding-json, which escape control characters as \uXXXX, and the project restricts the analogous remote lnwire.Error text to printable ASCII before printing (lnwire/error.go:150-159); the two human-readable code paths above are the only places remote strings are written raw. Root cause: CWE-150, failure to neutralise control/escape sequences in attacker-supplied strings before writing them to a terminal in a security decision context.

Assumption: go-pretty v6.2.7 (go.mod) preserves ANSI escape sequences inside cells (it computes widths ignoring escape sequences by design), so table rendering does not strip them.

## Evidence
1. [cmd/commands/cmd\_payments.go:298–311](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/cmd/commands/cmd_payments.go#L298-L311)
   confirmPayReq writes resp.GetDescription() (the BOLT11 'd' field chosen by the payee) to stdout with fmt.Printf and no escaping, immediately before the 'Amount', 'Fee limit' and 'Destination' lines and the yes/no prompt (promptForConfirmation, commands.go:1486) the operator uses to decide whether to pay. Embedded newlines forge lncli-looking lines; ESC-introduced CSI/SGR/OSC sequences (conceal, fg=bg colour, cursor hide) are interpreted by the terminal and hide the genuine lines that follow.
2. [cmd/commands/cmd\_payments.go:597–628](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/cmd/commands/cmd_payments.go#L597-L628)
   SendPaymentRequest (reached by both 'sendpayment --pay_req' and 'payinvoice') decodes the invoice via DecodePayReq, takes the amount from the invoice when present (line 607-610), and unless --force is set (default false, line 622) hands the decoded response to confirmPayReq; approval proceeds to SendPaymentV2 with the invoice's real amount.
3. [rpcserver.go:7221–7223](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/rpcserver.go#L7221-L7223)
   DecodePayReq copies *payReq.Description verbatim into desc, which becomes lnrpc.PayReq.Description at line 7266; no control-character filtering happens server-side.
4. [zpay32/decode.go:476–489](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/zpay32/decode.go#L476-L489)
   parseDescription accepts any UTF-8-valid byte sequence (BOLT11 field limit 639 bytes). ESC (0x1b), BEL, CR, LF and other C0 bytes are valid UTF-8, so a payee can embed arbitrary ANSI/VT escape sequences and newlines in the description.
5. [cmd/commands/cmd\_payments.go:864–900](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/cmd/commands/cmd_payments.go#L864-L900)
   Secondary path: formatPayment inserts node aliases from aliasCache.get (GetNodeInfo -> rpcserver.go:6612 node.Alias, set by whichever gossip participant announced the node; lnwire/node_announcement.go:43-57 checks only length <= 32 and UTF-8 validity) unescaped into the live payment table that PrintLivePayment prints and redraws with clearLines (lines 752-767, clearCode at 2158). Any hop on the route can inject sequences that alter or hide the 'Payment status'/'preimage' footer.
6. [lnwire/error.go:150–159](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwire/error.go#L150-L159)
   Contrast: for the analogous remote-authored text (lnwire.Error data) the project restricts rendering to printable ASCII 32-126 before it is printed, showing the project treats control bytes in remote strings as something to neutralise; the invoice description and alias paths lack this guard.

## Impact
Integrity: the operator is induced to authorise a payment whose amount, fee limit and destination differ from what the confirmation screen shows, so the attacker controls the funds leaving the node, bounded only by the operator's outbound liquidity and the default fee limit computed from the real amount. The confirmation prompt is the sole control for this in lncli. The secondary alias path lets a route hop forge the live payment status footer. No confidentiality or availability impact on the node.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker is any payee (merchant, counterparty, anyone who hands the operator a BOLT11 invoice over a web page, chat or QR code) and needs no privileges on the node. They encode newlines and escape sequences in the invoice description and set the invoice amount they want. The operator must carry the invoice into the local CLI and run `lncli payinvoice <invoice>` on the default, non-`--force` path, read the forged confirmation screen and type `yes` (UI:ACTIVE); the terminal's output rendering that is subverted is not bound to the network stack and the attacker relies on another person's interaction to deliver the payload, which CVSS 4.0 rates as AV:LOCAL. No race or special configuration: every mainstream terminal emulator honours SGR colour/conceal and cursor-visibility sequences.

## Recommended fix
1. confirmPayReq prints the payee-chosen invoice description verbatim to the terminal, so control/escape sequences in it are executed by the terminal and can forge or hide the amount, fee limit, destination and prompt that the operator relies on. Fix criteria: Any remote-origin string shown in the confirmation prompt (description, and any future free-text field) must be rendered with all non-printable and control characters (C0, DEL, C1, ESC-introduced sequences) escaped or stripped, e.g. by printing a quoted/escaped form, and the security-relevant lines (amount, fee limit, destination) should be unaffected by preceding output. Verify with an invoice whose description contains '\n', '\x1b[8m' and '\x1b[2K\x1b[1A': the printed amount and prompt remain fully visible and the description shows as escaped text.
2. formatPayment/aliasCache insert gossip-controlled node aliases unsanitised into the live payment table that is printed and redrawn with terminal control codes. Fix criteria: Aliases (and any other graph-sourced text) rendered in human-readable lncli output are sanitised of control and escape characters before display, or replaced by the pubkey prefix when they contain such characters. Verify that a route hop whose alias contains '\x1b[8m' or newlines does not alter the rendering of the payment status footer.

# processRemoteAdds misindexes partially-acked forwarding packages on restart, corrupting ack state

## Details
channelLink.processRemoteAdds (htlcswitch/link.go) is run on link start for every forwarding package whose AckFilter is not full (resolveFwdPkg, line 1148). For a package already in FwdStateProcessed it skips adds whose index is set in AckFilter and collects the rest into unackedAdds (3001-3030). It then iterates unackedAdds and uses the position in that *filtered* slice as the forwarding-package index: idx := uint16(i); sourceRef := fwdPkg.SourceRef(idx) (3052-3054), and fwdPkg.FwdFilter.Contains(idx) (3231). The package contract (channeldb/forwarding_package.go PkgFilter/SourceRef; lnwallet ReceiveRevocation assigns AddRef.Index as the add's position in the package, channel.go:6003-6010) requires the index into fwdPkg.Adds. Whenever at least one lower-index add of the package has been acked before a restart, every remaining add is processed with an index that is too small.

Consequences, traced:
1. Wrong AddRef. For an exit-hop HTLC that is still held (hodl invoice, AMP/MPP set awaiting parts) the shifted sourceRef is stored in hodlMap (3540) and later passed to SettleHTLC/FailHTLC; createCommitDiff/AppendRemoteCommitChain then ack the lower, already-acked index, and the HTLC's own index is never acked. The package never reaches FwdStateCompleted and is never garbage-collected.
2. Permanent link failure. On the next restart the never-completed package is replayed again. The HTLC has since been settled and removed from the channel; the invoice registry answers ResultReplayToSettled (invoices/update.go resolveReplayedHtlc), settleHTLC calls lnwallet SettleHTLC, which returns ErrUnknownHtlcIndex (channel.go:6513-6522), and processRemoteAdds converts the error into l.failf(ErrInternalError) (3193-3203). The link fails at every start from then on, so the channel can no longer be used off-chain; the only way out is a force close.
3. Wrong FwdFilter decision. A forwarded add inherits its lower neighbour's bit. If the neighbour was not forwarded, the forwarded add is not re-sent to the switch after a restart (an add whose outgoing packet was lost in the mailbox stays stuck until the upstream peer times it out on chain). If the neighbour was forwarded and the add itself was already resolved (its circuit deleted), the replay commits a *new* circuit (circuit_map.go CommitCircuits, 862-899) and the switch sends a brand-new outgoing HTLC for an incoming HTLC that no longer exists; if the downstream node settles it the node pays out without being paid. This third path needs the shifted ack to have hit a forwarded add first (circuit loaded from disk without keystone, or the exit-hop case above) and is therefore a compound, lower-probability consequence.

Attacker control: the upstream channel counterparty chooses which adds are locked in together (one commitment_signed carrying several update_add_htlc) and which of them fail instantly (e.g. an unknown payment hash or a malformed onion that is failed back and acked once the fail is signed) versus which stay pending (an HTLC paying one of the victim's hodl invoices, or an HTLC held by an attacker-controlled downstream node). Partially-acked processed packages are also the normal state of any busy routing node. The trigger is a restart of the victim's lnd (routine upgrade/reboot), which the attacker waits for; a single restart suffices to corrupt the persisted ack state, and the second restart or reconnect makes the link unrecoverable. The same code also runs on every link re-add after a disconnect (resumeLink -> resolveFwdPkgs), so a reconnect of the channel peer while such a package exists also triggers the replay.

No earlier record exists at this location; lead-link-3001-a73c pointed here without a traced conclusion.

## Evidence
1. [htlcswitch/link.go:3001–3030](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/htlcswitch/link.go#L3001-L3030)
   For a FwdStateProcessed package the first loop skips every add whose index is already in AckFilter and appends only the remaining adds to unackedAdds, so positions in unackedAdds no longer equal positions in fwdPkg.Adds once any lower-index add has been acked.
2. [htlcswitch/link.go:3052–3054](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/htlcswitch/link.go#L3052-L3054)
   The second loop iterates unackedAdds and uses its position as the package index: idx := uint16(i); sourceRef := fwdPkg.SourceRef(idx). Every reprocessed add therefore carries an AddRef that is too small by the number of skipped (acked) adds.
3. [htlcswitch/link.go:3231–3232](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/htlcswitch/link.go#L3231-L3232)
   The same shifted idx decides fwdPkg.FwdFilter.Contains(idx): the forwarding decision recorded for a lower add is applied to this one.
4. [channeldb/forwarding\_package.go:294–301](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/channeldb/forwarding_package.go#L294-L301)
   SourceRef(i) builds AddRef{Height, Index: i}; PkgFilter indices are documented as the indices of the Adds as written in the FwdPkg, and AckAddHtlcs (789-840) sets exactly the bit named by AddRef.Index.
5. [lnwallet/channel.go:6003–6010](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwallet/channel.go#L6003-L6010)
   ReceiveRevocation assigns AddRef.Index as the running position of the add inside the forwarding package (addIndex++); this is the contract the shifted idx violates.
6. [htlcswitch/link.go:1148–1151](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/htlcswitch/link.go#L1148-L1151)
   resolveFwdPkg calls processRemoteAdds for every package whose AckFilter is not full, so a partially-acked FwdStateProcessed package is reprocessed on every link start.
7. [htlcswitch/link.go:4024](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/htlcswitch/link.go#L4024)
   resumeLink runs resolveFwdPkgs on every link start. A link is re-created on every peer connection (peer/brontide.go loadActiveChannels -> addLink(..., syncStates=true, ...)), so the channel counterparty triggers the replay at will by disconnecting and reconnecting; a node restart is not required.
8. [htlcswitch/link.go:3536–3545](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/htlcswitch/link.go#L3536-L3545)
   processExitHop stores the shifted sourceRef in hodlMap for a held exit-hop HTLC (hodl invoice, partial MPP/AMP set); processHodlQueue later passes it to settleHTLC/SettleHTLC, so the ack lands on the already-acked lower index and the HTLC's own index is never acked; the package never completes.
9. [htlcswitch/link.go:3193–3203](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/htlcswitch/link.go#L3193-L3203)
   On the next link start the now-settled exit HTLC is replayed again (its bit was never acked): the registry returns ResultReplayToSettled, settleHTLC calls SettleHTLC, which fails because the HTLC is gone from the restored remote log, and the error becomes failf(ErrInternalError) - the link fails on every subsequent start.
10. [lnwallet/channel.go:6534–6544](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwallet/channel.go#L6534-L6544)
   SettleHTLC returns ErrUnknownHtlcIndex when the HTLC index is absent from the remote update log (restoreStateLogs only restores HTLCs still present on a commitment), and ErrHtlcIndexAlreadySettled if it is present with a modification; either error fails the link via the exit-hop path.
11. [htlcswitch/circuit\_map.go:862–899](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/htlcswitch/circuit_map.go#L862-L899)
   Compound path for forwarded adds: a replayed add whose circuit was loaded from disk without keystone is failed back via failAddPacket carrying the shifted packet.sourceRef (ack lands on the wrong index); once its circuit is deleted, a later replay commits a brand-new circuit and the switch emits a new outgoing HTLC for an incoming HTLC that no longer exists.

## Impact
Persisted forwarding-package ack state of the affected channel is corrupted (bookkeeping integrity) and the channel's link fails at every start thereafter, so the channel cannot be used off-chain and HTLCs routed over it are stranded until it is force closed. The node and its other channels keep running, and the counterparty could already stall or close this one channel by sanctioned means, so availability is rated LOW. The compound re-forward path (new outgoing HTLC with no matching incoming HTLC, paying out without being paid) additionally needs a keystone-less circuit surviving a full node restart and is not attacker-controlled, so integrity is rated LOW.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker: the upstream channel counterparty (any peer with a channel to the victim; no privileges). Step 1: in one commitment_signed send add A0 that is failed at once (unknown payment hash) and add A1 that is held at the exit hop (pays a victim hodl invoice, a partial MPP set for a victim invoice, or a partial AMP set on an accept-amp node). Once the victim signs the commitment carrying A0's fail, AckFilter={0} and the package is FwdStateProcessed but not complete. Step 2: disconnect and reconnect (or wait for any victim restart); the link is re-created, resumeLink -> resolveFwdPkgs -> processRemoteAdds reprocesses A1 with idx 0, and its later settle acks index 0 again, so index 1 is never acked. Step 3: reconnect once more after the settle is revoked; A1 is replayed as ResultReplayToSettled, SettleHTLC returns ErrUnknownHtlcIndex, and the link fails with ErrInternalError on every subsequent start. The attack requires the victim to accept a holdable exit-hop payment (hodl/MPP invoice issued to the attacker, or accept-amp), hence AT:P; the restarts themselves are under the counterparty's control.

## Recommended fix
processRemoteAdds derives the forwarding-package index from the position in the filtered unackedAdds slice instead of from the add's position in fwdPkg.Adds, violating the AddRef/PkgFilter index contract when earlier adds are already acked. Fix criteria: Every reprocessed add must be handled with its original index into fwdPkg.Adds for SourceRef, FwdFilter.Contains and FwdFilter.Set, regardless of how many lower-index adds were skipped. Verify with a package of two adds where index 0 is acked before restart: after restart, index 1 must be acked when its HTLC resolves, the package must reach FwdStateCompleted, and a further restart must not fail the link or re-forward the resolved add.
