# WalletKit SignPsbt under onchain:write signs with any lnd channel/identity key family

## Details
lnd's macaroon model splits on-chain wallet authority (`onchain:write`: SendCoins/SendMany/PublishTransaction/FundPsbt) from raw key-signing authority (`signer:generate`: signrpc SignOutputRaw/ComputeInputScript/SignMessage, which accept arbitrary 1017' key locators, signer_server.go:56-61) and from channel authority (`offchain:write`; CloseChannel and OpenChannel need onchain:write AND offchain:write, rpcserver.go:335-341). `/walletrpc.WalletKit/SignPsbt` is gated by `onchain:write` alone (walletkit_server.go:161-164, registered verbatim into the interceptor chain at rpcserver.go:837-843), yet its implementation is an unrestricted signing oracle over lnd's internal key tree:

* WalletKit.SignPsbt (walletkit_server.go:2507-2552) only requires a UTXO field per input and hands the packet to BtcWallet.SignPsbt (lnwallet/btcwallet/psbt.go:196-235), which takes the signing key from the caller-supplied `Bip32Derivation[0].Bip32Path`. deriveKeyByBIP32Path (lnwallet/btcwallet/signer.go:103-117) accepts any hardened account under purpose 1017' as `keychain.KeyFamily(account)` with no allow-list, so funding multisig (family 0), revocation/HTLC/payment/delay bases (1-4), revocation root (5) and node identity (6, index 0; lnd.go:507-510) are all derivable at any index via deriveKeyByLocator -> wallet.DeriveFromKeyPathAddAccount. The only binding is that the derived pubkey equals the caller-supplied pubkey; funding pubkeys are known to the channel counterparty (exchanged in open_channel/accept_channel) and the node key is public, and the index is found by iterating calls until `SignedInputs` is non-empty (non-matching inputs are silently skipped, psbt.go:209-230).
* Caller-supplied single/double tweaks are applied from proprietary PSBT fields (maybeTweakPrivKeyPsbt).
* signSegWitV0 (psbt.go:442-469) signs the BIP143 digest over the caller's WitnessScript (prepareScriptsV0 returns in.WitnessScript without checking it hashes to the P2WSH WitnessUtxo.PkScript), the caller's amount and the caller's 4-byte SighashType.

The shipped default `walletkit.macaroon` is minted with exactly address:read/write + onchain:read/write (walletkit_server.go:55-73), so a standard artifact occupies the attacker position. Consequences for its holder (or any custom onchain:write-only macaroon, e.g. for payout tooling):

1. Channel-fund theft with a counterparty. The attacker controls or colludes with a peer C holding a non-taproot channel with victim V in which V has balance (anyone can open an inbound channel and shift balance to V by routing through it). They build a transaction spending the funding outpoint to their own address, attach the 2-of-2 witness script, V's funding pubkey and path m/1017'/coin'/0'/0/i (funding keys are DeriveNextKey(KeyFamilyMultiSig), lnwallet/wallet.go:1409-1411), call SignPsbt until the index matches, add C's signature and broadcast (PublishTransaction is also onchain:write). V's channel balance is spent by a transaction V's channel state machine never agreed to; the sanctioned route to those funds (CloseChannel) requires offchain:write as well and pays V's balance back to V's wallet.
2. Node-identity signature forgery. With path m/1017'/coin'/6'/0/0 and V's public node key, SignPsbt returns an ECDSA signature over sha256d(BIP143 preimage). The preimage is nVersion(4)||hashPrevouts(32)||hashSequence(32)||outpoint(36)||varbytes(WitnessScript)||amount(8)||nSequence(4)||hashOutputs(32)||nLocktime(4)||hashType(4); nVersion, outpoint, WitnessScript, amount, nSequence, nLocktime and hashType are caller-chosen, and with SIGHASH_NONE|ANYONECANPAY in the low hashType byte the three hash fields are all-zero. Laid out as a node_announcement body (first two bytes = features length covering the hash fields, timestamp/node_id/rgb/alias/addresses inside the WitnessScript with the fixed node_id wrapped in a push opcode so the script still parses, trailing 52 bytes as one odd-type TLV record satisfying ExtraOpaqueData.ValidateTLV), the result verifies under netann.ValidateNodeAnnSignature (ECDSA over DoubleHashB(DataToSign), netann/node_announcement.go:125-146); the gossiper accepts any non-zero timestamp newer than the stored one (discovery/gossiper.go:2591-2605). The attacker can therefore publish a forged node_announcement for V with attacker-chosen addresses/alias/features, i.e. message:write/peers:write authority from onchain:write. Lightning SignMessage and channel_update digests begin with a fixed prefix/chain hash that falls in the hash-field region and cannot be forged this way.

The defect is in the permission table and the absence of any key-family policy in SignPsbt: an operation that signs with channel and identity keys over caller-structured digests is classified as a wallet write. The project's own statements of the boundary are the distinct signer:generate entity on signrpc, the two-entity requirement on CloseChannel, and docs/remote-signing.md, which bakes `signer:generate` alongside `onchain:write` for the remote signer and describes the 1017' accounts as 'internal to lnd, used for node identity, channel keys, watchtower sessions' (lines 100 and 193-195). Assumptions on dependencies (not read in this checkout): btcd txscript (v0.25.1-pre) RawTxInWitnessSignature requires the scriptCode to parse but does not validate it against the prevout and hashes the BIP143 preimage with double-SHA256, zeroing hashPrevouts/hashSequence/hashOutputs per BIP143 for ANYONECANPAY/NONE; btcwallet (v0.16.20-pre) DeriveFromKeyPathAddAccount derives any requested 1017' account/index.

## Evidence
1. [lnrpc/walletrpc/walletkit\_server.go:161–164](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnrpc/walletrpc/walletkit_server.go#L161-L164)
   The WalletKit permission table gates /walletrpc.WalletKit/SignPsbt behind the single pair onchain:write; registered verbatim into the interceptor chain (rpcserver.go:837-843), it is the only authorization check on the method. This is the entry the fix must change.
2. [lnrpc/walletrpc/walletkit\_server.go:2507–2551](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnrpc/walletrpc/walletkit_server.go#L2507-L2551)
   The handler parses the caller's PSBT, only requires a UTXO field per input, and hands the packet straight to Wallet.SignPsbt; no restriction on which keys the PSBT's BIP32 derivation info may address.
3. [lnwallet/btcwallet/psbt.go:196–234](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwallet/btcwallet/psbt.go#L196-L234)
   BtcWallet.SignPsbt takes the signing key purely from the caller-supplied Bip32Derivation[0].Bip32Path (deriveKeyByBIP32Path), accepts it when the derived pubkey equals the caller-supplied pubkey (silently skipping otherwise, which lets the caller iterate the index), then applies caller-supplied single/double tweaks from proprietary PSBT fields (maybeTweakPrivKeyPsbt).
4. [lnwallet/btcwallet/signer.go:103–117](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwallet/btcwallet/signer.go#L103-L117)
   For purpose 1017' the path's account element becomes keychain.KeyFamily(account) with no allow-list: funding multisig (0), revocation base (1), HTLC base (2), payment base (3), delay base (4), revocation root (5) and node identity (6) are all derivable, at any index, via deriveKeyByLocator (lines 181-199).
5. [lnwallet/btcwallet/psbt.go:442–468](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwallet/btcwallet/psbt.go#L442-L468)
   signSegWitV0 signs the BIP143 sighash computed over the caller's WitnessScript (prepareScriptsV0 returns in.WitnessScript unverified against the P2WSH WitnessUtxo.PkScript), caller's amount and caller's 4-byte sighash type, so the signed digest is sha256d over a caller-structured preimage.
6. [lnrpc/signrpc/signer\_server.go:56–60](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnrpc/signrpc/signer_server.go#L56-L60)
   The maintainers' own boundary: signing an arbitrary input with an arbitrary 1017' key locator (SignOutputRaw/ComputeInputScript/SignMessage) requires signer:generate, a distinct entity that onchain:write-only macaroons do not carry.
7. [rpcserver.go:335–341](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/rpcserver.go#L335-L341)
   Spending channel funds through the sanctioned path (CloseChannel) requires onchain:write AND offchain:write; SignPsbt lets onchain:write alone co-sign a spend of a channel funding output.
8. [lnwallet/wallet.go:1409–1412](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwallet/wallet.go#L1409-L1412)
   Channel funding (multisig) keys are ordinary DeriveNextKey results from KeyFamilyMultiSig (family 0), i.e. m/1017'/coin'/0'/0/i, exactly the paths SignPsbt will sign for.
9. [lnd.go:507–510](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnd.go#L507-L510)
   The node identity key is KeyLocator{Family: KeyFamilyNodeKey (6), Index: 0}, i.e. m/1017'/coin'/6'/0/0, a path deriveKeyByBIP32Path accepts and whose pubkey is public.
10. [lnrpc/walletrpc/walletkit\_server.go:55–72](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnrpc/walletrpc/walletkit_server.go#L55-L72)
   The default walletkit.macaroon lnd mints carries exactly address:read/write and onchain:read/write — no signer:generate, no offchain:write — so a shipped artifact occupies the attacker position.
11. [netann/node\_announcement.go:125–145](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/netann/node_announcement.go#L125-L145)
   Gossip node_announcement signatures are ECDSA over chainhash.DoubleHashB(DataToSign), the same double-SHA256 construction as the BIP143 sighash, so a signature SignPsbt produces with the node identity key over a preimage laid out as an announcement body is a valid node_announcement signature.
12. [docs/remote-signing.md:100–101](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/docs/remote-signing.md#L100-L101)
   The documented remote-signing macaroon grants signer:generate together with onchain:write, and lines 193-195 describe the 1017' accounts as 'internal to lnd, used for node identity, channel keys, watchtower sessions'; nothing tells operators that onchain:write alone already carries signer:generate-equivalent authority through SignPsbt.

## Impact
Integrity: channel funds the macaroon's entities never covered are spent by a transaction the node did not authorize (loss of funds, up to the victim's balance in every channel with a colluding counterparty), and the node's gossip identity can be rewritten with a forged node_announcement. Confidentiality: signatures reveal no secrets. Availability: a forged announcement with wrong addresses or unknown required feature bits makes the network stop routing to/through the node and misdirects reconnects until the node re-announces — a partial, recoverable effect.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker holds a macaroon with onchain:write but no signer:generate/offchain:write (the shipped walletkit.macaroon or any onchain-only custom macaroon) and reaches gRPC 10009 or REST POST /v2/wallet/psbt/sign; walletrpc is in RELEASE_TAGS. For fund theft they additionally control a peer with a non-taproot channel to the victim in which the victim has balance (AT:PRESENT); they craft the funding-spend PSBT with the known funding pubkey and iterate the key index until SignedInputs is non-empty, co-sign and broadcast. For announcement forgery no channel is needed: one SignPsbt call with the public node key at m/1017'/coin'/6'/0/0 and a preimage shaped as a node_announcement body. No defensive mechanism beyond the macaroon check stands in the way; the pubkey-equality check binds only to a key the attacker already knows.

## Recommended fix
1. The permission table classifies SignPsbt as a wallet write (onchain:write) although it signs with any 1017' key family, so a macaroon without signer:generate obtains the same raw-signing authority signrpc reserves for that entity and can co-sign channel-fund spends that CloseChannel reserves for offchain:write. Fix criteria: Either SignPsbt requires signer:generate (or onchain:write plus signer:generate) whenever the PSBT addresses a purpose-1017' derivation path, or SignPsbt refuses 1017' key families that belong to channel/identity use (0-6, and any family not explicitly allow-listed) unless the caller's macaroon carries signer:generate. Verify: a macaroon baked with only onchain:write is rejected when the PSBT input's Bip32Path is m/1017'/coin'/0'/0/i or m/1017'/coin'/6'/0/0, while standard BIP49/84/86 wallet inputs still sign; the remote-signing flow (which holds signer:generate) is unaffected.
2. signSegWitV0 signs over a caller-supplied WitnessScript that is not checked against the P2WSH WitnessUtxo script, turning SignPsbt into a double-SHA256 ECDSA oracle over a caller-structured preimage. Fix criteria: Before signing a V0 input, the WitnessScript (or RedeemScript) must hash to the WitnessUtxo.PkScript program; inputs that fail this check are skipped or rejected. Verify that a PSBT whose WitnessScript does not match the UTXO's script hash produces no signature.

# Timeout resolver fails incoming HTLC upstream at first inclusion of the timeout spend; a reorg to the counterparty's preimage spend loses the HTLC

## Details
When an outgoing HTLC expires on chain, htlcTimeoutResolver claims it with the presigned second-level HTLC-timeout tx (our commitment, resolveTimeoutTx) or a direct timeout sweep (remote commitment, resolveRemoteCommitOutput). The downstream counterparty, who holds the preimage, can spend the same HTLC output with a preimage spend; the two conflict and whichever is in the canonical chain wins. BOLT #5 says to fail the corresponding incoming HTLC only 'once the resolving transaction has reached reasonable depth'. lnd fails it at inclusion: watchHtlcSpend returns on the first block containing a non-preimage spend (RegisterSpendNtfn dispatches Spend when the spending tx is first connected, chainntnfs/txnotifier.go:1405; consumeSpendEvents treats that block as 'the final judge'), and checkpointStageOne (htlc_timeout_resolver.go:1155-1163) / resolveRemoteCommitOutput (:1212-1226) immediately call DeliverResolutionMsg with FailPermanentChannelFailure. The switch persists it and forwards an UpdateFailHTLC to the incoming link straight away (htlcswitch/switch.go:1610-1665), so update_fail_htlc goes upstream and the incoming HTLC is irrevocably removed.

The TxNotifier does signal reorgs: DisconnectTip drains the Spend channel and sends on SpendEvent.Reorg for any spend within ReorgSafetyLimit (dispatchSpendReorg, txnotifier.go:2085-2105). Neither waitForSpend (commit_sweep_resolver.go:102-124) nor consumeSpendEvents reads Reorg (the comment at :905-907 defers it to 'a dedicated reorg system' that does not exist). If the block containing our timeout tx is disconnected and the replacement contains the counterparty's preimage spend, the HTLC output is theirs, the resolver sits in resolveTimeoutTxOutput waiting for a spend of an output that no longer exists, and the incoming HTLC has already been cancelled. Net loss is the full HTLC amount; the incoming CLTV delta (lnd default 80 blocks, minus DefaultIncomingBroadcastDelta 16) that exists to absorb exactly this race is unused.

Attacker: a channel counterparty who routes a payment through the node to itself (circular route), withholds the preimage so lnd goes on chain, and at expiry gets a preimage spend into a competing block. The mempool watcher (bitcoind/btcd only; h.Mempool is nil on neutrino) would extract a preimage seen in the node's own mempool, so the attacker submits the preimage spend privately to a miner or mines it itself and relies on a 1-block reorg replacing the block with our timeout tx; on success they keep the outgoing HTLC on chain while the upstream fail refunds them, so each failed attempt costs only channel open/close fees while success doubles the HTLC. The project's own release notes (0.21.0, PR #10331) state that treating a spend as final 'immediately on spend detection with no confirmation waiting' was reorg-unsafe and raised channel-close finality to 3-6 confirmations (lnwallet.CloseConfsForCapacity, min 3); the resolvers' irrevocable upstream fail was not given the same gate. The legacy nursery path (ConfDepth = 1, server.go:1320) has the same one-confirmation behaviour.

## Evidence
1. [contractcourt/htlc\_timeout\_resolver.go:1133–1167](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/htlc_timeout_resolver.go#L1133-L1167)
   checkpointStageOne runs as soon as the second-level timeout tx is first seen spending the HTLC output; it delivers FailPermanentChannelFailure for the incoming HTLC (irrevocably cancelling it upstream) and checkpoints. The comment 'sufficiently confirmed' is one block. This is the primary fix location.
2. [contractcourt/htlc\_timeout\_resolver.go:1195–1227](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/htlc_timeout_resolver.go#L1195-L1227)
   resolveRemoteCommitOutput (direct timeout sweep on the remote commitment) fails the incoming HTLC upstream right after the first confirmed non-preimage spend and marks itself resolved.
3. [contractcourt/htlc\_timeout\_resolver.go:1232–1287](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/htlc_timeout_resolver.go#L1232-L1287)
   resolveTimeoutTx calls watchHtlcSpend, which returns on the first block containing a spend, then checkpointStageOne; no depth is awaited and the resolver then only waits (resolveTimeoutTxOutput) for the spend of the possibly reorged-out timeout tx output.
4. [contractcourt/htlc\_timeout\_resolver.go:887–974](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/htlc_timeout_resolver.go#L887-L974)
   consumeSpendEvents treats the block spend from the 1-conf RegisterSpendNtfn as 'the final judge' and returns; the note at 905-907 acknowledges reorgs are not handled, and the SpendEvent's Reorg channel is never read.
5. [contractcourt/commit\_sweep\_resolver.go:102–123](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/commit_sweep_resolver.go#L102-L123)
   waitForSpend (used by waitForConfirmedSpend on neutrino and by resolveTimeoutTxOutput) selects only on spendNtfn.Spend and quit; the Reorg channel is ignored, so a reorged-out spend is never observed.
6. [chainntnfs/txnotifier.go:1400–1423](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/chainntnfs/txnotifier.go#L1400-L1423)
   A spend notification is dispatched on Event.Spend as soon as the spending tx is included in a connected block (one confirmation); the request is then tracked in spendsByHeight for reorg handling, confirming the resolvers act on a non-final state.
7. [chainntnfs/txnotifier.go:2085–2107](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/chainntnfs/txnotifier.go#L2085-L2107)
   dispatchSpendReorg (called from DisconnectTip for spends in the disconnected block) drains Spend and sends on Event.Reorg so clients can roll back; the resolvers never consume this signal.
8. [htlcswitch/switch.go:1610–1665](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/htlcswitch/switch.go#L1610-L1665)
   The resolution message is persisted and immediately mapped to an UpdateFailHTLC packet forwarded to the incoming link, so update_fail_htlc is sent upstream as soon as the resolver delivers it; nothing downstream delays or gates it.
9. [lnwallet/confscale\_prod.go:8–25](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwallet/confscale_prod.go#L8-L25)
   The project's own standard for acting on a channel-close spend is a minimum of 3 confirmations 'to provide better reorg protection'; the resolvers' irrevocable upstream fail has no equivalent depth gate.
10. [contractcourt/chain\_watcher.go:821–850](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/chain_watcher.go#L821-L850)
   The chain watcher registers an N-conf notification for the close spend and only dispatches after it, showing reorg-aware handling exists for closes but not for the resolver's upstream fail.

## Impact
Loss of the full HTLC value (up to channel capacity): the counterparty takes the outgoing HTLC on chain while the node has already irrevocably cancelled the incoming HTLC and cannot claim it. With a circular route the attacker is also refunded upstream. Funds integrity impact is high; no confidentiality or availability impact.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker is a channel counterparty of a forwarding node (channels are opened permissionlessly, but the attacker must hold an open channel and have an HTLC routed to it, so low privilege). It withholds the preimage so lnd goes on chain, and at HTLC expiry gets a preimage spend into a block competing with the one containing lnd's timeout spend, avoiding lnd's own mempool (private miner submission or own hash power; neutrino nodes have no mempool watch at all). lnd fails upstream during processing of the first block; the attack succeeds when a 1-block reorg replaces that block with the preimage spend. Winning the reorg race is the attack requirement; no user interaction; network reachable via normal Lightning routing.

## Recommended fix
1. checkpointStageOne and resolveRemoteCommitOutput deliver the irrevocable upstream failure as soon as the timeout spend is seen in a single block, with no confirmation depth, contrary to BOLT #5's 'reasonable depth' requirement and to the project's own 3-6 confirmation standard for close finality. Fix criteria: The incoming HTLC must only be failed upstream after the resolving timeout spend has reached a reorg-safe depth (at least the depth lnd uses for close detection, bounded so it still precedes the incoming HTLC's broadcast deadline), and while waiting the resolver must keep watching the HTLC output so that a preimage spend appearing after a reorg is still extracted and settled upstream. Verify that a timeout spend reorged out and replaced by a preimage spend results in the incoming HTLC being settled, not failed.
2. Resolver spend waiting (waitForSpend, consumeSpendEvents) ignores the notifier's SpendEvent.Reorg channel, so a reorged-out resolving transaction is treated as final. Fix criteria: Resolvers must consume reorg notifications for the spends they act on and roll back to the waiting state (re-registering for the spend) when the resolving transaction is disconnected before the required depth is reached.

# Gossip-shaped graph overflows Brandes path counter, yielding NaN scores that disable autopilot

## Details
The autopilot's default heuristic, top_centrality, computes Brandes betweenness centrality over the public gossip graph (autopilot/betweenness_centrality.go). The shortest-path counter `sigma` is a plain []int accumulated with unchecked additions (lines 139-142). The number of equal-length shortest paths between two vertices grows multiplicatively with the graph structure, and NewSimpleGraph (simple_graph.go:53-62) adds one adjacency entry per channel, so parallel channels between the same pair multiply the counts per hop.

Any gossip author can therefore build a cheap structure whose path count wraps int64: e.g. a chain of 65 attacker nodes (each with an advertised address so it is iterated) connected by 2 parallel channels per hop, hanging off the attacker's node that has one channel into the real graph. That is 128 channel_announcements, each needing only an existing dust P2WSH output (~330 sat; the gossiper enforces no minimum capacity, discovery/gossiper.go:2853-2949) — on the order of 0.001 BTC. From the chain head, sigma doubles each hop: 2^63 wraps to math.MinInt64 and the next hop wraps to exactly 0. The backward pass then computes float64(sigma[v])/float64(sigma[w]) with sigma[w]==0 (lines 158-161), producing -Inf, which propagates as +Inf/-Inf/NaN into centrality[] for the chain nodes (and NaN for honest nodes reached through the chain from other sources).

Refresh's min/max loop (lines 225-239) sets min=-Inf and/or max=+Inf; GetMetric (lines 252-268) then uses z = 1/(max-min) = 0 and v=(v-min)*z, which is Inf*0 = NaN for every finite node (or 0 for every honest node and NaN for attacker nodes when only max is infinite). TopCentrality.NodeScores returns these as scores. WeightedCombAttachment's only guard is `score < 0 || score > 1.0` (combinedattach.go:133), which NaN passes. chooseN/weightedChoice (choice.go:15-47) then computes a NaN sum, never satisfies `r <= 0`, and returns 'unable to make choice'; openChans (agent.go:667-671) aborts. Every subsequent wake-up (balance change, node announcement, channel close) repeats the failure, so the autopilot agent opens no channels at all for as long as the attacker keeps the structure alive in the graph (channel_updates every <2 weeks avoid zombie pruning). In the variant where honest nodes normalize to exactly 0 and the attacker's nodes have no addresses, the candidate set is empty and the agent likewise never opens a channel. The same NaN scores are returned to operators through autopilotrpc QueryScores, and by picking wrap values that leave small non-zero denominators an attacker can also make selected nodes' centrality astronomically large relative to honest nodes, biasing the weighted choice toward attacker-controlled peers.

The ledger item dismissed-autopilot-server-294-ce86 confirmed this NaN->'unable to make choice' sink but dismissed it because its source was an admin SetScores call; this finding supplies an unauthenticated remote gossip source for the same sink via integer overflow. Precondition: autopilot.active=true (off by default) with the default or any top_centrality-weighted heuristic.

## Evidence
1. [autopilot/betweenness\_centrality.go:104–143](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/autopilot/betweenness_centrality.go#L104-L143)
   sigma is a []int (int64) shortest-path counter accumulated with unchecked `sigma[w] += sigma[v]` for every adjacency entry; path counts grow multiplicatively along layered or parallel-edge structures and silently wrap.
2. [autopilot/betweenness\_centrality.go:158–166](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/autopilot/betweenness_centrality.go#L158-L166)
   The backward pass divides float64(sigma[v]) by float64(sigma[w]); a wrapped sigma[w]==0 produces +/-Inf (or NaN for 0/0), and a wrapped negative sigma produces negative dependencies. These values are summed into centrality[].
3. [autopilot/betweenness\_centrality.go:223–267](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/autopilot/betweenness_centrality.go#L223-L267)
   min/max tracking accepts -Inf/+Inf (NaN is ignored); GetMetric then computes z = 1/(max-min) = 0 and v=(v-min)*z, which is Inf*0 = NaN for every finite node when min=-Inf, or 0 for all honest nodes and NaN for the Inf ones when only max is infinite.
4. [autopilot/simple\_graph.go:53–67](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/autopilot/simple_graph.go#L53-L67)
   NewSimpleGraph appends one adjacency entry per channel, so k parallel channels between the same two nodes multiply the counted shortest paths by k per hop; a 65-node chain with 2 channels per hop gives 2^64 counted paths.
5. [autopilot/combinedattach.go:126–139](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/autopilot/combinedattach.go#L126-L139)
   The only range sanity check is `score < 0 || score > 1.0`; NaN compares false to both, so NaN combined scores are returned as valid candidates.
6. [autopilot/choice.go:15–46](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/autopilot/choice.go#L15-L46)
   weightedChoice sums the NaN scores (sum<=0 is false), r becomes NaN, `r <= 0` never holds, and it returns 'unable to make choice'; chooseN propagates this error.
7. [autopilot/agent.go:653–670](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/autopilot/agent.go#L653-L670)
   openChans aborts the whole round on a NodeScores or chooseN error, so every controller wake-up fails and the agent never opens a channel while the structure is in the graph.
8. [autopilot/top\_centrality.go:54–93](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/autopilot/top_centrality.go#L54-L93)
   TopCentrality recomputes centrality from the live gossip graph on every scoring call and passes the normalized values straight through as scores.
9. [config.go:737–746](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/config.go#L737-L746)
   top_centrality with weight 1.0 is the default autopilot heuristic, so any node that enables autopilot without changing the heuristic is affected.
10. [discovery/gossiper.go:2853–2948](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/gossiper.go#L2853-L2948)
   A channel_announcement is accepted if the funding output exists and matches the script; capacity is simply the output value with no minimum, so each edge in the attacker's structure costs a dust-sized (~330 sat) UTXO.

## Impact
No data is disclosed. Integrity: the autopilot's channel-open decisions and the scores reported by QueryScores are corrupted (NaN or steered), which can bias where the victim's funds are deployed. Availability: the autopilot feature is rendered permanently non-functional (no channels ever opened) while the structure persists; the rest of the node keeps running, so impact is partial.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker is any Lightning node able to have gossip relayed to the victim. They fund ~128 dust outputs on-chain, author 65 node_announcements with addresses and 128 channel_announcements forming a chain with two parallel channels per hop, and keep them alive with periodic channel_updates. Once the structure is in the victim's graph, every autopilot scoring round deterministically produces Inf/NaN centrality and fails. No authentication, no victim interaction, no defenses to bypass; the only condition is that the victim has enabled autopilot (non-default) using the default top_centrality heuristic.

## Recommended fix
1. The shortest-path counter sigma is a fixed-width integer accumulated without overflow detection, so adversarially shaped graphs make it wrap to zero or negative values that are then used as float divisors, producing Inf/NaN centrality. Fix criteria: Centrality computation must never produce non-finite or negative values for any input graph: use a saturating or floating-point path counter (or detect overflow and clamp), and verify with a layered/parallel-edge test graph with >2^64 counted shortest paths that all centrality values are finite and in range.
2. Downstream consumers (GetMetric normalization, WeightedCombAttachment range check, weightedChoice) assume finite scores; NaN slips through the `<0 || >1` check and turns one bad score into a failure of the whole selection round. Fix criteria: Score validation must reject or zero NaN/Inf values (e.g. math.IsNaN/IsInf checks in GetMetric and the combined sanity check), and weightedChoice must not fail the entire round because of a single invalid weight; a test feeding NaN scores must result in those nodes being skipped rather than an error.

# bbolt auto-compaction rewrites channel.db, macaroons.db, sphinxreplay.db and tower DBs with umask-default (0644) permissions instead of 0600

## Details
When db.bolt.auto-compact is enabled (off by default, but the configuration docs/forwarding_history_privacy.md tells operators to turn on), kvdb.GetBoltBackend calls compactAndSwap on every startup where the DB's .last-compacted marker is older than auto-compact-min-age (default 7 days). compactAndSwap pre-creates the destination with os.Create (O_RDWR|O_CREATE|O_TRUNC, mode 0666 & ~umask, i.e. 0644 under the usual 022) and closes it (kvdb/backend.go:161-167). The compacter then opens it with bbolt.Open(dstPath, fi.Mode(), ...) (kvdb/bolt_compact.go:103), intending to carry over the source file's mode; but bbolt v1.4.3 passes the mode to os.OpenFile with O_CREATE, which the kernel ignores for an already-existing file, so the mode argument is a no-op and the file keeps 0644. After filling it, os.Rename(tempDestFilePath, sourceFilePath) (kvdb/backend.go:209) replaces the live database inode with the wider-permission one. Nothing restores the mode on later starts: kvdb.Open is walletdb.Open with the bdb driver (kvdb/interface.go:52-63), which only applies its mode on creation.

The original files are owner-only. Assumption on the dependency: btcwallet/walletdb v1.5.1's bdb driver opens with bbolt.Open(path, 0600, ...), and lnd's own legacy channeldb code fixes dbFilePermission = 0600 (channeldb/migration_01_to_11/db.go:16); the adjacent .last-compacted marker is written 0600 (kvdb/backend.go:241). GetBackends applies the same AutoCompact config to channel.db, macaroons.db, sphinxreplay.db, wtclient.db and watchtower.db (lncfg/db.go:652-731), so all five are widened; wallet.db is opened through the btcwallet loader and is not affected.

channel.db holds every channel's full state: the local shachain RevocationProducer root (from which all local per-commitment secrets, including future ones, derive), the remote revocation log, commitment transactions and signatures, HTLC and invoice preimages, complete payment and forwarding history and peer data; macaroons.db holds the password-encrypted macaroon root key (offline brute force); wtclient.db/watchtower.db hold tower session state. None of this is exposed by the world-readable readonly.macaroon, which only grants RPC reads.

lnd decides which local users may read a secret by per-file mode, not by directory mode: lnd.go:53-60 and the 0.14 release notes justify admin.macaroon at 0640 by per-user groups ('This makes it easier to allow other users to manage LND'), and readonly/invoice macaroons are written 0644 so other local users can be granted RPC-only access. That scheme presumes other local users may reach the data directories, and relies on channel.db staying 0600 to keep channel state owner-only. lnd-created directories are 0700 (config.go makeDirectory, kvdb/backend.go:90), so the disclosure materialises in exactly the deployments the scheme anticipates — a data directory other local users can traverse (group-managed node, operator-supplied or restored directory tree, shared Docker volume); there, every compaction silently hands any local user the full channel database.

## Evidence
1. [kvdb/backend.go:159–167](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/kvdb/backend.go#L159-L167)
   compactAndSwap pre-creates the destination DB with os.Create(), i.e. O_CREATE mode 0666 masked by the process umask (0644 under the usual 022), then closes it. This file becomes the live database.
2. [kvdb/bolt\_compact.go:102–105](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/kvdb/bolt_compact.go#L102-L105)
   The compacter opens the destination with bbolt.Open(dstPath, fi.Mode(), ...) intending to preserve the source file's mode, but bbolt (v1.4.3) only passes the mode to os.OpenFile with O_CREATE, which has no effect on the already-existing file; the intent is defeated by the pre-creation.
3. [kvdb/backend.go:206–209](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/kvdb/backend.go#L206-L209)
   os.Rename moves the 0644 temp file over the original DB file, so the original 0600 protection is lost on every compaction and nothing restores it on later starts.
4. [kvdb/interface.go:52–63](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/kvdb/interface.go#L52-L63)
   kvdb.Create/Open are walletdb.Create/Open with the 'bdb' driver, which takes no mode parameter: the original 0600 comes from the driver's own bbolt.Open(path, 0600, ...) (assumption: btcwallet/walletdb v1.5.1), and Open on an existing file never re-applies it.
5. [kvdb/backend.go:236–242](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/kvdb/backend.go#L236-L242)
   Contrast: the adjacent .last-compacted marker is deliberately written 0600, showing the maintainers' expectation that DB-directory files are owner-only.
6. [lnd.go:48–60](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnd.go#L48-L60)
   lnd's security reasoning about local users is per-file mode: admin.macaroon is 0640 so that other local users in the lnd group can manage the node. That scheme presumes other local users may reach the data directories and relies on channel.db's 0600 to keep channel state owner-only.
7. [lncfg/db.go:651–731](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lncfg/db.go#L651-L731)
   The same AutoCompact/AutoCompactMinAge config is applied to channel.db, macaroons.db, sphinxreplay.db, wtclient.db and watchtower.db via GetBoltBackend, so all five files are widened.
8. [docs/forwarding\_history\_privacy.md:243–259](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/docs/forwarding_history_privacy.md#L243-L259)
   lnd's documentation instructs operators to enable db.bolt.auto-compact, making the non-default compaction path a recommended configuration.

## Impact
Read access to channel.db discloses the complete channel state (local revocation producer root, remote revocation secrets, commitment transactions, HTLC and invoice preimages), all payment/forwarding/invoice history and peer data; macaroons.db exposes the encrypted macaroon root key to offline attack; tower DBs expose session state. Files become readable, not writable, so no integrity or availability impact.

## Reproduction steps
1. A local, unprivileged user on the same host reads the database files directly; no interaction with lnd or its operator is needed and the widening is deterministic on every compaction run. Requires the non-default but documented db.bolt.auto-compact=true setting (AT:P). The attacker needs only an ordinary local account (PR:L).

## Recommended fix
1. compactAndSwap pre-creates the destination file with os.Create's default 0666 mode, and the later bbolt.Open(dst, fi.Mode()) cannot change the mode of an existing file, so the compacted copy loses the 0600 permission of the original. Fix criteria: The compacted file that replaces the live database must carry the original file's permission bits (0600 for lnd-created DBs) before the rename, e.g. by creating the temp file with the source mode or chmod-ing it to fi.Mode(); verify by compacting a 0600 database under umask 022 and confirming the resulting channel.db is still 0600.
2. Nothing on later startups re-tightens a bolt database file whose mode was already widened by a past compaction, so existing deployments stay exposed after the code fix. Fix criteria: On opening an existing bolt database lnd tightens its mode to owner-only (or warns loudly when it is wider), so that databases widened by earlier releases are restored on the next start.

# etcd kvdb backend reports transient RPC errors as 'key absent', callers overwrite state

## Details
The walletdb/kvdb bucket interface has no error return on Get/Sequence/NestedBucket/cursor methods. The etcd backend (kvdb/etcd, compiled into release binaries via the kvdb_etcd RELEASE_TAG, make/release_flags.mk:31) resolves this by swallowing the STM's DatabaseError and returning the 'not found' value: readWriteBucket.Get() -> nil (readwrite_bucket.go:107-112), Sequence() -> 0 (:386-391), NestedReadWriteBucket() -> nil (:134-139), cursor First/Last/Next/Prev/Seek -> (nil,nil) (readwrite_cursor.go). Each site carries a TODO acknowledging the error should propagate. By contrast CreateBucket/CreateBucketIfNotExists/DeleteNestedBucket/ForEach do return the STM error, and the sqlbase backend panics into catchPanic on a query error, so the intended semantics is 'abort the transaction'.

stm.fetch() (stm.go:664-711) returns the DatabaseError before rset.addItem(), so a failed read leaves no ModRevision guard in the read set and, if it was the first read, leaves s.revision at its reset value math.MaxInt64-1 (stm.go:1205). commit() (stm.go:1120-1152) validates only successfully-read keys (ModRevision ==) plus the write-set rule ModRevision(key) < revision+1, which an existing, older key always satisfies. When the Update closure reacts to the bogus 'absent' by writing a fresh value, the commit succeeds as soon as etcd answers the Txn RPC (a separate call with its own 30 s timeout). runSTM (stm.go:271-323) never learns a read failed.

When does fetch fail? Assumption on go.etcd.io/etcd/client/v3 v3.5.12 (go.mod:54): its retry interceptor retries Get on codes.Unavailable until the context deadline, so a single TCP reset is absorbed; what surfaces as DatabaseError is (a) the 30 s rpcTimeout (DeadlineExceeded) when the etcd link is down or the cluster is leaderless for 30 s, (b) non-retryable server errors such as 'required revision is a future revision' when a serializable WithRev read lands on a lagging member in a multi-endpoint configuration, or 'required revision has been compacted', (c) auth failures. Once the link recovers before the closure reaches commit, the overwrite is committed.

Confirmed consumers whose authors assumed these calls 'cannot fail inside Update':
- macaroons.RootKeyStorage.RootKey() (store.go:304-331, used when baking macaroons): Get(id)==nil triggers generateAndStoreNewRootKey over the existing root key; every macaroon minted under that id (admin/readonly/invoice for id 0) stops verifying. RootKeyStorage.Get() (verification) fails closed with a spurious error.
- htlcswitch persistentSequencer.NextID() (sequencer.go:90-107): Sequence()==0 persists SetSequence(1000) and re-issues attempt IDs 1..999, which key the switch's circuit map, network-result store and payments-DB HTLC attempt buckets.
- payments/db nextPaymentSequence() (kv_store.go:683-695), channeldb addIndex.NextSequence() (invoices.go:1208-1218), wtdb towerIndex.NextSequence() (client_db.go:401) and keyIndex.Sequence() (client_db.go:732-738): the counter restarts and Put() under the reused sequence overwrites existing index entries or reuses a session key index.
- Cursor-based iteration ends early and returns partial sets.

The maintainers' tests (kvdb/etcd/stm_test.go, readwrite_tx_test.go) never exercise a failing fetch.

## Evidence
1. [kvdb/etcd/readwrite\_bucket.go:100–119](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/kvdb/etcd/readwrite_bucket.go#L100-L119)
   Get() calls stm.Get; on a DatabaseError (etcd RPC failure/timeout) it returns nil, which every kvdb caller interprets as 'key does not exist'. Nothing marks the transaction as failed (TODO at :109-110 acknowledges it).
2. [kvdb/etcd/readwrite\_bucket.go:385–403](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/kvdb/etcd/readwrite_bucket.go#L385-L403)
   Sequence() returns 0 on an etcd error; NextSequence()/SetSequence then persist 1 (or horizon+0), resetting the bucket's monotonic counter. The write commits because the failed read left no revision guard.
3. [kvdb/etcd/readwrite\_bucket.go:127–147](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/kvdb/etcd/readwrite_bucket.go#L127-L147)
   NestedReadWriteBucket returns nil on error, indistinguishable from 'bucket missing'; callers that treat nil as 'initialise' re-create state, others spuriously fail. Contrast CreateBucketIfNotExists (:238-241), which does return the error.
4. [kvdb/etcd/stm.go:664–711](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/kvdb/etcd/stm.go#L664-L711)
   fetch() returns the DatabaseError before rset.addItem() and before setting s.revision/getOpts, so the commit's compare set has no ModRevision guard for the key whose read failed.
5. [kvdb/etcd/stm.go:1120–1181](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/kvdb/etcd/stm.go#L1120-L1181)
   commit() compares only read-set keys (ModRevision ==) and write-set keys (ModRevision < revision+1; revision is MaxInt64-1 if no read succeeded, stm.go:1205). An existing key that was never successfully read passes, so the overwrite commits once etcd answers the Txn RPC.
6. [kvdb/etcd/stm.go:271–323](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/kvdb/etcd/stm.go#L271-L323)
   runSTM runs apply() then commit(); it has no knowledge that a read inside apply failed, so a closure that saw a swallowed error is committed like any other.
7. [kvdb/etcd/readwrite\_cursor.go:29–114](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/kvdb/etcd/readwrite_cursor.go#L29-L114)
   First/Last/Next/Prev/Seek also swallow STM errors and return (nil,nil), which callers treat as 'bucket empty / iteration finished', yielding partial result sets.
8. [macaroons/store.go:304–331](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/macaroons/store.go#L304-L331)
   RootKey() (called when baking macaroons): if bucket.Get(id) returns empty, a brand-new root key is generated and stored under the same id, invalidating every macaroon previously minted under it (admin/readonly/invoice for id 0).
9. [htlcswitch/sequencer.go:90–107](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/htlcswitch/sequencer.go#L90-L107)
   NextID() trusts nextIDBkt.Sequence() ('cannot fail when used in Update') and persists Sequence()+1000; a swallowed error resets the HTLC attempt-ID counter so previously used attempt IDs are re-issued.
10. [payments/db/kv\_store.go:683–695](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/payments/db/kv_store.go#L683-L695)
   nextPaymentSequence() has the same pattern for the payment sequence/index; channeldb/invoices.go:1208 (addIndex.NextSequence), watchtower/wtdb/client_db.go:401 (towerIndex.NextSequence) and :732 (keyIndex.Sequence) likewise.
11. [kvdb/sqlbase/readwrite\_bucket.go:84–90](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/kvdb/sqlbase/readwrite_bucket.go#L84-L90)
   Contrast: the SQL backend panics on a query error and catchPanic converts it to a transaction failure, so the same callers abort instead of writing. Only the etcd backend turns errors into 'absent'.

## Impact
Integrity: persistent counters and keyed state in the replicated channel/payment/invoice/macaroon/tower databases are silently reset or overwritten (root key replaced, attempt-ID and sequence reuse clobbering index entries, partial cursor reads). The attacker controls when but not what is written, and only transactions in flight during the outage are affected, so integrity is LOW rather than HIGH. Availability: a macaroon bake in flight locks the operator out until macaroons are re-baked; reused attempt IDs can fail payment attempts; the node keeps running. No disclosure.

## Reproduction steps
1. Requires db.backend=etcd (non-default, shipped in release builds). An adversary on the lnd-to-etcd network path blackholes the link for >=30 s (the etcd client retries Unavailable, so a single reset is absorbed; the 30 s rpcTimeout is not), then restores it: every Update whose read was in flight sees 'absent' and its subsequent write commits on the restored link. The same happens with no adversary on a 30 s etcd outage or a non-retryable error from a lagging member. The attacker does not choose which transactions are in flight.

## Recommended fix
1. kvdb/etcd bucket and cursor methods map STM DatabaseError to the 'not found' return value, so transient RPC failures are indistinguishable from absent data and the enclosing transaction continues. Fix criteria: A failed etcd read must make the enclosing Update/View fail (or retry) instead of returning nil/0: e.g. record the error on the transaction and have Commit()/runSTM refuse to commit (as sqlbase does via panic/catchPanic). After the fix, a dropped Get RPC during RootKey(), NextID() or NextSequence() must yield an error from kvdb.Update and leave the stored key/sequence unchanged.
2. stm.fetch() adds no read-set entry when the RPC fails, so the later commit has no revision guard for the key and accepts the overwrite. Fix criteria: A transaction in which any read failed must never reach a successful Txn commit; verify that commit() is not invoked (or returns an error) once the STM has observed a DatabaseError.

# Tor-mode config validation resolves custom tor.dns host via clearnet before Tor proxy is installed

## Details
lnd's Tor mode (`tor.active=1`) promises that hostname resolution and dialing go through Tor so the node's clearnet IP is not tied to its Lightning activity (config.go:1317-1321, lnd.go startup log). `ValidateConfig` breaks this for the `tor.dns` option because of an ordering defect: the Tor SOCKS, DNS and Control addresses are normalised with `cfg.net.ResolveTCPAddr` at config.go:1260-1289, but `cfg.net` is still the `&tor.ClearNet{}` from `DefaultConfig` (config.go:767); `tor.ProxyNet` is only assigned at config.go:1322-1329, after those lookups.

For `tor.socks` and `tor.control` this is unavoidable and harmless (they must be resolved before Tor is usable and are normally loopback). For `tor.dns` it is a leak: whenever the configured string differs from the exact default `soa.nodes.lightning.directory:53` (config.go:1271) — e.g. the documented example `tor.dns=nodes.lightning.directory` (sample-lnd.conf:1009), a custom seed, or even the default host written without `:53` — `lncfg.ParseAddressString` (lncfg/address.go:254-280) hands the hostname to `net.ResolveTCPAddr` (tor/net.go:70-72), i.e. the operating-system resolver. A clearnet DNS query for a Lightning-specific DNS-seed hostname leaves the node's real IP towards its recursive resolver and from there to the zone's authoritative server. The resolved `IP:53` string then replaces `cfg.Tor.DNS` and all subsequent SRV traffic is correctly carried over SOCKS (`ProxyNet.LookupSRV` -> `tor.LookupSRV` -> `dialProxy(dnsServer, socks…)`, tor/net.go:122-129, tor/tor.go:151-160), so the single startup query is the only exposure — but it repeats on every lnd start.

This is distinct from the recorded finding `lncfg-parseaddress-tor-failure-falls-back-to-system-dns-leak`, which concerns the *failure fallback* inside `ParseAddressString` when the Tor resolver is consulted and fails. Here the Tor resolver is never consulted at all, so that record's remediation (do not fall back to the system resolver when Tor cannot resolve) would not close this path. A Tor-proxied resolution was available: `tor.socks` is parsed first (config.go:1260-1267), and `tor.ResolveTCPAddr(address, socksAddr)` (tor/tor.go:204-222) needs only the SOCKS address.

Who sees it: any passive observer of the node's DNS path (ISP, recursive-resolver operator, on-path network) and the operator of the chosen seed's authoritative zone learn that this clearnet IP runs an lnd node in Tor mode and which seed it bootstraps from. The node pubkey is not disclosed, so the impact is a location/fingerprint leak (C:L), not full deanonymisation. Non-default `tor.dns` is a precondition.

## Evidence
1. [config.go:1269–1280](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/config.go#L1269-L1280)
   Primary location / fix point. When tor.dns differs from the default string, ValidateConfig calls lncfg.ParseAddressString(cfg.Tor.DNS, "53", cfg.net.ResolveTCPAddr). At this point cfg.net is still the &tor.ClearNet{} set by DefaultConfig (line 767); the Tor ProxyNet is only assigned at line 1322. So the DNS-seed hostname is sent to the operating-system resolver over clearnet from the node's real IP, even though tor.active is set. The resolved IP:port string then replaces cfg.Tor.DNS.
2. [config.go:1317–1329](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/config.go#L1317-L1329)
   ProxyNet is installed only here, after the Tor SOCKS/DNS/Control addresses were already resolved. The comment states the maintainers' guarantee: Tor-proxy functions are used 'in order to avoid leaking our real information'. The ordering defeats that guarantee for the tor.dns lookup. cfg.Tor.SOCKS was already parsed at 1260-1267, so a Tor-proxied resolution (tor.ResolveTCPAddr(address, socks)) was available for the DNS host.
3. [config.go:767](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/config.go#L767)
   DefaultConfig initialises cfg.net to &tor.ClearNet{}; this is the resolver in force during the Tor address parsing.
4. [tor/net.go:70–72](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/tor/net.go#L70-L72)
   ClearNet.ResolveTCPAddr is a direct call to net.ResolveTCPAddr, i.e. the Go system resolver (hosts file, then the configured recursive DNS over clearnet UDP/TCP).
5. [lncfg/address.go:254–280](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lncfg/address.go#L254-L280)
   For a hostname that is not an IP literal, .onion, loopback, IPv6 or unspecified, ParseAddressString invokes the supplied tcpResolver — here the clearnet one — so the hostname leaves the host as a DNS query. The Tor resolver is never consulted on this path, so the separately recorded failure-fallback defect at line 272 is not what fires here.
6. [config.go:1654–1667](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/config.go#L1654-L1667)
   Contrast: the RPC/REST listener (and, at 1725-1740, p2p listener and externalip) normalisation runs after ProxyNet is installed and therefore resolves through Tor under tor.active, showing the intended order; only the tor.* block at 1260-1289 precedes the ProxyNet switch.
7. [tor/tor.go:151–162](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/tor/tor.go#L151-L162)
   After startup, LookupSRV dials the (now numeric) DNS server through the SOCKS proxy via dialProxy, showing the design intends all DNS-seed traffic to be Tor-only; with the default (unresolved) tor.dns value Tor itself resolves the seed hostname, so the one clearnet query is the startup resolution of a custom server hostname.
8. [tor/tor.go:204–222](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/tor/tor.go#L204-L222)
   tor.ResolveTCPAddr short-circuits IP literals and otherwise resolves via Tor using only the SOCKS address — the Tor-safe alternative that could have been used since tor.socks is parsed first.
9. [lnd.go:526–529](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnd.go#L526-L529)
   With tor.active and without skip-proxy-for-clearnet-targets lnd logs 'Proxying all network traffic via Tor!'; the clearnet lookup of the tor.dns host at config time contradicts this promise with no operator opt-in.
10. [sample-lnd.conf:1007–1009](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/sample-lnd.conf#L1007-L1009)
   The shipped sample config documents example values such as tor.dns=nodes.lightning.directory and tor.dns=soa.nodes.lightning.directory:53; any string that is not byte-identical to the default 'soa.nodes.lightning.directory:53' (including the default host without ':53') takes the clearnet-resolution branch.

## Impact
Confidentiality only: the node's clearnet IP (or its resolver's IP/ISP/geography) is linked to a Lightning-DNS-seed lookup, revealing that the host runs an lnd node in Tor mode and which seed it uses — defeating the location privacy Tor mode is configured to provide. No keys, funds, channel state or node pubkey are exposed, so the loss is a single fingerprinting datum (LOW). No integrity or availability effect.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker is a passive observer on the node's DNS path (ISP/recursive resolver) or the authoritative-zone operator of the configured seed host. They need no input or privilege: every start of a tor.active lnd whose tor.dns string is not byte-identical to the default emits one clearnet DNS query for the seed hostname from the node's real IP. Preconditions outside the attacker's control: Tor mode with a non-default tor.dns value (documented examples do exactly this) and a vantage point on the DNS path, hence AT:PRESENT. No user action beyond normally running the node.

## Recommended fix
ValidateConfig resolves the operator-supplied tor.dns hostname with cfg.net while cfg.net is still tor.ClearNet; the tor.ProxyNet that is supposed to carry all name resolution under tor.active is only installed afterwards, so the Tor-only resolution guarantee is violated by ordering. Fix criteria: Under tor.active (without skip-proxy-for-clearnet-targets), no DNS query for the tor.dns host may be issued through the system resolver: either resolve it via the Tor SOCKS proxy (which is already parsed), defer resolution until ProxyNet is in place, or keep the hostname unresolved and let the Tor-proxied dial resolve it (as already happens for the default value). Verify by starting lnd with tor.active=1 and a non-default tor.dns hostname while capturing traffic on the host's DNS port: no query for that name may appear outside the SOCKS connection.

# SubscribeInvoices backlog query nests base-connection query inside read tx, exhausting native SQL pool

## Details
When `db.use-native-sql` is enabled (a supported, documented backend choice: sample-lnd.conf:1599-1605; `kvdb_sqlite`/`kvdb_postgres` are in RELEASE_TAGS, make/release_flags.mk:31), `SQLStore.InvoicesSettledSince` (invoices/sql_store.go:837) opens a read-only transaction through `i.db.ExecTx(ctx, ReadTxOpt(), ...)` and, still inside that closure, calls `i.db.FetchSettledAMPSubInvoices(...)` (line 889) instead of `db.FetchSettledAMPSubInvoices(...)` on the transaction handle. `i.db` is the `sqldb.TransactionExecutor`, whose embedded `BatchedQuerier` is `baseDB` (config_builder.go:1294-1298); `BaseDB.Queries` is `sqlc.New(db)` bound to the `*sql.DB` pool (sqldb/sqlite.go:142, sqldb/postgres.go:134), and the generated query runs `q.db.QueryContext` on it (sqldb/sqlc/amp_invoices.sql.go:183). The open `*sql.Tx` already pins one pooled connection, so the nested call must acquire a second one from the same pool; `database/sql` blocks until a connection is freed or `ctx` is cancelled.

The pool is shared by the invoice, graph and payments stores (config_builder.go:1294-1335 build all three executors on one `baseDB`) and is small: `sqldb.DefaultSqliteMaxConns = 2` (sqldb/config.go:39, applied at sqldb/sqlite.go:139; lncfg/db.go:128; sample-lnd.conf:1742), 50 for Postgres (lncfg/db.go:42, sqldb/postgres.go:126-130). `BaseDB.BeginTx` sets no timeout and the sqldb `Timeout` option is never applied to native queries (no use of it in sqldb/*.go).

Attack: a caller holding only an `invoices:read` macaroon (rpcserver.go:411-414) opens N >= pool-size concurrent `SubscribeInvoices` streams with `settle_index >= 1` (`idx == 0` returns early). `SubscribeNotifications` runs `deliverBacklogEvents` -> `InvoicesSettledSince` for each stream with no serialisation (invoiceregistry.go:1764, 498), so each stream begins a transaction (pinning one connection), iterates every settled invoice with per-row `fetchInvoiceData` calls, then blocks at line 889 waiting for a connection that only a transaction holder could release. `database/sql` hands freed connections to arbitrary waiters, so with N concurrent streams the pool converges on a state where every connection is held by a transaction whose nested query is waiting: a deadlock that persists until the attacker's stream contexts are cancelled (the gRPC stream context carries no deadline). While it holds, every other native-SQL operation blocks on the pool: `UpdateInvoice` for HTLC settlement/cancellation is called with `context.Background()` (invoiceregistry.go:1033, 1179), so links and contract-court resolvers hang indefinitely; graph reads for pathfinding, gossip writes and payment persistence stall as well. The node stops settling or failing incoming HTLCs and stops paying, risking HTLC timeout windows. The same wedge can occur accidentally when two legitimate subscribers resume with non-zero settle indexes on a SQLite node.

Dependency assumptions: for SQLite the permanent deadlock relies on modernc.org/sqlite v1.59.0 (sqldb/go.mod) issuing a plain `BEGIN` for `TxOptions.ReadOnly=true` even with `_txlock=immediate`, so two read transactions coexist in WAL mode and each pins a connection (if it issued `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` instead, the second BeginTx would fail after busy_timeout and the wedge would degrade to repeated stalls rather than a permanent deadlock). For Postgres (pgx/v5 v5.11.0) read-only SERIALIZABLE transactions always coexist, so 50 concurrent streams suffice regardless.

The lead `lead-sql-store-887-74da` asked whether this nesting is merely a consistency issue; it is a pool-exhaustion deadlock reachable by a limited-privilege RPC caller. Related but distinct from `forwardinghistory-listpayments-listinvoices-unbounded-page-size` (unbounded page size), which does not involve connection pinning.

## Evidence
1. [invoices/sql\_store.go:887–893](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/sql_store.go#L887-L893)
   Inside the ExecTx(ReadTxOpt) closure, FetchSettledAMPSubInvoices is invoked on i.db (the TransactionExecutor whose embedded BatchedQuerier is the base pool) rather than on the tx handle `db` passed to the closure; this acquires a second pooled connection while the transaction already pins one. This is the line the fix must change.
2. [invoices/sql\_store.go:836–837](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/sql_store.go#L836-L837)
   The surrounding read transaction is opened via i.db.ExecTx; its *sql.Tx pins one pooled connection for the whole closure, including the nested base call.
3. [sqldb/interfaces.go:165–171](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/sqldb/interfaces.go#L165-L171)
   TransactionExecutor embeds BatchedQuerier, so any i.db.<Query> call dispatches to the base querier (baseDB) bound to the *sql.DB pool, not to the transaction.
4. [sqldb/sqlc/amp\_invoices.sql.go:182–183](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/sqldb/sqlc/amp_invoices.sql.go#L182-L183)
   The generated FetchSettledAMPSubInvoices runs q.db.QueryContext; for the base Queries, q.db is the *sql.DB, which must check a connection out of the pool and blocks when none is free.
5. [sqldb/interfaces.go:417–423](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/sqldb/interfaces.go#L417-L423)
   BaseDB.BeginTx calls sql.DB.BeginTx with ReadOnly from ReadTxOpt and no timeout; the *sql.Tx pins a pool connection until Commit/Rollback.
6. [invoices/sql\_store.go:159–161](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/sql_store.go#L159-L161)
   FetchSettledAMPSubInvoices is a member of the SQLInvoiceQueries interface, so the transaction handle `db` could have been used; the base-connection call is an oversight, not a necessity.
7. [sqldb/config.go:33–65](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/sqldb/config.go#L33-L65)
   DefaultSqliteMaxConns = 2 and MaxConns() returns it when unset; lncfg DefaultDB sets Sqlite.MaxConnections to this value, so the native SQLite pool holds two connections by default.
8. [sqldb/sqlite.go:139–142](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/sqldb/sqlite.go#L139-L142)
   SetMaxOpenConns(cfg.MaxConns()) caps the shared pool at 2 for SQLite, and sqlc.New(db) binds the base Queries to that *sql.DB (50 via defaultPostgresMaxConnections for Postgres, sqldb/postgres.go:126-130).
9. [config\_builder.go:1294–1334](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/config_builder.go#L1294-L1334)
   The invoice, graph and payments executors are all built on the same baseDB (one *sql.DB pool), so exhausting it wedges every native SQL store, not just invoices.
10. [invoices/invoiceregistry.go:1759–1767](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/invoiceregistry.go#L1759-L1767)
   SubscribeNotifications calls deliverBacklogEvents -> InvoicesSettledSince (invoiceregistry.go:498) with no mutex held, so N concurrent subscribers run N concurrent read transactions.
11. [invoices/invoiceregistry.go:1179–1180](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/invoiceregistry.go#L1179-L1180)
   HTLC settlement/cancellation calls UpdateInvoice with context.Background(), so once the pool is pinned these updates block indefinitely rather than failing, stalling HTLC resolution.
12. [rpcserver.go:6050–6055](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/rpcserver.go#L6050-L6055)
   SubscribeInvoices passes the caller-chosen settle_index straight into SubscribeNotifications with the stream context (no deadline); any value >= 1 reaches the vulnerable path (idx == 0 returns early).
13. [rpcserver.go:411–413](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/rpcserver.go#L411-L413)
   The entry point requires only the invoices:read macaroon permission.

## Impact
All native SQL stores (invoices, graph, payments) share the exhausted pool, so HTLC settlement/cancellation on invoices, pathfinding, gossip persistence and payment persistence stall indefinitely while the streams stay open; links and contract-court resolvers block on invoice updates, so the node cannot resolve incoming HTLCs before expiry. No confidentiality or integrity impact.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker: RPC client with an invoices:read macaroon (or any admin), over gRPC/REST. Delivery: open two (SQLite default pool) or fifty (Postgres default) concurrent SubscribeInvoices streams with settle_index=1 and keep them open. Each handler pins a pool connection in a read tx, then blocks at sql_store.go:889 waiting for another; once the pool is fully pinned no connection is ever released. No defence mechanism intervenes; the only precondition is the non-default db.use-native-sql deployment with sqlite/postgres backend.

## Recommended fix
1. InvoicesSettledSince executes a query on the base connection pool (i.db) from inside an open transaction closure, violating the invariant that all work inside ExecTx uses the transaction handle and that a transaction never waits on the pool it is pinning. Fix criteria: Inside the ExecTx closure, FetchSettledAMPSubInvoices (and every other query) must run on the transaction handle `db`. Verify by auditing that no `i.db.<Query>` call occurs inside any ExecTx closure in the SQL stores, and that opening pool-size concurrent SubscribeInvoices streams with settle_index>=1 completes without blocking other store operations.
2. The sqldb executor offers no guard against pool-pinning misuse: BeginTx has no acquisition timeout and the sqldb Timeout setting is not applied to native queries, so a nested acquisition hangs forever instead of failing. Fix criteria: A query that cannot obtain a pool connection within a bounded time must fail with an error rather than wait indefinitely (e.g. apply the configured store timeout to native transactions/queries), so that a pool-exhaustion bug degrades to errors that unwind rather than a permanent node-wide stall.

# Prometheus exporter serves DefaultServeMux, exposing pprof debug endpoints unauthenticated

## Details
When Prometheus export is enabled (--prometheus.enable; lncfg.Prometheus, compiled in by the `monitoring` tag that is part of RELEASE_TAGS and of the Dockerfile's `make release-install`), lnd starts its metrics server with http.ListenAndServe(cfg.Listen, nil) (monitoring/monitoring_on.go:46-48). A nil handler selects http.DefaultServeMux. lnd.go:14 imports net/http/pprof (non-blank, for pprof.Index etc.), so that package's init() has already registered the /debug/pprof/ index, cmdline, profile, symbol and trace handlers on DefaultServeMux (Go stdlib behaviour; go.mod pins go 1.26.8, where the patterns are registered as 'GET /debug/pprof/...'). Every pprof endpoint is therefore served on the Prometheus port, in plaintext and unauthenticated, regardless of whether --profile is set.

This bypasses the shipped control for this surface: lnd.go:218-266 builds a private http.NewServeMux() for the opt-in --profile feature precisely so that pprof is reachable only on the explicitly configured profiling address. The Prometheus listener, enabled for an unrelated purpose, re-exposes it. No documentation tells operators to fence the metrics port; sample-lnd.conf:630-634 gives prometheus.listen=0.0.0.0:8989 as the example (default is 127.0.0.1:8989, lncfg/monitoring_on.go:30).

Condition: holds when prometheus.enable=true and the listener is reachable by the attacker (any non-loopback bind, as in the sample config example; on the loopback default only same-host clients are affected).

What an unauthenticated client on that port obtains:
- /debug/pprof/cmdline: os.Args verbatim. The repository's own container entrypoint docker/lnd/start-lnd.sh:66-90 passes --bitcoind.rpcpass / --btcd.rpcpass on the command line; --db.postgres.dsn, --db.etcd.pass and --tor.password are likewise CLI flags (lncfg/bitcoind.go:21, lncfg/btcd.go:10, kvdb/postgres/config.go:9, kvdb/etcd/config.go:21, lncfg/tor.go:14). These are credentials to the chain backend and database that the node's funds safety depends on.
- /debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=2, /debug/pprof/heap and the index: full goroutine stacks, allocation sites, internal paths and exact build fingerprint.
- /debug/pprof/profile?seconds=N and /debug/pprof/trace?seconds=N: start CPU profiling / execution tracing on demand; goroutine and heap dumps stop the world. Repeated requests impose sustained overhead on a daemon whose timeliness (HTLC and breach deadlines) is funds-relevant.

The server also runs with package-level http defaults (no ReadHeaderTimeout, unlike the --profile server at lnd.go:252-256), but the material defect is the unintended pprof surface. Related, distinct record: the dismissal dismissed-lnd-218-93cd concerns the explicit --profile listener (operator opt-in); this finding is pprof leaking onto a port the operator enabled for a different purpose.

## Evidence
1. [monitoring/monitoring\_on.go:46–48](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/monitoring/monitoring_on.go#L46-L48)
   The exporter registers /metrics on the global http.DefaultServeMux and calls http.ListenAndServe(cfg.Listen, nil); a nil handler means every pattern registered on DefaultServeMux by any package init() is served on the Prometheus port, with no TLS, auth, or request timeouts.
2. [lnd.go:14](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnd.go#L14)
   The lnd package imports net/http/pprof. That package's init() unconditionally registers /debug/pprof/, /debug/pprof/cmdline, /debug/pprof/profile, /debug/pprof/symbol and /debug/pprof/trace on http.DefaultServeMux, so they are present on the Prometheus listener whether or not --profile is set.
3. [lnd.go:218–266](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnd.go#L218-L266)
   For the opt-in --profile feature the maintainers build a dedicated http.NewServeMux(), register the pprof handlers on it and serve it with its own http.Server (with ReadHeaderTimeout) bound to the operator-chosen profiling address; this is the shipped control that confines pprof to an explicit opt-in port. Serving DefaultServeMux from the Prometheus exporter goes around it.
4. [make/release\_flags.mk:31](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/make/release_flags.mk#L31)
   The 'monitoring' build tag is part of RELEASE_TAGS, so monitoring_on.go is compiled into the shipped lnd binaries (and Docker images), not only into developer builds.
5. [lncfg/monitoring\_on.go:28–32](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lncfg/monitoring_on.go#L28-L32)
   Default listen address is 127.0.0.1:8989; sample-lnd.conf:630-634 documents prometheus.listen=0.0.0.0:8989 as the example for scraping from another host, which is the common deployment for a metrics exporter.
6. [docker/lnd/start-lnd.sh:66–89](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/docker/lnd/start-lnd.sh#L66-L89)
   The repository's own container entrypoint passes --<backend>.rpcuser and --<backend>.rpcpass on the lnd command line. /debug/pprof/cmdline returns argv verbatim, so in this deployment the chain backend RPC credentials are readable by anyone who can reach the metrics port.

## Impact
Confidentiality: process argv (which the project's own container entrypoint fills with the chain backend RPC password, and which may carry the postgres DSN, etcd password or Tor control password), goroutine stacks and heap allocation sites are disclosed; wallet seed/keys and macaroon root key are not dumped, so LOW rather than HIGH. Integrity: none. Availability: on-demand CPU profiling, execution tracing and stop-the-world goroutine/heap dumps can be triggered repeatedly by any client, degrading a daemon whose timeliness is funds-relevant - LOW (degradation, not outage). Subsequent-system impact: Where credentials are passed on the command line - as docker/lnd/start-lnd.sh does for the bitcoind/btcd RPC password - /debug/pprof/cmdline hands the attacker the chain backend's RPC credentials; if the attacker can also reach that RPC port they gain read access to the backend's state and can stop it, invalidate blocks or disturb the mempool lnd relies on. Rated LOW across because it is conditional on that deployment style and on separate reachability of the backend.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker: anyone who can open a TCP connection to the Prometheus listen address. Delivery: plain HTTP GET to http://host:8989/debug/pprof/cmdline (or goroutine, heap, profile, trace). No credentials, TLS or user interaction. Preconditions outside the attacker's control: prometheus.enable=true (feature off by default) and the listener bound to an interface the attacker can reach (default loopback; the sample config's example is 0.0.0.0:8989 and no doc tells the operator to fence it) - hence attack requirements PRESENT. Assumes Go stdlib net/http/pprof init() registration on DefaultServeMux (go 1.26.8 per go.mod).

## Recommended fix
1. monitoring_on.go serves http.DefaultServeMux (nil handler), inheriting every handler any imported package registered globally — in particular net/http/pprof's debug endpoints — on the metrics port. Fix criteria: The Prometheus listener must serve only the metrics handler: a dedicated mux (or http.Server with an explicit Handler) that exposes /metrics and nothing else, with sane header/read timeouts. Verification: with prometheus.enable=true and --profile unset, GET /debug/pprof/cmdline on the Prometheus port returns 404 and no pprof routes are reachable there.
2. Importing net/http/pprof registers handlers on the global default mux as a side effect, so any future use of DefaultServeMux in lnd re-exposes pprof. Fix criteria: lnd should not depend on DefaultServeMux anywhere, or should guarantee pprof is never registered on it (e.g. only register pprof handlers explicitly on the --profile mux). Verification: http.DefaultServeMux has no /debug/pprof routes at runtime in a release build.
