# Session key-index reservation key truncates TowerID to its zero high bytes, sharing reservations across towers

## Details
The watchtower client reserves a session-key derivation index per tower before negotiating, so that a session identity shown to one tower is never reused with another (NextSessionKeyIndex docstring, client_db.go:698-703; comment at 1048-1052: 'created as tower-id||blob-type'). createSessionKeyIndexKey (client_db.go:1053-1062) builds that key with `copy(keyBytes[:4], towerID.Bytes())`. TowerID.Bytes() (tower.go:44-49) is the 8-byte big-endian encoding and tower IDs are small bucket sequence numbers (towerIndex.NextSequence(), client_db.go:401), so the four bytes copied are the always-zero high half. Every tower therefore maps to the identical key 00000000||blobType and the 'per-tower' reservation is a single global slot per blob type.

Traced through the negotiator (session_negotiator.go:300-335): NextSessionKeyIndex(towerA, bt, false) hands out index N; createSession derives P_N and tryAddress (399-460) dials tower A with P_N as the brontide static key, so A learns P_N in handshake Act 3 (brontide/noise.go:701) before any CreateSession reply. If the attempt with A fails for anything other than AlreadyExists (A returns a reject code, drops the connection, times out, or the client-side CreateClientSession fails after CodeOK), the reservation is left in place and the negotiator moves to the next candidate B. NextSessionKeyIndex(towerB, bt, false) finds N under the shared key and returns it; the client creates its session with B under the same identity P_N (the tower uses the remote static pubkey as the SessionID, wtserver/server.go:219), and CreateClientSession then deletes the reservation.

Impact: the per-session ephemeral key is the protocol's mechanism for limiting tower-side tracking (docs/watchtower.md:19-22). After any failover, the tower A that saw P_N (and, if it had replied CodeOK, holds an idle server-side session P_N) and the tower B that holds the live session P_N can deterministically link the two observations as the same client — a link the per-tower reservation exists to prevent and which, when the client connects over Tor, no other observable (source IP) provides. A registered hostile tower can force this on every negotiation simply by rejecting CreateSession. A holds no backup data under P_N, so what is linked is the client's attempt at A (time, policy, network path) with its live session at B; no blobs, hints, keys or funds are exposed. Integrity and availability are unaffected: CreateClientSession rejects duplicate SessionIDs and the negotiator is serial per blob type, so no two stored client sessions share an index. Distinct root cause from wtclient-negotiator-alreadyexists-unbounded-loop-key-index-exhaustion, which concerns the bucket-wide sequence, not the reservation key. The unit test (client_db_test.go:383-397) exercises one tower only and does not catch the loss of isolation.

## Evidence
1. [watchtower/wtdb/client\_db.go:1053–1061](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtdb/client_db.go#L1053-L1061)
   createSessionKeyIndexKey builds the 'tower-id||blob-type' key by copying towerID.Bytes()[0:4] into keyBytes[:4]. TowerID.Bytes() (tower.go:45-49) is the 8-byte big-endian encoding, so bytes 0..3 are the most-significant half, which is 0x00000000 for every tower ID the DB ever assigns (towerIndex.NextSequence() at client_db.go:401 starts at 1). The resulting key is therefore 00000000||blobType for all towers: the reservation is global per blob type, not per tower as the function and the NextSessionKeyIndex docstring (lines 698-703) state.
2. [watchtower/wtdb/client\_db.go:715–724](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtdb/client_db.go#L715-L724)
   NextSessionKeyIndex with forceNext=false first calls getSessionKeyIndex(keyIndex, towerID, blobType); because the key ignores the tower, a reservation left behind by a failed negotiation with tower A is returned verbatim to tower B, so both towers are handed the same key index and hence the same session key/SessionID.
3. [watchtower/wtdb/client\_db.go:1064–1089](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtdb/client_db.go#L1064-L1089)
   getSessionKeyIndex looks up the truncated key; only the legacy fallback for TypeAltruistCommit (towerID.Bytes(), full 8 bytes) is actually tower-specific, showing the per-tower intent that the new format lost.
4. [watchtower/wtclient/session\_negotiator.go:300–334](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtclient/session_negotiator.go#L300-L334)
   On any createSession error other than ErrSessionKeyAlreadyUsed the negotiator goes to retryWithBackoff/tryNextCandidate and calls NextSessionKeyIndex(nextTower.ID, blobType, false) for the next tower without releasing the previous reservation; that call returns the index already shown to the failed tower.
5. [watchtower/wtclient/session\_negotiator.go:399–459](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtclient/session_negotiator.go#L399-L459)
   tryAddress dials the tower with the derived session key (brontide Noise_XK reveals the client's static session pubkey to the tower in Act 3) before CreateSession is answered, so a tower that rejects the session (codes RejectBlobType/MaxUpdates/RewardRate/SweepFeeRate, or simply closing the connection) has already learned the session pubkey that will subsequently be reused with the next tower.
6. [watchtower/wtdb/tower.go:44–48](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtdb/tower.go#L44-L48)
   TowerID.Bytes() is big-endian, so the first four bytes copied by createSessionKeyIndexKey are the always-zero high half.

## Impact
Confidentiality: a session identity shown to one tower is reused with the next, so colluding or co-operated towers (or a tower whose CodeOK reply was lost and therefore holds the same SessionID) can deterministically link the client's attempt at one tower to its live session at another, defeating the per-tower unlinkability the design and docs intend — low, because the rejecting tower holds no backup data under the reused key and the link ties one attempt to one session. Integrity: none, duplicate SessionIDs are rejected and the negotiator is serial per blob type. Availability: none.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker is a watchtower the victim has registered (the threat model's lying-tower adversary) that colludes with, or also operates, a second tower the victim has registered; the victim must have at least two towers configured so negotiation fails over. The hostile tower completes the brontide handshake (learning the session pubkey) and returns any CreateSession reject code or drops the connection; the client's next candidate tower receives the session under the identical pubkey. No privileges on the victim and no user interaction; the attack requirement is the attacker's position at two of the victim's towers.

## Recommended fix
createSessionKeyIndexKey copies the high (always zero) four bytes of the 8-byte big-endian TowerID, so the reservation key does not depend on the tower and the per-tower reservation invariant documented for NextSessionKeyIndex does not hold. Fix criteria: The reservation key must be unique per (tower, blob type): reserving an index for tower A and then calling NextSessionKeyIndex for tower B with the same blob type must return a different index, and a session key index shown to one tower must never be used to create a session with another tower. Existing on-disk reservations under the degenerate key must be handled (migrated or invalidated) so that the fix does not strand them. Verify with a test that reserves for two towers and asserts distinct indexes.

# Native-SQL graph store regroups node addresses by type, so relayed node_announcements carry a signature over a different address order

## Details
When lnd runs with db.use-native-sql=true (sample-lnd.conf:1600-1605; config_builder.go:1123 selects graphdb.NewSQLStore for the graph), the graph store does not preserve the cross-type order of a node_announcement's address list. collectAddressRecords (graph/db/sql_store.go:4835-4876) buckets addresses into per-type lists and upsertNodeAddresses (:4878-4917) stores (node_id, type, position) with position meaningful only within a type; GetNodeAddresses/GetNodeAddressesBatch (sqldb/sqlc/queries/graph.sql:215-227) read them back ORDER BY type, position; buildNodeAddresses (:6100-6124) rebuilds node.Addresses in that type-sorted order while buildNodeWithBatchData attaches the stored AuthSigBytes unchanged. The schema comment (000008_graph.up.sql:79-83) and upsertNodeAddresses' comment state the intent to keep the order 'so that the signature of the announcement remains valid'; the implementation only does so within a type.

BOLT 7 requires senders to place address descriptors in ascending type order, but lnd's decoder (lnwire/lnwire.go:721-764, ReadAddress :834) and netann.ValidateNodeAnnFields (:98-121) accept any order, and the gossiper's addNode (discovery/gossiper.go:2191-2202) verifies the signature over the wire order and then stores the message verbatim. The announcement is only accepted for a node already in the channel graph (graph/builder.go:931-950), so the attacker needs one announced public channel. A remote node can therefore send a validly signed node_announcement with addresses e.g. [onion_v3, ipv4]; the victim verifies and stores it, and every DB-backed re-encoding — ChanSeries.UpdatesInHorizon for gossip_timestamp_range syncs (discovery/chan_series.go:186-205) and FetchChanAnns for query_short_channel_ids replies (:300-345, which runs only ValidateNodeAnnFields, not a signature check, before sending) — emits [ipv4, onion_v3] under the original signature via models.Node.NodeAnnouncement (graph/db/models/node.go:193-228). The immediate re-broadcast of the received wire message is unaffected; the kv store (graph/db/addr.go SerializeAddr loop, kv_store.go:4708) preserves slice order, so this is a native-SQL-only divergence.

Consequence: a native-SQL lnd serves, to every peer that syncs from it, node_announcements whose signatures do not verify, and its stored copy of the announcement differs from what was signed. Receiving lnd peers log an error and drop the message (gossiper handleNodeAnnouncement; the ban manager only scores channel-announcement failures, handleBadPeer :4047), so against lnd peers the effect is that the affected node's address information does not propagate through the victim and the victim is logged as a source of invalid gossip; how CLN/LDK/Eclair treat a peer sending invalid-signature gossip (warning, possible disconnect) is a dependency behaviour not verified in this checkout. The same defect makes the victim's own announcement fail signature verification when served from the store if its externalip list is not type-sorted (lnd does not sort self addresses: lncfg.NormalizeAddresses, server.go:5757), though that is operator-driven rather than attacker-driven. No funds, confidentiality or availability impact on the vulnerable node itself; integrity of relayed signed gossip is degraded.

## Evidence
1. [graph/db/sql\_store.go:4835–4876](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/sql_store.go#L4835-L4876)
   collectAddressRecords buckets the announcement's addresses into per-type lists (IPv4, IPv6, TorV2, TorV3, DNS, opaque), discarding the cross-type order they had on the wire; position is only tracked within a type. This is the code the fix must change.
2. [graph/db/sql\_store.go:4878–4917](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/sql_store.go#L4878-L4917)
   upsertNodeAddresses writes (node_id, type, position) rows from those buckets; its comment claims the original order is preserved so the signature stays valid, but only intra-type order is.
3. [sqldb/sqlc/queries/graph.sql:215–226](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/sqldb/sqlc/queries/graph.sql#L215-L226)
   GetNodeAddresses / GetNodeAddressesBatch return rows ORDER BY type, position, so on read the addresses always come back sorted by type regardless of wire order.
4. [graph/db/sql\_store.go:6100–6124](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/sql_store.go#L6100-L6124)
   buildNodeAddresses rebuilds node.Addresses in that type-sorted order; buildNodeWithBatchData (:4385-4445) attaches the stored AuthSigBytes unchanged.
5. [graph/db/models/node.go:193–228](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/models/node.go#L193-L228)
   Node.NodeAnnouncement(true) re-encodes Addresses in stored slice order and attaches AuthSigBytes, producing a message whose signature no longer covers its content.
6. [discovery/chan\_series.go:300–344](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/chan_series.go#L300-L344)
   FetchChanAnns (query_short_channel_ids replies) sends the DB-reconstructed node announcement after only ValidateNodeAnnFields (DNS check), with no signature re-check; UpdatesInHorizon (:186-205) yields it with no check at all.
7. [discovery/gossiper.go:2191–2202](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/gossiper.go#L2191-L2202)
   addNode verifies the signature over the wire-order address list and stores the message verbatim via models.NodeFromWireAnnouncement; no type-order enforcement.
8. [lnwire/lnwire.go:721–764](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwire/lnwire.go#L721-L764)
   The wire decoder accepts address descriptors in any type order (no ascending-type check), so a remote announcement with e.g. [tor, ipv4] is accepted and signature-verified in that order.
9. [netann/node\_announcement.go:98–149](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/netann/node_announcement.go#L98-L149)
   ValidateNodeAnnFields checks only the DNS address constraint; ValidateNodeAnnSignature verifies over DataToSign(), which serialises Addresses in slice order.
10. [graph/builder.go:931–949](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/builder.go#L931-L949)
   assertNodeAnnFreshness ignores announcements for nodes not in the channel graph, so the attacker needs one announced public channel (attack requirement).
11. [config\_builder.go:1123](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/config_builder.go#L1123)
   The production build selects the native-SQL graph store when db.use-native-sql is set; the defect is reachable only in that configuration.
12. [graph/db/addr.go:311–325](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/addr.go#L311-L325)
   The kv store sibling serialises addresses one by one in slice order (SerializeAddr), preserving wire order; the SQL store diverges.

## Impact
Integrity (low): the node persists an address list that differs from the one it verified and relays node announcements whose signature does not verify to every syncing peer, so the affected node's addresses are blocked at this relay and the victim appears to peers as a source of invalid gossip. lnd peers only log and drop such messages; no confidentiality or availability impact on the vulnerable node.

## Reproduction steps
1. Any gossip node with one announced public channel sends a validly signed node_announcement whose addresses are not in ascending type order; lnd accepts it (no ordering check on receipt) and the native-SQL store regroups them. Every later DB-backed re-encoding by the victim (gossip_timestamp_range sync, query_short_channel_ids replies) carries a signature that no longer verifies. No authentication or interaction needed; requires the victim to run the non-default db.use-native-sql=true backend.

## Recommended fix
1. graph_node_addresses records order only within a type bucket, so the signed cross-type order of the announcement is lost and the stored signature no longer matches the data reconstructed from the store. Fix criteria: The store round-trips the exact address order covered by the signature (e.g. a global position across all address types, with reads ordered by that position), and an accepted announcement with [onion_v3, ipv4] re-serialises via Node.NodeAnnouncement(true) to bytes that verify under the stored signature.
2. Ingestion accepts address lists that violate BOLT 7's ascending-type ordering without either rejecting them or guaranteeing lossless storage. Fix criteria: Either announcements whose addresses are not in ascending type order are rejected at ingest (making type-sorted storage lossless), or the DB-backed serving paths (ChanSeries.UpdatesInHorizon, FetchChanAnns) re-verify the reconstructed announcement's signature and skip ones that fail rather than relaying them.

# Failure-embedded channel_update skips gossip future-timestamp check; node relays it and is ban-scored by peers

## Details
lnd applies channel_updates found in onion failure messages to its public graph through a side door that lacks the timestamp plausibility check applied to gossip. routing/payment_lifecycle.go handleFailureMessage passes the update extracted from any non-local failure source (intermediate hop or payee; failure codes listed in routing/router.go extractChannelUpdate) to Builder.ApplyChannelUpdate (graph/builder.go:982). ApplyChannelUpdate verifies the signature against the channel's stored node key for the flagged direction and validates max_htlc, then calls updateEdge, which only requires the timestamp to be strictly newer than the stored one and persists LastUpdate = time.Unix(uint32 Timestamp) with no upper bound (graph/db has no future/skew check). The gossiper's handleChanUpdate, by contrast, rejects any remote update whose timestamp is more than DefaultChannelPruneExpiry (14 days) in the future and increments the ban score of the peer that delivered it (discovery/gossiper.go:3227-3251).

Attack: a routing node Y (any hop on a route we chose, or the payee) with at least one public channel in our graph fails our HTLC with e.g. FailTemporaryChannelFailure carrying a channel_update for Y's own channel direction, validly signed by Y, with Timestamp set decades ahead (up to the uint32 maximum, 2106). Our node persists it.

Consequences:
1. Relay and ban shifted onto us. We re-serve stored policies verbatim: netann.ChannelUpdateFromEdge rebuilds the wire message from policy.LastUpdate and policy.SigBytes, and ChanSeries.UpdatesInHorizon only filters on AuthProof and max_htlc fields. Every lnd peer that selects us as an active or pinned syncer sends gossip_timestamp_range (now, math.MaxUint32) (discovery/syncer.go:786-788, 2037-2039), so ApplyGossipFilter's horizon ends ~136 years out and the far-future policy is included in each backlog dump; anyone sending query_short_channel_ids for the SCID receives it too (FetchChanAnns). The receiving lnd node runs IsStaleEdgePolicy (false, since it never accepted the update) and then the future check, treats us as the bad peer and calls handleBadPeer: +1 ban score per message (discovery/ban.go:249). This rejection path does not populate recentRejects (puts exist only at gossiper.go:3141, 3343, 3466), so every re-sync re-increments, and the score only resets after 48 h without increments (resetDelta). At DefaultBanThreshold=100 (config.go:838) a Y controlling ~100 public channel directions bans us at a peer after one sync; smaller Y's accumulate across the peer's reconnects. A banned node is disconnected by non-channel peers (gossiper.go:4062) and its inbound connections are refused for 48 h (accessman.go:150-164 ErrGossiperBan, server.go:4497-4510 conn.Close()), degrading our gossip connectivity and bootstrap ability. Via the sanctioned gossip path the same message would be dropped and Y, not us, would be ban-scored.
2. Uncorrectable graph entry. The far-future LastUpdate wins every later monotonicity comparison in both updateEdge and IsStaleEdgePolicy, so Y's genuine later updates (e.g. disabling the channel, changing fees) are rejected as outdated, and isPolicyZombie never considers the direction stale, so with default non-strict pruning the channel is never zombie-pruned. Our pathfinding keeps using Y's policy of choice until an on-chain close is observed.

The fix belongs to the router entry (routing/payment_lifecycle.go:1021 / Builder.ApplyChannelUpdate) and to the graph layer: a failure-embedded update must meet the same timestamp plausibility bound as gossip, and the graph should never persist or relay a policy whose LastUpdate is far in the future.

## Evidence
1. [routing/payment\_lifecycle.go:957–1025](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/payment_lifecycle.go#L957-L1025)
   handleFailureMessage takes the channel_update extracted from a remote hop's onion failure (any errorSourceIdx > 0, intermediate or final hop) and hands it straight to cfg.ApplyChannelUpdate, bypassing the gossiper's handleChanUpdate pipeline that all other channel_updates pass through.
2. [graph/builder.go:982–1029](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/builder.go#L982-L1029)
   ApplyChannelUpdate validates only the signature against the stored key for the flagged direction and the max_htlc fields, then calls UpdateEdge. No plausibility check on msg.Timestamp.
3. [graph/builder.go:1194–1278](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/builder.go#L1194-L1278)
   updateEdge accepts any policy whose LastUpdate is strictly newer than the stored one (lines 1241-1263) and persists it with UpdateEdgePolicy. There is no upper bound on LastUpdate, so a timestamp decades in the future is stored and permanently wins the monotonicity check against all later genuine updates.
4. [discovery/gossiper.go:3225–3251](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/gossiper.go#L3225-L3251)
   The gossip path rejects a channel_update whose timestamp is more than DefaultChannelPruneExpiry (14 days) in the future and calls handleBadPeer on the peer that delivered it (ban score +1, disconnect if not a channel peer). This is both the check the router path bypasses and the penalty our node later incurs when it relays the stored update. This rejection path does not populate recentRejects, so each relayed copy re-increments the score.
5. [discovery/syncer.go:1613–1659](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/syncer.go#L1613-L1659)
   ApplyGossipFilter serves every stored policy with LastUpdate in [FirstTimestamp, FirstTimestamp+TimestampRange) to the requesting peer via ChanSeries.UpdatesInHorizon; lnd active and pinned syncers request (now, math.MaxUint32) (syncer.go:786-788 and 2037-2039), so a far-future policy is included in every backlog dump to such peers. The relay filter (chan_series.go ValidateChannelUpdateFields) checks only max_htlc fields, not the timestamp.
6. [netann/channel\_update.go:165–179](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/netann/channel_update.go#L165-L179)
   ChannelUpdateFromEdge rebuilds the wire message from the stored policy, using policy.LastUpdate as Timestamp and policy.SigBytes as the signature, so the relayed message is byte-identical to the attacker-signed far-future update.
7. [discovery/ban.go:249–266](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/ban.go#L249-L266)
   incrementBanScore adds 1 per bad message; DefaultBanThreshold is 100 and a banned non-channel peer is disconnected (gossiper.go:4048-4066) and refused on reconnect for banTime=48h via accessman.assignPeerPerms (accessman.go:150-164, ErrGossiperBan).
8. [routing/router.go:1306–1327](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/router.go#L1306-L1327)
   extractChannelUpdate: the failure codes (ExpiryTooSoon, AmountBelowMinimum, FeeInsufficient, IncorrectCltvExpiry, ChannelDisabled, TemporaryChannelFailure) through which any remote hop can attach a channel_update to a payment failure.

## Impact
Integrity: our graph DB persistently holds an attacker-chosen policy for the attacker's channel directions that no later legitimate update can replace and that zombie pruning never removes, skewing pathfinding. Availability: our node emits protocol-invalid gossip and is ban-scored by every lnd peer that syncs the poisoned updates from us (active/pinned syncers and SCID queriers); at threshold 100 non-channel peers disconnect us and refuse our connections for 48 h, degrading gossip connectivity. Reach is limited to gossip connectivity with non-channel peers; channel peers are never disconnected by the ban. No confidentiality impact.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker is any Lightning node we route a payment through, or a payee we pay; both can return onion failures carrying a channel_update (threat model: downstream nodes control failure bytes). It needs one public channel known to our graph and signs an update for its own direction with a far-future timestamp, returning it in a TemporaryChannelFailure/FeeInsufficient/etc. Our router applies it with only a signature check. No privileges or user interaction; the requirement is being on one of our payment routes with a public channel, and reaching the ban threshold at a given peer needs ~100 such directions or accumulation across that peer's re-syncs within 48 h windows.

## Recommended fix
1. Channel updates obtained from payment failures reach the graph via Builder.ApplyChannelUpdate without the timestamp plausibility bound the gossiper enforces, so a validly signed far-future update is persisted. Fix criteria: An update delivered through a payment failure whose timestamp is further in the future than the gossip bound (DefaultChannelPruneExpiry) must be rejected before UpdateEdge; verify by returning such an update in a failure and confirming the stored policy's LastUpdate is unchanged and nothing is served to a syncing peer.
2. updateEdge/UpdateEdgePolicy accept any strictly-newer LastUpdate and the relay path serves stored policies verbatim, so a single far-future value permanently blocks genuine updates and is relayed to peers who ban-score this node. Fix criteria: The graph layer must refuse to persist a policy whose LastUpdate exceeds now plus the accepted skew regardless of caller, and the sync/relay path must never send a channel_update a compliant peer would reject on timestamp; verify that after the attack a later genuine update from the channel owner is applied and that a peer's handleChanUpdate does not flag our node.

# Legacy HTLC success path ignores counterparty timeout spend; resolver and nursery stall forever

## Details
On non-anchor channels (legacy and static-remote-key/'tweakless' types, which lnd still accepts today: funding/commitment_type_negotiation.go:228-232 accepts an explicit StaticRemoteKeyRequired-only channel_type and :485-491 falls back to CommitmentTypeTweakless whenever the peer withholds the anchors feature bit), HtlcSignDetails returns nil (lnwallet/commitment.go:393-397), so an incoming HTLC on our own commitment for which we hold the preimage is resolved by htlcSuccessResolver.Resolve's default branch, resolveLegacySuccessTx: it publishes the presigned, fixed-fee HTLC-success transaction and hands the second-level output to the UTXO nursery as a preschool output. Neither component accounts for the fact that the counterparty can spend the same HTLC output through the CLTV timeout path (their own signature only, valid once cltv_expiry has passed). The legacy success tx cannot be fee-bumped (SignDetails nil, its only output CSV-locked) and carries nSequence 0 (lnwallet/commitment.go:408-414), i.e. it is BIP125-replaceable, so if it has not confirmed by expiry the counterparty's higher-fee timeout spend replaces it; lnd's own htlcTimeoutResolver.sweepDirectHtlcOutput does exactly this with a deadline-driven sweeper budget, so an ordinary lnd counterparty triggers the condition whenever our success tx is still unconfirmed at expiry, and a deliberate one can hold the commitment feerate low as initiator and then outbid.

When the counterparty's spend wins, every path stalls deterministically:

1. If the counterparty's spend is already confirmed (or conflicting in the mempool) when the resolver runs - including on every restart, and including the HtlcClaimAction case where the preimage was known at close and no expiry check precedes the success resolver: PublishTx -> testmempoolaccept rejects -> mapRpcclientError returns lnwallet.ErrDoubleSpend -> resolveLegacySuccessTx returns the error. ChannelArbitrator.resolveContract logs 'unable to progress' and the goroutine exits; handleBlockbeat's launchResolvers() on later blocks only calls Launch(), whose default branch is a no-op for this path. The resolver never checkpoints, never calls PutFinalHtlcOutcome/NotifyFinalHtlcEvent, and never resolves.

2. If our success tx made it to the mempool and was then replaced: the nursery's registerPreschoolConf/waitForPreschoolConf wait for a confirmation of our success txid that can never come (they never watch the HTLC input for a competing spend, unlike waitForSweepConf's ErrRemoteSpend handling), and the resolver's resolveSuccessTxOutput waits via waitForSpend for a spend of ClaimOutpoint, an output that will never exist. After a restart, outputIncubating is true but the publish at line 925 runs first and fails as in (1); reloadPreschool re-registers the dead confirmation each time.

Consequences: the channel arbitrator stays in StateWaitingFullResolution forever, ChainArbitrator.ResolveContract/MarkChanFullyClosed is never called so the close summary remains pending and the arbitrator and chain watcher are recreated on every start, the HTLC's final outcome is never recorded, the nursery channel bucket is never removed (IsMatureChannel requires all-grad), PendingChannels reports the HTLC value as limbo indefinitely (rpcserver.go:4670-4684 takes LimboBalance from NurseryReport), and each start repeats the failing publish and leaves a blocked goroutine plus a notifier registration for the process lifetime. The anchor-channel sibling (resolveSuccessTx) handles this exact case via waitForSpend + matchSecondLevelOutput + checkpointForeignSpend; the legacy path and the nursery have no equivalent. The HTLC value itself is lost to the on-chain race (a protocol property of non-anchor channels), not to this defect; the defect is the permanent, counterparty-triggerable liveness failure of the channel's resolution and its unbounded repetition across restarts. The only operator remedy is AbandonChannel with i_know_what_i_am_doing (rpcserver.go:3305-3306), which discards the channel's history.

This resolves ledger lead lead-htlc-success-resolver-882-7bfc. Assumes btcwallet v0.16.20-pre's chain.MapRPCErr maps bitcoind/btcd 'missing-inputs'/'bad-txns-inputs-missingorspent'/'txn-mempool-conflict' reject reasons to chain.ErrMissingInputs / chain.ErrMempoolConflict, as lnd's mapping at btcwallet.go:1289-1297 expects; the stall in case (2) does not depend on that mapping.

## Evidence
1. [contractcourt/htlc\_success\_resolver.go:912–957](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/htlc_success_resolver.go#L912-L957)
   resolveLegacySuccessTx publishes the presigned, fixed-fee SignedSuccessTx unconditionally (line 925) with no check whether the HTLC outpoint it spends has already been spent by the counterparty's CLTV-timeout claim. When that spend is confirmed (or in the mempool), PublishTx returns lnwallet.ErrDoubleSpend and the function returns the error before any checkpoint or spend-detection; the outputIncubating fast-forward (line 932) and the IncubateOutputs/Checkpoint steps are only reached after a successful publish, so on every restart the same publish fails again and the resolver can never progress.
2. [contractcourt/utxonursery.go:1172–1250](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/utxonursery.go#L1172-L1250)
   registerPreschoolConf/waitForPreschoolConf only register a confirmation notification for the success tx (txid = ClaimOutpoint.Hash). Nothing watches the HTLC input for a competing spend, so if the counterparty's timeout spend confirms after our success tx entered the mempool, the goroutine blocks until shutdown and the 'pscl' entry is never advanced or removed. There is no analogue of the ErrRemoteSpend handling that waitForSweepConf has for kindergarten outputs.
3. [contractcourt/utxonursery.go:763–801](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/utxonursery.go#L763-L801)
   reloadPreschool re-registers the same never-confirming confirmation on every restart, so the stuck preschool entry, its goroutine and its notifier registration recur indefinitely; closeAndRemoveIfMature can never remove the channel bucket because IsMatureChannel requires every output to be 'grad'.
4. [contractcourt/htlc\_success\_resolver.go:1019–1039](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/htlc_success_resolver.go#L1019-L1039)
   After a successful publish the resolver waits in resolveSuccessTxOutput for a spend of ClaimOutpoint, an output of a transaction that can no longer confirm. waitForSpend never fires, so checkpointClaim/PutFinalHtlcOutcome are never reached and the resolver never marks itself resolved.
5. [contractcourt/channel\_arbitrator.go:2759–2768](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/channel_arbitrator.go#L2759-L2768)
   resolveContract exits the resolver goroutine on any Resolve() error with only a log line; the per-block launchResolvers() calls only Launch(), which is a no-op for the legacy success resolver (Launch default branch returns nil). The resolver is therefore not retried until the next restart, where the identical error recurs, leaving the arbitrator in StateWaitingFullResolution permanently.
6. [contractcourt/htlc\_success\_resolver.go:962–990](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/htlc_success_resolver.go#L962-L990)
   Contrast: the anchor-channel sibling resolveSuccessTx waits for the spend of the HTLC outpoint, validates it, and on a non-matching (foreign) spend calls checkpointForeignSpend to record the outcome and resolve. The legacy path has no equivalent, which is the missing protection.
7. [lnwallet/btcwallet/btcwallet.go:1285–1308](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwallet/btcwallet/btcwallet.go#L1285-L1308)
   mapRpcclientError maps chain.ErrMissingInputs / chain.ErrMempoolConflict / ErrTxAlreadyConfirmed to lnwallet.ErrDoubleSpend, which is the error resolveLegacySuccessTx returns when the HTLC output is already spent (confirmed) or conflicted (mempool) by the counterparty's timeout claim.

## Impact
No confidentiality impact. Integrity: the HTLC's final outcome is never persisted, the channel's close summary stays pending indefinitely, the nursery store retains an unremovable entry and PendingChannels reports a false limbo balance. Availability: one channel arbitrator, its chain watcher and its resolver are permanently stuck and recreated on every start, each start repeats the failing publish and leaves a blocked goroutine and notifier registration; the node otherwise keeps operating, other outputs of the same channel are swept by their own resolvers, and the leak is bounded by the number of such HTLCs, so both impacts are low.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker is the channel counterparty on a non-anchor channel who offered us an HTLC. They can select that channel type at open by withholding the anchors feature bit (lnd falls back to CommitmentTypeTweakless) or by requesting StaticRemoteKeyRequired explicitly, and pre-anchor channels already exist. Once our commitment is on chain and the HTLC's cltv_expiry passes, they broadcast their timeout spend of the HTLC output with a fee above our fixed, BIP125-replaceable presigned success tx (or before our commitment confirms, if we closed late). When their spend confirms, our resolver's publish fails with ErrDoubleSpend, or our nursery/resolver wait on a confirmation/spend that can never occur; this repeats on every restart with no remedy except AbandonChannel. Requires a non-anchor channel and winning the on-chain fee race, hence AT:P; no privileges or user interaction.

## Recommended fix
1. resolveLegacySuccessTx publishes the success tx and then waits only for the second-level output, never observing a competing spend of the HTLC outpoint; a publish failure caused by that competing spend is returned as a fatal error with no checkpoint, so the resolver can never conclude. Fix criteria: On the legacy path, the resolver must detect that the HTLC outpoint was spent by a transaction other than our success tx (before publishing, and while waiting), record the foreign outcome (as checkpointForeignSpend does for anchor channels) and mark itself resolved. Verify: with a legacy channel where the counterparty's timeout spend confirms first, the arbitrator reaches StateFullyResolved and the restart no longer re-runs a failing publish.
2. The nursery's preschool (and crib) stages register only a confirmation of our second-level transaction and never a spend of its input, so an entry whose second-level tx can no longer confirm is never advanced or removed, and reloadPreschool/reloadClasses re-register it forever. Fix criteria: A preschool or crib output whose first-stage input has been spent by a foreign transaction must be removed from the nursery store (or marked graduated/lost) so IsMatureChannel can succeed and no dead confirmation registration is re-created on restart. Verify: after such a spend, the channel bucket is removed from the nursery store and NurseryReport no longer reports the HTLC as limbo.

# Topology client cancel races async notifier: send on closed channel crashes lnd

## Details
ChannelGraph's topology notification machinery assumes that notification fan-out and client cancellation are serialised on the `handleTopologySubscriptions` goroutine (see the NOTE on notifyTopologyChange, graph/db/notifications.go:156-157). That invariant no longer holds: graph/db/graph.go:176-177 dispatches each topology update with `go c.handleTopologyUpdate(ctx, update)` (the TODO(elle) at 173-175 acknowledges this), while the cancel branch (graph.go:186-197) still runs inline and does `LoadAndDelete(clientID)`, `close(client.exit)`, `client.wg.Wait()`, `close(client.ntfnChan)`. The notifier goroutine performs a DB read (`FetchChannelEdgesByID`, notifications.go:415 for policy updates) before it fans out, so it genuinely runs concurrently with the handler's processing of subsequent cancel requests.

notifyTopologyChange (notifications.go:158-198) iterates the clients with sync.Map.Range, and for each client calls `client.wg.Add(1)` and spawns a goroutine that does `select { case t.ntfnChan <- topologyDiff: case <-t.exit: case <-c.quit: }`. If the cancel branch runs between the Range yielding the client and `wg.Add(1)`, `wg.Wait()` sees a zero counter and returns immediately, `ntfnChan` is closed, and the sender goroutine is then started with both `t.ntfnChan` (closed) and `t.exit` (closed) ready. In Go's select a send on a closed channel is an eligible case and panics when selected; selection among ready cases is pseudo-random, so roughly half of such interleavings raise `panic: send on closed channel` in a goroutine that has no recover, terminating the whole lnd process. A neighbouring interleaving from the same root cause panics too: when the handler is blocked in `client.wg.Wait()` (senders pending) and a late `wg.Add(1)` for the same client lands around the last sender's `Done`, Go's WaitGroup raises `sync: WaitGroup misuse: Add called concurrently with Wait` or `sync: WaitGroup is reused before previous Wait has returned` (the latter in the handler goroutine itself), likewise unrecovered.

Runtime assumptions (toolchain pinned `go 1.26.8` in go.mod): sync.Map.Range may yield a value for a key that is concurrently LoadAndDelete'd (documented: Range reflects any mapping for that key from any point during the call); select visits ready cases in random poll order and a send case on a closed channel panics when visited first (runtime selectgo `sclose`). Neither is contradicted by anything in the tree.

The notify side is driven by every accepted gossip message (AddNode / AddChannelEdge / UpdateEdgePolicy / PruneGraph all push to `topologyUpdate`, graph.go:384-388, 413-417, 647-651, 572-576), i.e. by the public network at the normal mainnet rate. The cancel side is driven by any topology subscriber ending: `SubscribeChannelGraph` (rpcserver.go:6819-6871, permission info:read at rpcserver.go:451, present in the stock readonly macaroon written from `readPermissions` at lnd.go:859, also exposed over REST/WebSocket at /v1/graph/subscribe) does `defer client.Cancel()` whenever the stream ends. An RPC client holding only a read-only macaroon can therefore hold many SubscribeChannelGraph streams and churn them (open, then close while gossip is being fanned out); each (update, cancel) pair has a small but non-zero chance of hitting the window, attempts are free and unlimited, and a single hit that resolves to the send case crashes the node. The gRPC panic-recovery interceptor (rpcperms/interceptor.go:683-700) covers only the RPC handler goroutine, not goroutines spawned by ChannelGraph. The same race can fire with no attacker at all when an honest subscriber (lncli, a dashboard, autopilot shutdown in autopilot/manager.go:135-149, server.go:472) disconnects while an update is being fanned out.

This is distinct from the verified record `subscribechannelgraph-unbounded-goroutine-per-gossip-update` (slow subscriber -> unbounded goroutines); this finding is the lifetime/ordering defect between cancellation and the asynchronous notifier, whose consequence is an unrecovered panic rather than memory growth.

## Evidence
1. [graph/db/graph.go:172–197](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/graph.go#L172-L197)
   handleTopologySubscriptions dispatches every topology update asynchronously (`go c.handleTopologyUpdate`, lines 176-177) yet handles client cancellation inline (lines 189-201): LoadAndDelete the client, close(client.exit), client.wg.Wait(), then close(client.ntfnChan). Because the notifier now runs concurrently, wg.Wait() can return (counter 0) before a concurrent notifyTopologyChange has called wg.Add(1) for the same client, so ntfnChan is closed while a sender for it is about to be spawned.
2. [graph/db/notifications.go:158–197](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/notifications.go#L158-L197)
   notifyTopologyChange ranges over topologyClients, calls client.wg.Add(1) (162) and spawns a goroutine whose select includes the send case `t.ntfnChan <- topologyDiff` (178). If ntfnChan was closed in the window between the Range loading the client and wg.Add(1), the send case is 'ready' (closed) alongside `<-t.exit`; Go's select picks pseudo-randomly, so ~1/2 of the time the send on the closed channel is chosen and panics. The NOTE at 156-157 records the original invariant (only called from the handler's call stack) that the `go` at graph.go:177 breaks.
3. [rpcserver.go:6819–6870](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/rpcserver.go#L6819-L6870)
   SubscribeChannelGraph (info:read) registers a topology client and `defer client.Cancel()`s it when the stream ends for any reason, so every stream open/close by a read-only RPC caller drives the cancel side of the race while gossip drives the notify side.
4. [graph/db/notifications.go:121–132](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/notifications.go#L121-L132)
   Cancel sends a cancel request to ntfnClientUpdates, which is processed by handleTopologySubscriptions on its own goroutine, concurrently with any in-flight handleTopologyUpdate goroutines.
5. [graph/db/graph.go:384–387](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/graph/db/graph.go#L384-L387)
   Every AddNode/AddChannelEdge/UpdateEdgePolicy/PruneGraph pushes to topologyUpdate; the gossip network therefore sets the rate at which notifier goroutines (and race windows) are produced.
6. [rpcperms/interceptor.go:683–699](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/rpcperms/interceptor.go#L683-L699)
   The gRPC panic-recovery interceptor only covers the handler goroutine; the panicking sender goroutine is spawned from the ChannelGraph's own goroutines, so the panic is unrecovered and terminates the lnd process.

## Impact
An unrecovered panic in a ChannelGraph-spawned goroutine terminates the entire lnd process: channels go offline and HTLC timeouts and breach remedies are unmonitored until an operator restarts. No confidentiality or integrity impact.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker is a network RPC client with a macaroon granting info:read (stock readonly.macaroon) reaching gRPC 10009 or REST 8080. They repeatedly open and close SubscribeChannelGraph streams while the node ingests ordinary gossip; each stream close triggers the inline cancel path while in-flight handleTopologyUpdate goroutines range over the client set. Winning requires the cancel to land in the microsecond window between Range yielding the client and wg.Add(1), and the sender's select to pick the closed send case (~1/2), so this is a race that must be won (AT:P) with no other defence to defeat (AC:L). Attempts are free and unlimited.

## Recommended fix
1. Client cancellation (close of ntfnChan after wg.Wait) and notification fan-out (wg.Add + spawn sender) are no longer serialised, because handleTopologyUpdate is dispatched asynchronously; a sender can be created for a client whose channel is already closed. Fix criteria: No goroutine may ever attempt to send on a topology client's ntfnChan after it has been closed. Either fan-out and cancellation are performed on the same goroutine (restore the documented invariant), or the client's registration/wg.Add is made atomic with respect to removal (e.g. a per-client mutex or state flag checked under lock before Add, and ntfnChan never closed while a sender may still be created). Verify by stress-testing concurrent SubscribeTopology/Cancel against a steady stream of topology updates under the race detector with no panic.
2. The sender goroutine's select contains a send on a channel that another goroutine closes, making the closed channel a panic sink rather than a benign signal. Fix criteria: Deliver 'client gone' exclusively through the exit channel; the receiving side (rpcserver/autopilot) is informed of termination without the producer side closing a channel that producers may still send on. Verify that cancelling a client while notifications are in flight never results in 'send on closed channel'.

# KV-to-SQL invoice migration panics on stale AMP InvoiceKeys left by settled-set re-use in the bbolt store

## Details
The KV-to-SQL invoice migration (invoices/sql_migration.go:389-404 and 434-443) iterates AMPState[setID].InvoiceKeys and dereferences invoice.Htlcs[circuitKey] (htlc.AcceptTime, htlc.AMP.Record) without checking that the HTLC exists; the 'missing htlc' guard at line 438 sits after the first dereference. Htlcs is map[CircuitKey]*InvoiceHTLC, so a circuit key present in InvoiceKeys but absent from the stored HTLC sets is a nil pointer and a runtime panic.

The bbolt invoice store produces exactly that inconsistency when a settled AMP set is re-used. updateMpp (invoices/update.go:277-320) admits an HTLC into set S purely from inv.State (always Open for AMP invoices) and HTLCSet(S, Accepted), which is empty once S's HTLCs are Settled; AMPState[S].State is never consulted. If the new HTLC N alone satisfies total_msat, reconstructAMPPreimages runs over the empty prior set and the sender's own share validates it, so the update becomes an AddHTLCsUpdate that settles S again. In addHTLCs, acceptHtlcsAmp → getUpdatedInvoiceAmpState(Accepted) (update_invoice.go:687-729) finds the existing entry, keeps State=Settled and adds N to InvoiceKeys (now {A, N}). kvInvoiceUpdater.UpdateAmpState (channeldb/invoices.go:818-862) switches on that set state: its Settled branch seeds updatedAmpHtlcs[S] with an empty map and adds only N. The old settled HTLC A is never re-added, because trySettle (update_invoice.go:757-760) returns no-change for a non-Accepted HTLC and settleHtlcsAmp is therefore not called for it. updateAMPInvoices (1031-1052) then Put()s {N} under invoiceNum||S, erasing A's record, while the invoice body is written with InvoiceKeys={A, N}. (The cancel-then-retry route does not produce this: after cancelSingleHtlc the set state is Canceled and UpdateAmpState's Canceled branch merges Accepted ∪ Canceled, preserving the canceled shard.)

Nothing on the KV runtime path reads InvoiceKeys, so the divergence is latent and permanent (invoices are retained by default and the AMP invoice stays Open). When the operator later enables db.use-native-sql on a SQLite/Postgres backend (config_builder.go:1139-1167; ApplyAllMigrations at 1240), MigrateInvoicesToSQL runs inside sqldb ExecTx (sqldb/migrations.go:501-532) with no recover(). KV QueryInvoices → fetchInvoice (channeldb/invoices.go:1572-1613, called with nil set IDs at line 566) loads AMPState from the body and Htlcs={N} from the per-set keys independently; MigrateSingleInvoice dereferences nil for A and lnd panics. The transaction never commits, so the panic recurs on every start until the operator reverts to KV or sets db.skip-native-sql-migration, which per lncfg/db.go abandons the entire invoice history.

Preconditions: the victim has an AMP invoice the attacker has paid once (a static invoice issued with addinvoice --amp, or spontaneous AMP via --accept-amp where the attacker first pays a trivial amount), and the operator later runs the documented KV→native-SQL invoice migration (docs/db_migration_guide.md: 'Start LND — invoice migration runs automatically'). The admission of re-used settled set IDs and the erasure of settled HTLC records are recorded in amp-settled-set-reuse-fails-exit-link; this finding records the resulting InvoiceKeys/storage divergence and the migration crash sink, which need their own fix (the migration must tolerate or reconcile stale keys).

## Evidence
1. [invoices/sql\_migration.go:389–403](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/sql_migration.go#L389-L403)
   MigrateSingleInvoice iterates ampState.InvoiceKeys and does htlc := invoice.Htlcs[circuitKey] then htlc.AcceptTime.UTC() with no nil check. Htlcs is map[CircuitKey]*InvoiceHTLC, so a circuit key present in InvoiceKeys but absent from the stored per-set HTLC blobs yields a nil pointer and a runtime panic. This is the code the fix must change.
2. [invoices/sql\_migration.go:434–442](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/sql_migration.go#L434-L442)
   Second loop over InvoiceKeys dereferences htlc.AMP.Record.RootShare() at line 436 before the 'missing htlc' check at 438, so the guard never runs for a missing HTLC.
3. [channeldb/invoices.go:818–861](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/channeldb/invoices.go#L818-L861)
   kvInvoiceUpdater.UpdateAmpState switches on the *set* state (InvoiceStateAMP.State), not the HTLC state. When the first update for a set in this tx finds the set state Settled, it seeds updatedAmpHtlcs[setID] with an empty map and adds only the HTLCs touched in this tx, so a shard accepted into an already-settled set produces a stored set containing only the new HTLC. (The Canceled branch merges Accepted ∪ Canceled, so the cancel-then-retry route preserves canceled shards and does not produce stale keys.)
4. [channeldb/invoices.go:1031–1051](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/channeldb/invoices.go#L1031-L1051)
   updateAMPInvoices serializes exactly that map and Put()s it under invoiceNum||setID, replacing the previously stored HTLC set; the records of the earlier settled shards are erased from disk.
5. [invoices/update\_invoice.go:687–728](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/update_invoice.go#L687-L728)
   getUpdatedInvoiceAmpState for an Accepted HTLC on an existing set keeps State as-is (Settled) and only ever adds the circuit key to InvoiceKeys (line 726); nothing removes a key when its HTLC is dropped from storage, so AMPState (serialized in the invoice body) becomes {old, new} while the per-set storage holds {new}.
6. [invoices/update\_invoice.go:757–759](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/update_invoice.go#L757-L759)
   trySettle returns (false, state, nil) for any HTLC not in HtlcStateAccepted, so the previously Settled HTLCs of the re-used set are never passed to settleHtlcsAmp/UpdateAmpState in addHTLCs (lines 336-353) and are not re-added to the rewritten set.
7. [invoices/update.go:277–319](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/update.go#L277-L319)
   updateMpp admits the new HTLC because inv.State is Open (AMP top-level invoices never leave Open) and HTLCSet(setID, Accepted) is empty for a settled set; AMPState[setID].State is never consulted. An HTLC with amt >= total_msat >= invoice value completes the set alone, and reconstructAMPPreimages over the empty prior set validates it from the sender's own share, yielding an AddHTLCsUpdate that settles the set again.
8. [channeldb/invoices.go:1572–1612](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/channeldb/invoices.go#L1572-L1612)
   fetchInvoice deserializes AMPState from the invoice body and, for AMP invoices (whose body carries no HTLCs), loads the HTLCs from the per-set keys independently with no reconciliation. QueryInvoices (line 566) calls it with nil set IDs, so the migration receives Htlcs={new} and AMPState[S].InvoiceKeys={old,new}.
9. [sqldb/migrations.go:501–531](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/sqldb/migrations.go#L501-L531)
   The custom invoice MigrationFn runs inside ExecTx during ApplyAllMigrations at startup; there is no recover() in sqldb or the startup path, so the panic terminates the lnd process before the transaction commits, and the same panic recurs on every start.
10. [config\_builder.go:1139–1166](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/config_builder.go#L1139-L1166)
   The migration is attached whenever db.use-native-sql is set and db.skip-native-sql-migration is not, and ApplyAllMigrations runs synchronously at startup (line 1240); the only escapes are reverting to KV or setting skip-native-sql-migration, which per lncfg/db.go abandons the invoice history.

## Impact
Availability: once the state is planted, lnd panics during the startup migration on every start while db.use-native-sql is set; service is restored by reverting the flag, so this is a blocked operator-initiated upgrade with an operator-controlled outage window rather than downtime of a running node, and the attacker cannot choose its timing — LOW. Integrity: the stored records of the set's previously settled shards are erased and AMPState permanently disagrees with the stored HTLCs; completing the migration then requires db.skip-native-sql-migration, which discards the whole invoice history — LOW. No confidentiality impact.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker is any Lightning node able to route an HTLC to the victim that has once paid an AMP set to it (static AMP invoice, or --accept-amp spontaneous payment of a trivial amount), so it knows payment_addr and its own set_id. It sends one more HTLC with the same payment_addr/set_id, total_msat >= invoice value and amt >= total_msat (zero-value or spontaneous AMP invoices make this trivially cheap); the victim settles it and its bbolt store now carries InvoiceKeys referencing an erased HTLC. No credentials or user action are needed to plant the state. The crash fires deterministically, but only when the operator later turns on db.use-native-sql (non-default) on a SQLite/Postgres backend — an attack requirement the attacker does not control.

## Recommended fix
1. MigrateSingleInvoice trusts that every circuit key in AMPState[setID].InvoiceKeys has a matching entry in invoice.Htlcs and dereferences the map value before checking it, turning a KV data inconsistency into a process crash that blocks startup. Fix criteria: The migration must never panic on an InvoiceKeys entry with no stored HTLC: it must either drop/reconcile the stale key (recomputing InvoiceKeys and AmtPaid from the HTLCs actually present) or return a descriptive error naming the invoice and set ID. Verify by migrating a KV invoice whose AMPState references a circuit key absent from its stored HTLC set: lnd starts or fails with a clear error, not a nil-pointer panic.
2. kvInvoiceUpdater.UpdateAmpState rewrites a set's per-set HTLC blob from an empty map when the set's recorded state is Settled, while getUpdatedInvoiceAmpState only ever adds to InvoiceKeys, so an HTLC accepted into an already-settled set erases the set's earlier HTLC records and leaves InvoiceKeys and AmtPaid referencing them. Fix criteria: After any AMP update on the KV store, the stored HTLC set for a set ID must contain every HTLC whose circuit key is in AMPState[setID].InvoiceKeys (all states) — e.g. seed the rewrite from all existing HTLCs of the set regardless of state — or keys must be removed when their HTLCs are dropped; independently, HTLCs naming an already-settled set should be rejected (amp-settled-set-reuse-fails-exit-link). Verify by settling a set, accepting a new HTLC under the same set ID, then reloading the invoice: InvoiceKeys and Htlcs agree and the original HTLC records remain.

# Peer-chosen scid_alias makes node sign channel_updates for arbitrary SCIDs including its own public channels

## Details
Reachable only when the operator has enabled protocol.option-scid-alias (off by default: sample-lnd.conf:1441, server.go:746 unsets ScidAliasOptional otherwise; required for zero-conf/LSP setups). With it enabled, any private channel negotiated with a peer that also signals the feature gets channeldb.ScidAliasFeatureBit (lnwallet/reservation.go:473), and the funding manager stores whatever alias_scid the peer puts in channel_ready (funding/manager.go:4210 -> aliasmgr.PutPeerAlias), re-storing it on every duplicate channel_ready (funding/manager.go:4106-4118). lnd deliberately does not range-check it (aliasmgr.IsAlias comment: peers are free to use any range) and never compares it with the SCIDs of its own channels. Inbound private channels of the option_scid_alias channel type are accepted from any peer without a channel acceptor (funding/manager.go:1645 rejects only the public variant).

Every channel_update we later produce for that private channel is rewritten by the gossiper after the real-SCID copy has been stored in our graph: the SCID is replaced with the stored peer alias and the message is re-signed with our node identity key via SignAliasUpdate = server.signAliasUpdate (gossiper.go:3483-3510 for ChanStatusManager updates via server.applyChannelUpdate(useAlias=private); gossiper.go:2001-2020 for UpdateChannelPolicy), then delivered to the peer through the reliable sender.

An attacker-peer therefore sets alias_scid = SCID of one of our public channels X with a third party T. We emit a channel_update for X carrying a valid signature by our node key. The attacker chooses its own node key so that its lexicographic order relative to ours matches T's (funding/manager.go:4575, 4596), making the direction bit our side of X. Timestamp is now, fees/timelock are our defaults for the private channel, htlc_minimum/htlc_maximum derive from the attacker's open_channel parameters and capacity (funding/manager.go:1752-1753 -> extractAnnounceParams 3647-3661), so the message passes validateChannelUpdate1Fields (netann/channel_update.go:276-301) and verifyChannelUpdate1Signature at every node, including our own gossiper, which filters remote announcements for own channels only for ChannelAnnouncement1 (gossiper.go:955) and accepts a remote ChannelUpdate1 for X in our direction once the signature verifies (gossiper.go:3365-3385, UpdateEdge at 3449), overwriting our own stored policy for X; subsequent genuine updates built by ExtractChannelUpdate from the graph (chan_status_manager.go:629-648) carry the forged fields forward.

Triggers under the attacker's control: sending shutdown makes chancloser.ReceiveShutdown -> initChanShutdown call DisableChannel -> ChanStatusManager.RequestDisable (peer/brontide.go:3869) -> processDisableRequest -> signAndSendNextUpdate(disabled=true) (chancloser.go:525, chan_status_manager.go:455-465, 629-648), producing a signed disabled update for X; getOrInitChanStatus loads any channel from the graph so private channels are not excluded on this path. Operator-driven triggers are routine: every global UpdateChannelPolicy re-signs an update for each private channel, giving a fresh forged update for the currently targeted SCID, which the attacker can re-target at will by re-sending channel_ready.

Impact: an anonymous peer with one small private channel obtains a channel_update signing oracle over our identity key for arbitrary SCIDs. It can broadcast a disabled or crippled (tiny max_htlc, large min_htlc, default fees) policy for any of our public channels, removing them from the network's routing view in our direction and overwriting our configured policies in third-party graphs and in our own; third parties cannot distinguish the forged updates from genuine ones. The htlcswitch failure path is not affected: failAliasUpdate only substitutes our own, range-checked aliases.

## Evidence
1. [discovery/gossiper.go:3478–3510](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/gossiper.go#L3478-L3510)
   handleChanUpdate: for every local update of a private channel the SCID of the already-stored update is overwritten with the peer-supplied remoteAlias and the message is re-signed with the node identity key (SignAliasUpdate) and sent to the peer. No check that the alias is in the alias range or is not the real SCID of one of our channels.
2. [discovery/gossiper.go:1994–2025](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/gossiper.go#L1994-L2025)
   processChanPolicyUpdate (UpdateChannelPolicy RPC path): same replacement of ShortChannelID with d.cfg.GetAlias(chanID) (the peer alias) followed by SignAliasUpdate, without validating the alias value.
3. [funding/manager.go:4196–4213](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/funding/manager.go#L4196-L4213)
   handleChannelReady stores msg.AliasScid from the remote channel_ready verbatim via PutPeerAlias; nothing checks it against the alias range or the SCIDs of our own channels.
4. [funding/manager.go:4106–4118](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/funding/manager.go#L4106-L4118)
   Duplicate channel_ready refreshes the stored peer alias at any later time, so the peer can re-target the SCID whenever it wants.
5. [aliasmgr/aliasmgr.go:492–519](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/aliasmgr/aliasmgr.go#L492-L519)
   PutPeerAlias persists any 8-byte value; GetPeerAlias hands it unchanged to the gossiper/server consumers.
6. [aliasmgr/aliasmgr.go:708–716](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/aliasmgr/aliasmgr.go#L708-L716)
   IsAlias documents that the range check applies only to aliases we generate and that peers are free to use any range; this is what lets a real SCID flow into our signed updates.
7. [server.go:2026–2035](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/server.go#L2026-L2035)
   signAliasUpdate signs ChannelUpdate1.DataToSign() (which includes ShortChannelID) with the node identity key; the result is indistinguishable from a legitimate channel_update by this node for whatever SCID the message carries.
8. [server.go:5455–5477](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/server.go#L5455-L5477)
   applyChannelUpdate (ChanStatusManager.ApplyChannelUpdate) fetches the peer alias for private channels and passes it as RemoteAlias to the gossiper, so disable/enable updates take the re-sign path.
9. [lnwallet/chancloser/chancloser.go:522–527](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnwallet/chancloser/chancloser.go#L522-L527)
   initChanShutdown, reached from ReceiveShutdown (closeIdle case) when the peer initiates, calls DisableChannel -> ChanStatusManager.RequestDisable -> signAndSendNextUpdate(disabled=true): the peer triggers a signed disabled update for the chosen SCID on demand by sending shutdown.
10. [netann/chan\_status\_manager.go:629–647](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/netann/chan_status_manager.go#L629-L647)
   signAndSendNextUpdate builds the update from the graph policy, signs it and hands it to ApplyChannelUpdate with private=true (AuthProof==nil), enabling the alias replacement; getOrInitChanStatus (702-726) loads any channel from the graph, so private channels are reachable on the RequestDisable path.
11. [server.go:746](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/server.go#L746)
   NoOptionScidAlias = !cfg.ProtocolOptions.ScidAlias(): the scid-alias feature bits are unset unless the operator sets protocol.option-scid-alias (default false, sample-lnd.conf:1441), which is the deployment condition for this finding.
12. [funding/manager.go:1645–1655](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/funding/manager.go#L1645-L1655)
   Inbound private channels with the option_scid_alias channel type are accepted from any peer; only the public variant is rejected and, unlike zero-conf, no channel acceptor is required.
13. [funding/manager.go:4571–4596](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/funding/manager.go#L4571-L4596)
   The direction bit of our update is derived from the lexicographic order of our key and the peer's key; the attacker chooses its node key, so it can make the bit match our side of the targeted public channel.
14. [funding/manager.go:3640–3664](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/funding/manager.go#L3640-L3664)
   htlc_minimum/htlc_maximum of our update derive from funder-chosen open_channel parameters (LocalChanCfg.MinHTLC / MaxPendingAmount set from msg.HtlcMinimum / msg.MaxValueInFlight at 1752-1753) and capacity, so the attacker also controls these fields of the forged update and can keep max_htlc below the target channel's capacity.
15. [netann/channel\_update.go:276–301](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/netann/channel_update.go#L276-L301)
   validateChannelUpdate1Fields at receiving nodes checks only the max_htlc flag, min<=max and max_htlc<=capacity; with the signature verified against the node key for the direction bit, the forged update for X is accepted.
16. [discovery/gossiper.go:3365–3385](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/gossiper.go#L3365-L3385)
   Our own gossiper, receiving the forged update back from the network, selects our node key by direction bit and accepts it after ValidateChannelUpdateAnn; the own-channel filter at 955 exists only for ChannelAnnouncement1, so our own graph policy for X is overwritten too.

## Impact
Integrity: the node's authenticated gossip is forged; the attacker chooses SCID, direction, min/max htlc and the disabled flag of a channel_update that every node, including the victim's own gossiper, accepts as the victim's policy for a public channel (bounded set of fields, hence LOW). Availability: targeted public channels are marked disabled network-wide in our direction so no payments are routed through them until a genuine update supersedes the forgery; the daemon itself keeps running (LOW). No confidentiality impact.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker is an anonymous remote peer. Precondition is a deployment setting: the victim must run with protocol.option-scid-alias=true (default false, sample-lnd.conf:1441), a feature commonly enabled for zero-conf/LSP operation, hence AT:P. The attacker generates a node key whose ordering relative to ours matches the third party in target channel X (one bit, trivial), opens a private channel with the option_scid_alias channel type (accepted without acceptor), and after confirmation sends channel_ready with alias_scid = X. Sending shutdown (or waiting for the operator's next UpdateChannelPolicy) yields a channel_update for X signed by the victim, which it relays to the network. No security mechanism has to be defeated.

## Recommended fix
1. The peer-supplied alias_scid from channel_ready is stored and later used as the short_channel_id of node-signed channel_updates without validating that it is an alias rather than a real SCID, violating the property that the node only signs policy statements for the channel they describe. Fix criteria: A peer alias that lies outside the alias range or equals the SCID of any channel this node is party to is rejected or ignored before it can appear in a signed channel_update. Verify by sending channel_ready with alias_scid equal to one of the node's public channel SCIDs and confirming that no signed channel_update carrying that SCID is ever produced (shutdown, force close, UpdateChannelPolicy, zero-conf first update).
2. Both gossiper re-sign sites (handleChanUpdate RemoteAlias path and processChanPolicyUpdate) substitute the SCID and call SignAliasUpdate without re-checking what is being signed. Fix criteria: Every call that re-signs a channel_update with a substituted SCID asserts the replacement is a non-real alias SCID; a substitution that fails the assertion results in the update being sent with the channel's real SCID or not at all, never signed for a different channel.
