# Failed one-shot historical rescan leaves spend/conf request pending forever, never delivered

## Details
Every ChainNotifier backend implements historical lookups as a single fire-and-forget operation: TxNotifier.RegisterSpend/RegisterConf flips the request set to rescanPending (chainntnfs/txnotifier.go:1168, :748) and returns a HistoricalDispatch; the backend scans once and is expected to call UpdateSpendDetails/UpdateConfDetails with the result (possibly nil), which is the only transition back to rescanComplete other than seeing the event in a newly connected block (handleSpendDetailsAtTip, :1704-1710). On any error the backend goroutines in bitcoindnotify/bitcoind.go (:313-326 spend, :268-281 conf), btcdnotify/btcd.go (:971-976; the rpcclient handlers at :132-136 register no OnRescanFinished, so even a successful btcd rescan never calls UpdateSpendDetails) and neutrinonotify/neutrino.go (:886-889, any GetUtxo error other than 'not found') only log and return. TxNotifier is never informed and has no failure transition, timeout or retry: the set stays rescanPending with nil details until the process exits.

Consequences in the state machine: (1) spends/confirmations in blocks connected after registration are still detected by ConnectTip/filterTx; (2) a spend or confirmation that already happened before registration is never delivered; (3) every later RegisterSpend/RegisterConf for the same request hits `case rescanPending` (:1131-1140, :714-727) and returns HistoricalDispatch == nil, so no caller (chain watcher re-registration on NegativeConf at chain_watcher.go:1021, a resolver restart, an RPC client) can trigger a retry; (4) unspentRequests/unconfirmedRequests (:2007-2021, :1986-2000) skip the set so its hint is frozen; (5) only an lnd restart creates a fresh set.

Funds-critical consumer: contractcourt's chain watcher registers one spend notification per open channel funding outpoint at startup (chain_watcher.go:394-397, from ChainArbitrator.loadOpenChannels) with DeriveHeightHint(), and both closeObserver (:948) and handleBlockbeat/checkFundingSpend (:2009, :2082) only read that one Spend channel; there is no other mechanism by which lnd learns that a channel's funding output was spent while it was offline. If the single historical rescan for that outpoint errors (backend RPC failure, connection blip, bitcoind restarting or saturated during the startup burst of per-channel rescans, neutrino unable to fetch filters/blocks), the chain watcher believes the channel is still open for the rest of the process lifetime: a counterparty force close or revoked-commitment broadcast that confirmed while the node was down is never handled, HTLCs are never resolved on chain and a breach is never punished while the remote CSV window elapses. The operator sees only one 'Rescan to determine the spend details ... failed' log line.

This finding holds only when the single historical rescan errors. The channel counterparty controls the attacker-side input (which commitment to broadcast and when, choosing a time the victim is offline) but not the backend fault, so exploitation depends on a runtime condition outside the attacker's control (CVSS AT:P); once that fault occurs the loss of the notification is deterministic and unrecoverable without a restart. docs/safety.md imposes no operator obligation that fences this path (it only recommends a non-pruned bitcoind with -txindex for performance). This record files the ledger item lead-bitcoind-261-0da9.

## Evidence
1. [chainntnfs/txnotifier.go:1131–1147](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/chainntnfs/txnotifier.go#L1131-L1147)
   RegisterSpend: when the set is rescanPending the new client gets no HistoricalDispatch. The state leaves rescanPending only via UpdateSpendDetails (backend reports rescan result) or handleSpendDetailsAtTip (spend seen in a newly connected block). If the backend's single rescan errors, neither happens for a historical spend, so every later registration for the same outpoint is silently told to wait at tip.
2. [chainntnfs/bitcoindnotify/bitcoind.go:310–352](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/chainntnfs/bitcoindnotify/bitcoind.go#L310-L352)
   Historical spend rescan goroutine: on any error from historicalSpendDetails (GetBlockHash/GetBlock per block, lines 881-890) it logs and returns without calling UpdateSpendDetails; the TODO acknowledges there is no retry. Lines 265-299 do the same for confirmations.
3. [chainntnfs/btcdnotify/btcd.go:132–135](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/chainntnfs/btcdnotify/btcd.go#L132-L135)
   btcd: the rpcclient NotificationHandlers register only OnBlockConnected/OnBlockDisconnected/OnRedeemingTx and no OnRescanFinished, so UpdateSpendDetails is never invoked for the historical path even on success; a RescanAsync failure (lines 968-978, and 853-861 for conf) is only logged, so a historical spend is delivered only if the rescan's OnRedeemingTx happens to fire.
4. [chainntnfs/neutrinonotify/neutrino.go:864–889](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/chainntnfs/neutrinonotify/neutrino.go#L864-L889)
   neutrino: GetUtxo error other than 'not found' returns without UpdateSpendDetails.
5. [chainntnfs/txnotifier.go:714–726](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/chainntnfs/txnotifier.go#L714-L726)
   RegisterConf has the identical rescanPending short-circuit for confirmation requests (used e.g. by the chain watcher for the close tx and by the funding manager).
6. [chainntnfs/txnotifier.go:2007–2022](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/chainntnfs/txnotifier.go#L2007-L2022)
   unspentRequests skips rescanPending sets so the spend hint is frozen; nothing in the notifier ever times out or re-queues a pending rescan. The only recovery is restarting lnd (new TxNotifier, fresh rescanNotStarted).
7. [contractcourt/chain\_watcher.go:392–402](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/chain_watcher.go#L392-L402)
   The chain watcher registers exactly once at startup with the channel's height hint and relies on the historical dispatch to learn of a funding spend (force close / breach) that confirmed while the node was offline. handleBlockbeat/checkFundingSpend (2000-2025, 2060-2092) only perform a non-blocking read of the same Spend channel, so they cannot detect a historical spend either.

## Impact
The node silently never learns that a channel was closed on chain: HTLC timeouts/claims are not enforced and a revoked commitment is not punished within the CSV window, which is direct loss of channel funds (integrity of the node's funds-controlling state). Confidentiality is unaffected; the process keeps running.

## Reproduction steps
1. A channel counterparty broadcasts a (possibly revoked) commitment while the victim node is offline. On restart the victim's chain watcher registers the funding spend and the backend's one-shot historical rescan must fail (any RPC error from bitcoind/btcd, or a non-'not found' GetUtxo error from neutrino whose peers the threat model treats as untrusted). No defense is bypassed, no user interaction is needed, and the counterparty needs only an open channel; but the backend fault is a runtime condition the attacker does not control, so attack requirements are PRESENT. Assumption: the pinned RPC layers (btcd v0.25.1-pre rpcclient, btcwallet v0.16.20-pre chain client, neutrino v0.17.1 GetUtxo) do not themselves retry a failed historical fetch; lnd's own code performs no retry and its TODO comments acknowledge this.

## Recommended fix
1. Backend historical rescan goroutines treat an error as terminal and never report it to TxNotifier, so a request's rescan state can remain rescanPending for the life of the process and historical events are lost. Fix criteria: A failed historical rescan must either be retried (with bounded backoff) until it completes, or reported to TxNotifier so the set returns to a state in which the next registration re-dispatches the rescan (or the registering caller receives an error). Verify by making the backend's first rescan fail for an outpoint already spent below tip, then re-registering (or waiting for the retry) and asserting the Spend notification is delivered without restarting the notifier.
2. TxNotifier.RegisterSpend/RegisterConf unconditionally short-circuit on rescanPending with no way to detect an abandoned rescan, so no client can recover the request. Fix criteria: TxNotifier exposes a failure path (e.g. a method the backend calls on rescan error, or a pending-age/attempt check) after which rescanPending is cleared and a subsequent registration yields a HistoricalDispatch again. Verify with a unit test: register, simulate rescan failure, register again, and assert the second registration returns a non-nil HistoricalDispatch.

# KV-to-SQL invoice migration leaves settle_index sequence at zero; new settlements reuse old indexes

## Details
The KV invoice store assigns settle indexes from the bbolt sequence of the invoice-settle-index bucket (channeldb/invoices.go:982, first value 1), so a node with N settlements holds indexes 1..N. The SQL store assigns them from invoice_sequences.settle_index via NextInvoiceSettleIndex (sqldb/sqlc/queries/invoices.sql:141-145), which schema migration 000001 initialises to 0 when the native SQL schema is created — for a migrating node, immediately before the KV-to-SQL invoice migration (sqldb/migrations.go:64-77, version 7). MigrateSingleInvoice copies each KV invoice's original settle_index into the new row (invoices/sql_migration.go:285-304) and does the same for AMP sub-invoices (412-431), but neither MigrateInvoicesToSQL (513-589) nor the driver that attaches it (config_builder.go:1138-1150) ever sets invoice_sequences.settle_index to the maximum migrated value. NextInvoiceSettleIndex is the only writer of that row anywhere in the tree, and settle_index carries no UNIQUE constraint on invoices or amp_sub_invoices.

Consequently, on a node that had N settled invoices before migrating, the first settlement after migration is assigned settle_index 1, the second 2, and so on: each new settlement reuses an index already held by a migrated row. sqlInvoiceUpdater.UpdateInvoiceState (invoices/sql_store.go:1373-1393) and UpdateAmpState (1463-1485) write that reused index into the row and into the returned Invoice, so it is what the registry dispatches and what lnrpc reports.

lightning.proto:3926-3929 documents settle_index as monotonically increasing and as the SubscribeInvoices resumption cursor. Two shipped consumers break on the violated contract: (a) InvoiceRegistry.dispatchToClients (invoices/invoiceregistry.go:403-407) skips a settle event when client.settleIndex >= invoice.SettleIndex, so a subscriber that resumed with its pre-migration cursor N (the documented use, rpcserver.go:6050-6055 → SubscribeNotifications) silently drops every post-migration settlement whose reused index is <= N; (b) InvoicesSettledSince(N) (sql_store.go:836-885, FilterInvoicesBySettleIndex settle_index >= N+1) never returns those settlements either, so re-subscribing with the cursor cannot recover them. Up to N post-migration payments are therefore permanently invisible to cursor-based consumers, and settle-index-keyed records become ambiguous (two invoices per index). Subscribers that start from cursor 0 after migration, and LookupInvoice/ListInvoices, are unaffected.

The defective state is seeded by the operator following the sanctioned migration path (db.use-native-sql on an existing SQLite/Postgres KV node; release-notes-0.19.0.md:531 'Migrate KV invoices to SQL'; the docs/sqlite.md note about not migrating refers to switching the kvdb backend, not to this migration). The actor who then exercises it is any Lightning payer: paying any invoice after migration yields a settlement the merchant's event-stream consumer never sees while the payer holds the preimage. Assumption: bbolt's Bucket.NextSequence (go.etcd.io/bbolt as pinned in go.mod) returns 1 on first use, as the SQL store's own comment at sql_store.go:833 ('The index starts from 1') also states.

## Evidence
1. [invoices/sql\_migration.go:285–314](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/sql_migration.go#L285-L314)
   MigrateSingleInvoice copies the KV invoice's SettleIndex verbatim into the new row via InsertMigratedInvoice; AMP sub-invoices are handled the same way at lines 412-431. Nowhere in this file, including MigrateInvoicesToSQL (513-589), is invoice_sequences.settle_index advanced to the maximum migrated value; this is where the fix belongs.
2. [sqldb/sqlc/queries/invoices.sql:141–144](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/sqldb/sqlc/queries/invoices.sql#L141-L144)
   NextInvoiceSettleIndex is the only writer of invoice_sequences anywhere in the tree (UPDATE ... SET current_value = current_value + 1 RETURNING current_value). After migration the first live settlement receives settle_index 1, the second 2, regardless of how many migrated rows already hold those values.
3. [sqldb/sqlc/migrations/000001\_invoices.up.sql:1–11](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/sqldb/sqlc/migrations/000001_invoices.up.sql#L1-L11)
   The settle_index sequence is created with current_value 0 when the native SQL schema is initialised, which for a migrating node happens immediately before the version-7 KV invoice migration (sqldb/migrations.go:64-77).
4. [sqldb/sqlc/migrations/000001\_invoices.up.sql:26–29](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/sqldb/sqlc/migrations/000001_invoices.up.sql#L26-L29)
   settle_index on invoices has no UNIQUE constraint (likewise amp_sub_invoices.settle_index in 000002_amp_invoices.up.sql:17-20), so the duplicate assignment is accepted silently instead of failing the settlement.
5. [invoices/sql\_store.go:1373–1392](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/sql_store.go#L1373-L1392)
   sqlInvoiceUpdater.UpdateInvoiceState assigns the value returned by NextInvoiceSettleIndex to the row and to the returned Invoice (line 1432), so registry notifications carry the colliding index. UpdateAmpState (1463-1485, 1513) does the same for AMP sets.
6. [invoices/invoiceregistry.go:403–406](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/invoiceregistry.go#L403-L406)
   Live dispatch to SubscribeInvoices clients skips a settle event when client.settleIndex >= invoice.SettleIndex. A client that resumed with its pre-migration cursor N (SubscribeNotifications seeds client.settleIndex from the RPC request, 1674-1681) silently loses every post-migration settlement whose reused index is <= N.
7. [invoices/sql\_store.go:836–884](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/invoices/sql_store.go#L836-L884)
   InvoicesSettledSince(idx) returns rows with settle_index >= idx+1, so backlog recovery for a client with cursor N never returns the post-migration settlements with reused indexes 1..N; those payments are permanently invisible to cursor-based consumers.
8. [config\_builder.go:1138–1150](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/config_builder.go#L1138-L1150)
   The production driver attaches MigrateInvoicesToSQL as the version-7 custom migration whenever db.use-native-sql is set and skip-native-sql-migration is not; after it returns, it only sets the KV tombstone. No step here or in any later schema migration (000007-000015) synchronises the settle_index sequence.

## Impact
Integrity of the node's invoice data is affected: settle_index, documented as unique and monotonic (lightning.proto:3926-3929), is duplicated for up to N post-migration settlements, those settlements are suppressed for cursor-resuming SubscribeInvoices clients and can never be fetched via InvoicesSettledSince. Rated LOW rather than HIGH: the payer does not choose which index collides or which records are affected beyond their own payments, invoice rows, preimages, channel state and funds are otherwise intact, and LookupInvoice/ListInvoices still show the settlement. No confidentiality impact; the node stays available.

## Reproduction steps
1. The inconsistent state is seeded by the operator following the sanctioned, shipped migration path (config_builder.go:1138-1150; release-notes-0.19.0.md:531), not by misconfiguration, so it is not an attack requirement the operator must have failed. The actor who exercises it is any Lightning payer: settling any invoice over the P2P network after migration yields a colliding settle index with no privileges and no user interaction. Attack requirements are present because the node must have migrated from a KV store holding settled invoices and the affected consumer must resume SubscribeInvoices by settle_index cursor; given that, the outcome is deterministic.

## Recommended fix
1. MigrateInvoicesToSQL copies KV settle indexes into the SQL rows but does not synchronise the invoice_sequences.settle_index counter that NextInvoiceSettleIndex increments, so the SQL store resumes numbering from 0 and violates the uniqueness/monotonicity that the registry's deduplication and InvoicesSettledSince assume. Fix criteria: After migration, the settle_index sequence must be at least the maximum settle_index present in invoices and amp_sub_invoices, so every subsequent settlement receives a strictly greater index. Verify by migrating a KV database with settled invoices, settling a new invoice, and checking that its settle_index exceeds all migrated ones and that a SubscribeInvoices client resuming from the pre-migration cursor receives the new settlement.
2. settle_index is not constrained unique on invoices or amp_sub_invoices, so the duplicate assignment is silently accepted rather than surfacing as an error. Fix criteria: A duplicate settle index assignment must be detected (a uniqueness constraint or an explicit check in the updater) so that a numbering regression fails loudly instead of corrupting the event stream; verify that inserting a second row with an existing settle_index is rejected.

# Unsynchronized feature set map: UpdateNodeAnnouncement RPC races RPC readers and can crash lnd

## Details
feature.Manager (feature/manager.go) stores its per-set raw feature vectors in a plain Go map, fsets, and has no mutex: GetRaw (line 280) and ListSets (line 303) read or iterate the map, and setRaw (line 289) writes it. UpdateFeatureSets (lines 315-359) validates the proposed sets and then unconditionally executes m.fsets[set] = features.Clone() for every set in the update map, even when the vector is unchanged.

At runtime the writer is server.genNodeAnnouncement (server.go:3559), which runs under server.mu. It is reached from the peersrpc UpdateNodeAnnouncement RPC (lnrpc/peersrpc/peers_server.go:309-402): the handler always passes a non-nil features vector (nodeAnnFeatures, initialised from currentNodeAnn.Features) to cfg.UpdateNodeAnnouncement -> server.updateAndBroadcastSelfNode, so every accepted call, including an alias- or colour-only change, performs the map write. The RPC is gated only by the peers:write macaroon permission (peers_server.go:33-36) and is neither rate limited nor serialized.

The readers do not take server.mu: updateAndBroadcastSelfNode itself reads featureMgr.Get(SetNodeAnn) at server.go:3632 after genNodeAnnouncement has released the lock; peerConnected reads Get(SetInit)/Get(SetLegacyGlobal) at server.go:4525-4526 on every connection; rpcserver.go reads the map in OpenChannel (2144), GetInfo (3440-3444, including a map iteration via ListSets) and the AddInvoice feature closures (776/779, 5798/5820). Two concurrent UpdateNodeAnnouncement calls alone therefore race one call's write against the other's unlocked read, with no second credential needed.

With go.mod pinning go 1.26.8, the runtime detects a map read or iteration overlapping a map write and terminates the process with 'fatal error: concurrent map read and map write'; this is a runtime fatal, not a panic, so the gRPC panic-recovery interceptor (rpcperms/interceptor.go:553-557) cannot catch it and lnd exits. The write window is a single small-map assignment, so each attempt succeeds only probabilistically, but the holder of the limited peers:write macaroon can issue concurrent calls indefinitely; each accepted call also re-signs and broadcasts a node announcement. A peers:write credential is entitled to connect/disconnect peers and edit the node announcement, not to stop the daemon (StopDaemon requires info:write, rpcserver.go:447-450); an lnd that is down cannot punish breaches or resolve HTLCs, which the threat model treats as a security impact.

## Evidence
1. [feature/manager.go:288–290](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/feature/manager.go#L288-L290)
   setRaw assigns m.fsets[set] with no synchronization; Manager has no mutex and the feature package imports no sync primitive. This is the write side of the race and the location the fix must change.
2. [feature/manager.go:279–307](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/feature/manager.go#L279-L307)
   GetRaw reads m.fsets[set], Get wraps it, and ListSets ranges over the map, all without synchronization; a read or iteration overlapping setRaw is detected by the Go runtime (go.mod: go 1.26.8) as 'concurrent map read and map write' / 'concurrent map iteration and map write', a runtime fatal that cannot be recovered.
3. [feature/manager.go:315–358](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/feature/manager.go#L315-L358)
   UpdateFeatureSets validates each proposed set then unconditionally calls setRaw for every set in the update map (lines 354-356), even when the vector is identical to the current one, so every caller that passes a non-nil features vector performs the map write.
4. [server.go:3542–3570](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/server.go#L3542-L3570)
   genNodeAnnouncement takes s.mu and, whenever features != nil, calls featureMgr.UpdateFeatureSets (line 3559). s.mu serializes writers against each other but none of the readers below take s.mu.
5. [server.go:3611–3632](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/server.go#L3611-L3632)
   updateAndBroadcastSelfNode calls genNodeAnnouncement (releasing s.mu on return) and then reads featureMgr.Get(SetNodeAnn) at line 3632 outside any lock. Two concurrent UpdateNodeAnnouncement RPCs therefore race one call's map write (3559, under s.mu) against the other's unlocked read (3632): the peers:write holder alone supplies both sides.
6. [lnrpc/peersrpc/peers\_server.go:316–333](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnrpc/peersrpc/peers_server.go#L316-L333)
   nodeAnnFeatures is initialised from currentNodeAnn.Features (a non-nil *RawFeatureVector set at startup, server.go:5876) and is passed to cfg.UpdateNodeAnnouncement on every call (lines 395-397), so even an alias- or colour-only update reaches UpdateFeatureSets and writes the map; a feature update toggling an unknown bit is also accepted by ValidateUpdate (lnwire/features.go:486-525).
7. [lnrpc/peersrpc/peers\_server.go:32–37](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnrpc/peersrpc/peers_server.go#L32-L37)
   UpdateNodeAnnouncement is gated only by the peers:write macaroon permission, a limited credential also used for ConnectPeer/DisconnectPeer; there is no rate limit or serialization of concurrent calls.
8. [server.go:4525–4526](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/server.go#L4525-L4526)
   peerConnected reads featureMgr.Get(SetInit)/Get(SetLegacyGlobal) without s.mu for every inbound or outbound connection, a second reader the same peers:write holder can drive via ConnectPeer, and that any anonymous peer connecting to 9735 drives.
9. [rpcserver.go:2144](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/rpcserver.go#L2144)
   OpenChannel reads featureMgr.Get(SetNodeAnn) from a gRPC handler goroutine without s.mu.
10. [rpcserver.go:3440–3444](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/rpcserver.go#L3440-L3444)
   GetInfo calls featureMgr.ListSets (map iteration) and Get for each set without s.mu; ordinary operator monitoring thus continuously supplies readers for the race.
11. [rpcserver.go:775–780](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/rpcserver.go#L775-L780)
   Invoice feature generation closures (AddInvoice path via invoicesrpc) read featureMgr.Get(SetInvoice/SetInvoiceAmp) without s.mu.

## Impact
The outcome is an unrecoverable runtime fatal error that terminates the lnd process: complete loss of availability of the node until an operator or supervisor restarts it, repeatable by the attacker for as long as the peers:write credential remains valid. While down the node cannot monitor the chain, sweep HTLCs or punish revoked commitments. No confidentiality or integrity impact is established by the code.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker: any gRPC/REST client holding a macaroon with peers:write (not admin). It issues many concurrent UpdateNodeAnnouncement calls that alternate alias or colour (or toggle an unknown feature bit); each call writes fsets under server.mu at server.go:3559 and then reads it unlocked at :3632, so the attacker's own calls supply both sides of the race, and ordinary GetInfo/AddInvoice/peer-connection traffic adds further unlocked readers. When a read overlaps the map assignment the Go 1.26 runtime aborts lnd. No defence must be defeated; the narrow window must be hit, so success per attempt is probabilistic but unbounded retries are available.

## Recommended fix
1. feature.Manager.fsets is a plain map read by GetRaw/Get/ListSets and written by setRaw from different goroutines without any synchronization, so UpdateFeatureSets running from the UpdateNodeAnnouncement RPC can overlap a reader and trigger the Go runtime's unrecoverable concurrent-map fatal. Fix criteria: Every read, iteration and write of the manager's feature set map is serialized inside feature.Manager (e.g. an RWMutex, or copy-on-write with an atomic pointer swap) so that no caller of Get/GetRaw/ListSets can observe a concurrent write regardless of the caller's locking. Verify with a race-detector test that runs UpdateFeatureSets concurrently with Get/ListSets in a loop and completes without a race report or fatal.
2. UpdateNodeAnnouncement performs the feature-set write on every call because the handler always passes a non-nil features vector, even when no feature bit changed, maximising the writer's frequency. Fix criteria: The write path is entered only when the proposed feature vector differs from the current one (or the manager treats an identical update as a no-op), so announcement-only updates do not mutate the shared map. Verify that an alias-only UpdateNodeAnnouncement call leaves the manager untouched.

# Direct peer's malformed invalid_onion_blinding failure is never penalized, forcing identical retries

## Details
Mission control's interpretation of a failure with source index 0 (routing/result_interpretation.go processPaymentOutcomeSelf) assumes such failures 'originate from ourselves' and therefore applies a penalty only for the three classic malformed-onion codes (invalid_onion_version/hmac/key), treating everything else as a transient local condition to be retried without learning anything.

However, the htlcswitch also routes peer-authored failures through the index-0 path. When our direct channel peer answers one of our own HTLCs with update_fail_malformed_htlc, the link converts the failure code into a plaintext lnwire failure padded to 260 bytes (htlcswitch/link.go processRemoteUpdateFailMalformedHTLC), processRemoteSettleFails marks the packet convertedError from that length, the switch treats it as `unencrypted` and parseFailedPayment returns a LinkError rather than a ForwardingError, and payment_lifecycle.handleSwitchErr maps any non-ForwardingError ClearTextError to failureSourceIdx = 0.

For failure_code invalid_onion_blinding (0xC018) the link produces lnwire.FailInvalidBlinding, which processPaymentOutcomeSelf does not list. The resulting interpretedResult has no pair results, no node failure and no finalFailureReason. Mission control records nothing, the bandwidth hints for the local channel are unchanged (the HTLC was removed), AllowMoreAttempts imposes no cap on failed attempts, and paymentSession.RequestRoute consults only mission-control probability and bandwidth hints, so the next route is the identical route through the same peer. The loop repeats -- one add/commit/fail/revoke round trip and one persisted HTLCAttempt record per iteration -- until the payment context deadline expires (payment_lifecycle.go checkContext; 60 s default in lncli, caller-supplied timeout_seconds in SendPaymentV2), at which point the payment fails even though other first hops were available.

Compare with the alternatives available to the same peer: a normal encrypted failure (index 1) or a malformed failure with the onion-version/hmac/key codes causes failNode(1)/failPairBalance, after which pathfinding routes around the peer and the payment can still succeed. The invalid_onion_blinding code is the one choice that lets a direct peer veto all of the victim's payments whose cheapest first hop it is, without being penalized or de-prioritized in mission control, while churning attempt records into the payments database for the duration of each payment.

Note on spec conformance: BOLT 4 has nodes inside a blinded route (those receiving path_key in update_add_htlc) use update_fail_malformed_htlc(invalid_onion_blinding), while an introduction node returns the encrypted form; lnd's own link does exactly this (link.go:3718-3752). A sender never sets path_key on its own first-hop add (sendAttempt builds the UpdateAddHTLC without one), so a direct peer sending this malformed code for one of our own HTLCs is non-compliant -- precisely the case in which the sender is expected to penalize it, and the one processPaymentOutcomeSelf silently ignores.

## Evidence
1. [routing/result\_interpretation.go:208–235](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/result_interpretation.go#L208-L235)
   processPaymentOutcomeSelf (sourceIdx 0) penalizes the first hop only for FailInvalidOnionVersion/Hmac/Key. Every other failure type, including FailInvalidBlinding, falls to the default branch, which only logs and records no pair/node result and no final failure reason, on the assumption that an index-0 failure 'originates from ourselves'. This is the location the fix must change.
2. [htlcswitch/link.go:4191–4258](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/htlcswitch/link.go#L4191-L4258)
   When our direct peer sends update_fail_malformed_htlc for an HTLC we originated, processRemoteUpdateFailMalformedHTLC maps failure_code invalid_onion_blinding to a plaintext-encoded lnwire.FailInvalidBlinding (lines 4218-4221), encodes it with EncodeFailure (256-byte padded body + 4 length bytes) and feeds it into the channel via ReceiveFailHTLC as a normal fail.
3. [htlcswitch/link.go:2952–2954](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/htlcswitch/link.go#L2952-L2954)
   processRemoteSettleFails flags the resulting packet as convertedError because the 260-byte reason has no HMAC.
4. [htlcswitch/switch.go:986](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/htlcswitch/switch.go#L986)
   handleLocalResponse treats convertedError as `unencrypted`, so the peer-authored failure is stored and later handled on the local-failure path.
5. [htlcswitch/switch.go:1093–1115](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/htlcswitch/switch.go#L1093-L1115)
   parseFailedPayment decodes the plaintext reason and returns NewLinkError(FailInvalidBlinding) -- a LinkError, not a ForwardingError -- even though the message was authored by the remote peer.
6. [routing/payment\_lifecycle.go:929–952](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/payment_lifecycle.go#L929-L952)
   handleSwitchErr sets failureSourceIdx = 0 for any non-ForwardingError ClearTextError, skips channel-update handling (idx 0) and reports (0, FailInvalidBlinding) to mission control, which via processPaymentOutcomeSelf learns nothing; reportAndFail then only fails the attempt and the lifecycle requests a new route.
7. [routing/payment\_lifecycle.go:248](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/payment_lifecycle.go#L248)
   The resumePayment loop's only time bound is checkContext (defined at line 364), i.e. the payment context deadline; there is no retry or attempt count limit.
8. [routing/payment\_session.go:260–284](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/routing/payment_session.go#L260-L284)
   RequestRoute selects the route from mission-control probability (ProbabilitySource) and fresh bandwidth hints only; with no mission-control result recorded and the failed HTLC's bandwidth restored, it returns the identical route through the same peer on every iteration.
9. [payments/db/payment.go:622–663](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/payments/db/payment.go#L622-L663)
   AllowMoreAttempts permits a new attempt whenever RemainingAmt is non-zero and the payment is registrable; it imposes no cap on the number of failed attempts.

## Impact
Availability (limited): the victim's payments that start over the malicious peer fail after spinning for the full payment timeout, generating one commitment round-trip and one persisted attempt record per iteration; payments via other peers are unaffected, and the node itself stays up. No confidentiality impact; no integrity impact on funds or state beyond the attempt-record churn.

## Reproduction steps
1. The attacker must be a direct channel counterparty of the victim that pathfinding selects as the first hop (cheap/large channel). For each HTLC the victim originates through it, the peer replies with update_fail_malformed_htlc carrying failure_code invalid_onion_blinding (any sha256_of_onion). The victim records nothing, re-sends the same attempt, and repeats until the payment deadline; the payment fails instead of being rerouted via another peer. No authentication beyond the existing channel is required and the behaviour is deterministic.

## Recommended fix
processPaymentOutcomeSelf assumes every index-0 failure is self-originated and ignores peer-authored converted malformed failures other than the three onion codes, so FailInvalidBlinding (and any future malformed code) yields no penalty and no terminal decision. Fix criteria: A failure that the switch converted from the direct peer's update_fail_malformed_htlc must be attributed to the peer (index 1 or an explicit converted-error marker) and interpreted with the existing first-hop/blinded-route rules, so that the peer's pair/node is penalized or the blinded route is failed and the payment is rerouted or terminated. Verify with a test where hop 1 returns malformed invalid_onion_blinding: mission control must record a result for the first hop and the lifecycle must not re-select the identical route.

# Backup dispatcher spins forever when stashed prevTask's channel closes before a new session arrives

## Details
backupDispatcher keeps one stashed task, c.prevTask, when the active sessionQueue rejects a backup with status sessionQueueExhausted or sessionQueueShuttingDown (client.go:947-971). Once a new sessionQueue is active the branch at client.go:774-782 replays it: `if c.prevTask != nil { c.processTask(c.prevTask); continue }`. processTask (client.go:854-861) first asks Manager.getSweepScript for the task's channel; if the channel is no longer in Manager.chanInfos it logs 'not processing task for unregistered channel' at Info level and returns without clearing c.prevTask and without touching c.sessionQueue. The dispatcher `continue`s into the same case and repeats: a hot loop with no blocking operation, no select on c.quit, and one log line per iteration. The normal pipeline path (client.go:810-815) drops a task for an unregistered channel correctly; only the prevTask replay lacks the reset.

How prevTask becomes set: a task is rejected with sessionQueueExhausted only when a session that is already full is made the active queue (taskAccepted clears prevTask when a task fills a session, so ordinary exhaustion never stashes one). ExhaustedSessionFilter (client.go:73-77) deliberately keeps a session whose stored SeqNum == Policy.MaxUpdates as a candidate when it still has un-acked committed updates (wtdb CommitUpdate increments SeqNum when the update is committed, before the tower acks). Such a session is loaded as a candidate at client construction and on AddTower (client.go:259, 1256-1259); nextSessionQueue (client.go:517-556) may select it, sessionQueue.status() (session_queue.go:715-724) reports exhausted, and the next revoked state read from the pipeline is rejected and stashed as prevTask while a new session is requested (client.go:700-703). Un-acked updates at restart exist whenever the tower was unreachable, or chose not to ack, the final updates of a session. (sessionQueueShuttingDown cannot produce a stash from inside the dispatcher: handleStaleTower/handleDeactivateTower/handleTerminateSession nil c.sessionQueue themselves.)

How the channel disappears: Manager.handleClosedChannel (manager.go:807-842) runs in its own goroutine on every ClosedChannelEvent (emitted from contractcourt/chain_arbitrator.go:507 for cooperative, force and breach closes, and from rpcserver AbandonChannel) and deletes the channel from chanInfos. If the channel owning prevTask closes and confirms while the dispatcher is still in awaitSession — a window the tower controls, because the negotiator retries CreateSession indefinitely with backoff up to 5 min — the first session that arrives puts the dispatcher into the infinite loop.

Consequences: the dispatcher of that blob-type client spins at 100% of one core and floods the log; it never reads another task from the pipeline, so no further revoked state of any channel of that commitment type is backed up to any tower (tasks accumulate in the DiskOverflowQueue's unbounded input list and disk queue) and no error is surfaced to the operator; and because client.stop closes c.quit and waits on c.wg (client.go:456-458), Manager.Stop and server.Stop block forever — the signal interceptor ignores repeated signals ('Already shutting down...', signal/signal.go:160-163) — so lnd must be SIGKILLed, discarding the in-memory queue contents that are only persisted on a clean stop.

A registered tower (an adversary in the recorded threat model) controls both the un-acked state at restart and the delay before a session is granted; any channel counterparty can force-close at will to supply the channel close; the same sequence also arises accidentally during a tower outage that spans an lnd restart and a channel close.

## Evidence
1. [watchtower/wtclient/client.go:774–782](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtclient/client.go#L774-L782)
   prevTask replay branch of backupDispatcher: whenever c.sessionQueue != nil and c.prevTask != nil it calls processTask(c.prevTask) and unconditionally `continue`s, never selecting on c.quit or the pipeline. Termination relies entirely on processTask clearing prevTask or nil-ing sessionQueue. This is the code the fix must change.
2. [watchtower/wtclient/client.go:854–861](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtclient/client.go#L854-L861)
   processTask returns early when c.cfg.getSweepScript reports the channel is not registered, logging at Info level, without clearing c.prevTask and without reaching AcceptTask/taskAccepted/taskRejected (the only places prevTask is cleared). Combined with evidence[0] this is a hot infinite loop.
3. [watchtower/wtclient/client.go:947–971](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtclient/client.go#L947-L971)
   taskRejected stashes the task in c.prevTask and nils c.sessionQueue when AcceptTask reports sessionQueueExhausted (or sessionQueueShuttingDown); the task is held until a new sessionQueue is active.
4. [watchtower/wtclient/client.go:73–77](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtclient/client.go#L73-L77)
   ExhaustedSessionFilter keeps a session with SeqNum == MaxUpdates as a candidate if it has un-acked committed updates. This is the path by which an already-exhausted session becomes the active queue (via nextSessionQueue after restart or AddTower) and rejects the next pipeline task into prevTask; the tower controls whether the final updates of a session are left un-acked.
5. [watchtower/wtclient/session\_queue.go:715–725](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtclient/session_queue.go#L715-L725)
   status() reports sessionQueueExhausted when seqNum (initialised from the stored session SeqNum) plus pending >= MaxUpdates; AcceptTask (session_queue.go:298-300) then rejects the task with that status, which is what causes taskRejected to stash prevTask.
6. [watchtower/wtclient/manager.go:807–842](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtclient/manager.go#L807-L842)
   handleClosedChannel runs in the Manager's handleChannelCloses goroutine, concurrently with the dispatcher, on every ClosedChannelEvent and deletes the channel from m.chanInfos; afterwards getSweepScript (manager.go:965-975) returns false for that channel, so a stashed prevTask for it can never be accepted or cleared.
7. [watchtower/wtclient/client.go:456–458](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/watchtower/wtclient/client.go#L456-L458)
   client.stop closes c.quit and waits on c.wg for backupDispatcher; a dispatcher in the hot loop never observes quit, so Manager.Stop and server.Stop hang and lnd cannot shut down without SIGKILL.

## Impact
No confidentiality or integrity impact. Availability: the tower client for that commitment type stops processing every backup silently (no further revoked states reach any tower, tasks pile up in the pipeline), one CPU core is pegged and the log floods, and lnd cannot shut down gracefully (Manager.Stop waits on the stuck goroutine; repeated signals are ignored) so it must be killed, discarding in-memory queued backups. lnd's channel operation, forwarding and HTLC resolution continue while it is online, so this is a partial loss of the daemon's availability rather than a total one; the loss of offline breach protection is a consequence conditional on further events and is not rated as a separate system.

## Reproduction steps
1. The attacker is a watchtower server the victim backs up to (remote, no credentials on lnd; named as an adversary in the threat model) and/or a channel counterparty. The tower leaves the final committed updates of a full session un-acked (offline or deliberately), so after the victim's next lnd restart or AddTower that session is re-selected as the active queue and the first revoked state is stashed as prevTask; the tower then withholds CreateSession (the negotiator retries indefinitely) until one of the victim's channels — which a counterparty can force-close at any time — closes and confirms, then grants a session. The required ordering (exhausted-with-unacked session re-activated, channel close inside the negotiation window) is runtime state the attacker influences but does not fully control, hence AT:PRESENT; the same state also arises without an attacker during a tower outage spanning a restart and a channel close.

## Recommended fix
1. processTask's early return for an unregistered channel leaves c.prevTask set, and the dispatcher's prevTask replay branch has no exit other than prevTask being cleared or sessionQueue being nil-ed, so a stashed task for a closed channel is retried forever without blocking. Fix criteria: A stashed prevTask whose channel is no longer registered is discarded (prevTask cleared) and the dispatcher returns to normal pipeline/quit processing. Verify by activating an exhausted session that still has an un-acked update (restart or AddTower), queuing one backup so it is stashed, closing that channel while no session is available, then supplying a session: the dispatcher must continue processing other tasks and the client must stop cleanly.
2. The backupDispatcher loop contains an iteration path (the prevTask replay) that can run without making progress and without observing c.quit. Fix criteria: Every iteration of backupDispatcher that does not make progress must be able to observe c.quit (or otherwise be guaranteed to make progress), so that client.stop() always returns.

# WalletKit NextAddr/DeriveNextKey/DeriveKey mutate wallet derivation state under address:read

## Details
The WalletKit sub-server's permission table (lnrpc/walletrpc/walletkit_server.go:77-88) gates DeriveNextKey, DeriveKey and NextAddr behind `address:read`, and rpcserver.go:837-843 registers that table into the macaroon interceptor as the only authorization gate for those methods. `address:read` is a member of `readPermissions` (rpcserver.go:116), the list from which lnd bakes the shipped `readonly.macaroon` (lnd.go:857-860); docs/macaroons.md:54-56 defines that macaroon as one that "permits only methods that don't change the state of lnd". These three methods are the only users of `address:read` in any permission table, while the main Lightning service requires `address:write` for NewAddress (rpcserver.go:294-297).

None of the three is side-effect free:

* NextAddr (walletkit_server.go:673-702) calls Wallet.NewAddress(addrType, req.Change, account) — the identical call rpcserver.NewAddress makes under address:write — which lnwallet/btcwallet/btcwallet.go:516-533 maps to btcwallet NewAddress/NewChangeAddress, deriving and persisting a fresh external or internal address and advancing that branch's next index.
* DeriveNextKey (walletkit_server.go:631-648) casts the caller's int32 key_family to keychain.KeyFamily without validation and calls BtcWalletKeyRing.DeriveNextKey (keychain/btcwallet.go:145-201), which opens a walletdb.Update transaction, creates the m/1017'/coin'/<family>' account if absent (createAccountIfNotExists -> scope.NewRawAccount) and stores the family's next external address, permanently advancing its index.
* DeriveKey (walletkit_server.go:652-670 -> keychain/btcwallet.go:208-254) likewise runs walletdb.Update and createAccountIfNotExists for any family on a non-watch-only wallet.

The defect is the authorization table, not the wallet code: operations that write wallet.db (account creation, derivation-index advancement, stored addresses) are classified read-level, so every holder of the read-only macaroon — and of any custom macaroon carrying address:read, such as the one docs/remote-signing.md:100-101 tells operators to bake — can mutate derivation state the project documents as off-limits to it. Behaviour assumed of btcwallet v0.16.20-pre (go.mod): wallet.NewAddress/NewChangeAddress and waddrmgr NextExternalAddresses persist each derived address and advance the account index; NewRawAccount stores a record for any not-yet-existing account number below the hardened limit; seed recovery stops after `recovery_window` consecutive unused addresses, as docs/recovery.md:124-129 states.

## Evidence
1. [lnrpc/walletrpc/walletkit\_server.go:77–88](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnrpc/walletrpc/walletkit_server.go#L77-L88)
   macPermissions gates /walletrpc.WalletKit/DeriveNextKey, DeriveKey and NextAddr behind address:read only. These are the only three users of address:read in any permission table and the entries the fix must change; lnrpc.Lightning/NewAddress (rpcserver.go:294-297) requires address:write for the identical wallet call.
2. [lnrpc/walletrpc/walletkit\_server.go:673–702](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnrpc/walletrpc/walletkit_server.go#L673-L702)
   NextAddr calls w.cfg.Wallet.NewAddress(addrType, req.Change, account) with caller-chosen type, change flag and account name — the same call rpcserver.NewAddress makes under address:write (rpcserver.go:1672-1710). lnwallet/btcwallet/btcwallet.go:516-533 maps it to btcwallet NewAddress/NewChangeAddress, which derives and persists a new address and advances the branch index.
3. [lnrpc/walletrpc/walletkit\_server.go:631–670](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnrpc/walletrpc/walletkit_server.go#L631-L670)
   DeriveNextKey and DeriveKey cast the caller's int32 key_family straight to keychain.KeyFamily (uint32) with no validation, so any account number in the m/1017' scope can be targeted, including the live channel key families (multisig 0, revocation base 1, HTLC 2, payment 3, delay 4, revocation root 5, node key 6) and arbitrary never-used families.
4. [keychain/btcwallet.go:145–201](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/keychain/btcwallet.go#L145-L201)
   BtcWalletKeyRing.DeriveNextKey runs walletdb.Update: createAccountIfNotExists -> scope.NewRawAccount creates a new account in the 1017' scope for any family not yet present, then NextExternalAddresses(ns, family, 1) derives and stores the next address, permanently advancing the family's index. Both are wallet.db writes performed for an address:read caller.
5. [keychain/btcwallet.go:208–254](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/keychain/btcwallet.go#L208-L254)
   DeriveKey also runs walletdb.Update and createAccountIfNotExists on a non-watch-only wallet, so even the arbitrary-key lookup RPC creates persistent accounts for every family number the caller names.
6. [rpcserver.go:105–144](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/rpcserver.go#L105-L144)
   readPermissions includes address:read (line 116); this list defines what the read-only macaroon may do.
7. [lnd.go:857–860](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/lnd.go#L857-L860)
   genDefaultMacaroons bakes the shipped readonly.macaroon from readPermissions, so every holder of that file can call the three mutating WalletKit RPCs. docs/macaroons.md:54-56 documents this macaroon as permitting only methods that do not change lnd state.
8. [rpcserver.go:294–297](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/rpcserver.go#L294-L297)
   The main Lightning service requires address:write for NewAddress, which performs the same Wallet.NewAddress call. The sub-server's weaker requirement is the inconsistency that lets a read-only caller perform the write.
9. [rpcserver.go:837–843](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/rpcserver.go#L837-L843)
   Sub-server permission tables are registered into the macaroon interceptor chain verbatim, so the address:read entry is the only authorization gate on these methods; no further check exists in the handlers.

## Impact
Integrity: a principal the docs say may not change lnd state writes wallet.db — creates up to ~2^31 accounts in the 1017' scope, advances channel key-family indices, and burns default-account receive and change addresses. Burning more than the default 2500-address recovery look-ahead puts addresses the operator later issues beyond the gap, so a seed-only restore with the default window misses funds received there until the operator guesses a larger window (docs/recovery.md:124-129). Availability: every call leaves a persistent record, so wallet.db and the address set every rescan and filter match must cover grow without bound and stay grown after the attack stops. No confidential data beyond public keys address:read already exposes.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker holds a macaroon carrying address:read — the shipped readonly.macaroon or the documented remote-signing macaroon — and can reach gRPC 10009 or REST 8080. They call NextAddr (POST /v2/wallet/address/next), DeriveNextKey (/v2/wallet/key/next) or DeriveKey (/v2/wallet/key) repeatedly; the interceptor admits each call on address:read and each call deterministically writes wallet.db. No further check, key_family validation or rate limit exists.

## Recommended fix
The WalletKit permission table assigns address:read to RPCs whose effect is a wallet-state write (new address derivation, account creation, index advancement), inconsistent with the main server's address:write requirement for the same Wallet.NewAddress operation and with the documented read-only macaroon contract, so read-only macaroon holders mutate derivation state. Fix criteria: NextAddr, DeriveNextKey and DeriveKey require a write-level permission (address:write) consistent with lnrpc.Lightning/NewAddress, or are made side-effect free (no account creation, no index advancement, no wallet.db write) when invoked under a read-level permission. Verify that each RPC called with readonly.macaroon is rejected or leaves ListAccounts/ListAddresses and wallet.db unchanged, that admin and remote-signing flows still work, and that docs/remote-signing.md is updated if the documented custom macaroon must change.

# Set-level retry fee rate permanently strands lower-budget inputs after partial sweep failure

## Details
The budget aggregator batches inputs that share a deadline height into one sweep transaction; the fee bumper runs a single linear fee function for the whole set whose ending rate is min(sum(budgets)/txWeight, MaxFeeRate) (fee_bumper.go MaxFeeRateAllowed). When the transaction fails partway - TxUnknownSpend because a counterparty confirmed a spend of one of the batched inputs, or TxFailed from ErrNotEnoughBudget/ErrNotEnoughInputs/ErrMaxPosition/publish errors - fee_bumper.calculateRetryFeeRate produces the set-level rate stepped one position further and sweeper.markInputsPublishFailed stores that one rate as StartingFeeRate on every surviving input (sweeper.go:1005).

On the retry, aggregator.filterInputs (aggregator.go:246-258) compares each input's own Budget with StartingFeeRate x that input's own weight and skips the input when the budget is smaller. For a set containing a large and a small HTLC the set rate is dominated by the large one (HTLC budgets are 50% of value by default, weights are equal), so once the fee function has advanced past the small input's own budget density the small input fails this check. It is not removed, not failed, not signalled; it sits in s.inputs in state PublishFailed and is re-skipped on every block with only a log.Errorf. updateSweeperInputs never terminates it (no attempt cap), nothing in the sweeper clears StartingFeeRate, and the timeout resolver's Launch() is guarded by isLaunched(), so only a node restart (resolver re-offer through handleExistingInput) or an operator BumpFee replaces the params. The resolver discarded the SweepInput result channel, so nothing alerts.

Attack path (channel counterparty): the attacker routes two HTLCs through the victim to itself with equal CLTVs so they share a deadline (e.g. 5,000,000 sat and 50,000 sat), lets them go on-chain, and waits. The victim batches both timeout claims (deadline = incoming expiry). The set's ending rate is capped at MaxFeeRate 250,000 sat/kw and ramps linearly over the ~80-block window; the small HTLC's density is 25,000 sat / ~450 WU ~ 55,000 sat/kw, reached after roughly a quarter of the window. The attacker keeps the victim's sweep unconfirmed with a conflicting preimage claim of the large HTLC (each RBF round makes createRBFCompliantTx step the set's fee function further) and lets its claim confirm once the set rate exceeds the small input's density. The bumper reports TxUnknownSpend, the small HTLC gets StartingFeeRate above its own density, and filterInputs skips it on every subsequent block. The victim's timeout claim of the small HTLC is never broadcast; the attacker (also upstream) collects the incoming HTLC by timeout and later claims the stranded output with the preimage, netting the small HTLC's value. Several small HTLCs batched with one large one are all stranded at once. The same stranding occurs non-adversarially whenever a batched sweep fails partway.

The per-input check in filterInputs is sound for operator-supplied starting rates, but applying a set-level rate to individual inputs violates the invariant that an input's starting rate never exceeds its own budget density (the TODO above createInputSets acknowledges the missing grouping).

## Evidence
1. [sweep/sweeper.go:968–1006](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/sweep/sweeper.go#L968-L1006)
   markInputsPublishFailed writes the single, set-level feeRate carried by the BumpResult into every surviving input's params.StartingFeeRate (line 1005). The rate was derived from the whole set's budget/weight (dominated by the largest input) and nothing in the sweeper ever resets it; only a resolver re-offer on restart (handleExistingInput) or an operator BumpFee (handleUpdateReq) replaces params.
2. [sweep/aggregator.go:246–257](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/sweep/aggregator.go#L246-L257)
   filterInputs drops any input whose own Budget is below StartingFeeRate x its own weight (InputSize + witness upper bound) with only a log.Errorf. An input carrying a set-level rate above its own budget density is skipped here on every block; it remains in s.inputs in state PublishFailed, is never clustered, never swept, never marked Fatal and never signalled.
3. [sweep/sweeper.go:1971–2031](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/sweep/sweeper.go#L1971-L2031)
   handleBumpEventTxUnknownSpend runs when a third party (the channel counterparty) confirms a spend of one input of a batched sweep (detected by processRecords/getSpentInputs/isUnknownSpent). It calls markInputsPublishFailed with the set-level retry rate, marks the surviving inputs Immediate and retries; the retry goes through filterInputs, which silently drops the lower-density survivors.
4. [sweep/fee\_bumper.go:1898–1951](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/sweep/fee_bumper.go#L1898-L1951)
   calculateRetryFeeRate returns the set's fee function stepped one position further and ignores ErrMaxPosition; its value is the rate written into every surviving input.
5. [sweep/fee\_bumper.go:180–221](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/sweep/fee_bumper.go#L180-L221)
   MaxFeeRateAllowed computes the fee function's ending rate from the whole set: min(sum(Budget)/txWeight, MaxFeeRate). With default 50% HTLC budgets this is dominated by the largest co-batched input, so the set rate exceeds a smaller input's own Budget/weight once the function has advanced.
6. [sweep/sweeper.go:1708–1723](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/sweep/sweeper.go#L1708-L1723)
   handleBumpEventTxFailed (ErrNotEnoughBudget / ErrNotEnoughInputs / ErrMaxPosition / publish errors) also writes the set-level retry rate into every input via markInputsPublishFailed, so the same stranding occurs without an adversary whenever a batched sweep fails.
7. [sweep/sweeper.go:1522–1579](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/sweep/sweeper.go#L1522-L1579)
   updateSweeperInputs only removes inputs in Fatal/Swept/Excluded and returns PublishFailed inputs for sweeping each block; there is no publish-attempt cap, so the stranded input cycles through filterInputs forever.
8. [contractcourt/htlc\_timeout\_resolver.go:580–591](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/contractcourt/htlc_timeout_resolver.go#L580-L591)
   The timeout resolver offers the outgoing HTLC with Budget = 50% of its value (calculateBudget, contractcourt/config.go:118) and DeadlineHeight = incomingHTLCExpiryHeight (attacker-chosen via the onion CLTVs, so two HTLCs are batched), and discards the result channel; Launch() is guarded by isLaunched(), so the input is re-offered only on restart. No component observes that the input is never swept.

## Impact
The victim's deadline-bound HTLC timeout claim is never broadcast, so the HTLC value is lost to the counterparty (upstream refund by timeout plus downstream preimage claim of the stranded output); multiple small HTLCs co-batched with a large one are lost together. No confidentiality impact; node availability is unaffected. Recovery requires an operator restart or manual BumpFee before the counterparty claims, with no result signalled to the resolver and only a log line.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker is a channel counterparty who is also upstream/downstream of the same payments. They choose HTLC amounts and CLTVs so two HTLCs of very different value share a deadline, force the channel on-chain, keep the victim's batched sweep unconfirmed with a conflicting preimage claim until the set's fee function has advanced past the small HTLC's budget density (createRBFCompliantTx increments the set function on every RBF conflict, so this takes few blocks), then let the claim confirm. All steps are ordinary protocol and on-chain actions; the stranding then follows deterministically from the code with no user interaction and no alert. The exploit depends on runtime conditions - a batched set with heterogeneous budgets and the fee function having advanced before the partial failure, which is a timing race the attacker must win - hence AT:PRESENT. Having a channel with the victim is the only privilege (PR:LOW).

## Recommended fix
1. markInputsPublishFailed stores the set-level retry fee rate as each input's StartingFeeRate, so an input can carry a starting rate its own budget cannot cover. Fix criteria: After a partial failure, each surviving input's StartingFeeRate must be bounded by its own Budget divided by its own weight (or left unset), so that no input is excluded from re-clustering solely because of a rate inherited from a larger co-batched input. Verify by batching a large and a small HTLC, spending the large one by a third party after several bumps, and confirming the small one is re-swept on the next block.
2. filterInputs silently skips inputs whose budget cannot cover the starting fee, leaving them in PublishFailed with no retry path, no result signalled and no state change. Fix criteria: An input that cannot be swept at its recorded starting rate must either be retried at a lower rate or be surfaced as a terminal result to its listeners/operator rather than silently skipped on every block. Verify that no input can remain in PublishFailed indefinitely without a signalled result.

# Tor-mode SRV lookup has no read deadline; stalled DNS server hangs bootstrapper and shutdown

## Details
When lnd runs with `tor.active=1`, DNS-seed bootstrapping resolves the BOLT-10 `_nodes._tcp.<seed>` SRV record via `tor.LookupSRV` (tor/tor.go:151). That function opens a plaintext TCP connection through the Tor SOCKS proxy to the configured `tor.dns` server (default `soa.nodes.lightning.directory:53`, a third-party host; config.go:82-83,347) and then does `dnsConn.WriteMsg(msg)` / `dnsConn.ReadMsg()` (tor/tor.go:173-176). No read or write deadline is ever set on the connection: the `timeout` argument is consumed only by `net.Dialer{Timeout: timeout}` inside `dialProxy` (tor/tor.go:112), which bounds the connect to the *local* SOCKS proxy. Once the stream is established, `ReadMsg` blocks until the remote peer sends a complete length-prefixed message or closes the stream.

Both siblings that perform the same operation are bounded: `ClearNet.LookupSRV` (tor/net.go:60-68) wraps the resolver call in `context.WithTimeout`, and `DNSSeedBootstrapper.fallBackSRVLookup` (discovery/bootstrapper.go:397) calls `conn.SetDeadline` on its DNS connection before the identical WriteMsg/ReadMsg exchange. Only the Tor path is missing the deadline.

Who controls the stall: the operator of the `tor.dns` server, or any Tor exit relay carrying the stream (the exchange is unauthenticated plaintext DNS over TCP, so the exit can hold the connection open or hand back a 2-byte length prefix such as 0xFFFF followed by nothing). The local TCP connection to the SOCKS proxy stays healthy, so Go's dialer keep-alive does not help.

Consequences, deterministic once the stall is in place: (1) `DNSSeedBootstrapper.SampleNodeAddrs` (discovery/bootstrapper.go:473, which ignores its ctx) -> `MultiSourceBootstrap` -> `peerBootstrapper`/`initialPeerBootstrap` (server.go:3210, 3287, 3396) block forever; automatic peer bootstrapping (maintaining `defaultMinPeers`=3 outbound peers) never runs again for the life of the process, and on a fresh node that is the only way it finds peers other than manual `lncli connect`. (2) `peerBootstrapper` is tracked by `s.wg` (server.go:2735, 3203), so `server.Stop` blocks at `s.wg.Wait()` (server.go:2919) after the other subsystems have already been stopped; the signal interceptor ignores further signals (signal/signal.go:159-172) and `lnd.Main` only returns after the deferred `server.Stop()` (lnd.go:757-763), so a graceful `lncli stop`/SIGINT shutdown never completes until the process is SIGKILLed (the shipped systemd unit waits TimeoutStopSec=3600 before doing so). Channel peers are maintained by the persistent-peer connection manager, so channel operation continues until the operator requests shutdown; the impact is loss of the bootstrapping component and of clean shutdown, not of funds.

Preconditions: `tor.active=1` (a documented, supported configuration whose docs call `tor.dns` 'required in order to be able to properly automatically bootstrap'), a network with DNS seeds (mainnet/testnet/testnet4/signet, chainreg/chainregistry.go:878), `nobootstrap` unset (default), and a bootstrap round in progress (fewer than 3 connected peers: every startup, and every 15 s to 5 min thereafter while under-connected; the DNS seed is consulted with high probability since bootstrappers are shuffled).

Dependency assumptions (not vendored, stated rather than verified): github.com/miekg/dns v1.1.43 `Conn.ReadMsg` on a TCP conn performs blocking `io.ReadFull` reads of the 2-byte length and body and sets no deadline of its own; golang.org/x/net v0.57.0 `proxy.SOCKS5(...).Dial` returns the raw stream with no deadline set; the Tor daemon does not time out an established idle stream.

This is a sibling of the verified `tor-lookupsrv-unchecked-assertion-crashes-bootstrap` (a panic on the parsed answer at tor/tor.go:190); this record is the distinct liveness defect on the same connection before any answer is parsed.

## Evidence
1. [tor/tor.go:156–176](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/tor/tor.go#L156-L176)
   LookupSRV dials the DNS server through dialProxy, wraps the net.Conn in a dns.Conn and calls WriteMsg (173) and ReadMsg (176) without ever calling SetDeadline/SetReadDeadline on the connection. The `timeout` parameter is consumed only by dialProxy's `net.Dialer{Timeout: timeout}` (line 112), which bounds the TCP connect to the local SOCKS proxy (or, with skip-proxy, the connect to the DNS host), not the DNS exchange. ReadMsg blocks until the remote end sends a complete length-prefixed message or closes the stream. This is the location the fix must change.
2. [discovery/bootstrapper.go:393–397](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/bootstrapper.go#L393-L397)
   The clearnet fallback for the same seed query, fallBackSRVLookup, dials with d.timeout and then explicitly does `conn.SetDeadline(time.Now().Add(d.timeout))` (line 397) before the identical dns.Conn WriteMsg/ReadMsg exchange, showing the maintainers intend the DNS exchange to be deadline-bounded. tor.LookupSRV lacks the equivalent.
3. [tor/net.go:60–67](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/tor/net.go#L60-L67)
   The clearnet sibling ClearNet.LookupSRV wraps the resolver call in context.WithTimeout(timeout), so on clearnet the whole lookup is bounded. ProxyNet.LookupSRV (lines 122-129) forwards the same timeout to tor.LookupSRV, where it is not applied to the read.
4. [discovery/bootstrapper.go:468–475](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/discovery/bootstrapper.go#L468-L475)
   DNSSeedBootstrapper.SampleNodeAddrs calls d.net.LookupSRV synchronously for each configured seed and ignores its ctx argument (named `_`). Under tor.active, d.net is the *tor.ProxyNet (config.go:1322-1329), so this is the call that blocks; no caller wraps it in a select on quit or a timeout.
5. [server.go:2728–2738](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/server.go#L2728-L2738)
   Unless nobootstrap is set, Start does s.wg.Add(1) and launches peerBootstrapper as a wg-tracked goroutine (defer s.wg.Done() at 3203). It calls discovery.MultiSourceBootstrap synchronously (initialPeerBootstrap at 3396-3398 and the ticker loop at 3287-3289), and MultiSourceBootstrap (discovery/bootstrapper.go:67-93) calls each bootstrapper's SampleNodeAddrs synchronously. While LookupSRV is blocked, no bootstrap round can complete for the life of the process.
6. [server.go:2917–2919](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/server.go#L2917-L2919)
   server.Stop closes s.quit and stops the subsystems, then waits on s.wg.Wait(). peerBootstrapper's deferred wg.Done never runs while it is blocked inside LookupSRV (the quit channel is only consulted between rounds), so a graceful shutdown of lnd blocks here indefinitely.
7. [signal/signal.go:159–171](https://github.com/Halbarevi/lqwd1/blob/17c16878a0246420e1dec11ce46ce92fba9065d5/signal/signal.go#L159-L171)
   The interrupt handler ignores every signal after the first ('Already shutting down...') and nothing in signal/ or cmd/lnd/main.go forces os.Exit while server.Stop is in progress; lnd.go:757-763 runs server.Stop in a defer before Main returns. So once wg.Wait blocks, only SIGKILL ends the process (the shipped systemd unit contrib/init/lnd.service sets TimeoutStopSec=3600).

## Impact
No data is disclosed or altered. The peer-bootstrapping goroutine is permanently wedged so the node stops acquiring bootstrap peers for the rest of the process lifetime, and graceful shutdown blocks on s.wg.Wait (server.go:2919) after the other subsystems have stopped, until the process is SIGKILLed (up to TimeoutStopSec=3600 under the shipped systemd unit). Channel peers and HTLC processing continue via the persistent-peer manager until shutdown is requested, so availability impact is partial rather than total.

## Reproduction steps
1. Attacker is the configured `tor.dns` server operator (a third party by default, config.go:82-83,347) or a Tor exit relay on the path of the plaintext TCP DNS stream (tor/tor.go:126-133 dials through SOCKS with no authentication or integrity protection). They accept lnd's TCP connection to port 53 and either send nothing or a length prefix without a body; tor/tor.go:176 `dnsConn.ReadMsg()` then blocks forever because no deadline was set on the conn (the only deadline-bearing object is the net.Dialer at tor/tor.go:112, which bounds the connect to the local SOCKS proxy). lnd must be running with tor.active=1 on a network with DNS seeds, without nobootstrap, and be in a bootstrap round (fewer than defaultMinPeers=3 connected peers: every startup and every 15 s to 5 min thereafter while under-connected). No credentials, no user interaction; the hang is deterministic and persists for the process lifetime. Dependency assumptions: github.com/miekg/dns v1.1.43 Conn.ReadMsg blocks on io.ReadFull without an implicit deadline; golang.org/x/net v0.57.0 proxy.SOCKS5 Dial returns the stream with no deadline; the Tor daemon keeps an established idle stream open.

## Recommended fix
1. tor.LookupSRV performs a blocking DNS exchange with a remote, untrusted server over a connection that has no read/write deadline; the timeout it receives only bounds the dial to the local SOCKS proxy. Fix criteria: The entire SRV exchange (write and read) must be bounded by the caller-supplied timeout so that a server that accepts the connection but never answers causes LookupSRV to return an error within that timeout. Verify with a stub DNS server that accepts TCP and sends nothing while lnd runs with tor.active: bootstrap must proceed to the next seed/round and `lncli stop` must complete.
2. The bootstrapper goroutines call network-dependent samplers synchronously and ignore the context they are given, so any unbounded wait inside a bootstrapper wedges peer bootstrapping and server shutdown. Fix criteria: A stalled bootstrapper must not prevent server.Stop from completing nor block subsequent bootstrap rounds; cancellation via the quit signal/context should unblock in-flight lookups. Confirm by stalling one bootstrapper and observing shutdown finishes.
